Ahem I'd recommend grabbing a snack. 

(This review is mainly for people looking to buy the game.)
(Some details are omitted for spoiler purposes)

Graphics: I personally adore the graphic style, it is not at all "realistic" if that is the style of games you're looking for. It's a game that has a "cartoony" vibe with dark undertones. Think, 2d platformer smashed with a 3d dungeon crawler then add some gore. It's a stylized look, as I'm sure you can tell from the pictures. There isn't much to say about the graphics besides they are awesome if you love tarot cards.

Gameplay: Personally I dont give a rats ass if the game is repetitive, if you dislike repetitive games DO NOT GET THIS GAME. I've seen reviews of people talking about how they HATE the gameplay loop. Allow me to describe the game loop to you quickly. 

Lamb (You) has a cult (Think animal crossing village), and to get materials, they need to leave the cult. Which is where the dungeon crawler comes in. 

You go through an area, get your materials, come back to the cult, build shit, then leave. 

Seems repetitive, which it is. However there are some things I glossed over like the fact you can leave the dungeon anytime (If you have the cloak for it, a cloak upgrade is basically when you defeat a big boss you get something to get a new cloak, and an ability of one of those cloaks is you can teleport out of the dungeon whenever you want with a short windup). So you're not "forced" to go through the full dungeon. Plus, I've actually seen people completely skip over the dungeon crawler portion, which I find kinda insane. The dungeon crawler is a key component of the game, but you CAN avoid it, HOWEVER it is SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult to deal with your cult.

 Basically what I'm stating here is: If you don't like dungeon crawlers this isn't the game for you, but if you love the game enough (stubborn enough) you could avoid that part of the game. You will be missing the story however so it's not recommended. 

Alright lets talk about the difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself now that everyone who hates dungeon crawlers has left. 

The difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself is player focused/skill. There are things that can assist, or make it more difficult for players either looking for a challenge or simplicity, which I will not get into much as that leads to spoilers. But lets simplify it, lets say you're just using vanilla lamb (basic/starter kit). Here's the basic dungeon rundown:

When you go into a dungeon, the dungeon will show multiple types of rooms. A dungeon run is called a CRUSADE. There's 14 total types of rooms. I would highly recommend searching “Cult Of The Lamb: Level Types” if you're a visual learner. I'll list all the rooms you'll come across keeping one out for spoiler purposes. If not, I'll try to explain here. The brackets are the symbols you'll see

Normal fight (Sword Symbol), Hearts (Heart), Coins (Coin), Food (The Food of that Dungeon), Lumber (Chopped Wood), Stone (Rocks), Bones (Crossbones), Tarot (Card), Shop (Shop), Event (Question Mark), New follower (Stick Figure Kneeling, Holding Hands upward), Miniboss (Skull and Crossbones). 

Okay Now ill briefly explain what each room actually IS;

Normal Fight: I will come back to this one to not confuse you

Hearts: You get Health

Coins: You get Money

Food: You get Food for your Cult

Lumber: You get Wood for your Cult

Stone: You get Stone for your Cult

Bones: You get Bones for your Cult 

Tarot: You get an NPC that gives you a temporary bonus ability ONLY for that run

Shop: You can buy shit there. Do you not know what a store is? Touch grass.

Event: This one basically has a chance of a few different rooms and I will avoid stating because of spoilers.


New Follower: You get the CHANCE to free a NPC to join your cult

Miniboss: This one will ONLY EVER appear at the end of the dungeon run. It is exactly as it's said. It's a miniboss. 

Alright now you know what rooms are congrats. Let's go back to the Normal Fight room. You will ALWAYS start a Crusade in a Normal Fight Room. A normal fight room is basically where you go through multiple smaller rooms freeroam (you get a minimap) and you fight shit. Make sure you explore everywhere because most of the time you have the chance of running into a Tarot type room, or an NPC, or Treasure. What's Treasure? Treasure can vary. Coins, Materials, or Weapons to use in the dungeon. During the start of the Crusade when you enter the Normal Fight Room you will get 2 weapons. A physical one, and a ranged one, and yes you carry this weapon throughout your entire crusade.

If your fucking confused. Think of a Russian nesting doll. There are the General levels, which I mentioned. Then the Normal Fight Rooms.

Okay enough about the gameplay, if you really need to know more search up a video stupid. 

Audio: The audio is heavenly, you just gotta hear it for yourself. Sadly the person who made the original music passed away. RIP your music was beautiful. 

PC Requirements: It's pretty average. You don't need a super computer, but you still have a decent computer. The size is workable, there really isn't much to talk about here, idk what computer you have. Figure it out yourself.

Grind: There isn't a grind. UNLESS you care about achievements. If you do, Well… have fun. 

Story: I will not go into the story at all as this is mostly a spoiler free review. However, the story is good, and the Final Boss Fight is awesome. Highly recommended.

Game Time: It gets repetitive, the game will go as long as you can go. 

Price: For me it's highly worth the price, and if you don't think so, just wait for it to go on sale. It goes on sale very often. I bought it full price, with every possible DLC. (Jumping on Woolhaven the second its OFFICIALLY out).

Bugs: Very Minor Bugs, If you do find any, report to the discord. They deal with it pretty quickly.

For me? 10/10 I love being a psychopathic lamb that runs a cult.

Soft-ish spoilers in here, really just Monster names. (If you don't want to know the names for some reason, avoid this?)

Out of all the "modern" Monster Hunter games, this is the one that shines the most, you're not going to get the performance issues of Wilds, or the baby'd-down combat of Rise.

If you're interested in a story for some reason, this game has one, but you're probably going to be mentally checked out until the end of the base-game, then back to checking out until Iceborne where the combat is shining and the gaps between story beats are a little longer.

I would absolutely under all circumstances recommend you DO NOT start with the Defender Armor or weapons, it was designed for people wanting to skip to high rank on new characters, not for first time playthroughs, it circumvents the armor and weapon system and prevents you from learning the gearing loop.

All of low-rank is your tutorial, they're going to gloss over a lot of systems and hand the reins over to you a bit but you're going to be closing a lot of dialogues that do and don't explain everything you need to know.
The intro is extremely hand-holdy and if you have functioning brain cells during the tutorial section of the game it is going to try to turn them off, it's really really slow.

The systems in the game won't baby as much you once you're getting into high-rank, you're going to slowly taper off off the in-game tutorials and guides and reach a point where you need to become self sufficient and either play extremely well solo or be extremely communicative in groups.

Difficulty across the game is very subjective, personally before getting deep into the combat systems I could get away with soloing literally everything [u]without clutch claw[/u] up until mid-Iceborne (Around Rajang, Zinogre, etc.). The skill floor starts rising once you hit that point, monsters are going to stop pulling their punches and you're going to have to start learning monster mechanics and double down on practicing some runs instead of first time clearing everything.

Iceborne is a double edged blade for most people who play this game, a lot of the traditional hunters do not like clutch claw, a lot of people who [u]aren't[/u] traditional hunters don't like clutch claw.
The introduction of the claw saw all of the game being rebalanced with the claw in mind, meaning if you don't own Iceborne, you still have to deal with monsters that have Iceborne health, if you do own it, you're incentivised to use it at almost every point possible, with how it was designed, this can completely break low/high-rank content.
The intent for the claw is to tenderize and add some variety so you can capitalize on gaps in monster behaviours for damage by creating tenderized parts, however the existence of "clagging" has subverted that idea and it can be used to trivialize a lot of fights up until around Alatreon. If you want to preserve the sense of difficulty just don't engage in clagging and ignore the developers ham-fisted attempt to give players a broken tool to deal with harder hitting monsters. Believe in the you that you can become, the you that can absolutely kill that difficult monster without handouts, not the you that wants to just get the kill at all costs.

Combat is absolutely as fluid as you can play it, you're going to find yourself trying out weapons and finding gaps to absolutely decimate monsters. You're going to find a weapon that fits your needs and requirements for as fun playstyle, try out weapons you have no idea how to play. The crafting system is engaging and gives you clear goals that you control, and you don't need to put in that extra X% damage just to try out a weapon on some monsters.

Armor crafting and skills are somewhat diverse (All roads lead to Weakness Exploit, Critical Eye and Crit Damage :( ), Defense as a stat is not extremely useful after a certain point, Raw and Elemental Damage at all points will be your bread and butter, and maximizing Crit and Crit damage will see you clearing monsters as if you're in the training room hitting barrels.

If you're looking for a sandbox, this game is a massive one, there are plenty of unique build setups (Less optimal than crit, but they still exist, shout out to Part Breaker, Airborne and Latent Power you janky beautiful skills), plenty of team compositions for you and other hunters to attempt, the skill floor and skill ceiling are far enough apart that you can feel the progression as you learn and understand the systems in place.

The one quirky jank big downside to combat is the hitboxes and hurtboxes can be very off in some situations and you can find yourself being hit by attacks from a monster a good distance away from you or staggered from the monster just moving. It's most noticeable on Insect Glaive (In the air), Longsword (When you're in the middle of weeb combo slicing down) or when you're behind a monsters tail and it decides to rush in a direction away from you.

Even though this can be a large point of contention and frustration, it can also be a plus, it means that you're preparing to be knocked back, so you play safer and play cleaner, you're avoiding any and all instances of damage and it raises the skill ceiling, as well as unfortunately the skill floor.

Post-game, Guiding lands can be 50/50 for enjoyment, on one hand, you have an infinite source of monster hunting, back to back to back to back to you get the idea...
On the other hand, this system is extremely grindy and is not for everyone, a lot of people just use mods to circumvent leveling zones, which is not a bad suggestion if you don't like the system.

Layered armor is barely explained but it is the keystone reward to Guiding Lands for most people, you're going to need to beat the story of Iceborne -> farm guiding lands and do event quests to get layered armor, it's not explained in game but some sets won't be available until you craft the corresponding armor sets normally.

When funds and manpower were short, it was literally passion that kept the project going. Valve eventually even gave them their blessing. 

The story remains the same, as players take the role as Gordon Freeman in the Black Mesa Research Facility. An experiment goes awry and a rift opens up, allowing creatures from another world to infiltrate and cause havoc. The military is sent in to contain the situation, and eliminate ANY witnesses that are present, including the science team and facility staff. Gordon finds himself on a journey to close the rift, while battling both aliens and soldiers, and has multiple interactions with the enigmatic G-man along the way. 

The gameplay is faithful to the original, but with improvements to elevate it to modern day standards. Enemy AI is vastly improved, creating more dynamic situations. Of course the visuals have received a complete overhaul. Textures and models are beautifully rendered. The use of light and shadows is amplified thanks to the Source engine. Half-Life was known for its impressive level design and Black Mesa builds on this foundation. Many levels retain their iconic look and feel but have more expansive functionality. Visually so beautiful and underlined with a soundtrack that will give you goosebumps.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1755365916}, {"review_text": "Black Mesa is a bold and lovingly crafted reimagining of Valve’s iconic 1998 first-person shooter Half-Life, developed by the dedicated team at Crowbar Collective. More than just a remake, Black Mesa is a testament to fan devotion and creative vision, meticulously rebuilding the world of Gordon Freeman with modern technology while preserving the essence that made the original so beloved. Released in full in 2020 after years in early access, the game offers both longtime fans and newcomers a deeply polished, atmospheric, and narrative-driven FPS experience that stands tall on its own merits.

From the outset, Black Mesa impresses with its visual fidelity and attention to environmental detail. The Black Mesa Research Facility has been completely overhauled with high-resolution textures, dynamic lighting, and more expansive and immersive level design. Gone are the blocky, low-polygon corridors of 1998; in their place are sprawling, believable industrial and scientific complexes that feel like functional spaces rather than simple backdrops for gunfights. The game’s visual storytelling is subtle and powerful, evoking a sense of realism and dread as players witness the slow unraveling of the facility after the infamous resonance cascade. Every lab, tunnel, and security checkpoint is infused with the eerie quiet of a disaster in progress, amplifying the game's sense of isolation and tension.

The core gameplay remains faithful to Half-Life’s pioneering blend of combat, exploration, and environmental puzzle-solving, but Black Mesa enhances it with refined AI, tighter gunplay, and smoother platforming. Enemy soldiers and alien creatures are far more challenging than in the original, employing smarter tactics and more aggressive flanking maneuvers, which keeps the player constantly on edge. The weaponry, though largely unchanged in its roster, feels punchier and more satisfying to use, especially classics like the shotgun, revolver, and the experimental Tau Cannon. The crowbar, of course, still reigns supreme as Freeman’s iconic blunt instrument of survival.

One of Black Mesa’s most notable achievements lies in its reimagining of the controversial Xen chapters, which in the original game were widely criticized for being rushed, repetitive, and disorienting. Crowbar Collective chose to expand Xen into a sprawling, visually stunning, multi-hour experience that transforms what was once a low point into a narrative and gameplay high. The alien world is richly textured and imaginative, with bizarre flora, treacherous platforming, and some genuinely awe-inspiring scenery. New gameplay mechanics are introduced here, including elements of low-gravity movement and environmental interaction, which keep the final act feeling fresh and otherworldly without deviating too far from the game’s established tone.

On the audio front, Black Mesa excels with a powerful and atmospheric soundtrack that underscores the game’s tension, mystery, and moments of chaos. The music swells at key moments, reinforcing the pacing and emotional beats of the story. Sound design is equally commendable—every alien screech, weapon discharge, and ambient machinery hum contributes to the immersive soundscape. Voice acting, although limited mostly to incidental dialogue from scientists and security guards, maintains the dry wit and nervous energy that defined the original characters, further grounding the game in its darkly humorous tone.

Performance-wise, Black Mesa runs smoothly on a wide range of hardware, with the Source engine’s modifications offering modern rendering features without sacrificing optimization. Occasional bugs and glitches do appear, particularly in complex AI encounters or during physics-heavy sequences, but they are infrequent and rarely game-breaking. Crowbar Collective has shown a strong commitment to patching and supporting the game post-release, reinforcing the sense that Black Mesa is a labor of love, not just a nostalgia cash-in.

In terms of narrative, Black Mesa doesn’t rewrite Half-Life’s story so much as it enriches it. The story of Gordon Freeman—a silent MIT physicist thrown into a nightmarish alien invasion—is told through the world rather than cutscenes, and Black Mesa excels at environmental storytelling. The game expands and deepens the original’s pacing and mood, taking its time to build tension before plunging the player into high-stakes action. Despite knowing the beats of the plot, returning players will find themselves captivated again by the sense of dread, wonder, and escalating catastrophe.

Ultimately, Black Mesa succeeds not just as a remake but as a fully realized reimagining that brings Half-Life into the modern era with reverence and creativity. It honors the past while improving on nearly every aspect of the original—gameplay, graphics, level design, and atmosphere—making it both a perfect entry point for newcomers and a worthy tribute for veterans. It is a rare example of a fan-made project reaching—and arguably surpassing—the standards of the official source material. Black Mesa is not only a love letter to one of gaming’s most influential titles, but a masterpiece in its own right.

[{"review_text": "Portal 1 is lightning in a bottle. Apart from maybe some dated graphics etc, its the perfect game.

I got so tired of hearing my dad talk about how mind-blowing this game was that I finally asked him to let me try it. It was all true. There's so much to love: No timer, no cut-scenes, and the ability to make you feel like a genius after solving each chamber.

I played Portal for the first time when I was in grade 4 with my brother who was in grade 3. Just imagine a 10 year old and an 8 year old trying desperately to play this really complex and hard puzzle game 24/7 for about a month. I remember we would ask our dad to translate every pice of dialogue (or monologue) because we couldn't understand any English yet (we are from Greece). Many years later it is still my favorite game ever and we have been playing it almost every summer just for the nostalgia. I am so sad that we won't get a Portal 3... you have no idea.

Portal 1 is lonely and isolated to the point where you form a strong attachment to a simple thing like a cube with a heart on it. I loved the melancholic, lonely feel of the game. Something about its eerie atmosphere just resonated with me. And the darker tone of the game made it feel more real. I can't even fully explain it but it's just a ton of little things, such as the empty offices, the huge white rooms filled with artificial light, the way they impliment the soundtrack in this game, the ratman stuff you find later on, the behind the scenes feeling of the lab feeling like you shouldn't be there... I can go on and on but in my first playthrough there would be times where all of these things added up and I got tense almost as if I was in a psychological horror game. I definetly might be the only guy who felt that way to that extent about this game, but I really do think that's something that isn't said enough about Portal 1.

I also typically don't like games that I can finish in one sitting but Portal 1 is that rare exception. Not only that, it's one of my favorite games of all time, probably because it made you WANT to complete it to the very end. There's a reason I don't beat very many games; I have no reason to at all. What do I acheive other than bragging rights and completionism? Sure the story is something to drive you but most games IMO simply don't compel you enough to finish them for the story. I play games for their unique experience, so for this game to wrap so much depth and entertainment into roughly (for me) 5 hours of gameplay is something marvelous.

Portal 1 is basically video game perfection, literally nothing about it should be changed. Nothing is wasted, and nothing is unnecessary. The difficulty curve flawlessly keeps puzzles from being frustrating while still making you feel clever for solving them, the writing is clever and subtle, the story never hinders the gameplay, and the runtime keeps it from outstaying its welcome. To conclude, Portal 1 is just one of the best-made games I’ve ever experienced, and if by any chance you still haven’t tried it to this day… what the  hell are you waiting for?

The plot is essentially that you're in a lab as a research subject learning to use various in order to solve puzzles and make it to the exit of each test chamber. You'll slowly learn how room elements work such as boxes, pressure switches, and of course portals. This main mechanic of the game consists of two portals, a blue one and an orange one. Early on you'll be given a blue portal gun to work with alongside fixed orange portal placements to learn how this works. Essentially, entering either portal will have you exit the other portal. Once you've had enough testing time to familiarize yourself with this concept, the game will give you the dual portal gun which will allow you to create both blue and orange portals. Only one of each color can exist at a time. They can only be placed on white surfaces and if the surfaces moves then the portal will disappear. The goal is simple: solve all of the puzzles to complete every test chamber and you'll be reward with cake!

While using the portals to solve puzzles is the main goal, you'll need to manipulate other objects along the way. There are companion cubes that can be picked up, placed, and dropped. Often these will need to be placed on pressure switches in order to open the exit. You may need to reach buttons to spawn the boxes in the first place or to activate other mechanisms in the room. Some mechanisms will require power. To supply it you'll need to get an energy orb from a shooter and get it to the power node. You'll also start to have obstacles and hazards to impede your progress. Barriers exist that will destroy all items the pass through them and also remove all existing portals if you yourself pass through them. Stationary turret robots with machine guns will gun you down if you get within their line of sight. You'll need to find a way around them or knock them down to deactivate them. Water is the most dangerous hazard of all as it will kill you very quickly upon contact. Death results in respawning at the last checkpoint. There is no real fail-state in the game. Complete all 19 test chambers to conclude the research the computer requires of you.

GLaDOS the computer has some funny lines yet also some unsettling ones as well. The atmosphere of the game is very good at being ambiguous as to if you should trust these experiments or not. You're often left to wonder what exactly you're doing here and what this testing is in service of. The mechanics are fantastic. The concept of using portals can be difficult to wrap your head around at first, but it's used in so many different ways along with the other test chamber elements. I really appreciate that the game really makes the most out of the simple portal mechanic. It never feels like moving from gimmick room to gimmick room because anything new is always adding to the main mechanics of using the portals. I'm sure it's a technical marvel to make this work in terms of programming as well, but even just taking that for granted the concept is so unique and executed incredibly well.

That's not to say the game is flawless, though. For one thing, it's a bit on the short side. It's also a bit on the clunky side when it comes to action segments. Platforming is difficult due to very poor jumping ability. If you jump too soon you won't make it and jumping too late will just end up in you falling instead. It can also be difficult to line up portals to increase your momentum. There are multiple instances where you need to create a portal to fall into, one to fall out of, and then shoot again while falling to create enough momentum to launch yourself somewhere. This can be hard to do on the fly when the portal width is so narrow. You often just get caught on the sides and ruin the momentum. Worse yet is that if you make an infinite loop to fall through with portals without very particular placement, you'll be twisting around as you fall out of them and trying to aim to where the next portal needs to go while still falling will put you just enough out of alignment to catch the edge of the portal and stop your necessary loop.

So overall, the action sections are a pain, but the puzzles sections are excellent. This game is still quite unique and well-regarded for a reason. I did try a bit of the bonus levels but I'll admit I didn't do too many of them. There are extra stages that are harder variants of the normal test chambers, but I quit as soon as one had a hard action section. And the challenge stages are doing the main levels in a limited amount of time, steps, or portal placements. I'll also admit that this game was probably much more jaw-dropping to play when it originally released many years ago, but even so I still think it's a great experience. I'm very happy to have finally played it for myself. And the good news is that it goes for fairly low prices on basically all platforms these days. Personally I played it on my Steam Deck and loved it, but no matter where you play it, Portal is Portal. Now if you'll excuse me, I have some cake to go eat. Is it just me or is it getting kind of warm in here? Huh.

[h1]Puzzles for the non-puzzler[/h1]

Well, first order of business: what, exactly, [b]is[/b] [i]Portal[/i]?

Yes, it's a puzzle game, but unlike many puzzle games, this game doesn't expect you to use science/math logic, at least not beyond common sense logic that everyone should have. I always did really well in school but it has been a while and even in spite of that, I hated math (and advanced science); I've never been one to think with cold logic and numbers, I've always been more of a "see the paths ahead of you" sort of guy and I can safely say that [i]Portal[/i] is that kind of game.

You are expected to get from one end of the map to the other, and you have to do so by evaluating the layout, knowing how the mechanics work, and sometimes you need good timing as well. A good example of this is a sequence where you have to open a portal on a platform, drop down a deep pit and open a second portal there. This flings you up into the air and while you're mid-air, you want to switch out the pit portal for a new portal on a higher platform. You continue this onward until the end of the sequence, which requires some good timing and continued momentum in addition to the logic.

It also justifies these puzzles with story, stating that you're a test subject for Aperture Science, a company who developed wormhole technology and you're a tester for that tech. This justification is a huge part of what makes [i]Portal[/i] compelling to people like me, who usually play games for the story.

[h1]Sci-fi intrigue and comedic goofiness[/h1]

Speaking of the story, this game's plot is actually very interesting, though you wouldn't assume that from looking at it. You start off as the test subject, locked in a doorless cell with a bed, toilet, radio, coffee mug and notepad. This subtle setup does a great job at environmental storytelling, showing you your first hint as to what Aperture Science is like. This, combined with a female robotic voice you'll begin hearing, begins to subtly unravel story about Aperture, your role with them, and the world at large outside of the facility.

It also has loads of environmental storytelling, starting with a few areas where you can go a little outside of the normal testing chamber grounds. In these offset areas, you'll encounter clues that show you that you're not the first subject, and that your precursor(s) may have been fleeing from something. This comes to a head when you reach the end of the test chambers: [spoiler]while that robotic voice is trying to kill you off, you have the opportunity to flee and this ends up taking you through loads of 'unapproved' areas of the Aperture facility[/spoiler].

What's funny is that all of this leads to a real sense of adventure and even a bit of a pulse-pounding adrenaline rush in some segments. All the while, as you're trying to progress, you begin to uncover more and more that really starts to paint a clear picture of what's going on. I won't spoil that, though; all I'll say is that if you're a Valve fan, you're going to like the story of these games.

[h1]Timeless art[/h1]

Despite releasing in 2007, this game still looks fantastic, even without the ray tracing version (a free DLC). The Source Engine still holds up quite well today. It's very difficult to have a realistic, sci-fi art style that doesn't age poorly as graphic tech advances but [i]Portal[/i] had no such difficulties. Sure, it doesn't look [b]new[/b], by any means, but it still looks appealing.

I think part of this has to do with the fact that you never see any sort of human characters, aside from brief reflections of your character that you might see if the portals line up just right. Character design tends to age the worst in game graphics, so this worked out great in retrospect. However, the overall art design, color palette and graphics tech work together to give you a very, very good-looking game even in the 2020s.

The funniest thing, though, is how it starts off deceptively monochrome. You see the sterile whites and grays of the test chambers, with a nice, subtle hint of bright blue and orange thanks to the portals you open. However, as the game goes on and you advance beyond the test chambers themselves, you get a really crazy palette shift toward dingy browns, rusty reds and oranges, yellowish lighting and so forth. This shift feels both natural and jarring, which I'm certain was intentional.

All of that comes together to create a game that I'm comfortable saying is still [b]beautiful[/b] by today's standards. Oh, and let's not forget the simple elegance of Source Engine GUI design! It worked well in [i]Half-Life 2[/i] but it looks even better here because of the pseudo-utopian corporate aesthetics of the art design.

[h1]A classic epitomized[/h1]

Regardless of whether you're normally a fan of puzzle games, I feel like you really need to give [i]Portal[/i] a try. Not only should all of the above be reason enough, but it's also a total classic that I think everyone needs to try at least once.

It's not a puzzle game in the sense of [i]Myst[/i]'s obtuse difficulty, nor is it a puzzle game in the sense of some cheap puzzle game you'd find in the Walmart electronics section for $3. It's more like a first-person adventure game centered around logic puzzles where it's easy to pick up but a bit more difficult to master.

Besides, with the [i]Orange Box[/i] pack and the Valve Complete Pack, you can grab it alongside some other downright incredible games (including the vastly improved sequel) for an affordable price point. What makes the situation worse is that these marginal updates are marketed as full-priced new entries, effectively turning the series into a cashgrab. Players are paying top dollar for what is, in essence, a lightly modified version of the same game they've already purchased one or more times before. The developers, GIANTS Software, seem to rely on the loyal modding community to fill the gaps in creativity and depth, while delivering the bare minimum in terms of technical or gameplay evolution themselves.

At its core, Farming Simulator fails to live up to its genre’s potential. Despite its name, the game lacks the intricate depth that one would expect from a true simulation. Crop management, soil chemistry, equipment wear and tear, dynamic weather systems - elements that should add meaningful layers of realism - are either simplified to the point of irrelevance or entirely absent. Farming in the real world is a complex, constantly evolving process, but Farming Simulator presents it as a rinse-and-repeat grind with little nuance or challenge.

Even worse, many longstanding bugs persist despite years of feedback. Issues with AI workers getting stuck, poor pathfinding, clipping problems, janky vehicle physics, and multiplayer desyncs remain unresolved, making the experience feel unpolished and frustrating—especially given how long the series has been around. These aren't minor quirks; they're quality-of-life issues that have been present since multiple earlier titles and simply should not still exist.

However, the game is also severely held back by its story, which is among the worst in the series[/code]

Initially [url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-02-09/ubisoft-plans-new-assassin-s-creed-game-to-help-fill-schedule?sref=6UP70zYf]planned as another DLC expansion[/url] for [i]Assassin’s Creed: Valhalla[/i], a game that was [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dreamylotus/recommended/2208920/]already way too bloated[/url], [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] is a surprising return to the basics of the long running-franchise. As the series has moved into an action-RPG direction starting with 2017’s [i]Assassin’s Creed Origins[/i], which resulted in massive 70+h experiences that favoured open combat a lot more than stealth approaches, seeing publisher Ubisoft return to the previous gameplay formula was unexpected but not unwelcome – while the reinvention of the franchise drew in a lot of new players, some fans still preferred the “classic” [i]Assassin’s Creed[/i] experience.

Enter [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i], which was [url=https://www.ign.com/articles/future-assassins-creed-games-will-not-all-be-150-hour-rpgs]created with the intention of celebrating the franchise’s 15th anniversary[/url]: Set in Baghdad during the Islamic Golden Age, the game follows the early life of street-thief Basim, who made his first appearance in [i]Assassin’s Creed Valhalla[/i]. Despite essentially acting as a prequel however, [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] goes huge lengths to avoid forming any meaningful connections to the plot of its predecessor, which does come with the benefit of allowing new players to experience [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] without the risk of any spoilers as well. However, the self-contained nature of the plot also severely limits the narrative potential of [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i], which results in a pretty generic plot that doesn’t really commit itself to Basim as a character and has no impact on the current-day storyline.

To be blunt here, the story and its presentation are easily the biggest aspects that stop [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] from becoming anything more than an enjoyable return to the roots of the franchise. What you get is a boring excuse for eliminating certain targets in Baghdad after slowly uncovering their identity, which is told through the most basic cutscenes and dialogues. Basim is reduced to a generic protagonist without much personality throughout most of the game, the supporting cast is one-dimensional due to their limited screentime, and the villains are only given the lowest possible amount of “evil backstory” to make the player feel justified about killing them. All of this culminates in a rushed and unsatisfying ending, which easily suffers the most from the forcibly limited connections to [i]Assassin’s Creed Valhalla[/i], as [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] unsuccessfully tries to set up future events while simultaneously not wanting to talk about what’s to come. As a result, the game’s story essentially feels like filler material, entirely lacking in both memorable characters and moments. While [i]Assassin’s Creed Valhalla[/i] might’ve featured a story that was bloated to no end, it at least managed to carve out an identity and place in the franchise for itself.

What makes this story fiasco so much worse is that the gameplay of [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] is actually pretty fun and a decently short palate-cleanser after the enormous [i]Assassin’s Creed Origins, Odyssey & Valhalla[/i], focussing on parkour and stealth kills once again. All of the RPG elements have either been removed entirely or severely reduced – most importantly, there’s no XP-based level system anymore as you automatically raise your “Hidden One rank” while completing main missions. Additionally, while equipment still offers various bonusses and can be upgraded, it doesn’t have as much of an impact, as assassinations are one-hit kills regardless of equipment - the better stats only have a slight effect during open combat, really. And while a skill tree system returns, it’s vastly smaller than the one from [i]Assassin’s Creed Valhalla[/i] and only offers actively noticeable benefits (e.g. time slowing down when you’re using throwing knives while in the air).

That alone doesn’t make [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] play a lot more similar to the initial games in the franchise though, which is why further design choices have been implemented: Open combat is a lot more dangerous know due to Basim’s limited health and a focus on parrying, which makes stealth approaches a lot more viable. Many features from older games also see a return, such as the “Notoriety System” from [i]Assassin’s Creed II[/i], which increasingly punishes the player for performing illegal actions when witnesses are nearby and requires them to perform certain actions (e.g. ripping off wanted posters) to become invisible again. Parkour has also been expanded upon, with the small but dense city of Baghdad providing plenty of opportunities to make your escape when chased by guards. However, as [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] runs on the same engine as [i]Assassin’s Creed Valhalla[/i], even the enhanced parkour system still suffers from similar problems, like parkour down working a lot worse than going up.

Finally, key target assassinations include the option to choose from different approaches, as Ubisoft already experimented with during [i]Assassin’s Creed Unity & Syndicate[/i]. For example, a stronghold might offer multiple ways to get in, from bribing workers to get the right key to jumping in from the right window – while being limited to smaller things like these, these options do shake up the gameplay occasionally, as they prevent the player from simply performing the same methods every time. In my opinion however, this is only a small step in the right direction, as the key target assassinations are still severely lacking in terms of presentation and can all be “solved” through open combat to a certain degree.

Still, as someone who’ve played through all mainline [i]Assassin’s Creed[/i] titles, I found [i]Mirage[/i] to be a decent return to the old franchise formula in terms of gameplay. It’s short enough to not overstay it’s welcome, stealth and parkour are finally more important again and the city of Baghdad is fun to run across - even if the mostly empty wilderness surrounding it could’ve been cut in my opinion. There’s also a refreshingly low amount of side content, which can easily be ignored without consequences if you just want to play through the main story.

In short, [i]Assassin’s Creed Mirage[/i] may not the best title in the franchise by a long shot but if you’ve missed how the old titles played, this is a decent reminder when bought on sale. While there’s still a lot of room for improvement, it’s a great palate-cleanser for those tired of the expansive action-RPGs in the franchise and a fitting way to celebrate the legacy of a franchise that has been through various ups and downs as well.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1737935861}, {"review_text": "Yes, it's the old AC again, but it brings all the bad things with it, makes something even worse and barely improves anything.

THE GOOD

The parkour controls have been taken from the newer instalments, which is fine — they're definitely better than the controls from the older games. They're still not perfect, but Ubisoft apparently has no idea how to improve them at this point.
Parkour is great fun; after the modern AC games, which barely feature any parkour, it was refreshing to have so many movement options again.

THE BAD

Combat is probably the worst in the entire series. When you are attacked, you are supposed to either dodge or parry, depending on the colour of the telegraphed attack. The problem is that the colour prompt appears for such a brief moment before the actual attack that, even after hours of playing, I am physically unable to react that quickly. Ultimately, I just mashed buttons and hoped for the best.

For some reason, restricted areas are not indicated on the map, and the HUD indicator is very easy to overlook. This caused me to constantly trigger alarms when I just wanted to travel around the city.

The game uses the same key for both a normal attack and a silent assassination. It happens quite often that you intend to stealthily assassinate someone, but instead attack them, blowing your cover and sometimes failing the whole mission in the process.

There are also some technical problems. For me, the most apparent was that the display settings constantly reset, forcing me to go to the settings menu and select full-screen mode and vsync every time I ran the game.

THE UGLY

The writing in the AC series has always been poor, but here it's almost insulting. I played this game right after Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, and I was shocked at how much worse the writing was. Even the smallest quests and the most insignificant NPCs in KCD had better dialogue and backstory than the main quest in AC Mirage.
No one in this game sounds like a real human. Everyone speaks like a mystic or a philosopher, either giving you exposition or drowning you in endless, empty, metaphorical babbling. Later in the game I started skipping most of the dialogue because it was unbearable to listen to.

Is there really no one left at Ubisoft who can write believable dialogue between two flesh-and-blood characters?

Overall, Mirage is not a terrible game, but it's so mediocre and forgettable, even within the Assassin's Creed franchise, that I cannot recommend it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1751288052}, {"review_text": "---{ Graphics }---

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
The world is only a shell of its former self, ravaged by madness and purposelessness after the Shattering of the Elden Ring. Born as one of many Tarnished, you too would be destined to roam this endless limbo; however, that was not meant to be. Gifted with the ability to see the elusive remnants of divine Grace, you’re set on a journey to follow them through a broken world, with the ultimate goal of mending the Elden Ring, restoring the world to what it once was, or mold it into something different. 

It’s an obscure narrative, that doesn’t get more clear as you progress, unless you spend time reading all the fine print on items you acquire, exhaust all optional dialogues, and figure things out on your own. As cloudy as it might be, there’s a surprising depth and meaning in each character, friendly or otherwise, that you may encounter, as there is in each perilous fortress, dungeon or ruin you may venture into. Such obscurity may feel unwarranted, but it’s rewarding in its own way, as it allows players to piece together the story, motives and lore bit by bit instead of dumping it linearly as most games do. It’s written extremely well, and gives a new dimension to the exploration component, where items aren’t only tools, but also a source of understanding.

The world is nothing short of spectacular, both visually and artistically. From vast plains and labyrinthine cities to dark dungeons and putrid swamps, there’s enough variety to keep exploration fresh for more than a hundred hours, and that’s certainly something. Each location feels coherent in its characters, ambience and visual style, perfectly matching the background lore and events that may have occurred there. 

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore the world on either foot or horseback, your summonable steed an essential tool to traverse the large swathes of land between each dungeon, fortress or point of interest. Other than offering convenient functions like crafting, leveling and weapon ability swapping, Grace sites also act as fast travel beacons, and are conveniently placed all over the world. Of course, using them also means respawning all enemies except bosses. Unlike other Souls, there’s a map, with custom markers even, but nothing more than that. 

You’ll have to find places on your own, with nothing hinting that a hidden dungeon, cave or whole parts of the world may be hidden past the most remote crevices and corners. Despite that, the superb map design always gives you hints and landmarks to figure out if there’s still something left to find. It’s supremely rewarding to comb every tidbit of land, because when you least expect it, you’ll always find a unique item, a hidden NPC, a portal to a secret location; it’s the definition of organically rewarding exploration. 

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
Given the hundreds of available weapons, spells, and armor sets available, you’ll be able to shape your character into whatever most suits your playstyle. Be a powerful mage and destroy your foes from a distance, a swift rogue banking it all on attack speed and critical strikes after a parry, or a mighty warrior hitting foes hard enough to break their poise, exposing them to a deadly finisher. Or why not, a mix of all of the above and more; there isn’t a right or wrong build, as everything is equally viable if used correctly. 

Combat is, above all, based on individual skill, precise dodges, learning enemy patterns and picking your fights wisely. It’s a learning process, where each death makes you stronger in experience, despite the Runes (souls) you might have lost. More than in any other Souls however, Elden Ring puts emphasis on builds, giving you passive tools like talismans, interchangeable weapon skills and a wide variety of buffs and utilities to find the perfect combination to overcome your foes.

Enemies are deadly and merciless at all times. Those who recklessly rush, or button mash, will be demolished even by common trash mobs. Elden Ring is almost never unfair, but it’s impossibly difficult if you don’t approach it in the correct way and refuse to play by its rules. That only is more true for bosses, most of which have evolving movesets and even double phases, so that once you think you have mastered their moveset and found a strategy, a higher challenge presents itself. A wide array of status effects, damage types, resistances and weaknesses you’ll have to figure out on your own are present to make some fights much easier, and only through trying and failing many times will you be able to find the right strategy. 

[h3]Character Progression[/h3]
As you level up with Runes gathered from defeating enemies and using certain items, your attributes will allow you to use more powerful weapons, many of which having unique special abilities, and even normal ones can be customized with the skills you like the most, through a simple yet deep crafting system. Elden Ring isn’t as gear-dependent as classic RPGs may be, but unless you’re a tryharder masochist, having good gear to complement your build definitely makes all the difference in not getting one-shot by everything and not taking forever in killing bosses.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 29, "timestamp_created": 1741374349}, {"review_text": "An extraordinary milestone that will likely cast as long of a shadow over other open world games as Dark Souls already did over most action RPGs during the last decade.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1754072605}, {"review_text": "Spend 3 hours building character

Anyways, it's still a fun game, even if I feel a bit cheated.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1740234878}, {"review_text": "As an engineer and physics teacher, I find it a pleasure to write a review for "Oxygen Not Included." This game has captivated me for over 600 hours, and for good reason. It’s one of those rare titles that can make you lose track of time, often at the expense of a good night’s sleep, thanks to its deep and engaging base-building and management mechanics.

The gameplay and art are top-notch, as expected from the creators of "Don’t Starve." The game’s incorporation of real-world physics, chemistry, and even a hint of biology sets it apart from typical base-building titles. Concepts like denser gases sinking, thermal conductivity of materials, and gas flow mechanics aren’t just visual flourishes—they’re crucial to mastering the game’s systems. I’ve even recommended it to some of my students as a fun way to engage with these scientific ideas in a practical context.

One area that feels like a missed opportunity, however, is the game’s approach to electricity. While it introduces the concept of transformers to manage potential differences, it falls short of incorporating more sophisticated concepts like series and parallel circuits. Given the game’s 2D aesthetic, I believe the addition of more realistic electrical systems could have been a natural and engaging fit for players to experiment with.

Make no mistake, this is a challenging game. Your duplicants (the characters you manage) will suffer and perish in various ways—hunger, heat, and oxygen shortages, to name a few—until you master the balancing act required for survival. Problems often reveal themselves too late, forcing you to start over from scratch. But therein lies the charm of "Oxygen Not Included": every failure is a lesson learned. The experience of rebuilding from scratch, armed with newfound knowledge, makes for an incredibly rewarding gameplay loop.

For those who enjoy base-building games, I wholeheartedly recommend "Oxygen Not Included." It’s not always a smooth ride, and losing a base after dozens of hours can be disheartening, but the lessons learned with each restart make every new base a little smarter and more efficient than the last.

The expansions are promising, though I’ve only scratched the surface of the newer ones. Mods, on the other hand, are a mixed bag. There’s a rich modding community offering everything from quality-of-life improvements to full gameplay overhauls. Personally, I’m a bit of a purist, preferring cosmetic mods over those that make the game easier. The only caveat is that mods often break after updates and require patching to work again.

All in all, "Oxygen Not Included" is a meticulously crafted, mentally stimulating, and sometimes brutally unforgiving game. If you’re up for the challenge, it’s well worth your time—just don’t be surprised if it ends up taking more of it than you expected.

1000/10 would recommend", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1748312856}, {"review_text": "If you're the kind of player who thrives on depth, complexity, and the thrill of solving problems with increasingly elegant systems, Oxygen Not Included might be your next obsession. After 1700 hours, I can say without hesitation: this game has earned every minute.

Depth That Never Runs Dry
What looks like a quirky space-colony sim quickly reveals itself as a brutally intricate simulation of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, gas exchange, agriculture, industrial automation, psychology, and even rocket science. And yet, it’s all packed into a charming, side-scrolling aesthetic with expressive Duplicants and satisfying sound design.

Even after thousands of cycles across multiple colonies, I'm still refining my designs, optimizing layouts, and discovering new strategies. There's no “one solution” — just more refined ones.

Engineering Playground
You’re not just surviving; you’re building systems. Water loops, oxygen production, heat management, food chains, power grids, automation, and late-game interplanetary logistics — this is a game where planning matters, and poor choices 100 cycles ago can come back to melt your base.

Mistakes teach. Recovery is a puzzle. Mastery is satisfying.

Endless Replayability
Every asteroid type demands new thinking. Traits, biomes, geysers — all randomized. You’re never playing the same game twice. Want a relaxed experience? Play Terra and build at your own pace. Want a challenge? Start on Rime and deal with the cold. Or try modded asteroids and explore community-curated chaos.

Systems Nerd Heaven
If you enjoy games like Factorio, Dwarf Fortress, or RimWorld, but crave more simulation and fewer guns, this is your game. ONI is about processes. It’s a colony sim where how you do something is often more important than what you do. That’s a rare design choice — and it's beautifully executed.

Minor Critiques
The early game can feel like a trap for new players who don’t understand heat, gas stratification, or resource scarcity.

Performance can drop in large colonies with lots of automation and piping.

There’s no hand-holding — but the Wiki and community are incredibly helpful.

Final Verdict: 10/10
Oxygen Not Included isn't a game you play. It's a game you inhabit. It's a slow-burn obsession for systems thinkers, tinkerers, and masochists who enjoy watching colonies implode because they forgot to vent CO₂. It’s also one of the most rewarding games I’ve ever touched.

This game starts with acting like its cute and rewarding and pretty easy. Everything looks and feels so lovely and after 2 or 3 hours of gameplay it lets you know "nope your cleaned water isn't clean, it's full of germs which gives your colony a slow but unavoidable death". You have to study the game on youtube and the Steam forums. Then you come back, confident, create a germ-killer, you are unbeatable at this game! You play it for like 5-10 hours. Then.. the next problem arrives. I love the way the game just cascades complexity at you and almost every solution you come up with to the current problem creates a new problem or resource bottleneck somewhere down the line.

Everything in ONI has byproducts. In most craft/simcity style games, you need 1 wood 1 fiber to make an axe, use an axe to get more wood, 10 wood makes a plank, 2 planks and one iron makes a board, etc. In ONI, 10 wood makes a plank AND sawdust. Which builds up and becomes a problem over time. It's that little bit of polluted water the generators make, that little bit of CO2 the dupes breathe out, that little bit of heat that EVERYTHING makes, in ONI you craft and unlock better craftables to make things more efficiently just like every other game, but you ALSO have to deal with the long term problems that everything you've done so far has created. It is a subtle change to the gameplay loop but it makes the game so much more interesting. Complex and detailed system games are my favorite. When a game gives me the ability to actually think and create a scientific solution or at least do something that lets you feel like you invented something, that is the best feeling ever.

I think this is one of those games that's really fun to figure out on your own because it's almost like a roguelike but for RTS. You definitely learn from your failures, and pretty quickly. If you've played Fallout Shelter or something similar, it's very similar to that in look and feel, but there are about a million more ways to build your little colony. I think there's fun in exploring, but if you're failure/risk averse, then a How to Get Started tutorial won't ruin the experience.

This might get me burned, but I found Oxygen Not Included much more engaging and creative than Factorio. Both deal with managing systems, but where ONI's concept is colorful and varied, Factorio's is one simple idea multiplied a million times over. If ONI is a chess set, Factorio is more like a huge game of checkers. Thanks to the large amount of different and interconnected aspects of the simulation, ONI can keep the problems and solutions fresh well into the endgame. It also somehow manages to find that thin line of giving you just enough information that it feels like you're finding the solutions by yourself, not following a manual. Your solutions probably won't be perfect, but that's the fun part. In many games there is only one way to do something. In ONI there are many and people are constantly finding new ones. Some are better than others but you can do it plenty of ways.

The complexity and how the many systems interact with each other are the best part of the game, and unlike Factorio, having to manage these systems by necessity made me much more engaged and invested in what I was building. To me having bathrooms, handwashing etc made the game that much more engaging because it fed into the core gameplay loop, how to manage your resources, inputs, outputs and waste products while keeping everything balanced. In most other games, bathrooms are just a thing you build, but in Oxygen not included, bathrooms are a thing you design. How you get renewable water into your bathrooms, how to dispose of the germy waste water, and how if you work out the math the whole loop is actually beneficial bc it's water positive so you can easily make it a closed loop system as long as you handle the germs.

Having problems that initially seem small but slowly pile up into a catastrophe actually highlights the brilliance of the simulation. The key thing is nothing about those disasters are random. This game ruins your experience over and over. For me it's an drug addiction: everything is fine in the beginning, then you can't stop, then your only thought is "i will f*** you back!". Set during the vibrant and dangerous period of the Italian Renaissance, the story follows Ezio Auditore da Firenze, a nobleman-turned-assassin after a devastating family betrayal. Ezio isn’t just a protagonist — he’s a character arc incarnate, evolving from a brash, arrogant youth to a cunning and wise Assassin bent on justice, not vengeance.

His journey spans decades, cities, and conspiracies, involving historical figures like Leonardo da Vinci, Lorenzo de’ Medici, and Rodrigo Borgia, woven seamlessly into a narrative about loyalty, loss, and legacy.

Ezio's charm, relatability, and development make him not just the heart of this game, but arguably the heart of the entire franchise.

Combat, while still simple, is tighter and more fluid than before, introducing new weapons, counters, and tools like smoke bombs and poison blades.

For a 2009 title, Assassin’s Creed II is visually stunning. The attention to architectural detail, Renaissance artwork, and the natural beauty of Italy give the world a timeless quality. Animations are smoother than the original, and crowd density brings each city to life.

Assassin’s Creed II didn’t just fix the first game’s flaws — it became the template for every successful AC game that followed. Its blend of historical fiction, character growth, and open-world exploration hit a sweet spot that fans still praise today.

Even over a decade later, Ezio’s debut adventure remains deeply playable, emotionally resonant, and mechanically solid. Whether you’re new to the series or a returning fan, this is an essential chapter that never loses its charm.

Avoid If:
You need ultra-modern graphics or expect deep RPG elements (those came later in the series).

Assassin’s Creed II is a genre-defining sequel that balances style, substance, and storytelling in a way few games have managed since. Ezio Auditore’s journey is not just iconic — it’s unforgettable.

I consider myself a staunch defender of Age of Empires IV. In fact, I think it is one of the finest RTS games ever made, and it deserves far more recognition than it gets. For me, this is not just another installment in the series, this is the perfect spiritual successor to Age of Empires II, built with modern design principles and an incredible attention to detail.

AoE4 takes the core magic of AoE2 and turns the depth dial up to eleven. Every single civilization is truly unique. Not just slightly different bonuses or tech trees, but entirely different playstyles, mechanics, and strategies. Playing the French feels nothing like playing the Mongols, which feels nothing like playing the Chinese, which feels nothing like playing the Malians. The variety is staggering, and it fundamentally changes how you approach the game depending on your faction.

Even the presentation is outstanding. Civilizations are not only visually distinct, they are culturally alive. Your units speak in their own historical languages, their architecture evolves through the ages in a way that reflects their heritage, and the attention to detail in animations, unit design, and map variety makes the world feel authentic and vibrant. Few RTS games have ever achieved this level of immersion.

The gameplay itself is razor sharp. It keeps the accessibility that makes AoE approachable while adding layers of complexity and asymmetry that reward mastery. This is a game where learning a new civilization feels like learning a whole new game, and that is a rare achievement in the RTS genre.

If there is one problem, it is not in the game design itself, but in the amount of post-launch content it receives. Compared to Age of Empires II Definitive Edition, which gets new civilizations, campaigns, and maps at an incredible pace, AoE4 feels like it is only receiving a fraction of that love. That is a shame, because if the developers poured the same amount of attention and expansions into AoE4 as they do with AoE2, I genuinely believe it would become the greatest Age of Empires game ever made, no contest.

As it stands, it is already a masterpiece in my eyes. It is a game with immense potential, already delivering a fantastic experience, and capable of becoming the definitive RTS of our era if given the support it deserves. I will keep playing it, I will keep recommending it, and I will keep defending it, because AoE4 is not just good, it is the future of the franchise!

I love how AoEIV had taken the time and effort to bring us a historically-accurate stories that are tied to the gameplay. I think this is the part that I love the most.

Each of the civilizations feel unique, although not as unique as in Age of Empires III (AoEIII), in my opinion, with exceptions, naturally. I think it a bit as a combination between Age of empires II (AoEII) and AoEIII, leaning a little bit towards AoEII, which, by the way, is my favorite Age of Empires due to several reasons. The strategies and battles are surely good and I enjoy having different kinds of the same group of units, each with different functions. The walls' mechanics are also a good addition and adds a lot in terms of strategies and siege.

I know for a fact that many of the updates have solved many of the issues that player the player base have experienced by now and I applaud this; it was actually the bugs that led me to abandon the game some time ago, hoping for it to get better after some updates. And it really happened, even releasing a DLC. Reading this DLC's reviews, which I won't buy at least for now, shows me that AoEIV may be in a limbo where instead of taking advantage of what it is, it is just a bit nervous about the steps they need to follow to earn new and old fans of the series.

One of the things I don't like at all is that there's too little focus on the single-player experience. What I loved about AoEII was the different heroes, scenarios and setting of the campaigns, and that is also one of the things that made AoEII so memorable for many people; the amount of content that you could experience on your own was tremendous and adding the multiplayer was just perfect for all types of players. AoEIV is lacking heavily on this side: there's only half the campaigns for each of the civilizations that you can play. [{"review_text": "One of the best sim racing experiences you can get, even years later.

Assetto Corsa might be getting old, but it’s aged like fine wine - especially once you dive into the modding scene. The base game alone is solid but a bit barebones by today’s standards. The real magic happens once you install Content Manager and Custom Shaders Patch (CSP). Those two completely transform the game -better lighting, weather, physics tweaks, smoother performance, and tons of quality-of-life features. It honestly feels like a new title after that.

Then you’ve got the mods - cars, tracks, visuals, sound packs, everything you can imagine. The community support is insane, and there’s something for every kind of driver, from casual track day enthusiasts to full-on sim racers. You can go from drifting in Japan to racing GT3s at Spa, or even just cruising through city maps at sunset.

If you’re playing on a controller, don’t worry - there are some amazing Gamepad FX scripts that completely change how Assetto Corsa feels without a wheel.

For grip racing, there’s Advanced Gamepad Assist, which smooths out steering, reduces twitchiness, and gives you way more precision when braking and cornering. It makes racing with a controller feel natural and consistent.

For drifting, there’s a different script called A7 Assist, designed specifically for smoother countersteering. It makes it much easier to catch slides and hold long drifts without the car snapping or feeling unpredictable.

Both are absolute game-changers depending on your driving style.

Performance-wise, it runs great on most modern PCs, and the visuals can look stunning once you tune everything with CSP and a good graphics preset (would definitely check out Pure if I were you)

All in all, Assetto Corsa is one of those games that grows with you - the deeper you go, the better it gets. It’s not perfect out of the box, but with the right setup, it’s easily one of the best and most flexible sim racing platforms ever made.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762949551}, {"review_text": "---{ Graphics }---

AC: Origins was the game that pushed the series into a new direction after people were getting tired of yearly releases that all felt similar to play. In some ways, it succeeded, in others, it didn't, but overall it's a great game that I enjoyed enough to play all its DLCs and hunt down all achievements.

The game sends you to Ptolemaic Egypt, where you play as Bayek, a guardian of the country who ends up founding the precursor of what would later become the Assassin order. Your journey leads you from Greek cities like Alexandria to ancient Egyptian religious centers like Memphis and Krokodilopolis. The world design is excellent, you get to visit many historically important locations and they're all gorgeous to look at, and you can climb all the way to the top of every building in good old Assassin's Creed fashion.

The variety of environments is great. Greek cities, ancient Egyptian temples, valleys of ruined monuments, and later in the game Roman forts as Caesar establishes a foothold. The landscapes are just as varied as the architecture: the fertile floodplains of the Nile, rocky and sandy deserts, forested hills, grand mountains.

Exploration is the game's greatest strength. In a surprising move for an Ubisoft game, it's actually very playable without markers. I played through the entire game with the interface set to minimal, only using quest markers when I couldn't find a quest location myself. Most questgivers will give you simple directions where you need to go, which lets you solve the quests without having to follow markers. Sometimes there are tracks in the sand to follow, and other visual indicators like that. I'd say about 70% of the game's quests can be solved entirely without markers, the rest is vague enough that you'll need to check them - still, a pretty good track record for a modern AAA game.

Speaking of quests, the writing of the side quests is pretty solid, and many quests are inspired by actual historic practices of ancient Egypt. Several quests are related to mummies, one even has you investigate mummies that have been improperly preserved and you need to find the person at fault. The only problem is that the quests are completely linear and can't be sequence broken. If a quest requires you to kill an officer in a fort, that officer will only spawn once you accept the quest. If you already cleared the fort before, the officer wasn't there yet, so you have to go back and clear it again. The silliest example was a quest where I had to retrieve an ancient artifact from a pyramid. I had already been through the pyramids and looted all the treasure, but the one quest-specific chest only spawned after I took the quest, so I had to return into an already looted dungeon to open a chest that hadn't been there before. It's just silly.

Now for the questionable parts: the biggest difference to older AC titles is the introduction of "RPG elements". I'm putting those in quotation marks because it isn't a real RPG at all - in fact, it's the greatest misunderstanding of what an RPG should be that I have ever seen. There are experience points, levelups, and a skill tree, but the implementation has several problems. While the skill tree has some interesting choices that can change your playstyle, leveling up itself is designed in the worst way possible. Being higher level inherently raises your damage and health by a significant amount, and enemies who outlevel you are pretty much unkillable HP sponges. The main RPG mechanic of this game is that numbers get bigger as you level up, and tremendously so. The biggest problem is that unless you have the interface set to full (which I didn't, as I prefer playing with an unobtrusive minimal interface) you can't tell what level an enemy is, so you'll attempt to fight a bunch of soldiers and figure out they're ten levels higher than you by landing thirty hits barely dealing damage, then they kill you in a single strike. Levels are the most important stat in this game, far more important than any of the skills you invest points into, or any of the equipment you can upgrade.

The level system really is the game's greatest drawback. While I like RPGs that have zones of different levels, where you enter a dungeon that's too hard for you so you make a note to return later when you're stronger, I don't like it when levels give inherent bonuses to a character. I had the same problem with Divinity: Original Sin, where being just a few levels higher than any given enemy would make them trivial to defeat, while being just a few levels lower would make them almost impossible. Same here. To make things worse, your hidden blade now deals "assassination damage" and if the enemy has too many hitpoints, your stealth attack won't be an insta-kill, which makes it completely impossible to even attempt a stealth approach for high level enemy encampments.

The way levels work is that each province has a level zone: one province might be level 15 to 20, another might be 30 to 35, so all enemies in there will be in that level range - with a few exceptions of higher level forts in low level regions. There is no visual difference between a level 3 and a level 30 enemy, it's literally just numbers. They have the same character model, same equipment, same behavior. It's such a waste of potential because the game does have different enemy types in different regions, and later in the game Romans arrive who wear different armor to the local Hellenistic military. It would have worked much better to have all Greeks be of the same strength, and the Romans of higher strength, but alas. Strength is solely determined by numbers. Such a massive waste of what is actually a decent RPG system, because many of the skills in the skill tree are genuinely fun to unlock, giving you some wonderful horizontal character development rather than just dumb vertical number go up. Particularly the utility skills you can unlock are fun to play with (poison darts, fire bombs, etc).

Combat is also different from the earlier AC games, now playing much more like an action RPG. You got regular and heavy attacks, can parry enemy strikes, dodge out of the way - it almost feels inspired by Dark Souls style combat. Overall the combat is solid enough to be fun, but of course not quite at the level of a proper soulslike. I prefer the counter-based combat of the older games, but this is by no means bad. Except when you get into a boss fight. Those are terrible and feel completely out of place in an Assassin's Creed game.

Despite these issues, it's a very enjoyable game, particularly for the exploration. There's a lot of detail and many cool things to discover. A nice little bonus is the Discovery Tour, which gives you guided tours explaining the history of the places in the game. It's quite wonderful, and can be used as a genuine educational tool. I was a huge fan of ancient Egypt as a kid, and would have loved this. If you have kids and want to get them interested in history, this Discovery Tour mode is perfect for that.

If you don't mind the horrible "RPG system" bloat, I can thoroughly recommend this game. Plenty of content, gorgeous environments, fun stealth, decent combat, only marred by a flawed leveling system.

It trades the linear, parkour-heavy missions of previous entries for a sprawling, RPG-flavored experience set in ancient Egypt. The result is a game that sometimes struggles under its own ambition but manages to deliver a fresh and compelling take on a franchise that needed reinvention for better or worse.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
Origins completely revamps combat, ditching the old counter-heavy system for a more deliberate, RPG-style approach. Bayek now has access to a variety of weapons—swords, spears, bows—with distinct speed, damage, and stamina mechanics. Combat feels weightier and more tactical: timing blocks, dodges, and heavy attacks matters far more than in previous AC games. Boss fights and elite enemies are genuinely challenging, requiring strategy rather than button-mashing but a lot of the challenge also boils down to some enemies being huge bullet sponges.

RPG elements also play a huge role. Leveling up, upgrading gear, and choosing skill tree perks affects combat significantly. You can tailor Bayek to a stealth-focused build, a tanky brute, or a balanced fighter. The game isn’t perfect—some abilities are overpowered compared to others—but experimentation is encouraged and almost always rewarding.

Stealth feels more natural. Instead of being forced down corridors, you can climb, hide in tall grass, or use distractions. Guards are less predictable, but the AI isn’t great—you can still fool them easily. Encounters generally feel organic, though open-field battles can be inconsistent.

[b]Exploration[/b]
Exploration is one of Origins’ strongest suits. Ancient Egypt is massive, beautifully realized, and packed with secrets. From the Nile delta to the deserts and bustling cities, every location feels distinct and alive. The world encourages curiosity: tombs, hidden caves, and environmental storytelling reward players who take their time to look around.

The game also leans heavily into verticality. Rooftops and cliffs provide vantage points for scouting or stealth approaches, and climbing isn’t just for show—it’s integrated into exploration and puzzle-solving. The map is huge, but Origins makes it manageable with fast travel, synchronization points, and a clear sense of progression.

The scenery alone makes wandering worthwhile. Sunsets over the pyramids, wildlife in the deserts, and city markets feel alive, and the attention to detail can make simple traversal feel cinematic. There’s always something to discover, and the sense of scale makes the world feel epic without being overwhelming.

[b]Side Content[/b]
Side content in Origins is "okay". Optional quests and contracts usually have some story or context, which is nice, but a lot of them quickly fall into “go here, kill this, loot that” territory. Tombs and puzzles are the highlight—you actually have to think and explore to get rewards, and those moments feel earned. Random encounters can be fun, though they get repetitive after a while.

Elite targets stand out because they make you approach fights differently, but beyond that, most side content feels like filler padding the massive map rather than something genuinely memorable. The game gives you a lot to do, but don’t expect every side mission to be interesting—it’s hit or miss.

[b]Story[/b]
The game tells an intimate, personal story set against the sprawling backdrop of ancient Egypt. At its core, this is Bayek’s [spoiler]revenge[/spoiler] tale: he starts the game as the Medjay of Siwa, a protector of his people, but his life is shattered when [spoiler]his son Khemu is killed during an ambush orchestrated by the mysterious Order of the Ancients[/spoiler]. The game gradually expands from Bayek’s [spoiler]revenge[/spoiler] into the larger formation of the Assassin Brotherhood. Early on, Bayek is mostly reacting—tracking leads, interrogating enemies, and surviving ambushes—but as he uncovers the scope of the [spoiler]Order[/spoiler], his mission becomes about more than just [spoiler]personal vengeance[/spoiler]. The story does a good job showing how the Assassins emerge from chaos, rather than just starting as a pre-established organization.

[spoiler]The Order of the Ancients[/spoiler] itself is composed of individuals embedded across the political landscape of Egypt, from corrupt generals to scheming merchants.
