It’s not the giant spiders or falling off a cliff while placing a conveyor. It’s that little voice that says “just five more minutes.” Then the sun is coming up, your coffee is cold, and your factory hums like a cathedral of steel and motion.

This game nails the dopamine loop better than almost anything out there. Every time you fix one bottleneck, two more appear, but it never feels punishing. It’s addictive in the best way, full of small victories wrapped in the steady hum of machines and glowing lines of progress.

The gameplay loop is deceptively simple but endlessly deep. You start by mining iron and crafting parts by hand. Before long, you have automated the basics, then you are scaling up, building new tiers, unlocking trains and drones, and chasing efficiency that always feels just out of reach. Every upgrade feeds into a bigger idea, and every “temporary” setup somehow becomes permanent. It’s the kind of game that quietly trains you to think like an engineer, even if you never meant to.

One of the most satisfying parts is deciding how your factory will grow. Some players build tall, vertical complexes with layers upon layers of machines stacked into the sky. Others prefer wide, sprawling layouts that stretch across entire biomes, a maze of conveyors winding through forests and cliffs. There is no single right way to do it, which makes every player’s world feel personal, a reflection of their own version of order and chaos.

The visuals carry so much charm. Watching your factory come alive is a reward on its own. Conveyors glide like arteries, feeding into splitters and constructors that pulse with quiet precision. When everything works together, it’s oddly beautiful. And when it doesn’t, it’s still beautiful in its own way. A giant spaghetti mess of belts looping in every direction, machines somehow still running. Chaos that functions.

That said, there are a couple of things that can test your patience. The early game can feel slow, especially when you’re stuck handcrafting parts before automation kicks in. It’s satisfying once things get rolling, but that first stretch can feel like pushing a cart with square wheels. Later on, when your factory grows massive, performance and organization start to fight back. Belts pile up, power demands spike, and it can all become a bit of a balancing act that pulls you out of the calm rhythm the game builds so well.

That’s the magic of Satisfactory. It’s both a meditation and a madness. tl;dr: This is an incredibly good, fun game with an incredibly awful end game problem. Definitely buy it, definitely play it, definitely do not plan on finishing it.

Factorio is a classic in the genre of this type of game but it can be quite obtuse. And then once you're out of the obtuse stage, every moment of your Factorio life is trying to figure out what thing you're going to run out of next or not make enough of next. Things start out simply enough with a few short assembly lines making "iron line" components and "copper line" components that eventually merge into combined components. It's also a game where you're endlessly rebuilding and expanding, rebuilding and expanding your factory until it eventually it becomes a behemoth and you win the game. But before that happens, you are in endless calculation mode trying to balance out how much of this is needed to build that. And most people just eyeball it and are in an endless repetition of finding the bottlenecks in your production chains or finding more resources to pump into your production chains and fixing them over and over again.

At the end of the day, it couldn't be clearer that Satisfactory just started as 3D environment Factorio. And it opens quite a bit less obtuse than Factorio with the most solid tutorial I've seen in a game in a very long time. But soon enough, you're lowered gently to the dirt and are playing 3D Factorio. And the complications from that start instantly because there are endless variations to the (fixed map) terrain to challenge you, places to explore, places that are off-limits to you because of poison gas, too tough critters, or both. But quite soon, you have some constructors and assemblers going and the best robot assistant voice since GlaDOS is nudging you up the technology chain.

Two things spoil the fun, and they're related.

Because Satisfactory is both a 3D game where you have to look at things in front of you instead of from overhead, and because it's a 3D game that you have to move around in, constructing all those assemblers and conveyor belts is *much* more complicated and time-consuming than it appears at first glance. You have only limited opportunities to drag a conveyor belt from there to there and have it line up perfectly. Instead, you will be constantly, constantly trying to judge alignment and height and very often getting them wrong. The game gives you a few tools to help you (many have to be bought in a hysterical little "bonus store" that you unlock early in the proceedings) but mostly you start to build up experience at how to move things around. And finally, just before the late game, you get a hoverpack which is a freakin' godsend. On paper, it’s “just driving trucks,” but in practice it’s a surprisingly deep and rewarding experience that can easily soak up hours of your time without you even noticing.

The core gameplay loop is straightforward but highly satisfying: pick up cargo, plan your route, and haul it across beautifully recreated stretches of America. The maps are scaled down, but they’re crafted with such attention to detail that every drive feels unique. You’ll pass through small towns, open deserts, mountain passes, and busy cities, all with a strong sense of place. The developers clearly care about accuracy and atmosphere, and it shows.

Driving itself feels authentic without being punishing. The handling strikes a nice balance between realism and accessibility, so even players who aren’t hardcore sim fans can enjoy it. There’s something relaxing about settling into a long haul, keeping an eye on the road while listening to music, podcasts, or even the in-game radio stations. It’s the perfect “chill” game — the kind you can unwind with after a long day.

Where the game really shines is how it evolves over time. At first, you’re just a hired driver taking whatever jobs you can get. But as you earn money, you can buy and customize your own trucks, expand your garage, and eventually manage a full fleet with hired drivers working for you. This progression gives the game a strong sense of growth, turning what might seem like a casual experience into something deeper and more rewarding.

American Truck Simulator is also one of the best “time wasters” I’ve ever played — and I mean that in the most positive way. You can sit down for a quick 20–30 minute delivery or lose yourself in a multi-hour drive across multiple states. The pacing is entirely in your hands, and no matter how long you play, it always feels like time well spent.

On top of all that, the developers have been fantastic about supporting the game with regular updates and new DLC states. Each new addition expands the world and keeps the experience fresh, and it feels like the game just keeps getting better as the years go on.

review_texts:
[{"review_text": "fun game with great gunplay, but the maps/areas get really stale. the same maps in the same order again and again.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1736506812}, {"review_text": "I suppose it's about time I reviewed this game. Actually, it's been a while since I reviewed ANY game, but regardless.

Gunfire Reborn is if Risk of Rain and Borderlands made a baby, and then they took care for the baby to grow big and strong instead of leaving him in the ocean to drown.
It's a chinese game, which is frankly shocking, not just from the above-and-beyond quality, but the surprising lack of cancerous monetization. You buy the game, and then there's DLCs. That's it. No microtransactions, no lootboxes/gacha, no skins for sale, it's all just content upfront. And not just that, but consistently for years after release they put out free content updates that spiced up the game, and currently it's in the best state and I reckon it can only get better.

To put it in simple terms: Gunfire Reborn is a powerhouse simulator, in which you go with a build in mind and try and break the game with whatever you're given. Counting the DLCs, there's 12 characters, each with their own playstyle, and 3 ways to play: primary skill, secondary skill and weapons. With that said, nothing stops the creative mind to make up unorthodox builds. Example: Lei Luo(the snow leopard I believe) is the sniper character, with the upgrade tree basing around snipers and distance as well as crit. But there's a blessing that gives you a 50/50 chance to crit, which also applies to launchers, meaning nothing stops you to go ham with a mortar as you wreck havoc across the land. Paradoxically: there's a close quarters character (bird, idfk the chinese name). You are meant to play him as an "in your face" playstyle. But he also has a blessing that makes weapons hit twice, effectively doubling the damage. So giving him a sniper rifle to quickscope scrubs is a legit playstyle. And there's more examples like these, but you'll have to find them on your own.

Weapons are plentiful and inscriptions can be game changing. There are common and uncommon ones, that apply across most weapons, and then there's legendary ones that can change how a weapon functions. Some weapons have alternate firing modes, such as the mortar, with the normal shot being a cluster of non-self-damaging explosions at close range, while the right click instead launches projectiles, like how you'd expect a mortar to work. There's a legendary inscription that makes the right click fire the entire magazine. Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines is one of those rare gems—an immersive, darkly compelling RPG that takes you deep into a world of nightmarish intrigue, complex morality, and unforgettable characters. Released in 2004, it may have been ahead of its time, but it has since become a beloved classic, and for good reason. This is a game that not only captures the spirit of its source material but builds a world so rich, so nuanced, that it feels alive.

A World of Shadows and Secrets
From the moment you step into the shoes of a freshly turned vampire, Bloodlines introduces you to a world that is both beautifully sinister and intricately detailed. Set in modern-day Los Angeles, the game weaves a dark tale of political intrigue, personal conflict, and supernatural terror. The rich lore of the Vampire: The Masquerade tabletop RPG is brought to life in an almost seamless way, with each faction of vampires—whether it's the stoic Ventrue, the cunning Malkavians, or the fiery Brujah—adding layers of complexity to the story. This is a world where nothing is ever simple, and where every decision you make carries weight.

The setting itself, the urban sprawl of LA, is a masterwork of gothic atmosphere. The game’s locations—be it the seedy alleyways of Santa Monica or the terrifying depths of the haunted asylum—are meticulously crafted, with a level of detail that makes every corner feel like it holds a secret. You’re not just moving through a city; you’re navigating a sprawling, living ecosystem of power struggles and hidden threats.

Immersive Role-Playing Like No Other
What truly sets Bloodlines apart from other RPGs is its depth of character interaction and role-playing opportunities. The game is all about choice—and not just in how you approach combat or quests, but in how you choose to live your life as a vampire. Will you uphold the delicate balance of the Masquerade, hiding your true nature from humanity, or will you embrace your monstrous side and sow chaos? These choices aren’t just for show; they impact the way you’re treated by the various factions, your relationships with other characters, and even the game’s ending. There are no easy answers here, and that’s what makes it so compelling.

The character creation system is robust, allowing you to craft a vampire that fits your playstyle. You can invest in a variety of abilities, from brutal physical combat to stealthy persuasion and hacking skills. The power of your clan also plays a significant role in how you approach different challenges, and the supernatural abilities you gain as a vampire offer a variety of ways to approach problems. Whether you want to manipulate minds, become a fearsome force in combat, or sneak past enemies unnoticed, Bloodlines gives you the freedom to build your vampire exactly how you envision them.

A Story That Binds You
But it’s not just the gameplay that shines—it’s the narrative. Bloodlines offers a gripping, multi-layered story that is filled with moral ambiguity, unforgettable characters, and moments of genuine emotional weight. Whether you're trying to navigate the political machinations of the vampire factions or diving into a personal quest that challenges your own morals, the plot is constantly shifting and evolving. The main story is full of twists and turns, but it’s the side stories—the personal journeys of the NPCs—that really elevate the game. These characters are deeply written and full of life, each with their own motivations, quirks, and tragic backstories.

The voice acting is phenomenal, bringing every character to life with nuances and emotions that make them feel real. Whether you’re talking to a wise old vampire or a desperate fledgling, the dialogue is always engaging and never feels forced. review_texts:
[{"review_text": "Amazing how the people behind this game listen to the community!

I already enjoyed the game when it launched, even though it was obviously flawed in some regards. Over the last 2 years the game received numerous updates, and today I got recommended a video about update 2.0 launching, and it literally fixed EVERY SINGLE FLAW the game had. And even though I already own the game I really respect the game being on a 67% discount for 2 weeks right after the update drops, instead of making people pay the standard price of 60€ for it after upgrading its value this much.

I really hope this game will receive the love it deserves!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 14, "timestamp_created": 1744925479}, {"review_text": "After playing Demon's Souls, all the Dark Souls games, Elden Ring, Mortal Shell, Nioh (1 and 2), Lies of P, and even the goofy charm of Another Crab's Treasure, I finally got around to Lords of the Fallen 2.0 and I reaaaally loved it. I finished the game twice on my xbox series X with regular and adyr ending ng+, yet to finish it here. 

The combat is really polished. It feels a lot better than the original Lords of the Fallen which I also have finished on xbox, You’ve got a dedicated jump button now, which is honestly unnecessary but I think it's something some people asked and that's another point I liked, CI Games proved they listen us, and the many complaints people did at launch. The game also have some of that Elden Ring smoothness, but don’t expect the same level of freedom. And while the lock-on system is definitely improved, it’s still not as buttery as Dark Souls 3. Some weapons hit hard and feel super satisfying, kinda like Mortal Shell’s heavy crunch. I used radiance build in my first run and inferno build in my 2nd run, but I feel inferno is the most powerful one.

[b]This recommendation comes with some notable caveats though.[/b]

For the record:
- I am an avid Souls-like fan. 
- I haven't played this game prior to the 2.0 release. 
- I was playing in the much welcomed new co-op mode with my partner.
- I am aware that I'll be making the cardinal sin of comparing LotF to Elden Ring/Dark Souls, but I feel the points are justified nonetheless.

We started the game quite impressed with the visuals and sound design. I would have given the game a solid 7 out of 10 right there - which, in my books, is still a game definitely worth playing.

Though, there are some glaring issues that began to creep through the cracks the longer we played.

1. The biggest issue? The weapons. 

See, the multitude of various weapons you will find give an [i]illusion[/i] of variety, but in reality, each weapon of a type will attack the exact same way as any other weapon of that type.
Perhaps I have been spoiled by the massive variety presented in Elden Ring and Dark Souls, but it made finding new weapons extremely uninteresting as, apart from visual appeal and stat scaling, the move-sets are all [b]exactly[/b] the same.
Find a really cool looking short sword? Well, it will essentially operate the same as the one you're currently carrying. The only reason to change is whether the new one matches your stats/attributes more effectively.

I'll expound upon this point shortly, but it ties into point number two.

2. Gear (apart from armour)

Namely rings and pendants. There's very little in the way of variety here. 
Increase Holy defence. Increase Fire defence. Increase Poison Resistance. Increase Str. Increase Vit. Etc. You get the gist.
Essentially, all the basic-type talismans you'd find in Elden Ring are copy and pasted here. Except, none of the interesting ones that can change your build in fun ways.

Now, combining the aforementioned points, this is where I found my biggest source of frustration/boredom with LotF; there really isn't a lot of [b]true[/b] build variety.
Sure, you technically [i]could[/i] play as a pure Str mage, but it won't work out as you hope. It'll just be weak and sub-optimal.
The game almost expects you to use a very select few options of weapons/gear for your chosen attributes/stats. There's no effective way to change this (besides one niche end-game thing - for a single weapon - and not all types).

It was extremely disappointing, as I even had the benefit of having my partner able to drop me unique weapons so that I could dual wield them, but alas, there was really no point. Nothing was unique. No weapon operated any differently from it's genre-specific counterparts.
So, we settled on Great hammers. And whichever one matched our stats.

Note: There [b]are[/b] boss weapons that you get access to, from their remembrances (much like Elden Ring). And while they'll also have the exact same move-sets, [i]some[/i] of them have a ridiculously convoluted way of giving them a [i]slightly[/i] different attack. But I ask you, wouldn't it have just been better to have these moves operate differently from the outset? Otherwise, they simply aren't worth the time. We didn't even bother.
Which brings me to point number 3.

3. Boss rewards (especially from remembrances) 

...Pretty much useless, unless they had a specific spell you needed, or a specific armour set you thought looked cool. But mostly, you'll overlook the boss rewards as there isn't a lot worth taking.

4. Input reading

Some bosses and enemies have some of the most egregious input reading examples I have seen in a souls-like game.
I don't simply mean "They dodged two of my arrows", I mean "They are literally dodging, back-to-back, both my partner and I spamming ranged attacks."
It was literally that bad at times.

5. Over-use of branching paths

I appreciate, and quite enjoy the thoughtful and creative use of branching paths that create an intertwined world. Dark Souls 1 did this very well.
But LotF has an absolute metric f**k tonne of moments where you are given a choice of 'Left or right'. Then, when taking a path, there's another 'left or right' and so on.
Now, I can't quite articulate why, but it wasn't creating a sense of fun exploration for us. It was creating no small amount of tedium. Perhaps because we knew that any reward we found would be lacklustre anyway?
Either way, at around 80% completion of the game, we eventually just decided to ignore most branching paths just to streamline game-play.
And as a minor ancillary point to this, the game gives very poor direction as to what you're expected to do to proceed the story. NPC quests are constantly expecting you to randomly backtrack to random (and unintuitive) places, to proceed their arc. This aspect simply wasn't planned very well.

6. Exploration (for loot) is disincentivised.

Once you have your build organised, which can be sorted out quite early on once you realise weapons are all functionally identical, there really is no reason to explore for cool items and weapons. You simply wont find some cool sword that makes your character do amazing things.
And the best spells are easily purchased. You're better off just sticking to the path that gets you through the story.

7. Bugs and Glitches

Throughout our playtime, we probably had to restart the game around 4 times due to glitching through the floor and being stuck. It wasn't a huge inconvenience, but it was still frustrating when it happened.

Now, all that being said, LotF does do some things well. Credit where it's due.

- The story isn't bad. It's not [i]outstanding[/i] but it's serviceable.

- LotF is also one of the very few souls-like games that does ranged combat well. In fact, it makes it a viable option as a main strategy (if you build it right, and manage to have a backup for the worst input-reading offenders). The ranged system works similarly to the way magic works - but they simply substitute mana for ammunition, and mana stones for ammunition pouches. It's simple, but effective.

- The 'Shadow realm' gimmick is interesting. It can be annoying at times, sure, but it's an interesting approach.

- Co-op works very well.

- As mentioned above, the visuals are genuinely very nice.


Overall, by the end of our play-through, we became quite tired of a game that began to feel like a chore. So much so that we ended up putting the game aside, indefinitely - not even wanting to finish. And I found myself thinking "I think I'd much rather just play Elden Ring with a co-op mod. It'll feel more fulfilling."
And that just sucks, because I had some high hopes for LotF at the start.

After a few action-heavy missteps, Capcom takes a bold pivot back to its horror roots—and it’s nothing short of brilliant.

Trading in global bioterrorism for claustrophobic dread, the game places you in the shoes of Ethan Winters, an everyman searching for his missing wife. His journey leads him to the decaying estate of the Baker family, deep in the Louisiana bayou, where something has gone horribly, unnaturally wrong. From the first creaking door to the final grotesque showdown, RE7 immerses you in an atmosphere dripping with menace.

The biggest change is the shift to first-person perspective. It's a gamble that pays off. Every hallway becomes a tunnel of anxiety, every sound a potential threat. The intimacy of the view heightens the horror—when Jack Baker bursts through a wall with a shovel, you don’t just see it. You feel it.

What sets Biohazard apart is its pacing. It knows when to dial up the terror and when to give you a moment to breathe. The puzzles are satisfyingly old-school, and the resource management is classic survival horror—limited ammo, tight inventory, and tense decision-making.

The Bakers themselves are unforgettable antagonists: grotesque, charismatic, and terrifying. They’re not just monsters; they’re characters. Each member of the family offers a distinct brand of horror—from Jack’s relentless pursuit to Marguerite’s insect-infested madness.

Graphically, the game is stunning in a disgusting sort of way. The RE Engine delivers uncanny realism, from mold-caked walls to glistening entrails. Sound design, too, deserves praise—groans, whispers, and footsteps constantly gnaw at your nerves.

If there’s a drawback, it’s in the final act, where the narrative takes a more conventional turn, slightly pulling you out of the suffocating tension that defined the earlier hours. Still, it's a minor blemish on an otherwise masterful experience.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumphant resurrection of the series’ core identity. It’s brutal, unnerving, and deeply atmospheric—everything survival horror fans crave. Not just a great Resident Evil game, but one of the best horror titles of the last decade.

I’ll admit up front: I’m not a Souls-like veteran. I usually steer clear of games that punish your mistakes with brutal consequences. So I went into Sifu expecting frustration, maybe even regret. What I got instead was a challenging, elegant brawler that not only won me over, but pulled me in deep enough to play it again—this time, for the true ending.

The aging mechanic, where each death adds years to your life, is brilliant and the first game I played with this mechanic. It reinforces the central theme of revenge, discipline, and acceptance without ever needing to spell it out. Every time I got knocked down, I genuinely felt the cost—and every time I stood up and improved, it felt earned. Though admittedly, this mechanic can be cheesed, because the enemy health and toughness bar doesn't reset when you get up so it's basically having multiple lives and can be used as a brute forcing mechanic.

Combat is the star here, and it’s incredibly fluid. Learning enemy patterns and knowing when to commit or retreat is essential, and while it’s unforgiving at first, the game never feels unfair. If you mess up, it’s on you—and the game teaches you that lesson the hard way, but never without purpose.

The level design deserves praise too. Each stage is stylish, thematic, and distinct—from grimy clubs to surreal final showdowns, the environments not only look good but also subtly teach you how to play better. There’s a rhythm to each encounter, and once you’re in tune with it, fights start feeling like choreographed duels rather than frantic button mashing.

Coming from someone not used to this kind of difficulty curve, I’ll say: the early hours can be punishing. Bosses in particular can feel like brick walls if you haven’t internalized the game’s mechanics. But that’s the thing—Sifu doesn’t just expect you to get better; it makes you want to. I found myself restarting levels just to try new approaches, optimize routes, or walk away younger.

And then came the twist: there’s more to the story. That true ending teased a deeper message and gave me a reason to go back. My second run was less about revenge and more about understanding. That’s when Sifu really clicked. It’s not just about mastering your enemies—it’s about mastering yourself.



[h3]Final Verdict:[/h3]
Sifu is a striking, satisfying action game that rewards patience, precision, and persistence. Even if you're not into Souls-like games or tough-as-nails combat, there's something deeply rewarding here—especially if you’re willing to push through those first few humbling defeats. It's one of those rare games where every setback feels like a step forward. I didn’t expect to love it—but now, I can’t recommend it enough.

Sifu is in fact so close to Sekiro that the game essentially lifts two of its fundamental mechanic from it, those being the parry system and the posture gauge. If you're not familiar, parrying attacks (tapping the block button at the last moment before impact) will fill your enemy's posture gauge. Once it's full, you will be able to start a finishing blow animation that will immediately kill your opponent, regardless of how much HP they have left. The major departure from Sekiro's gameplay are in the way Sifu adopts the perilous attacks system, and the ability to fight with bare hands or different weapons found in the levels. By holding the block button and moving the analog stick in any direction, the player can avoid an attack by moving away from it rather than block or parry it. If the perilous attack is a low, you will need to avoid up, if it's a high you will have to avoid low, and so on. However, the player can still opt to parry or block perilous attacks, unlike in Sekiro, where they will go through your defenses and must be avoided. The tradeoff is that if the player fails to parry at the right time or simply blocks the perilous attack, they will take a large amount of damage--whether HP or posture.
The idea behind the avoid mechanic seems to be twofold: to introduce further depth to the gameplay, and to allow the player to recover some of their posture during long fights, since avoiding an attack (perilous or not) will remove some of the damage from your gauge. That opening village encounter hit like a freight train. I became obsessed. Every corner I turned, every building I entered, every enemy I encountered added to the story I was building in my mind and in my heart. I was not just watching Leon Kennedy. The action is fast paced and requires a lot of finesse. To start off, a constant in every game is the utterly phenomenal soundtrack by Yoko Shimomura. Her works are probably the most iconic part of the series and are easily the greatest feature of them. Even in the most seemingly mundane part of any given game, the music accompanying it elevates it beyond the sum of its parts and makes it far more memorable than it really has any right to be. This series is one of the catalysts for my love of video game soundtracks and, despite any complaints I may have with any game listed in this review, the music will always be a positive, with almost no exceptions.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Final Mix[/b] is one of the two most popular installments, with those two probably being the only ones most will play out of this collection. KH1 is a classic for a lot of people, and on replay all these years later, still holds up decently well. This is the simplest and most grounded story in the series, and holds up as a standalone. The stakes are well-defined and Sora's goals are clear-cut. In terms of exploration, KH1 is an outlier compared to practically the entire series in that there is no minimap system, and worlds have layouts that aren't entirely linear. Paired with the game rarely ever giving you explicit directions on where to go, it can be confusing on where to go during a first playthrough. For some, this is a positive, and others, a negative. Exploration and intrigue is a key part of KH1's design philosophy, so unless you look up walkthroughs, there's really no getting around this point. Many areas have tiny little secrets that could take several playthroughs to find, some of which I first found even on my most recent run. It's a gameplay experience you won't find in any future installments, so it's a unique aspect that this title alone holds. As for combat, it's apparent that the action RPG system was still finding its footing, but it's still solid enough to not be a total detriment. Attacks have weight to them and Sora is extremely grounded, leading to aerial fights feeling disadvantageous. Enemies themselves are generally simple, having a couple attacks and maybe some resistances and weaknesses, but elite enemies found in the late game can provide a challenge, especially in groups (which they will be in, often). Bosses on the other hand are where the bulk of the game's difficulty will come from, with a few notorious fights feeling almost out of place with the movement options you have. Overall, KH1 has its issues, and can be frustrating at times, but is an enjoyable experience at the end. I wouldn't say this is my favorite installment, but it is by far the most unique, and to this day, no other installment has captured the feeling this one has.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Re:Chain of Memories[/b] is a PS2 remake of a GBA game, remastered for modern systems. Re:CoM is the first game to deviate from the core aRPG gameplay (and won't be the last), delving into a card-based battle system. Combat is similar to KH1, but with every action tied to cards with numerical values, that must be higher than your opponents in order to connect, or else they will be deflected and leave you open to attack. This system is one of the most contested in the series, with the on-the-fly strategy required sometimes feeling unfair, especially in the late game. At the same time, the system is also easily exploited, with certain combos of cards trivializing most fights. The world system itself has also turned into cards, with each world being a re-hash of KH1 worlds. These worlds are made up of preset generic rooms you create with even more cards, and their stories round up to being quick one-note summaries of the originals. The main focus of the story is Sora and Riku, dealing with the internal conflicts within their memories, while also dealing with the external conflicts of what will be the main antagonists of the next game. Re:CoM was made to be a bridge between KH1 and KH2, and story-wise fills that role very well, with it being the highlight of the experience. Otherwise, the game is fairly average, with a passable gameplay concept, but a repetitive loop.

[b]Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix[/b] is contending with KH1 for most popular game and is a return to form. If you were to ask any single fan of the series which game was their favorite, if they didn't say KH1, they would probably say KH2. KH2's story picks up where KH Re:CoM left off, and introduces more elements to the story to set up the worldbuilding needed for later installments, namely Nobodies and the ever-looming Organization XIII. The story focuses more on these original concepts compared to KH1, and has a few outstanding highlights, but is generally on the lesser side compared to the previous 2 games. KH2 is radically different from 1 in a few ways, mainly straying away from exploration to focus more on combat. Worlds in KH2 are generally much more linear, with very little deviance in the main path. Treasures and collectibles are usually not too far from where you'll naturally go, and what you can't reach on your first visit is usually just obtained with movement options you unlock later in the game. This world design makes for clearer objectives, but erases any amount of discovery the game could have. What KH2 makes up for this is in its combat, which is the main highlight of this game. Combat in KH2 is fast, fluid, and flashy, and the addition of Reaction Commands and Drive Forms make for spectacles of fights from beginning to end. Enemies themselves are also much more dynamic, with many having attacks that can now combo and cover much more ground. Bosses are more well-rounded compared to KH1, and the endgame lets you test your mastery of the mechanics, though with a few exploits. KH2 is a game with a handful of glaring flaws, but I still admit I have a soft spot for it.

[b]Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep Final Mix[/b] was originally a PSP game with a multiplayer aspect. The game was remastered and the multiplayer shaved off to be a singleplayer experience. This game acts as a prequel to all previous games and lays the groundwork for Integrum Masterpiece's main antagonist, as well as worldbuilding for the universe and the rules of the Keyblade. The game is split into 3 parts, with you controlling 3 different characters and experiencing their perspective of the story. This leads to each character's individual personality feeling a bit flat, but the overarching narrative makes up for it by the end. Worlds are smaller and more tightly packed, but are divided up for each character's visit, meaning you can't see the entirety of most worlds from just one character's POV. Combat is mix of the numbered games' action and Re:CoM's deckbuilding, and strikes a mix that on revisit is much better than what I first saw it as. It provides a good amount of strategy while still allowing leeway for simple action. The deck system can still be abused greatly to decimate most of the game, but the amount of commands available still allow for freedom in your gameplay style. The difficulty in this game is a steep increase, with some bosses feeling almost unfair in their attacks (and a certain boss [i]actually[/i] being unfair). while enemies are just basic. BBS is divisive in almost every aspect, but I came to enjoy it more than before.

And to footnote the last two for completion because I'm running out of space, [b]358/2 Days and Re:Coded[/b] are just remastered collections of cutscenes with no gameplay. Days is the more enjoyable one by far with more overall plot importance. [b][u]Kingdom Hearts[/u][/b]

Kingdom Hearts follows the story of Sora as he embarks on a grand adventure with Donald and Goofy throughout various Disney worlds. While KH 1 is the most nostalgic, it aged the poorest due to stiff gameplay and an abysmal camera that has a spasm every time Sora faces a different target because of how close it is to him (change the camera from auto to manual). That being said, this game is a lot of fun with a great story, amazing world-building and exciting boss fights. It also has better partner AI customization (setting the frequency of regular & special attacks, support abilities and when to use items) and makes your partners much more useful than the succeeding titles (Donald especially as the magic system in KH 1 complements him more). The Gummi Ship system also didn’t age well as it isn’t very intuitive and is poorly explained in-game. While customizing the ship isn’t necessary, having a stronger ship at later stages helps as playing through the shooting segments in-between worlds is mandatory until late in the game when fast travel becomes available.

Re: CoM uses a card combat system that gets mixed reception. [b][u]Kingdom Hearts 2[/u][/b]

Everything about Kingdom Hearts 2 from the story featuring loveable characters, world-building, music, smooth gameplay (including a fully revamped Gummi Ship system), exciting boss fights and all the content it provides are the pinnacle of the entire franchise. [b]Nerfed Partner AI Customization[/b] – Partner AI customization is limited to the frequency of special attacks making partners less useful than they were in KH 1 (especially Donald as the magic system doesn’t complement him at all).

Taking place 10 years before KH 1, Birth by Sleep follows the stories of Terra, Aqua and Ventus as they go through their own journeys. The critiques I have of BBS are:

[b]Repetitive Nature[/b] – Because there are 3 stories, this means visiting the same worlds 3 times with minor changes made to them which in combination with tedious grinding, wears out the game’s welcome. 

[b]Command Melding & Grinding[/b] – Command melding, while not bad, is tedious without a guide to look up how to craft commands and abilities. I found that grinding commands and abilities as early as the second world helped as a lot of the commands necessary for melding are available by that point. This served as a fast way to max out abilities early on (unlocked when a crystal is melded with 2 maxed out commands and becomes permanent when the melded command is maxed out). There are also fast ways to grind levels:
 
Terra – Equip EXP Chance (remove EXP Walker), 2 Mega Flares and 1 Victory Pose, lower your health to 25% (flashing red), go into Skull Rock on Neverland and cast both Mega Flares while standing in place followed by Victory Pose. Ventus & Aqua – Equip EXP Chance (remove EXP Walker & Treasure Magnet), 2 Thundagas & Victory Poses (Thundaga followed by Victory Pose) and a keyblade with good magic. Lower your health to 25% (flashing red) and go to the Jungle Clearing in Neverland. While not the strongest entry in the series, BBS is still a fun experience and I give it a 7.5/10.

[b][u]Conclusion & Recommendation[/u][/b]

Everything about Kingdom Hearts from the story, loveable characters, world-building, beautiful music and fun gameplay make this a truly magical adventure worth owning. After everything, I give this collection a 7.5/10.

KH1 still holds up exceptionally well today and is definitely the most "deep" game of the series (it has by far the most tiny hidden details for exceptionally savvy players as evidenced by videos still being made about things no one noticed). The combat can feel just a little bit slow compared to the rest of the series and the camera is just a little too zoomed in but it's really not enough to significantly detract from the experience. The special enemies you  have to kill over and over for item synthesis are a real pain though definitely my least favorite part. The story is a great intro to the universe as a whole too, telling you just enough whilst still keeping the most juicy details secret for later. Definitely a first game, but that's not really a bad thing it was just what it needed to be.

Re:Com is probably my least favorite, the combat just doesn't really work on a base level and feels quite unsatisfying. It somehow manages to be too simple and needlessly complicated at the same time. Higher number wins except in the case of 0. Cards recharge except premium cards and first card used in sleights (combo moves). It seems interesting in concept but seeing it in execution I'm really not sure there's a way they could have made it particulary fun while not making any major changes. There was only one fight in the entire game that actually felt balanced and it was the very last one with Riku, everything else was either too hard or too easy usually leaning towards the latter. Having the cards you get be heavily RNG based is quite annoying as well, especially with the enemy cards since you need to kill the enemy with the cards you want last and even then it's only a chance whether you get it. Riku at least was a bit better since you just get the cards set for the world and don't need to do any grinding but again the combat is just not that fun. Didn't really like the minigames for this one in particular as well.

KH2 is the best in the series for sure. The combat is surprisingly deep (seriously people beating data fights in seconds with super advanced tech is crazy to watch), and the fights themselves are almost exclusively fantastic (reaction commands really made each encounter feel unique and added some great cinematic moments that made you feel like a badass). The story was definitely the most satisfying ending we've gotten in the series, I'm still glad they kept it going but if it ended here it would've been just fine. Organization XIII are definitely my favorite villains, and Roxas my favorite character. Riding around Twilight Town in the prologue on a skateboard really just hits different. The only complaint I can think of is the worlds are a bit flat and linear particularly when compared to other entries, but that's a very minor complaint overall. Grinding drive form levels also isn't great but the whole series has grinding and this is one of the less egregious examples. Gummi Ship is an absolute pain going for 100% too but at least the mandatory stuff is fun.

I'm really not a fan of BBS. I find it to be kinda clunky and stiff (seriously I can't be the only one who feels like there's a noticeable amount of landing lag after a jump), and this combined with making bosses stagger completely at random during fights as well as having some of the worst boss design in the series just makes them an absolute pain. Needing to level up your commands constantly for melding or else grind the arena to level instantly makes it worse. Still not a terrible game but in a series as good as it is falls pretty flat in my eyes.

358/2 Days isn't playable in this compilation, but if you still happen to have a DS or 3DS lying around somewhere I'd give it a go. [{"review_text": "Mahjong soul and Riichi city are the 2 most popular riichi mahjong platforms for westerners, and you'll find a good amount of skilled players on both. So what sets them apart?

Riichi city wins:
- Client & optimisation: First of all, Mahjong soul does not have a native MacOS client. Second, the browser and Windows clients are buggy and poorly optimised. I have experienced missing (or slowly loading) textures, low fps, stuck loading screens (causing me to lose east 1 rounds sometimes) and more. I've had no issues with Riichi city. Both platforms have good mobile apps though.
- Eye/ear candy: Riichi city has better animations, emotes, voice lines and voiced yaku (in Mahjong soul you need character bond for this), and in general is more pleasing to the eyes and ears. Mahjong soul has a more dated, old school look that is more functional (some may prefer this though.)
- Honour system: Riichi city has an honour system so I have seen slightly less ragequitting on there.
- Gacha & events: The gacha at Riichi city is way more friendly to free to play players. They often run events that actually yield a lot of free items for active players, and often include new limited characters. At Mahjong soul, getting characters without spending any money is much much more difficult. If you do spend money, you'll also get more for your money on Riichi city.
- Beginner friendly: Riichi city has a much better tutorial as well as tutor mode where you can solve quizzes and such, and a more in depth wiki/faq. In general, I think beginners will have an easier time on Riichi city.

Mahjong soul wins: 
- Analysis tools: Mahjong soul has a nicer ranking system for its AI analysis (I prefer the E to S+ ranking rather than Riichi city's weird star system), and it instantly performs analysis for all players rather than just one. More importantly though, it lets you see the expected value of decisions more clearly. In Riichi city you'll see the discards ranked in a list best to worst but you can't tell e.g. how much better is the discard in 1st vs the one in 2nd. This is a big issue as there are many cases where discard 1 is much much better than 2, but there are also many cases where it is roughly equal. This essentially makes Riichi city analysis unusable and you will have to use an external site like ekyu to analyse.
- Larger userbase: Mahjong soul is undeniably the more popular platform and most  mahjong players I've met in real life play on Mahjong soul rather than Riichi city. If you have friends that already play on Mahjong soul, it may be easier to play on there rather than convincing them to switch platforms. However, I think this not so much an intrinsic benefit of the platform itself.

Things each site does differently (and it's up to preference):
- Skimpy outfits: Riichi city has way more skimpy outfits and animations. There is a family mode setting that sets all character outfits to default and reduces this, but it may still be off-putting for some users. Personally, I actually find the outfits and animations to be well made, and a nice addition (Mahjong soul does not really even have win animations, so wins are less exciting.)
- Scoring system: At Mahjong soul you will lose a massive amount of rating for a 4th place finish, roughly break even with a 3rd place finish, and gain rating for 2nd and 1st (+ game point totals also matter a bit for rating.) On the other hand, Riichi city will punish you for a 3rd place finish but it won't hurt you anywhere near as badly on a 4th (+ game point totals do not matter, only final position). This leads to different play styles on both platforms (You can get away with playing less defensively on Riichi city) and which you prefer is up to preference.
- Tsumogiri discards: Mahjong soul is more realistic to a real game of mahjong in which it does not visually mark what tiles are tsumogiri and what tiles aren't, you have to pay a lot of attention to the animations to notice and remember. Riichi city simply marks all of them which I find is a nice QOL feature but some may find too unrealistic.

My personal conclusion is that Riichi city wins in many areas and is generally a nicer platform to play on. Oh and btw, please ignore most reviews whining about rigged chances, they're either Mahjong Soul shills or just can't accept they got a shit match.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1740700385}, {"review_text": "I grew up surrounded by Chinese women playing mahjong for up 10 hours every weekend for big money, so the rules I first learned were Hong Kong rules and I had absolutely no idea any other ruleset existed. Years later, I learned the Japanese riichi variant just enough to play lewd mahjong games on Mame. Decades from watching my mom and her friends throw chips around like it was encoded in their DNA, this game and its rival [i]Mahjong Soul[/i] has allowed me to really learn riichi in earnest because getting your ass handed to you by an actual player is very humbling compared to when the cartoon girl would cheat to get another quarter out of you.

Riichi - in comparison to HK rules - is batshit insane in terms of restrictions, but I think it stems from a need to play with 'points' instead of gambling for real, and it is honestly far more rewarding to navigate. It's almost like the difference between a relatively simple card game like [i]Asshole[/i] and a more complex one like [i]Bridge[/i], though I will admit that I will never... ever... understand [i]Bridge[/i]. In other words, learning riichi can be difficult, but it is the popular form of the game in the video game world because the games that feature it are developed in Japan, so it is worth learning for fun and also in case you run into it in the wild like in the Yakuza series.

That said, the obvious elephant in the room is the gacha element, which is also a feature of [i]Mahjong Soul[/i]. It is 100% meaningless. Though the artwork is actually very good, it absolutely doesn't do anything other than customize your experience like the character at the table, the designs of the tiles, the tabletop picture, etc. There is zero impact on the game itself and therefore you may be tempted to spend money only because you dig the aesthetics; there's no powers or anything that will give you an advantage.

This game and [i]Mahjong Soul[/i] are very similar in terms of presentation, so which one you choose to play is going to depend on only a few small things (or just play both). First, both are pretty beginner friendly with great resources, but I still think you're going to benefit from looking at an external source like the riichi wiki. [i]Riichi City[/i] is especially good to beginners as while its actual teaching is lacking, the methods by which it drills you in the "academy" really help you to nail down the rules; I found the scoring quizzes especially helpful, but only because I also did some reading-up outside of the game. In any case, the big thing to note about this game is that it enforces learning the game's romaji. In other words, for English speakers, it sticks to romanized Japanese terminology whereas [i]MS[/i] tends to favor the English equivalents. For example, you'll only ever hear and read 'honitsu' in this game, but the other one will say 'half flush'. If you are primarily focused on finding opponents, then [i]Soul[/i] most definitely has a higher player count at any given time and seems to be the more popular game. Finally, the aesthetics and presentation you prefer - this game is a bit more racy with its artwork and it is a big component of the game's UX. Conversely, I find [i]Mahjong Soul[/i] more muted and less about the lewdness and more about the cuteness, if you will. I primarily play this game only because there's a cheapo monthly pass that gives you an allowance of premium currency every day for 30 days and I figured with the hours I play, why not enjoy some of the fluff? Note that I cross-play this with the mobile version so my hour count is much higher than what's here.

In any case, if your goal is straight up just learning the game and/or playing it against other people, either game will suit your needs if you consider some of the things above. I like learning the romaji, even though it's really hard for my old brain to memorize it all (the quizzes help) and some of the social aspects of the game are more appealing to me, but I still flip over to the other game every once in a while. Despite [i]Soul[/i] being the obviously more-played game, I dig a lot of the fluff in [i]Riichi City[/i] more. The pallette is colorful and the gacha is more of a fun side thing than something you need to participate in. You can rank up and play to your heart's content without spending a single dime. I think the art is far better despite its propensity to be racy, but I honestly appreciate it for the skill level displayed - some of these are just great pieces even without the context. And the game itself is very generous. It pretty much just shits the lowest currency at you any chance it gets and like I said, there's a very cheap option to get into some of the premium currency stuff (there are several more currencies that outrank what you get here, mind you).

I love this game for 5 main reasons:

[olist]
    [*]Simple gameplay with high stakes, as your character moves through the levels automatically and you only need to control when it jumps, but if it hits just one obstacle, it dies and you have to restart the level from the very beginning! This creates a frustrating yet addictive experience, and it makes you want to try and try again, because you know where you messed up, and since the gameplay is so basic, you know what to do next time to get a little further into the level! Besides that, the game has a lot of level objects, from orbs that make you jump in the air when you click them, portals that change character's gravity and speed, to different character gamemodes, which change their jump to flight, switching gravity, teleporting and so on, and it all makes the gameplay fresh in every level so you won't get bored.
    [*]Strong sense of progression, because in a hard game such as this, you will clearly see your growth in skill, not in basic statistic, but in the levels you completed. At first, you are going to complete the easiest of levels, but eventually you'll move onto harder and harder ones. You will notice then how much confidence you have to complete the levels you previously feared. This brings a truly satisfying feeling, more than simply completing a game - you become skilled and confident enough to take on harder challenges. This sense of progression is further supported by showing you the amount of stars and demons, the hardest levels of the game, on your account. Additionaly, many icons for your character can only be unlocked by completing harder challenges, and by seeing how many icons you unlocked, you can see how far you've come in this simple game about jumping over spikes. 
    [*]Amazing level editor, which is THE selling point of Geometry Dash! This is the thing that gives truly limitless potential for the game, as I believe this is one of the best level editors in the game industry. Any object can be moved to any part of the grid, any object can be rotated to any degree you'd like, and any object can even be scaled by X and Y axis. This gives you a lot of potential for decoration in your levels! Besides that, level editor lets you place triggers, which manipulate the level in different ways. They can do something simple, like move objects or change their colors, and can do something drastic, like check collision or remember certain data. Triggers are what allow determined creators to change the level from a simple autoscroller to different game genres! And just when you think it can't get any better, the editor allows to use a vast majority of songs to be played in the level, like music from popular creative website Newgrounds.com, music from popular electronic music label NoCopyrightSounds, and a large music library from songs of various music composers! There are certain limits to this level editor, but as the creators push the limits of the game, the editor expands every update, bringing new features to create unbelievable levels!
    [*]Passionate community, because a good level editor isn't the only ingredient for a timeless game. Without the passionate community, that learned how to push the game and it's level editor to the limits, GD wouldn’t have come so far! This community is truly amazing, continuously supporting the game by creating artistic masterpieces, that sync with the song perfectly, that have beautiful decorations, and that have fun gameplay. Yeah, not all levels are this perfect, and you will find yourself disagreeing with many players, but this doesn't take away from the fact that this community loves the game very much to still keep it alive. Not only the creator side of the community is awesome, a big part of the playerbase are challenging themselves to the hardest levels in the game, which keeps raising the bar of difficulty of this already hard game!  
    [*]Passionate creator, Robert Topala, who has been working on this game all by himself since 2013, clearly showing how much he loves his game and its community. Though there's a lot I love about this game, it has some serious problems that really need fixing. 

First of all, lets get to the good. By far the best thing about this game is the level editor. The level is editor despite seeming very daunting, is actually pretty easy to learn. Despite being somewhat easily accessible, it provides for near limitless possibility. You can make pretty much anything in the level editor, from motion graphics to animations to entire full length adventure games. Due this limitlessness, there is a near infinite amount of community content that you can play, and if you play levels that are rated personally by the creator of the game, you get stars and such. There's also Gauntlets which although aren't always the greatest, can contain very good levels of varying difficulties that usually share a common theme. The gauntlets peak at hard demon, so they aren't always the most accessible to new players but there are a lot of easy gauntlets that contain really well made levels. Map packs are similar although most of the map packs are complete garbage due to the fact that they are very old. However aside from all that, my favourite thing about this game is the game play. This game is extremely satisfying to practice and complete, especially for levels around easy to medium demon difficulty once you get good enough for that. Attempting to Sightread levels when your able to is also very fun. However the best thing in this game is when your attempting a new hardest level. The best moments I've had in any game ever is when I've practised an extreme demon for over 40 hours and I finally beat it, showing that all that practice didn't go to waste. It is by far the most euphoric, most exhilarating feeling I've ever felt when playing a game, and nothing even comes close. Now that doesn't mean I'd recommend other people to go through the same thing as some of the most miserable moments I've had playing any game also come from this game, because once again, practising a level for over 40 hours and still not being very consistent can be discouraging to say the least. However pushing the limits of what you can handle is apart of the fun, and when you finally end up beating that level, nothing is more satisfying. This game pretty much embodies delayed gratification, and it helps you improve your planning and persistence for not just games, but anything in life. 

Now onto the bad, which I have a lot to say. If you haven't played this game or are new to it and trying to get into it, Geometry Dash hinges on one key mechanic that is pretty much required when you get into the harder levels: Practice Mode. I find that a lot of new players are easily frustrated and quit fairly quickly when trying to beat the main levels. The reason for this is usually very predictable, and that's because they refuse to use practice mode. And I don't blame them, practice mode in its default state is extremely boring, and that's largely because the practice music is very monotonous and boring to listen to, and the only way to change it so it actually matches the level your playing without mods is to unlock it with 2000 diamonds, which requires a fair bit playing already. By the time you've gotten 2k diamonds you've probably already beaten the main levels, which means you've probably already gotten used to the boring monotony that is the default practice music. It makes no sense that Practice music sync is locked behind getting collectables that take quite a bit of playtime to grind out, especially because practice mode is infinitely more enjoyable with it. The average player is not gonna try and install mods to unlock it like that either, so its either sit through the boring monotony of practice mode or grind the game until your used to it. This leads me to my second point is that the game is infinitely more enjoyable with QOL mods. It makes no sense why these mods aren't already in the game considering they are very simple to add in and have been around for forever. Lets take a mod called "Level thumbnails" for example. In Vanilla Geometry Dash when your scrolling through custom levels, all you see is the name, the length, and the song. That's it. Pretty much no information about the level itself. You have to go into the level yourself to see if it's worth playing. Level thumbnails shows a snapshot of the level beside the level name, making it way easier to select or filter things you wanna play, based on decoration for example. Why isn't this in the game? A few other examples include being able to remove the death effect or showing hitboxes on death, these are small things that vastly improved the quality of the game, it makes no sense how robtop worked nonstop for 7 years on the game and still has yet to implement these basic features while instead adding useless physics changes that make a bunch of old levels impossible. Now there are mods that send levels to robtop, but a lot of the time it can take him months to get to these levels. And how does one become a mod? Well simple, you just have to have robtop make you mod based on how he feels about you. On top of  all that, demons have an entirely different system where instead of individual mods sending them to robtop they vote on it. Why? Don't ask me. Obviously, this system is absolutely terrible and makes getting your level rated an absolute nightmare. Even worse, there's a ton of corruption and favouritism behind this system. If your friends with a mod, you can your level rated easily. And if you're not? Tough luck. Not only this, but due to the fact that levels are rated based on robtop's whims, rated levels can vary drastically in quality. For example, there's a level in the NCS gauntlets called "WANNACRY". Say what you want about the quality of these levels, they are not meant to be good, they are meant to be hard and they bring the most eyes to the game. The most notorious example of this is of a level called Crimson Planet, which despite being the hardest level in the game when it was verified, wasn't rated for an entire year. I'm sorry but that's just unacceptable, but unfortunately the community has become accustomed to it instead of demanding a new rating system. The game is riddled with these problems, that can be easily fixed, but unfortunately Rob doesn't care what anyone says.

Anyway that was a lot of complaining, but I'd be foolish to not recommend this game after spending so much time playing it. But these issues are seriously plaguing the game and they need to be fixed.

[{"review_text": "okay game but too many dlcs
alot of the dlcs should just be added as updates instead", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1756455563}, {"review_text": "Assuming you have no DLC packs, the game starts out slow. You begin as a level 1 hunter with a measly .243 rifle, only the best placed shots can take down medium sized game. You might spend a lot of time wrapping your head around the game mechanics as well as track a bunch of wounded animals at first, but soon you will start making some money and filling out your perk trees. I was left with a bad impression of the progression system at first but the strength you feel during the mid and late game definitely pays off. 

At the writing of this review, I have 170 hours of play time. I only have 1 / 19 maps completely explored. I chose to do the Layton Lake District map first (soon I will explain why I regret this decision)  and I have that map 100% explored and about 90% of the missions completed, so there is still more work to nickel and dime there as well. I hope this gives an accurate representation of just how much playtime you can get out of one map. I am currently working on exploring the Hirschfelden map and I have it ~60% completed with many missions left to go. At this rate, each of the 19 maps is offering me around 100-150 hours of gameplay, and even if I complete every mission there is nothing stopping me from continuing to hunt on the map.

I want to use this last bit here to share a few tips to anyone going into the game fresh. Earlier I stated I played the Layton Lake District map first. In hindsight, I would have much rather done Hirschfelden first because the map has more game animals that can be taken down by your free starting rifle and ammo, as well as many birds that can be hunted with the base shotgun (although this will come at a cost of the weapon itself and ammo). So in my experience, I started off on the harder of the two base maps which lead to me leveling up more slowly but also working harder. If you are playing a new vanilla game with no DLCs, please do yourself a favor and start off with hunting a bunch of Roe Buck and Red Fox on Hirschfelden Reserve. If you are willing to buy DLC weapons and maps, then by all means go crazy and start wherever you wish. My last piece of advice, there are two very powerful perks you want to acquire asap, which is Zeroing and Sight Spotting. Zeroing allows you to change the range your scope is zeroed in at with the press of a button. For example, for rifles it can be cycled between 75 m, 150 m, and 300 m, allowing you to take very precise shots at three preset distances. Sight Spotting allows you to mark and leave an outline on animals temporarily, especially useful when hunting at night. This mechanic can always be achieved with your binoculars, but this perk allows you to avoid the hassle of rotating between your binoculars and firearm, saving precious seconds. 

So yeah, I like this game a lot. I got a very good vanilla experience from the game before spending about $150 USD on DLC for this game during the summer sale. I would not be surprised if I accumulate 1,000 hours of playtime in the future. I grew up playing Cabela's hunting games on my PS2, then Hunting Unlimited for PC when I was older, and now playing Call of the Wild as an adult feels like the perfect way to progress this hobby.

The reason I'm saying this is because of the grind mechanic that becoming more and more prevalent with each new updated.

The game is absolutely beautiful. The animals look good enough and they're challenging enough to track and hunt to make it a fun game. My absolute favorite way to play is to go into a park and walk around to see what I find. I favor things with antlers, like deer and elk, so it is always exciting to see a red deer with an impressive rack walk by.

Now here is the issue; animal spawns are RNG based and set in such a way "rare" spawns (like albino and melanistic) are... well, very rare. You might be under the impression that, if you walk around for long enough, you will see these rare spawns, but the reality is that there is no guarantee that there is a single special animal in your population files at all. Your park could have not a single rare spawn at all, so you will spend hours walking around, seeing the same basic colored animals over and over again.

The only way to make the game spawn rare animals is to remove animals from the population so it has to spawn a new animal, and if you get lucky, it might be one of the 0.051% chance of getting an albino wolf, with the odds for Great Ones being likely even lower. People have gone on literal grinds of THOUSANDS of animals trying to get a Great One to spawn. There are 8 species in the game that can spawn a Great One, and 5 of these have multiple colors, 6 in the case of moose, 8 in pheasants, 7 in red fox and so on.

The way efficient grinding works is to set up tents near drink zones, teleport to the tent, cull certain leveled maled, reset time, got to another drink zone and repeat the whole process over and over and over again. It's tedious, to the point yesterday I realized I wasn't enjoying the game any more. I wasn't doing what I loved about the game, I was lost in a repetitive, boring task that made it feel like a job, not a leisurely game to disconnect and have some fun. There is something very wrong when a game makes you feel like you're working.

Not only that, but in a game that's basically a hunting simulator, a grind mechanic as the one describes completely destroys any immersion. To me, walking around the park and encountering that rare spawn without expecting it has always had far more value and been more exciting than grinding my way until the albino wolf appears. In the first case, seeing the rare spawn was awe-inspiring. In the second, it was more as relief. "Finally the thing has spawned!". No awe, no wonder, just relief that I was able to move on and do something else instead of the boring, repetitive grind. In my opinion, immersion is everything in a game like this.

Spawns should be common enough to be rare, but not unicorn rare, and they should appear in normal gameplay, not spawn after a tedious grind, or not at all (since the chance of them naturally spawning is VERY, VERY LOW). I understand making the game challenging, but challenging would be giving the Great One enhanced detection skills to the point it'd require a very skilled stalker to even approach to shooting range. Perhaps making it move all over the map so it's harder to track. Lowering the spawn rate so it forces you to shoot 5,000 whitetails while you camp their need zones is not challenging, it's just time-consuming and tedious.

Lets not forget something, these are games. We play these to disconnect from real life, to do the things we can't do in real life, to live a fantasy. Most hunters will never encounter an exceptionally colored animal in the wild, but that's precisely where games come in to play, to give you the chance to live that fantasy. Games should be challenging, but not mimic real life. Nobody plays Skyrim to have their same 8 to 5 accountant job.

I love the game, but I honestly think they need to take a step back and stop using mindless grinding and exaggerated rare spawns to boost game engagement. A game should NEVER expect its players a dedication akin to having a job just to have a chance at triggering the spawn of a rare animal. I’ve been waiting this game for years, probably over a decade. 
My favorite Dragon Ball game is Budokai Tenkaichi 3 and I played it a lot. This new game feels like BT3 with Super characters, some minor gameplay changes and unfortunately a few missing characters that really should’ve been added as DLC by now.
The story mode was fine, it included some what if scenarios that I really enjoyed. Honestly, I wish the game focused entirely on this direction, because replaying the same story over and over in every game is boring, at least for me. Still, it’s better than nothing.
Custom Battle is amazing. I knew right away I’d spend a lot of hours into it, recreating the what ifs I used to watch on YouTube, imagining in my head or discussing with friends. It could definitely be improved, but even as it is, it gives the game infinite replay value for me.

Now for the negatives.
Online was ridiculously unbalanced at launch and the developers took way too long to fix it, which drove away 90% of the player base. The game desperately needs more gamemodes (like Survival, Mission 100 or additional what if stories) as well as new outfits and accessories for all characters. The customization potential would be incredible: imagine Goku in old Saiyan armor or Frieza dressed as Goku with a saiyan tail. Some characters don’t even have a second outfit, which is unacceptable considering even BT3 gave everyone at least one alternate color.
The DLC situation is also very bad. The release time is way too slow. By now, we should’ve had most GT characters, full Daima, and maybe even some unique what if fighters like Gohan Black or Gohkan.

I’ve always been a big fan of the Budokai Tenkaichi series, so I pre-ordered Sparking Zero's Deluxe Edition to show both my excitement and support. Looking back, it’s remarkable that we actually received a sequel (/reboot) for this series after 17 years.

I’ve 100%’ed the game, unlocked all the achievements, and spent plenty of time in every mode. Now, almost a year after its release, I wanted to sit down and put my thoughts into a review.

In more detail:

[b]Positives[/b]

[list]
[*] Huge roster.
[*] Incredible graphics.
[*] Plenty of modes to choose from.
[*] On the topic of modes, I would like to state that in the story mode, there's a number of "what-if" scenarios with their own, fully-animated, "mini episodes", which I found very amusing. Since Dragon Ball Super's anime finale back in 2018, fans have been begging for a comeback/sequel. We don't have that yet, but the developers of this game made an effort to present us with some unique action sequences and story. A very pleasant surprise.
[*] Gameplay similar to Budokai Tenkaichi 3, though in some ways evolved (I am particularly thankful this is closer to BT3 than the Raging Blast series, because I found the latter very slow).
[*] Split-screen multiplayer support, for local fun like the old days.
[/list]

[b]Negatives[/b]

[list]
[*] Very limited character customization.
[*] Poor post-launch support (extra costumes, stages, tournaments, story episodes, etc.).
[*] Occasional clipping (e.g., Z LSSJ Broly’s win screen) and some awkward animations (mostly in story cutscenes (motion captured?)).
[*] Controls sometimes make no sense.
[*] Online is a hell-hole, filled with sweats and drug addicts. Very little character variety and people spamming techs that make you want to smash your controller against the wall. [*] Not the biggest fan of the OST. Too many tracks and most of them don't sound good to me (generic). It's clear that they've strayed away from the fusion rock of the original trilogy.
[/list]

[b]Suggestions[/b]

[list]
[*] Standardize health and damage across all characters in ranked matches. This would encourage players to use a larger variety of characters from this huge roster, instead of avoiding characters that currently put them at a major disadvantage.
[*] Add more stages, costumes, characters, and music through DLC (perhaps in a second season pass).
[*] Host more official tournaments and provide incentives for participation.
[*] Refine the controls: loosen the timing for Z-Vanish and Perfect Counter, limit how often they can be used consecutively, improve Super Blast and Rush Attack tracking so they connect more reliably (especially at steep angles, such as when knocking an opponent downward from the air), etc.
[*] Work on QOL improvements: include a random stage/track option, and make the game remember the last online search settings for each mode so players don’t need to re-enter parameters every time (e.g., Ranked → Singles, Similar Rank, Connection <4, Match Finish Rate High, etc.).

It's got so many characters (180ish in the base roster and 200+ with DLC) covering so many aspects of this great series. Z, Super, GT, Daima, and a little bit of OG DB as well! Even when two characters share a technique (like Super Kamehameha), it's animated slightly differently. I'm someone who grew up playing Raging Blast 2 and Tenkaichi Tag Team. My favorite thing to do was to go into an offline battle, select my characters and my opponent's characters, and fight against the CPU. It's what I've come to love about this series. Sparking Zero lets me do that but with a LOT more characters.

I never really cared for online play. It's not my thing. But that's where many fans are disappointed, specifically regarding Ranked Mode. Ranked Matches set up the expectations that there will be some amount of balancing so that both players are fighting at an equal level. But that's not what Tenkaichi is. Tenkaichi is built to be a game about power levels and the disparity between a weak character and a strong one. And that's what Sparking Zero is, too. Czech dubbing and period atmosphere – the iconic voices and authentic setting make both games a unique experience. The city feels alive, especially the opening winter chapters of Mafia II, which have an unforgettable charm.
Music – a soundtrack full of classic songs (Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and others) perfectly underscores the action and makes you feel like you’re really living in that era.
Well-written story and characters – a gangster drama that has it all: tension, humor, tragedy, and powerful moments. The characters are memorable, and their relationships still work after all these years.
Varied missions – from ordinary driving tasks to shootouts and “big hits.” Mafia II feels dynamic and never boring.
Simulation-style driving model – cars have weight, you can feel them, and each one behaves differently. Combined with police patrols, it elevates the atmosphere even further.
Nostalgia – Mafia II strongly recalls Driver 2, which is a huge plus for long-time gamers.
Mafia II DLCs – Joe’s Adventures and Jimmy’s Vendetta add plenty of extra content beyond the main story and make up for the fact that the city otherwise serves mostly as a backdrop.

Cons:
Dated gameplay – at its core it’s now just a classic cover shooter with no real innovations.
AI and technical flaws – enemies sometimes behave stiffly, and occasional bugs can appear.
Mafia II’s ending – deliberately open and controversial. For some it’s a brilliant narrative choice, for others a frustrating cliffhanger.
Mafia: Definitive Edition on PC – initially had issues running properly, which I only managed to fix thanks to a community solution I found on a forum.
Mafia II: Definitive Edition on PC – surprisingly lacks Steam Cloud support, which feels like a big oversight for a 2020 remaster.

Verdict:
Mafia I and II remain essential experiences for anyone who loves story-driven games and gangster films. Both have preserved their unique charm – from dubbing and music to city atmosphere and dramatic twists. The gameplay may have aged, but the strength of the story and atmosphere is timeless.
