There's this constant sense that he and his best friend Joe Barbarro never really get anywhere and this is reinforced by a careful structure and creative choices that reflect the protagonist's changing position. Across fifteen well directed chapters, the overall design puts you right in Vito's shoes; he is showered with money at one moment, only to lose it all the next.

Mafia II is far more gritty and unflinching than the original, a tale of loss, stagnation and grim consequences; something that runs counter to every other open-world game out there. The trifecta of third-person shooting, driving and stealth is present and accounted for. Once again it gets the job done with the plot being the main draw. You can buy clothes and guns, crush cars and take on wanted posters for some extra money, but the game always keeps you on task, waiting to drop the next big twist. When you're done, some extra DLC packs and collectables extend the game's length with Joe's Adventures being the best of the bunch, adding some extra detail to the narrative.

As for the Definitive Edition? It runs well enough, but there are some irritating glitches that dampen the immersion a bit. The environmental pop-in is the most glaring flaw, but I also encountered dialogue playing multiple times, strange looking facial expressions and a tailing mission that bugged out a couple of times when the target refused to move. Hanger 13 really should have remastered this game alongside its predecessor. You may want to stick to the 2010 original to experience Mafia II at its best, but if you're a fan of story-driven games, this title is a must-own.

[h3][Positives][/h3]
- Mostly faithful remake. It’s pretty neat to see all the iconic scenes are areas recreated.
- Solid story which has been expanded from the original. Most of the additions are really good.
- Good characters.
- Decent gameplay.
- Good pacing.
- Memorable missions.
- Tons of vehicles and solid driving mechanics.
- Great graphics and art style.
- Much more polished than the original game.
- A lot of padding was cut that was in the original.
- Cars are stored in an infinite garage now, so you don’t need to sacrifice cars when you unlock new ones.
- Paulie and Sam are more present in this game compared to the original, which helps flesh their characters out more. Other characters are expanded upon as well.

[h3][Mixed][/h3]
- Some missions were shortened from the original game, but also some missions were expanded.
- Some story details were changed. You may or may not like the changes, but I think they’re mostly fine.
-The game does a better job at directing the player compared to the original game, but sometimes this goes a little too far and makes the game feel too linear and hand holding.
- The open world is neat, but it’s pretty shallow. This isn’t a deal-breaker given that the game is mostly linear.
- The stealth mechanics are a bit better, but now they’re fairly generic. There’s no more hitting enemies with baseball bats from behind to knock them out. Now you just have a typical ‘Press B from behind’ takedown system.
- Cover mechanics in the combat are a questionable inclusion.
- The shooting while driving mechanics are still a bit clunky, so it’s a bit of a sidegrade.
- The Lucas Bertore sub-quests from the original games story were exchanged for free roam side missions instead.

[h3][Negatives][/h3]
- Combat and gunplay feel more generic compared to the original game. Most weapons feel worse than the original. The Tommy Gun being one of the most noticeable downgrades.
- The game was made significantly easier compared to the original. I’d recommend playing on Hard or Classic.
- The racing mission is notoriously difficult, especially on Classic difficulty.
- Some of the chase sequences are pretty scripted.
- Some of the collectibles are neat, but there’s too many of them and the in-game methods of tracking them are incredibly lacking.
- Various downgrades from the original. The city is a bit less interactive, being able to freely ride public transport was removed, car damage isn’t as impressive, some of the immersion feels weaker. The original game also felt fairly advanced for it’s time, this remake feels a bit too safe and generic in some ways.
- It's a bit of a movie game. Not much replayability.

[h3][Conclusion][/h3]
Mafia: Definitive Edition isn’t without it’s faults, but overall it’s a solid remake. I'd consider it to be (mostly) an improvement over the original. It’s not very replayable, but it’s worth a shot for the story alone.
7.5/10

Long version:
A disclaimer about my perspective - I haven't played much of this type of games in general (e.g. crime drama stuff), including GTA and stuff, and including the original game. Saw some hype towards the new game and remembered I'm actually having this one in my library and decided to give a go to the Mafia series.

The game is very good and I have enjoyed it, but you should know what to expect - at this point I guess most of us do, but I've just noticed the game has "Open World" as its first tag which is, I think, ridiculous and an insult to open world games :)

So what is Mafia?
This is a story driven action game, "story driven" meaning very cutscenes-driven here.
So we get a crime drama story which felt a tiny bit generic to me but I still liked it. The characters and script felt well written and voice overs felt well acted. Gameplay consists of generic action-type stuff as well, you'd drive around, you'd punch some guys at times, you'd shoot some guys at times, and you'd yet again drive, quite a lot, all separated by many cutscenes. From time to time there are some refreshing race\chase missions and rarely stealth ones, so all in all gameplay did feel varied enough for a relatively short campaign.
Missions are also very self contained in the sense that you mostly get ammunition and health restored in the beginning so no worried about conserving these from chapter to chapter.
As for difficulty, on "Normal" game actually felt pretty easy to me, there were some specific missions where I've died a couple of time but progress was mostly flowing.
Oh, and the soundtrack was very awesome, dramatic and fitting the game's atmosphere and story.
Driving, which is as I mentioned a crucial part of the game, was fun imo, it did feel a little janky at first and took some getting used to, but I grew to like it. There are some touches I found nice which are - you can drive on manual mode, and police can "realistically" (kinda) react to your behavior and if you're doing some shit (driving too fast, stealing cars, running over citizens) they'll start chasing you. These can be turned on and off via settings which is nice.

So, all in all, if you're in for a rather linear action adventure, with many (high quality) cutscenes and story parts, a lots of driving and shoot&cover missions, you should be really good to go with this one.

Another point I'm always mentioning in my reviews is whether games are "busy-player-friendly", as one who unfortunately no longer has so much time to spend on video games, and this one definitely is, with a not too long runtime (Took me ~13 hours and I'm sure for more experienced players would take 6-10 hours on Normal), auto save happens practically every few minutes, and missions aren't usually very long, all this made is very convenient for me to play short sessions as well and see the game to the end.

The game does have a "Free Ride" mode (I think that's what it was called) allowing to roam freely the city.
It's nice and impressive but I didn't find much use to it beside admiring the map and and they created a lively and vibrant vibes to the city.

It truly feels like being in a mafia movie, just like The Godfather, but in a playable version.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1735221452}, {"review_text": "Mafia: Definitive Edition is a masterclass in how to faithfully remake a classic without diluting its original identity. Hangar 13 has managed to respect the 2002 original while modernizing nearly every aspect to meet contemporary expectations, creating a cinematic crime experience that feels both nostalgic and fresh. It’s worth noting that some content from the original game has been trimmed, resulting in a slightly shorter overall experience, but this streamlining mostly benefits pacing and keeps the narrative tightly focused.

The gameplay is deliberate and rewarding. Driving, while intentionally weighty to reflect the period’s automotive design, feels satisfying and immersive. Gunplay has been upgraded to feel heavier and more impactful, with each shot reinforcing the tension of confrontations. While the game doesn’t offer the freedom of modern open-world titles, this linearity is deliberate: it ensures pacing remains tight, mission design purposeful, and narrative momentum uninterrupted. The world of Lost Heaven is densely crafted not sprawling, but every street, building, and ambient detail contributes to the city’s immersive noir atmosphere.

Storytelling remains the game’s core strength. Without spoiling any narrative beats, the characters are compelling, voice acting is top-notch, and cinematic direction elevates each scene. The missions are structured to complement the story perfectly, with a rhythm that balances action, tension, and quiet moments for reflection.

Visually, the remake shines. Lighting, textures, and environmental details all work in harmony to recreate the 1930s atmosphere with remarkable fidelity. Minor technical hiccups, such as occasional frame drops or slightly rigid NPC animations, are present but rarely detract from the experience. The sound design is exceptional: orchestral scoring, environmental audio, and weapon effects all enhance immersion, reinforcing the period’s tone and mood.

Technical Performance
Mafia: Definitive Edition performs reliably in most situations. Frame rates are stable, and optimization is solid even in denser city areas. Occasional minor bugs exist, but nothing critically hampers progression or breaks immersion. The game’s engine handles the detailed urban environments well, and crashes are rare under standard conditions.

Faithful remake with modern enhancements

Excellent storytelling and cinematic presentation

Deeply immersive city design with authentic atmosphere

Balanced and purposeful gameplay design

Strong sound design and orchestral score

Solid PC performance and optimization

Cons:

Linear structure may feel restrictive to some players

Minor frame drops and occasional rigid NPC animations

Slightly shorter than the original, with some cut content

[{"review_text": "[h1] Maximum Immersion Guide after 27 trips to Silent Hill [/h1]

Silent Hill 2 is in my Top 3 games of all time. I just finished my 27th playtrough including my runs in vanilla on PS2, Directors Cut on PC, the "not so HD" collection on PS3 and the Remake on PS5. I got 100% on all of those platforms, 75% on PC while writing this. The game is excellent on all levels so all I wanna do here is give you my top 5 tips for your ultimate "first-time" experience with the best horror game ever made. Follow these and you'll never forget this trip, promise.

1. Turn off the lights or even better, play alone in an abandoned hospital. Or just at home at night, thats fine as well. [b] Turn up your headphones [/b] (Akira Yamaoka is perfection).

2. Watch and listen. SH2 was made and intended to play slowly. Explore the town when outside. Walk instead of running around, especially indoors. [b] Check your map constantly. [/b] Take your time - read everything, question what you see, listen to the sounds of the city. Soak everything up. There is only one first playtrough, after that its gone, forever.

3. Start on both normal combat / riddle difficulty. Its the balance the devs have intended, imo its the perfect balance. Fighting is not the main focus of the game anyway and soon when you find the gun at the start of the game it gets ridiculously easy thanks to a little melee combo "trick" (a hint: knees). Also, you can easily dodge all attacks, even from bosses. The riddles are very well made and ingenious, so it would be a shame to waste this experience. Again, take your time, think a little, the riddles are not that hard, but fun! On hard, enemy damage doubles. Would not recommend for your first time.

4. For the best experience, turn off "Low health vignette" under Options/Gameplay. You can see how bad James is injured by how much blood is on his jacket, how he moves (when hurt badly) or by the "color" of your inventory. This is the way its meant to be played, the vignette just gives you a constant red corner which is super annoying.

5. Play with a controller. Its a way better and smoother experience!

Short notice about performance, the game is demanding, especially in 4K but also 1440p. DLSS Quality with 100% resolution scale and frame generation works well for most people as I heard but the newer your GPU, the better.

This concludes my thoughts about a game I spent WAY to much time playing it, but I regret nothing. You'll see why if you give this one a shot by yourself. For starters. I've been a HUGE Silent Hill fan for the past 10 years. I've played all the original Team Silent games multiple times, along with Origins and Shattered Memories. Silent Hill means a lot to me. 


As for Bloober Team's remake, they have exceeded my expectations! I could tell as I was playing that this game was made by dedicated fans, FOR fans. Their attention to detail, addition of Easter Eggs and homages to the other Silent Hill games has been a real treat for a fan like me. I have replayed the remake 8 times and with each play-through I kept discovering new Easter Eggs and details I happened to overlook. Aside from the original games, I have truly, genuinely, fully immersed myself in this game. Walking through these familiar streets feels like revisiting a town you grew up in, and that's exactly what this is. There's new places to explore, new buildings you can enter and different routes to take. Bloober Team made this experience feel fresh, and it was like I was playing Silent Hill 2 for the first time again! This remake has hit the nostalgia factor for me tenfold. The lore, environment, sound design, characters, story, music is 10/10 for both the original and remake of Silent Hill 2. The game-play was never this series' strongest suit, but I will mention that the addition of a dodge mechanic was a great change, and the Spider Mannequin variants kept me on edge!

I am pleased that Bloober Team did not diverge heavily from the core themes of the OG. I was worried they would tone down some parts, especially Angela's story line, since it touches on a very sensitive topic that people will be uncomfortable with. But the Abstract Daddy sequence SHOOK me to my core. I was not ready for something like that. It's as if I was experiencing Angela's trauma, but second-hand.

What SOLD me on this game were the performances. Luke Roberts as James Sunderland completely KNOCKED IT OUT OF THE PARK. He delivered one of the GREATEST video game performances of all time. He's right next to characters like Kratos, Arthur Morgan, Joel Miller, etc. I didn't think they could make an ending to rival In Water, but they DID with Stillness. As for the other characters, Angela, Eddie, Mary and Laura were perfect. They made Eddie more unsettling this time. In the OG, he came off goofy and silly. I could not take his character seriously. However with remake Eddie, you can tell right away there's something off about him, and as you progress he becomes increasingly psychopathic and unhinged. It's PERFECT.

As for some negative things to say: MARIA.
Maria has been a divisive topic with the remake. In some areas she delivers, and in others she falls short. This isn't to dog on the actress, though. She did a phenomenal job. This is more of an issue with the direction and writing. They wanted to take a subtle approach to Maria's character, especially when it came to her sex appeal and feistyness. This is not a game you simply “play.” It is a game that takes you apart, piece by piece, through subtle environmental cues, reimagined performances, deeply textured sound design, and a world that seems disturbingly aware of you. In a market oversaturated with horror games relying on loud noises, cheap shocks, and recycled tropes, Silent Hill 2 Remake stands out as a reminder of what horror is truly capable of — intimate, reflective, suffocating, and heartbreakingly human.

From the moment the title screen fades in, you are already being pulled into the mental and emotional space of James Sunderland. The fog isn’t merely a visual motif — it’s the boundary between memory and denial, clarity and confusion, guilt and the wish to forget. The town itself is an extension of James’s internal landscape, shaped by his trauma, his shame, and his desperate longing.

⭐ Graphics — A Town Rebuilt with Terrifying Intimacy

The graphical overhaul is astonishing in ways that are difficult to fully convey. This isn’t just an upgrade in textures or lighting; it’s a reconstruction of atmosphere. The fog isn’t uniform — it moves, flows, pulses. It feels alive. Light sources diffuse through the mist in unpredictable ways, creating the uneasy impression that the fog has moods. Shadows behave strangely too, bending in ways that make rational sense at first glance, but linger just long enough for you to question whether the world is obeying normal laws.

Character models are an enormous leap forward. James’s face carries the weight of sleepless nights and emotional exhaustion. Every line and twitch feels grounded in studied realism. Maria, whose presence is central to the emotional complexity of the story, is portrayed with incredible nuance — seductive yet vulnerable, manipulative yet sympathetic, confident yet wounded. Her animations alone add layers of subtext that were impossible to express in the PS2 era.

The monsters, grotesque manifestations of James’s internal struggles, look disturbingly organic. Their movements are erratic but purposeful. Their designs are faithful to the original but refined, more grounded yet more symbolic. They feel like half-living sculptures of guilt, fear, and suppressed desire.

Every environment tells a story. Hallways are lit with flickering lights that seem to tremble under the weight of the air. Walls decay in patterns that resemble bruises or burns. Abandoned rooms feel like memories left to rot. The level of detail invites close inspection, yet at the same time something inside you wants to look away.

Silent Hill 2 Remake doesn’t chase fluid combat or power fantasy. Instead, it designs systems that reflect vulnerability, clumsy fear, and the uncomfortable truth that James is not a trained fighter, but a damaged human being stumbling into situations he is wholly unprepared for.

Combat is heavier. Weapons have weight and delay. Every swing is a commitment. Enemies don’t behave like scripted obstacles — their movements reflect animalistic confusion and malicious curiosity. They react to sound, to light, and to your hesitation.

About grief.
About the unbearable weight of loving someone you cannot save.

Some sections are intentionally draining — long quiet walks through dense fog, lonely hallways where the only sound is your heartbeat echoing through your headphones, confrontations that feel like emotional confrontations with yourself.

It is difficult because it is supposed to be.

You don’t just finish Silent Hill 2 Remake.
You recover from it.

Silent Hill 2 Remake is respectful of its legacy while enhancing it with modern storytelling tools. It never feels like a cash grab. It never feels like an imitation. It feels like a passionate restoration of a timeless piece of psychological art.

Absolutely.

Worth the price?
More than worth it.

There are subtle elements of environmental storytelling that reinforce what’s already present in the lore files, or known by progressing in the story. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, as it should be in survival horror, and will never make you feel like you’re safe anywhere, in a city infested by monsters and horrors; even “safe rooms” will not feel as safe as they could in other titles of this genre, and that’s an intentional choice to keep the tension high.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore Silent Hill and its environs solely on foot, through maps that, generally, have a good degree of openness and aren’t entirely linear, but also couldn’t be defined as ‘open-world’. In fact, aside from optional areas you’re free to explore if you stumble upon them at all, most other sections of each level are barred behind critical items tied to story progression. There’s usually a precise, formulaic order in which you’ll acquire them and gain access to further parts of that map. There are no outright ‘secret’ areas or items to find, but there are many secondary locations that often house missable weapons, interactions and lore items that can make your run more interesting, and in some cases, less troublesome, if acquired. 

As with most survival horrors, being attentive, opening all containers and looking behind every corner is essential to scavenge enough ammo and healing to survive the frequent enemy encounters, and also collect notes, diaries and puzzle-related items. Exploration is interesting and compelling, given that you won’t know what to expect next, in a world where reality and figments of James’ mind intertwine the more you press forward. Other than always showing your position in a well-made layout, your map will automatically mark locked doors, important devices and landmarks; getting lost won’t ever be an issue.

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
You’ll fight several kinds of monsters, each representing a specific trauma from James’ past, during your travels in Silent Hill. On the Hard difficulty at least, each of them is a serious threat: just a few attacks can kill you, and earlier on these creatures are tough to defeat, and can also revive if you don’t make sure they stay dead by hitting their corpses. Most of the enemy moveset is melee, although some of them also have ranged attacks; dodging with near-perfect timing is an essential mechanic, as is learning each monster’s attack patterns to know when to strike in melee without risking a painful retaliation. Using ranged weapons gives you a decisive advantage, but ammo is scarce for most of the adventure, and should be saved for bosses and more demanding combat sections with multiple enemies. 

Unfortunately, the enemy variety is low, and soon enough you’ll be tired of fighting the same three or four archetypes recycled over and over. This doesn’t get better at any point, and I don’t see a reason why in this remake they couldn’t have added some more variants to spice up the gameplay. The melee system is weighty and satisfying to use, however, it’s also inconsistent and, at times, inaccurate. Boss fights are unique, and have hidden mechanics for you to figure out in most cases. For example, some of them are just tests of endurance where you don’t actually need to damage your foe, while others are more classic fights that may have specific weak points or ways to damage your enemy that aren’t immediately apparent; overall, they’re challenging and well-designed.

[h3]Puzzles & Character Progression[/h3]
There’s a high amount of puzzles in each area, often mandatory to progress. They’re mostly logic-based, and involve figuring out a combination, a code, or restoring a specific pattern of images, with the help of found documents or hints nearby the puzzle area. None of them are extremely difficult, but some will definitely test your patience and problem-solving skills. There are no levels, currency or other character progression to speak of. AoE2 takes historical figures — Joan of Arc, Saladin, Genghis Khan — and instead of burying them in dusty textbooks, lets you live their stories in beautifully crafted campaigns. The brilliance of AoE2 lies in how every tiny decision matters.

Economy management, map control, scouting, micro, macro — the game has layers upon layers of strategy that have kept both casual players and pros addicted for 25 years. You don’t just “play” AoE2 — you develop a lifestyle.⚒️🔥

🎨🎶-Graphics & Sound: Nostalgia Meets Modern Polish🎨🎶

The Definitive Edition somehow preserves the warmth of the original pixel art while making everything crisp, vivid, and animate in ways we never thought possible on modern screens.

⭐- Final Verdict

Age of Empires II is not just a real-time strategy game — it’s a generational masterpiece that refuses to die, refuses to age, and refuses to stop being relevant.
It’s emotional, competitive, educational, hilarious, frustrating, and unforgettable, all at the same time.

[h3][i]DMC[/i][/h3]
This is the game that made me a fan of this franchise and Capcom games in general, so my opinion on DMC will naturally have some form of bias, but personally speaking, I do not think this game has aged anywhere near as badly as what some people make it out to be.

The premise itself is fairly basic: main character Dante gets attacked by a mysterious woman named Trish at his office as a test and is then requested by her to enter a castle on Mallet Island to fight against the demon emperor Mundus, who is responsible for killing Dante’s brother and mother. There isn’t much plot in the game; it is mainly there to establish the setting and tone, but what’s there in the game does work. It’s simplistic and enjoyable for what it is.

The gameplay is rewarding and unique for its age. You slash down enemies with Dante’s sword and juggle enemies with your guns so you can increase your stylish rank. You are ranked based on your performance in each mission, so you’re encouraged to play better as you gain more red orbs, which act as a currency to buy items and moves for Dante. You can unlock Devil Trigger, which is a special transformation that lets Dante deal more effective attacks at lightning speed. DT is a very fun mechanic, and it will aid you the most during the game’s more difficult moments, so you’ll want to take advantage of it.

Unlike most of the games in the franchise, DMC is fundamentally designed with knowledge checks in mind. Certain attacks and weapons will deal more effective damage to specific enemies. If you’re familiar with any of the mainline Mega Man games and how they’re designed, you’ll have an idea of what to do in this game, but if you’re not willing to put in the time to figure out how the game works mechanically, then you likely won’t have the greatest time, especially on harder difficulties.

As for the camera, it is very similar to the use of fixed camera angles found in older Capcom titles. I do not mind how it functions in this game, but this will likely turn off some people who are particularly more used to camera control found in more modern games.

This game oozes atmosphere with its gothic environments, which stem from the game’s Resident Evil roots. The non-diegetic soundtrack helps the player settle into DMC’s dark world, and it really fits the mood of the game. 'Anarchy in the U.W.' and 'Flock Off!' are tracks I vibe with a lot.

While DMC is still very much an enjoyable classic, I feel that it unfortunately gets overshadowed by most of the games directed by Hideaki Itsuno. Hideki Kamiya’s vision of DMC is worth your time, and it’s still a fascinating experience that holds up today. Do not sleep on this game.
 
[h3][i]DMC2[/i][/h3]
DMC2 is a rushed abomination that Capcom somehow managed to release, with Itsuno being forced into the director’s chair last minute to finish up work on the game.

In this game, you play as two protagonists, Dante and Lucia. Dante controls like a slow tank with how he swings his sword around, and his guns deal far more effective damage than his sword, which straight up goes against what made his gameplay fun and interesting from the first game. As for Lucia, her gameplay is not much different from Dante’s. Her blades attack faster than Dante’s sword, and her selection of projectiles feels slow to use. New to this game is the ability to run on walls, but it really isn’t all that helpful to do for the most part.

The level design in DMC2 is filled with a lot of big open environments, which is in stark contrast with how the levels were designed in the first game. A lot of the time, you’ll be moving around with nothing interesting going on until you encounter an enemy and have to deal with the game’s atrocious camera. It’s abysmal with how it’s laser-focused on the enemies, and you’re forced to fight against the camera when you’re trying to navigate around the area during those encounters. It’s, without a doubt, worse than the camera from the first game. The gameplay is at its worst when you’re forced to do the underwater segments since you barely have any semblance of control while you’re swimming slowly and are forced to awkwardly attack enemies with your devil arms. Despite the changes, the gameplay of DMC2 does not have the technical nuance that made the first game special to play.

In regard to the story, it’s practically almost non-existent. Stuff just happens without any reason or build-up. The main antagonist is a meme, Lucia is boring, and Dante himself is severely depressed.

The least offensive aspect of the game is the soundtrack itself. While I don’t think it is objectively bad, it’s the least memorable out of all the mainline games. 'Parasitic Evil' is a standout track for me personally.

DMC2 simply does not have any of the special sauce that made DMC such a unique game. This game has little to no personality to its name, and I do not recommend it.

[h3][i]DMC3[/i][/h3]
This game is undoubtedly one of Capcom’s GOATs, and it’s objectively the best-designed game in this collection. Itsuno returned to direct this game to make up for the failure of the second game, and he absolutely cooked everything to near perfection with Dante’s Awakening.

Being a prequel to the first game, you play as a young Dante at his new shop who gets invited by an unknown man associated with Dante’s brother to visit Temen-ni-gru. Dante makes his way to the tower to fight his twin brother, Vergil. The premise itself is simple, but there is more to it as you play the game. I really appreciate the added details to the characters and established lore as a long-time fan of the franchise.

The gameplay provided in DMC3 streamlines a lot of what worked well in the previous games and sets the foundation for the rest of the franchise. Dante has access to different Styles that allow him to do many sorts of actions to aid the player. The extended amount of moves you can pull off while alternating between your weapons and Style on the fly is extremely satisfying when pulled off. It is similar to a fighting game in a sense with how many different moves you can dish out at once while also juggling enemies. Level design is mostly linear and is done in a manner that doesn’t pointlessly waste your time. The camera has been adjusted to make it easier to navigate, and you have more control of it.

The soundtrack in particular is fantastic. It’s got the most effort put in, with iconic tracks that are very much loved to this day, like 'Devils Never Cry', 'Taste The Blood' and 'Divine Hate'.

If you’re trying to get into character action games, this is an absolute must-play.

[{"review_text": "Counter-Strike 2: Not an Update, a Rebirth
At first glance, you think — oh, it's just CS:GO with ray tracing and protein shakes. Then you play it. And you realize: nope, this isn’t an update. It’s like your good old AK-47 suddenly developed a sense of smell.

CS2 is still that same adrenaline-fueled classic where one bullet can change the round, but now everything feels tangible. Source 2 didn’t just slap on better graphics — it poured a bucket of raw concrete into the game. You can feel things now: water droplets from explosions, the flicker of your teammate’s shadow around the corner, and smoke that doesn’t just exist — it lives.

Speaking of smoke — it’s no longer a wall. It’s a character. It moves, it breathes, it reacts to grenades like it’s got emotions. I wouldn’t be surprised if it starts streaming on Twitch next year.

The guns? Still the same arsenal, but every reload feels like you’re reloading your soul. The AWP doesn’t just boom anymore — it tears a hole in reality, pauses time, and gently lets you back into the match.

Servers finally hit 128-tick, and that’s like upgrading from smoke signals to quantum teleportation. Every movement is a dance. Every kill? Poetry. The feel is tighter, snappier, and your muscle memory comes back like a loyal dog that never really left.

It’s not perfect — hitboxes sometimes act like confused teenagers, and the UI is a bit extra. Matchmaking still throws you in with people who think the bomb site is a Spotify playlist. But that’s fine. CS2 is a foundation, not a fad. It's here to evolve.

The Verdict:
CS2 isn’t the second chapter. It’s a second life. For the aim gods and the eco warriors. For the smurfs, the noobs, the spray control philosophers. It’s not just a game — it’s the art of control, the sound of chaos, and the silence before the last shot.

[{"review_text": "[h3]Edited on 12th December, 2025[/h3]

I couldn't help but edit this review to make it up-to-date. Unfortunately, however, My thumb-down still holds. If you like to take a look at my original review posted last year, you can find it below. Consider this edit as an addition to the previous review to reflect what I think of the current state of Hunt: Showdown.

Crytek decided to give a huge load of F-you to its players. The Murder Circus has returned, and with that the obnoxious Shredder and Post Malone hunter skin. I will not elaborate on these two again; head over to the past review below to see why I dislike them. But to sum it up, the Shredder is OP and is not fun to fight against, and the real-life celebrities does not fit in Hunt's world, no matter their popularity and their love with Hunt: Showdown.

In the recent 2.6 patch, they turned to more worse monetization to have their players pay: Story Challenges and profile customization, which is a worrisome change regarding their content delivery. Story Challenges, as the name suggests, are sets of challenges you can finish for some rewards with some story. There are two storylines at this moment, but one of which is behind the paywall and cost almost double the amount of a single Battle Pass. It's also time-limited, meaning that you cannot obtain those rewards after the time limit in any way; not from Dark Tributes, not from Twitch Drops, whatsoever. What's worse is that it has less rewards than the current Battle Pass, but you also need to work more to earn those rewards. They could've released those rewards as another DLC or simply another in-game bundle items, but they decided to cost you more by manipulating the players' FOMO, both in money and in time.
Profile customization is another hideous stuff Crytek brought in. What this does is that it lets you customize what statistic values you want to show with your profile cards, for example, your K/D, the number of your maxed-out hunters, the total amount of Bounty cash earned, etc. The problem is that most of the weapon stats are locked behind the paywall, and will only start tracking [i]after[/i] you buy them. Which is nonsense because they did track them via the Book of Weapons before the 1896 re-launch, so they are clearly capable of doing so, but they chose not to in favor of monies. Not only that, you cannot choose your avatar background of hunter skins you own, no; you gotta pay extra to fancy up your profile card with your favorite hunter. No one asked for this feature, no one thought this is a good idea, but somehow, Crytek saw this as an opportunity to pull cash from their players and went to shove this in their face.

Now, many people will say that these are just cosmetics (like weapon skins and legendary hunters) and will not affect the core gameplay, and that I simply don't have to buy it if I don't like it. However, if we aren't vocal enough about these kind of things and let them pass with "they gotta make money somehow," I'm sure they'll try to push more greedy stuff solely for more profit while aggravating their players' experience even further.

It's a real shame that once one of my favorite game has gone downhill this far. Sure, there are some improvements and positive additions which I do like. However, the downside is too heavily outweighing the upside to defend Crytek's current stance. The Hunt right now is just a husk of its former self barely held together. I still had hope during the last event, hoping it will be better in Christmas season. Turned out it isn't, and will not going to be. I'm not saying that I'm going to stop playing Hunt entirely, but I'm not inclined to indulge into it as I have before anymore.

Just bring back the pre-1896 Hunt: Showdown, ffs.



[h3]Original review on 26th December, 2024[/h3]

I never thought I will be writing a "Not Recommended" review for this game.

As you can see from my playtime, I've poured quite a huge part of my free time into Hunt. That itself proves my fondness to this game.
I started playing right after its early access, back when there was no "1896" in its title. I was drawn into the grim, ruthless nature of the Hunt; everything around you can and will kill you, and you have to make the most of what you have―your equipment, your trait, your position and your knowledge of other enemies' equipment, trait and position. Forming a strategy is a must to at least survive, even though that means you're leaving without bounty. You need to traverse the map carefully, paying attention to the surroundings, and plan your next move deliberately. Failure to do so will result in your (and your partners') death, losing everything you brought in.
Every firearms had something to offer; each gun had its own strengths and weaknesses, so there was no such thing as "trash weapon" nor "superb weapon," meaning that you would always have a chance to topple over enemies, if you know how to play your gun right.
The world and environment is something that no other game would be able to pull off, its occult-esque darkness surrounding the world, which can be found both in-game in the lore book, i.e. the Book of Weapons and the Book of Monsters. The events pre-1896 were on track with its lore and brought interesting seasonal addition into the game in the form of short stories (and some cool narrations along with them).

But right now, after Hunt's 1896 reboot, everything matters no more. They completely removed all the books from the game, so we can't even have a look of the game's lores anytime you want (Crytek did announced that the books will be available on Hunt website, but why ripping them away from the game in the first place?).
Gunfight-wise, they've started to add more and more broken weapons and traits which makes any strategic aspects completely useless. They are now encouraging more fast-paced fights by implementing absurd equipment and buffing up more spammy weapons. They made every gun have all same custom ammo, made every shotgun buffed, made more expensive weapons powerful, and de-penalized being downed with Revive Bolt and Restoration Shot. The worst weapon so far is the "Shredder," a crossbow-ish weapon that shoots sawblades semi-auto that ricochet off the walls and home on enemies in proximity. That's the most absurd mechanics I've ever seen in any other shooter games (other than CoD), and it doesn't even fit into the game's original gunplay system in any way. They completely lost touch on what to do with equipment and are only focusing on attracting [i]major audience[/i] by steering away Hunt's core gameplay.

What dove a final nail in the coffin is the recent event, Post Malone's Murder Circus. Before this event, at least themes of each event were always on par with Hunt's originality. But the Murder Circus is all for Post Malone, a real-life celebrity (evident as shown in its title). Almost all weapon skin has a "PM" initials engraved, and there are two Post Malone Hunter skins in the battle pass. If I ever wanted to see a famous musician or actor, I'd go play CoD or Fortnite. I liked Hunt for its own unique atmosphere, not for having a real-life celebrity.

I don't know what to think of Hunt: Showdown anymore. This isn't [i]the[/i] Hunt I used to know. Once a dark, tense and slow-paced game, with an actually fine-balanced equipment, has become nothing but a so-called "Western" run-and-gun trigger-happy shooter. I may come back when my Hunt partners group up for a couple of matches, but I'm not going to actively play this game onwards.

I want this game to succeed and become better. I have no grudge against the Devs. That is why I give my honest feedback.

I would not recommend to start getting into this game unless you are a real masochist and enjoy dumping hundreds of hours in it to become somewhat decent and learn the ropes.

Recently I am loosing the fun with this game after almost 4.000 Hours because of the direction the game is heading. I am not saying it is wrong or bad in general, it is just not my cup of tea anymore.

- Ingame Voip and Chat not working properly
- UI Functions to equip your hunter are sometimes not working correctly
- Sound Bugs (sometimes a major inconvienience in a game that is designed for great audio)
- Server Performance sometimes randomly goes to hell with rubberbanding out of nowhere and lagging.
- Texture Loading Bugs and Derendering of walls or trees
- Reconnect Feature not working 
- Ingame map bugging and leading to stutters

And so on. Most of this is not the worst thing but in combination in intense situations it becomes very frustrating because this stuff happens often.

The Devs started to improve on communication again which I highly appreciate even though it is by far not as good as it was a few years ago.

The biggest issues that are making me leaving the game more and more are the following:

- The Instaburning meta.

For those who dont know. When you get killed in Hunt, your team mates can pick you up a few times and you loose part of your maximum health for every revive until you are at zero maximum health and red skulled. Then you can not be picked up again (besided when your team has the bounty, the main objective of the game). But even then they have to sacrifice their own health to get you back). When you are downed and people set you on fire, you rapidly loose your maximum health until you are redskulled.

I hated it when they implemented burning downed hunters long ago. But I see from a gamedesign perspective, that they needed some sort of mechanic to handle solos with self revive and stalemates from people that are just hiding and waiting until you leave, to pick up their team mates again. And I think it was fine how it was. But the devs decided not so long ago that it was not enough.

Before you had to bring a firebomb or find a lantern in the world to set hunters on fire. Which was fine because you had to invest ressources and time to burn a downed hunter and you had to move and take a risk because people could shoot you when you had to come close to burn a hunter.

Nowadays you can burn hunters with a million tools and consumables that are easy to restock and to bring and you can safely ignite hunters from behind cover with a flare pistol even from 50 meteres away. No ressources have to be invested, no risk taken. It is nowadays a surprise if you are not instantly getting set on fire even before your body has hit the ground.

And no that is not enough they even cranked up the burn speed by far so that if your mates do not instantly save you or throw a choke bomb (which is basically useless because it got also nerfed) you are out of the game in a very short time. Often enough you are not able to get your mate back because the bounty already left the game.

The official reason for this was they wanted to break up stalemates so people are not camping around dead bodies for hours. The effect is that people are even more camping now because the risk of getting burned is so high and punishing that it further promotes the passive meta, sitting around an waiting for others to make a move to third party them. Which means more stalemates and more boring camping.

Again everyone can play as they want and if people like to camp and sit around it is absolutely their right to do so and play the game this way. But I do not enjoy this at all, that is why the current development towards this gameplay is loosing me as a player.


- Matchmaking

Crytek changed the matchmaking system so that more players are in the six star bracket (the hightest bracket is six stars, most players are around 3-5 Stars). The Skill difference between a high six star player and a low six star players feels way bigger than the difference between 3 and low 5 star. In Six star you have a lot of bush camping snipers and a few shooter gods that are just very very good at the game.

Sometimes you get matches with a mix of 6, 3 and 4 Star Players in a trio that have a 5 Star Rating as a team. More in detail: this is a game about missed opportunities, which also reflects the history of the developers — once promising innovators, who over the years have lost their advantages and APIs.

It’s worth making a remark right away: I played all my hours exclusively with a friend who kept calling me into it; on my own, I regret every hour spent there after the eightieth, with rare exceptions only because of that friend.

[h3] Players [/h3]
First, an important point: the game is not widely known, the influx of new players is small. After each “major” update (more on that later), the number of players rises by about 50% — from ~20k to ~30k. When servers are divided by region for ping, this makes the pool quite small and closed.

And when we have a small community in one pseudo-hardcore game, we get annoying types you don’t want to meet. One of the main downsides is the unpleasant player base, which sticks to the meta, camps, and spams traps. Sure, that’s a matter of taste, but the game is extremely poor in counterplay options — there are few, if any.

Also, many belong to a rare breed of toxics who, after a match, if you killed them in a way they didn’t like, will pilgrimage to your Steam profile and tell you exactly what they think of your playstyle, you, and your relatives.

[h3] Game [/h3]
The concept isn’t new anymore: it’s a PvPvE extraction shooter. Today that sounds like the most clichéd thing Ubisoft could release. However, once upon a time, Hunt was one of the first in this field.

The game has a unique setting — 19th-century America with a mix of occultism, monsters, and dark magic, a variation on Supernatural. But here we hit problems that, in my opinion, are 100% the developers’ fault — unwillingness to risk, lack of staff or good designers. In fact, the setting isn’t revealed at all.

We have a bunch of weapons, which boil down to 4–5 types: rifles, pistols, shotguns, melee, and unique. They may have modifications — like sawn-off or scoped versions. The differences between them are pretty subjective within the same class and caliber.

The topic of magic isn’t revealed either. Recently we got an FPV drone — a magical beetle for scouting and small suicide damage — as well as a mine detonated with magic.

This season added Tarot cards, but there are two “buts.” In fact, they’re just consumables like heals or antidotes, only with different effects. The only difference is the way you obtain them.

There are also tons of traps — bear traps and tripwires, barbed or poisonous — and they come not by 1, but 2–3 per slot. You have to remove them manually or with a grenade; but grenades still trigger them, so they do their job of blocking paths and alerting others.

The gameplay is moving from one point to another, fighting zombies while searching for the boss and clues. Loop: collect three clues → find the boss → kill it → extract reward → other players attack → kill them or run like a sad weasel → extract → profit???

But there are hidden problems. Ammo is limited, and without resupply (fairly accessible), you may not have enough for two fights with players — let alone the boss and hunters chasing you.

Also, you don’t want to make noise — so suddenly you’re not in a shooter but in a Rambo simulator: sneaking past dogs, coops, branches, old lady Zina, and stabbing zombies with a knife.

Fights with players generally work, but the game is still oppressive. Headshots are one-shot kills from everything, so every time you peek, there’s a ~40% chance you’ll die instantly. Sure, friends can revive you — maybe — but nothing guarantees they won’t die, or you won’t be shot again. After a revive, you STAND UP immediately, even if you were crouched before — like a gopher in an open field.

But the main issue is the futility of it all. Bosses give ~500–800 currency for extraction. Enough for budget builds, but nothing else — only money and XP for hunters and account.

A hunter can take perks, most of which are useless except maybe four. If you hire a non-free hunter for 100, you instantly get 10 perk points to buy key ones.

Leveling the account unlocks gear and perks. At max level, you just get 1000 money per level, removing any money problems. You can reset to zero for prestige, but it gives nothing — only takes money and XP.

So we have no economy and complete futility in doing the main task, which is sometimes unpleasant by itself (like stabbing bosses with knives or shovels).

[h3] Developers [/h3]
The most depressing part is the so-called “game development.” Developers moved to a seasonal model. Each season brings minimal balance tweaks, usually like this:
“We’ve disabled bleed ammo because it’s too strong. Now you must find it on the map.”

There are almost no real number tweaks or weapon changes. “New” weapons are usually modifications. In a good update, we might get one truly new weapon and maybe a map.

Also, developers don’t add new mechanics permanently. They lock them in a season and then remove them.

For example, they added barbed branches. Sounds exciting, right? In practice, it was just a second type of branch: same crunch, but applied bleeding you had to stop. Not genius, not complex, just unpleasant. And after one season, they removed them.

Speaking of magic: in one season (maybe the same), there was a covenant mechanic. You could find spots, poke an object, and join a group. This could change perks and give one unique perk.

One group had a perk to deal damage once. It cast quickly, was convenient, and at least slightly revealed the magic theme.

New season — no covenants, no perk. Now we collect Tarot cards. Likely they’ll remove them too.

Thanks to this game, I fell into the grimdark rabbit hole of 40K lore—and I regret nothing!”", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1762527337}, {"review_text": "This review was written during the release of the Horde update, around 30th of June after I had some experience with it.

I've written this review of each part of the game.

[b]== Campaign ==[/b]
Short and to the point. Continues a few hundred years after the first game. You have two enemy factions and both are devastating and different enough. The story is you visiting the mothership, talking and taking in some lore parts and then going on missions that seemingly are impossible. Intertwined with the campaign are the co-op missions that an away-team does. You can do these missions too online with others and earn experience in the various classes. But about that later. 

The main campaign has very little freedom in terms of what weapons you carry or what ability you have. You're tied to Titus the entire run. That's fine and the campaign serves it's purpose and has a good ending. You have a few collectibles along the way but nothing else. A linear shooting experience that ends and leaves you to go explore the other aspects of the game: co-op and player versus player.

[b]== Co-op Mode ==[/b]
Mainly consists of 9 or so missions with difficulties going up from super easy to damn near impossible dice roll games. I would say the last 3 difficulties are the real normal, hard and impossible and everything before that most would avoid. The playerbase is rather small, even with cross platform, that all the limiting factors can sometimes mean you can't even find players at certain hours of the day. Even with quickplay and choosing Ruthless which I believe is the most common played difficulty mode because it's not too hard and gives the best rewards. 

Leveling in this mode takes forever since there's a prestige mode that goes up 4 times for each class and there are nearly 10 classes in the game. I've forgotten exactly how many, but they boil down to two categories: melee focused or ranged focused. 

Melee focused come with some defenses, but mainly the Bulwark class feels the best designed for later difficulties. As you get higher and higher you will challenge higher difficulties but don't be surprised that you'll never get a full combo off after a certain threashold and the game will boil down to counters, gun strikes and parries online combined with ranged combat. I've only managed to max prestige 2 classes in nearly 100 hours of game time and this is me repeating ruthless over and over again, doing whatever missions others are doing. The difficulties beyond that like Lethal are a dice roll if the mission will even be successful as the damage sustained seems to go up 4x times.

[b]== Horde mode ===[/b]
Newly released this comes with only two difficulties: normal and hard. Normal being insane beyond stages 15 with just the sheer number of enemies that flood your screen and hard being the absolute insane mode where only prestige 4 max'd out and optimized builds can survive. The resources you get don't feel meaningful because it's just health and ammo you have to invest it into and the others don't seem to make much of a difference. A dreadnaught is at best a distraction and gets stuck on map geometry and the other troops get tramped in seconds. I've yet to see anyone buy the buffs because of how expensive they are and they only last 5 minutes. 

Doesn't help that a single run rewards you with almost nothing. Same things as before and some recolors of pre-existing skins. Your average run can take up an hour of non-stop near-wipe moments only to get a single red skin of a weapon you might not even use. The experience is meaningless for those doing hard mode because they are max rank anyway and currency loses meaning quickly too, not to mention upgrade chips. 

In short: Horde mode does add some new challenge but it rewards you with LESS than what the campaign reruns would and doesn't allow you to be low level. If you try to level using the horde mode you're going to have a really bad time. 

[b]== PvP Mode ==[/b]
I've only tried a few games and I can't give a review of this mode. The arenas seemed small and since it's entirely separate from the PvE campaign you pretty much have to start from level 1. I'm guessing it takes hundreds of hours to get anywhere meaningful and the PvP doesn't seem to have any real depth I don't see how this appeals to people. The same classes are there and there are many players playing it it seems but expect just a lot of non-communicating Russian players if you're from the EU trying the PvP mode out. It's a nice extension to the game and perhaps something to jump into once you're done with the base game and PvE, but I saw no real depth in it. You see someone? Shoot. Oh he has a better gun? You lose. Rinse and repeat 10-20 lives. 

[b]== DLC ==[/b]
It's all cosmetic and it's kind of the bad greedy cosmetic type. Very expensive class-exclusive armor pieces that I wouldn't recommend buying unless you get them on a massive sale. That's about it. Even colors are locked behind DLC etc. and it's what it is. Not a fan. Not buying it unless they go down to 2€ / 2$ a piece or all together in a bundle for 10€. Just not worth my money as they add nothing to the gameplay.

[b]== Conclusion ==[/b]
The campaign and PvE of this game has had me entertained. The various guns and their perks combined with various classes together give enough wiggle room that you want to try a different build one more time. The armor rewards are also fancy and there's a lot to customize. It's a shame there is massive oversight in certain parts of the game, like no way to test builds in an arena and no damage numbers to see the effect of your perks. You just have no idea if one perk is better than another without locking them in and going through a 5 minute loading screen (waiting on console bros) and 20-30 minute mission just to test them out. 

Melee combat can also be very clunky at times. The game is 100% designed console first. Your character lunges at random enemies on PC unless you hold your WASD keys in the direction you want to go. Gun strikes and parries are also a must to learn and require skill. However especially in the horde mode with 10 big mobs on you a simple dodge will force you into a gunstrike and the animation for it twists your POV, blocking a possible other attack coming. 

I would even say that most deaths for veteran players come from this stupid camera angle twisting that you can't disable. You get locked into a gun strike and an enemy hits you from behind or behind your character and next thing you know you're stunlocked to death. Oh and there's plenty of dying from full health too from a surprise attack and sometimes the sound and effect that's supposed to warn you of a pending attack just forgets to trigger. So in short you get blinded by dumb camera, stunlocked by excess mobs and locked in a strike animation you didn't want to do. This can cause endless frustration for those trying to get better in the game and higher ranks. 

[b]== Recommendation ==[/b]
The game is stunning, has a good story and enough leveling and stuff to keep you entertained at least 40-50 hours. 100 if you like to complete things and love the lore and universe. There's plenty here to collect and immerse yourself in and frankly Warhammer 40k has had some good games recently and Space Marine 2 is the "console friendly" game that even PC gamers can enjoy for a while.

Story / Campaign. 

A solid solo or coop experience, a little short (six hours I think) looks good and is very (modern) Warhammer 40k - However the meat of the game isn't here....

PvP

Tacked on mode, quick bit of fun but some weird balancing (and no team balancing) taints the experience. Very old school third person shooter multiplayer feel.

PvE - Operations / Siege / Strategems 

This is the meat of the game, two factions Tyranids & Chaos:

Tyranids

9/10 - Look great and feel fantastic to fight, melee or ranged. Literally only objections are:
-Zoanthropes who have a buggy eye beam attack which can double hit you and hit you through walls.  
-Spore mines, have an incredible tendency to just nuke you from nowhere at certain times. Feels quite cheap. 

Chaos

7/10 - Chaos is just nowhere near as fun to fight. No blood and guts feedback, endless ranged poking. Chaos marines standing there shooting you while you hit them in the face. I would say 80% of my runs are Tyranid missions. However, Chaos has gotten better to fight over the game's lifetime.

Mechanics

Dodge / Parry & Gunstrike - I really like the implementation of this in Space Marine, it's not too hardcore but leaves plenty of room for skill expression. You need a mix of the two to survive and thrive. A criticism is that roll spamming is too effective and teaches new players bad habits. Gunstrikes (where you get a "critical" pistol attack animation after a perfect dodge or parry) are a fantastic mechanic. 

Health system & Contested HP - When you take health damage you have a small window to do damage to regain it. This is to promote Doom-esque aggressive play. Sadly it feels like the developers are determined to make this mechanic frustrating for players. So many things prevent you from regaining contested HP unless you have certain perks for your characters. It's deeply frustrating to land a powerful melee attack and watch your contested HP regain by a tiny sliver, or bug and not recover at all. This forces players into picking certain perks & (ranged) weapons that can actually get you your contested HP back.

"Healing" is really quite rare, especially on higher difficulties. Limited healing stim packs spawn and a few class perks can allow healing too. I actually like this implementation and just wish contested HP was a little better. 

Executes & Armour - Your other defensive tools, certain actions give you execution I-frames and also restore Armour. These animations looks incredible and are great fun. 

This combines for a fantastic ranged & melee experience. Getting better at the game and working up the difficulties feels great. 

Look & Sound

This game has phenomenal sound design, Only criticism is that the warning sound for "you need to dodge this attack" or "you need to parry this attack" are too similar. Overall the sounds of combat are just incredible the parry noise, the gunstrike noise, the noises each enemy makes. Wow. 

The game looks incredible, especially the marines and their armour & equipment. The free camera while you're performing an execution combined with custom FOV lets you really admire just how good the games looks in motion. 10/10. 

Customisation

One of the big draws to this game was the cosmetic customisation of your character/classes in PVE. Yes, you might need to buy some DLC to get juicy parts, but overall it has been a joy to build up my own roster of Space Marines. 

Now we come to the main flaws in the game:

Key criticism 1 - Matchmaking, the "hub" & loading screens

The "actually getting into a game" experience is really, really poor in Space Marine 2. The "hub" where you change your character and matchmake takes forever to load in and out of and this game does A LOT of loading in and out. 
>Load the game
> Wait to main menu to load, press enter, wait for it to load
>Press continue, wait to load

>Intro cutscene

For me this is an objective and fundamental flaw of this game. It wastes your time and is painful. It prevents you from getting to the gameplay, which is fantastic. 

Key criticism 2 - Bugs & janky mechanics 

I've said above that when you are in the flow of the combat loop, parrying, dodging, execute animatons the game feels incredible. The flip side are the things that "break" this loop. On higher difficulties mistakes are severely punished (which you expect!) but certain mechanics see you lose massive chunks of your HP or flatout die in an instant.

-Zoanthrope eye beams are deeply frustrating and countless time have nuked me through a wall or other substantial cover, regularly do "double damage" which will oneshot you at higher difficulties.
-Spore mines are an utter nightmare, you can get rid of a hundred of these but then one will just pop near you and goodbye to a massive chunk of your HP. 
-"grab" mechanic; certain enemies can grab you from an ambush attack. Often this is avoided due to a warning & a well timed dodge. Although this is typically only a major issue of higher difficulties when you fight large groups.Main gripe with these is that the Terminators continue to do them while you are at close range, which feels cheap and stupid. 

The above is a bit of a moan but it is so so frustrating to fight your way through a massive horde, come out without a scratch, feeling incredible. Next fight a spore mine or Zoan beam nukes you .

Conclusion

If you like Warhammer 40k & Spacemarines along with hack & slash horde shooters this is a wonderful game. If you want a solo or coop PVE experience that requires a bit of skill but isn't too hardcore this game is a fantastic fit. Yes, there are frustrating aspects which stop me from labelling this a truly great game but the core experience is so so good. Note: edited slightly after 8.0 Siege Mode patch

Space Marine 2 gets so many things right that the things it gets wrong are even more frustrating than they otherwise would be. A quick aside -- I enjoy the WH40K universe but I am not a giant lore junkie like some of my friends. That said, I have played a ton of WH games over the years. Being a WH40K fan is not required to enjoy the game.

First off, the things this game does right:
* The entire game is gorgeous, the environments are incredible, and the sound design is fantastic.
* You get to wield a great variety of Space Marine weaponry and most of it slaps HARD.
* There is a TON to unlock after the single-player game is done in Operations mode.
* Combat is INCREDIBLY well-done -- combined with the class, weapon, and heraldry upgrade systems the game loops work together to make an incredibly compelling whole.
* The execution animations are brutal and still fun even after dozens of hours.
* The game can practically be a Space Marine Heraldry Simulator -- there is a TON to unlock.
* Many new things for operations have been added since launch: missions, weapons, and enemy types. More are coming, even a new class and horde mode. (Edit: horde mode is out and it is SO SO GOOD)
* The modding community for this game is AWESOME. Look for the Astartes overhaul mod. You're welcome. :)
* Official mod support virtually guarantees this game will have interesting things to do for years to come, even when the developers wrap up.

Some of the things the game flubs a bit:
* Some of the dialog during the single-player campaign is ... just bad.
* The AI bots are fine for the campaign but they pretty much SUCK in the ongoing operations mode, especially as you increase the difficulty.
* There are several GLARING omissions in the heraldry selection, such as some decals only being available for the left pauldron or the right but not both. I am not an expert, but as I understand most of these omissions are not lore accurate. (Note: this will likely improve with future updates, this review was mostly written around patch 7.2 and later patch notes indicated major improvements are coming here)
* There are some niggling bugs that can be very frustrating, especially at higher difficulties where mistakes are incredibly punishing.

And the things that make this game wildly frustrating:
* Load times are unacceptably bad. Game launch to entering your first Operation can take well over 5 minutes, even on a good PC. I have watched task manager and nothing is particularly busy even though the loading progress bar isn't doing much. (I have had plenty of time to stare at it)
* You have to load into the game FAR too many times. I completely understand a big load when you launch a game, but the game seems to re-load nearly everything every time you return to the Operations hangar. Which you do after every mission. Or after failing to join a multiplayer game. Or after leaving a multiplayer game. You get the idea.
* Multiplayer matchmaking is an absolute travesty. You either start a game with a friend or 2 or you hope you get teamed up with someone. Unless you join a game where the class you wanted to play is already taken. Which you don't find out until AFTER you load into the mission. Or if you don't actually join an in-progress mission and instead show up at another player's hangar but they are AFK. Combine this with the load time issue and it can take up to 10 minutes to get into a game if you have to try several times to successfully join something. Why there isn't a list of games available for you to pick from or the ability to just start your own game is completely beyond me.
* And finally, these issues are intensified by matchmaking that just silently breaks which requires you to either return to the title screen (requiring two long-as-heck load screens) or quit entirely and restart.
* These 3 things combine to make for an INTENSELY frustrating experience. Normally I would just stop playing a game with this many negatives that reinforce each other, but the game is THAT good. It is STILL worth playing.

I want to end on a positive note -- this game is phenomenal. You can get around a lot of the matchmaking stuff by playing solo up to a difficulty you can manage with the AI or with friends / people from the official Discord server. At that point the load times are merely annoying as missions take 20-40 minutes to complete.

You can spend a silly amount of time just enjoying the Heraldry simulator. And then when you find a look that you like you can go punch a Terminid or a Chaos marine with your Power Fist. What I Like:

Tons of unique characters (called Legends), each with different weapons and styles.

The combat is smooth, fast-paced, and really fun.

You can play online, offline, ranked, or just casually with friends.

Cross-platform works great — I play with friends on console while I'm on PC.

It’s completely free and not pay-to-win.

Some matchmaking can feel unfair, especially at low ranks.

The community can be toxic sometimes, like in most competitive games.

Cosmetics are a bit expensive if you care about looks.

✅ Tons of Characters & Crossovers: From Rayman to WWE superstars, the roster keeps growing.
✅ Easy to Learn, Hard to Master: Simple controls but deep mechanics make it great for casuals and pros alike.
✅ Frequent Updates: New legends, skins, and balance patches keep things fresh.
✅ Cross-Platform & Stable Netcode: Play with friends on any platform with smooth online matches.

The Bad:
❌ Monetization Can Be Annoying: While the game is free, unlocking legends without spending money takes time.
❌ Floaty Combat Feel: Some players might not enjoy the aerial-heavy movement style.
❌ Matchmaking Can Be Hit or Miss: Ranked can sometimes feel unbalanced, especially for new players.

Final 
Brawlhalla is one of the best free-to-play fighters around, offering fun combat and a growing community. While it may not replace Smash Bros., it holds its own as a fantastic alternative for PC and consoles.

Overview
Hell Let Loose is a hardcore World War II first-person shooter that offers an unparalleled level of immersion and realism. With 103 hours of total game time and approximately 99 hours of combat time under my belt, I can confidently say that this game is not for the faint of heart.

Pros
Immersive Atmosphere
- Stunning sound design that puts you right in the middle of the battlefield
- Historically accurate recreations of WWII battlefields
- Intense and unpredictable combat scenarios

Realistic Gameplay
- Death can come from anywhere, at any time
- Snipers, bombing runs, and strafing attacks keep you on your toes
- Emphasizes tactical thinking and situational awareness

The planes look really good and together with the realistic landscape, clouds, rain effects etc. makes it a pleasure to fly. Just don't think of it like DCS or Flight Simulator. This is the kind of game that you would find in the Arcade: put in some coins, sit in a cockpit and shoot stuff. 

For the best experience I highly recommend using a controller. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
Most of the visuals are still good I especially enjoyed the clouds, landscapes, weather effects and the (massive amount of) planes as well as the sensation of speed. 

There is a variety of airplanes and the models look really good. I like that you can unlock mods to make them better and that you can get more planes: there is a huge variety of US, Soviet, Russian and some European airplanes. There are also some sci-fi planes (mostly through DLC) that are usually OP (and not recommended to use on the first run). 

It's cool that the environment can works against you (finding enemies hiding under a blanket of clouds), ice that affects the flight model. But sometimes the environment also helps you (using the trail of SAMs to locate SAM sites that are not yet on your radar).

There is a replay mode at the end of each mission and I love the tactical review when you've completed the missions. It's just small details but it adds a lot of immersion.

There are plenty of achievements to get and stuff to unlock.

Multiplayer is still available.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
If you're looking for a flight simulator then this is definitely not the game for you with planes carrying 100+ missiles. 

The story is cringe but thankfully you can skip it.

[H1]Bugs and glitches[/H1]
I didn't encounter any bugs.

There are 28 DLCs: many are included in the Season Pass. They add more playable planes to the game. None are required and for the first play through you probably want to just use the planes that the base game give you (or that you are able to unlock). It's worth getting them when on sale. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
Ace Combat 7 is a great arcade flight sim. The visuals are good; there are so many planes and there is even a cringe story. The landscape and the weather effects are impressive. It’s a bit like Animal Crossing, but with a more lively and magical vibe. Every character has their own personality, unique quests, and fun little interactions. You really start to get attached to them, and it feels like you’re part of the village. There’s a lot to unlock, tons of freedom with decorating and building, and you can easily spend hours just rearranging everything to make it your own.
There’s always something to do, gardening, cooking, mining, fishing, exploring, seasonal events... it's super varied. [h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

✔️ 45+ hours played

At first, I loved this game. It was cozy, charming. But over time, it turned into one of the most frustratingly greedy games I’ve spent money on.

If you're a big Disney fan, you'll probably still find joy here. But be warned: this game is no longer about fun and creativity. It's become a monetisation machine.

🎮 Gameplay

The core gameplay loop is relaxing and enjoyable

- Complete quests with Disney characters

- Decorate your valley

- Farm, mine, cook, and craft

- Explore themed realms

There's a ton of running back and forth, and certain quests feel like filler designed to slow you down and stretch playtime.

Post launch, there hasn't been meaningful progress on the main story in over a year. Most updates are just seasonal events, reskins, or content locked behind another paywall.

⚙️ Customisation & Progression

Customisation is the heart of the game. Outfits, furniture, valley layout, it’s all here and looks great. But so much of it is now locked behind:

- Premium currencies!

- FOMO-driven battle passes!

- A high-priced cash shop!

Oh, and if you want your valley to look amazing? Be ready to either spend money or feel like you're constantly missing out.

🪙 Monetisation Model

Here’s where it really falls apart

The game was originally promised to be Free-to-Play
Then they:

- Made it Buy-to-Play permanently....

- Kept the free-to-play-style monetisation system....

- Introduced a $38.99 (CAD) DLC the same day it left early access....

- Launched a premium shop with rotating FOMO items....

Continued with seasonal Battle Passes (Star Paths) that offer little on the free tier and hide the best content behind the paid track....

You pay full price for the game!
Then pay again for the DLC!
Then keep paying if you want premium outfits, furniture, or to access better rewards during events!

It's the worst of both worlds, a full-priced game with the cash shop of a mobile gacha....

📈 Content & Story

Content updates are frequent but often shallow

- New characters rarely have deep quests

- Still waiting to unlock areas teased since launch

- Events and new items mostly serve to push you into the shop or Battle Pass

There was a story about the Forgetting, the ruler of the valley, and mysterious magic, but it's barely moved in over a year. Everything since has felt like stalling.

🔁 Development & Communication

The developers started strong
But communication has dropped off

- Updates are often buggy

- Multiplayer was added, but it’s extremely limited

- Bug fixes are slow

- Key issues remain unfixed for months

Worse, they still show characters in trailers that aren’t in the game, even after two years

It really feels like the priority shifted from making a good game to maximizing profit.

❌ Downsides

- Microtransactions in a non-free game

- $40 DLC for features that should’ve been base game

- Star Path is FOMO-fueled and punishing if you skip it

- Premium shop uses paid currency, with tiny drip-feed earn rates

- Story is stagnant

- Customisation is great but often locked behind paywalls

- Major quality-of-life features still missing

- Still buggy after two years

- Very little depth once you’ve played 20-30 hours

- You can’t even sit on most furniture

✅ Final Thoughts

Is the game fun? Sometimes, yes
Is it worth the money? Not anymore

If you care about cozy sims and Disney, this might still hook you.
But if you care about ethical monetization and value for money? Skip this.

There are better, cheaper, and more honest cozy games out there.
