[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Story, Gameplay, Soundtrack & Downside[/h3]

Playing GTA: San Andreas back then was like diving into a massive, incredibly realistic world. Los Santos, which looked a lot like Los Angeles with its fancy parts and rough gang areas, is where it all began to get "mainstream". Then San Fierro transported me to a foggy, hilly version of San Francisco, and Las Venturas took me to the flashy heart of early-90s Las Vegas in the middle of the desert. San Andreas size was mind-blowing, making it much bigger than Vice City. Truth be told tough: Vice City remains my all time favorite based on atmosphere alone.

Many regard GTA: San Andreas as the standout title in the original trilogy, and for good reason. Its map is significantly larger than those of its predecessors and the main storyline is twice as long. The game features compelling characters such as Big Smoke, Officer Tenpenny, and the protagonist Carl 'CJ' Johnson, who is famous for the quote: 'Ah shit... here we go again'. As with other GTA games, the plot centres on gang warfare and police corruption, but there are also intriguing subplots that keep players engaged. I won't spoiler anything here because even though its old and a classic, there might be people interested on how the story unfolds, so let me just tell you: It's awesome.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3566111170

Returning to Los Santos after his mother's mysterious death turned out to be far more complicated than we thought. Corrupt cops framed the protagonist for a police officer's death and sent him into gang territory. The iconic characters, such as Sweet, and friends Big Smoke and Ryder, made the whole thing even more gripping. Honestly, it had one of the best stories in the series. From CJ’s conflicted return to his roots to the brutal betrayal and massive plot twists, the story felt awesome!

San Andreas stands out thanks to its attention to detail and the wide range of activities it offers. From diverse missions to side quests, there are plenty of ways to keep players entertained. The freedom to explore the vast map and interact with a variety of characters enhances the game’s replayability. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3567941619

Furthermore, the streets of San Andreas come alive with dynamic interactions that respond to Carl's appearance. If he is overweight and out of shape, he becomes the target of mockery from others. If he is fit and well-dressed, the townspeople acknowledge this positively, offering supportive comments. This feature exemplifies the game’s vibrant world, where players can witness drug deals, citizens fleeing non-player-controlled criminals and everyday traffic incidents. For a game from 2004, this was mindblowing back in the day. These elements merely scratch the surface of San Andreas immersive gameplay quality. Cars even accumulate dust and grime.

Construction workers engage in vocal interactions with passing women, and law enforcement officers diligently pursue their targets until completely out of sight. These nuanced details contribute to the game’s depth, making the virtual world feel remarkably alive and responsive to the player’s actions.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3574988834

Despite the passage of time, the gameplay mechanics of San Andreas remain solid, standing as a testament to the title’s enduring appeal. Whether engaging in intense shootouts, high-speed chases, or simply soaking in the atmosphere of its world, GTA: San Andreas delivers a gameplay experience that has become a benchmark within the GTA series and the reason GTA 5 is what it is today and probably what GTA 6 will even improve further.

The downside, though, is in the sound department. Sometimes there is crackling, because the sound files are heavily compressed. Also: even when you're standing still, the sound of driving faster sometimes loops making it sound like you accelerate on a bike, but you are not. Some bugs are unnecessary and shouldn't be here. The modern controls for swimming and flying feel awful sometimes and CJ dives into the water when I only want to swim faster and press the X button repeatedly.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

In the world of open-world gaming, GTA: San Andreas is a timeless masterpiece that transcends its era. With its massive map, diverse cities and captivating storyline, it effortlessly embodies the essence of great gameplay. Its iconic status is elevated by the attention to detail, from dynamic evolving graphics to a responsive and vibrant world. The trilogy is a must-have for everyone who wants to experience a classic in a new look and yes it is worth it. The initial release of the Definitive Edition trilogy was poor, but they patched it. Not perfect, but completely playable. As someone who has completed all the games multiple times and still plays Vice City to completion like once a year, I can say: they're beautiful!

I'm about to be a bit critical, so I'd like to open by saying that I'm recommending this game because it draws inspiration from other games in all the right ways, and is clearly being made with love. This is such an interesting concept, the weapons are really interesting and fun to use, the upgrade system with the bells and stuff is really cool, there's a tonn of immersive polish helping the overall feel of the game, and the general lore gives me a lot of hope for the content that's to come!
- To add to this, I've found increasing the toughness and amount of the enemies to be extremely useful, and borderline essential to this game. Definitely play with it as you go if you find that you're too OP!

So at about 3 hours into this game, I saw essentially all the content that exists. For a $20 game, that may be a little steep to some, the stupid dollar-an-hour rule wouldn't add up without some serious grinding. - Sometimes the summoner enemies fail to summon guys, or summon them out of bounds, and then none of them summon anything until you fully close/reopen the game.

The loading times are great! It is really quick to jump into. The best part is that the game saves your progress when you quit. If you were in the middle of a run, you can quit, and later jump straight back in. This makes the game very accessible, and friendly for people with little time. The travel system and movement is also very fast; travelling back to where you died is actually fun, not a slog like in some other games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742407435}, {"review_text": "I was initially inclined to leave a thumbs-down due to the lack of indicators, but hey it's early access (not using it as an excuse), I understand that plans can change, and they clearly have in this case. The game will no longer feature just 6 levels, but rather a significantly larger number, spanning across different biomes. Regarding the absence of indicators, the primary concern stems from the fact that the game currently offers only two playable levels. While it's possible to infer that the lack of a tome suggests no additional levels to unlock, this is not immediately obvious to players. However, I do appreciate the inclusion of a roadmap in the menus, as well as the "unstuck" button—thank you for those additions. It's clear that the developers care about the game's progression, but the overall scope and eventual endpoint remain somewhat unclear. It would be helpful if this were more transparently communicated. 

Visually, the game has a sleek design, and the traversal mechanics, though seemingly basic on the surface, feel fluid and satisfying. The core mechanics include dashes, a weapon throw for teleportation, and occasional grappling points. Combat is fluid and responsive, with dashing as the central feature, offering brief invincibility. Engaging enemies and landing hits gradually regenerates health, taking notes from the philosophy of Doom Eternal, where offense is the best form of defense.

There is a noticeable contrast between the first and second levels. The first is relatively linear and restricted, while the second offers much more exploration, with numerous points of interest and multiple layers to a degree of almost being a closed world in itself. There is loot to be discovered, and a strategic approach—where players complete expeditions to familiarize themselves with the map and gather resources before tackling the primary objective—seems beneficial. However, given that future maps are expected to be more numerous, but not necessarily as long (around two hours in dev's words), the quality of these new levels remains uncertain. While more content is always appreciated, it’s hard to predict whether the added quantity will match the quality of the initial levels.

The game also features elements of an extraction roguelite, not a roguelike (a distinction worth noting). This allows players to cleanse their equipment and retain it permanently. Additionally, equipment upgrades are available, and after reaching a certain tier, players will need to acquire duplicates of the same item to increase its "satiety." At the highest tier, RNG rolls come into play. Players can also level up their character to increase their overall damage output.

The game certainly holds promise, but I’ve witnessed many early access titles used primarily to fund development, a model that doesn't always succeed. While I’m not suggesting that this is the case here, some players may not fully grasp the valid concerns of the community. Being a solo developer is undoubtedly challenging, and I appreciate the developer’s commitment to continuously updating the roadmap and responding to every available feedback. That said, for some, the $20 price tag might feel steep although, with regional pricing and my own access to a free key, I felt my conscience wouldn’t allow me to take a personal hit on that. I’m genuinely invested in seeing where the game’s development goes, and I hope it lives up to its ambitions.

The review will be (kept) updated as the game continues to receive updates.

Absolutely crazy.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759943830}, {"review_text": "Already played the earlier versions/demos for 50+ hours as well so as of writing i have nearing 100 hour gameplay.

So are you one of those "gamers" who found TLOU the greatest gaming experience? Were you the one who spend hundreds of hours watching Geralt trailing his side hoes in W3? Maybe you are looking for a similar experience to a TES game? Then you are the wrong f*cking place my friend.

Voin doesn't have a story (i mean it does but its nearing a porn movie level). It doesn't have quest markers. It doesn't have dialogues. It has no handholding and pointing fingers. 

So what does Voin have then you might ask? Well. Gameplay. No wait, let me rephrase it and shout it into the eter:
 
G-A-M-E-P-L-A-Y

Voin feels like a huge throwback to the golden of the late 90s early 00s. The focus here is entirely in the game. You get thrown into the game, a short few minute tutorial section shows you the basic of controls and mechanics and that's it, you are already thrown into the world full of everything alive and trying to kill you. Sounds great eh? Well it is. 

The flow of this game is hard to capture in writing. Everything about this game feels fluid. Your char is not a slow realistic military guy like most of modern action games. No. Your character sports immense power , speed and tools of his disposal right from the start. Even just traversing around in this game is  a ton of fun. You get dashes, long dashes, multiple jumps, spells which makes you levitate and you can combine these tools to traverse the world. At first a novice player will spend long time walking while experts will cross the world in air without touching the ground once - mind you it takes a good few minutes as the playground is huge.

Game focuses in melee combat which is sadly rare and we don't have enough of these type of games. Sure you have soulslikes but they are pretty often play on the same side with slow 1o1 methodical combat while Voin happens at blazing game speed. You have a few set of RPG elements to make your char stronger and you have combinations of stuff which you can improve to increase the lethality of your guy.

What makes Voin truly outstanding is how it allows you to play around with the mechanics. Again late 90s eary 00s vibes. No handholding, no "this is balanced", no moral virtues. Fk no. Go and break the game the most you can.

Just an example , lets take a basic lightning weapon. You hit you do lightning occasionally. Sounds straightforward? But what if we combine it with another lightning effect which turns your lightning into chainjumping chainlightning mega nukes? Allright. But wait there's more. The weapon itself has abilities one of which makes you spin like a vortex (good ol' spin2win). You think the spinning will work with the on-hit effect of the lightnings? SUre it does! Will it proc on all enemies? I mean that would be op no? Heck no , blast those fukers apart. But wait there is still more. What is i tell you there is a special bossdrop hammer which also conjures more objects midfight on contacts summoning additional targets which can also be hit while spinning resulting in a loudspeaker shattering catastrophe of a lightning explosion?

And what if i tell you , that post this you still have the options of (currently) ice, fire, poison, pure phys, momentum and obscure versions of these weapons and abilities? The combination of your arsenal results in an insanely fun game which provides fun moment-to-moment gameplay which is fast lethal and very satisfying. On top of it the game has a trillion small extra nuance which enhances the gameplay. Most of these are hard to write down but if I'd have to then imagine small stuff like upgrading is not just N+1 "blacksmith hitting an anvil" but rather you use a sacrifical tollbell inside a magma room cleansing your equipment with a soundeffect so great you'll start upgrading your stuff 1 by 1 just to hear the bell tolling more. Or another instance is when i don't even know when was the lasts time where i just looked up to a mountain and said "yeah i'Ll climb that just for the fun of it!" did that and the game actually rewarded my exploration with some hidden enemies/loot leaving me with the satisfaction of playing the game for the sake of playing the game and not to fill meaningless achivement bars.

Last thing to note is that the game also has 1 last unusual option which is nice to have : the difficulty of this game is entirely on you. The game offers 3 set of bars in enemies density, quality, and toughness to choose on a scale of 1 to 6. So if you want you can make the game baby easy by putting everything down to 1 or go mega idiot mode by turning everything to the max. You can also do more specialised or more elegant versions say if you are a big dark souls fan you can put the density number down and toughness up , that way you can bossfight and enjoy duels more. While if you like more of an LeftforDead player you can crank numbers up while leaving them squishy to allow that for that grinding in enemies feel. 

This is a game made by a solo dev who has his clear vision on what he wants to do and hats off to it cuz it's working well so far. I can't eagerly wait till he finishes the final product. Haven't had such a fun gameplay focused game since the last Doom(2016) games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763647263}, {"review_text": "This game fucks so hard.

I think most people who've played a decent amount of games have probably at some point had a moment where, whilst playing a game that sucks but you can tell COULD'VE been good, they thought "Why did the developer/s not do this very obviously better thing? why did they choose to do this mechanic in this stupid way??" This game is like, In my opinion, if the dev actually did everything right.

While playing this game, every time I came across a decision that I've experienced being handled terribly in other games, I thought of how well it was handled in this game. The difficulty, the risk and reward, the upgrade system, travel/exploration, visuals, and almost certainly more that I'm forgetting.

The combat feels great. There's a certain weight to your swings that feels so meaty, and the speed of weapons overall isn't painfully slow like it is in other games. You're given frequent dodges and enemy attacks are clearly telegraphed so it feels sick when you perfectly dodge multiple attacks in a row, but it also does't make it too easy for you to dodge absolutely everything, between attack timing, attack variation, and just the amount of enemies there can be in a closed space sometimes.

The only downsides with the game I've encountered so far are:
1. A lack of playable content overall. As of writing this there's only two major locations, which you can run through decently quickly, in my experience.

2. A lack of story content. This just doesn't really exist at all at the moment. You get some very small tidbits, but that's about it as far as I can tell.

Both of the above are issues that are very obviously going to be fixed with time.

Look, I know I'm really hyping this game up a lot, but the fact of the matter is that at the end of the day, I REALLY like this game, and I really really hope it does well. If you have the money and like fast-paced combat focused games, buy this game. If you don't have the money and like fast-paced combat focused games, wait until a sale, and then buy this game.

Before reading my review I will admit I adore this game and those similar to it so my opinion may be slightly biased so take my words with a pinch of salt.

Voin is exactly what it says on the tin, A power fantasy hack and slash game. The only way I can describe it is an addicting mix of Doom (2016/Eternal) and Ultrakill giving you a game where you cleave through enemies in a immensely satisfying way with bursts of dopamine from loot drops. Without further ado let me talk about the parts of this game that I love.

The good:

- This is game is absolutely fantastic at a core level, with most aspects of the game being brief but well though-out.
- The weapons and other equipment (while limited) are very creative and allow for some very cool synergies especially when you get to the firstborn equipment. 
- Enemies have unique designs that make them easy to identify even when you are in the middle of combat.
- Movement feels extremely smooth without being so quick that it makes you dizzy, the added touch of drawing your weapon causing you to sacrifice some manoeuvrability was a really neat touch that makes the game a bit more immersive.
- The abilities we have access to at the moment feel very cathartic to use.My personal favourite being the lighting sting with its wind up and slow motion which makes you feel like a walking Demi-god when you rip through a pack of enemies with it.
- The world design is nearly perfect in my opinion, the areas look beautiful with the lighting and day/night cycle adding greatly to how good it looks. The areas themselves are very well though out with enemies, fast travel points, landmarks and secret loot all being placed in a very deliberate and methodical manner which reminds me greatly of the Dark souls games.

The Bad:
While I've listed this section as "the bad" this is really just small nitpicks and parts of the game that will definitely be addressed in future updates with the Dev communicating with the player-base in a very clear manner using a roadmap. With that in mind take all the point below not as massive flaws in the games design but things that people should likely know before buying.

- The game is definitely on the shorter side, even with exploring both maps as much as possible and multiple hours of grinding in order to get all my gear up to first born it only took me about 6 hours before I felt I had run out of things to do. 
- The enemy variety is overall great but it feels like the game could definitely use some more mini-boss type enemies that appear throughout the areas.
- Weapons are in a slightly weird situation where they, at a basic level, have good levels of variety between them but once you start getting into it the synergies, it feels like certain weapons have cool abilities but they almost always want to be used with an extremely fast attacking weapons in order to make their effect viable which limits what you can do when combining certain weapons greatly. 
- My final little nitpick is the Hub area, don't get me wrong it looks absolutely stunning but the distance between the portals to the different areas and the portals to get to the equipment/level rooms can definitely feel a little grating after a few hours.

Conclusion:
The game is a great example of why Indie games are always so beloved by the gaming community, The good parts of this game greatly out-weigh the bad parts to me but even if the issues I previously mentioned really ruin the game for you, put it on your wishlist and a give at a few months and I guarantee half my complaints will have literally disappeared completely. If you want to switch it up so you can just go in and farm ichor (the game's equivalent of souls) from plentiful weak enemies you can, or you can increase the strength of those enemies and get more ichor from killing them.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a multiplayer survival game by Klei Entertainment, building on the success of the original Don’t Starve. Players are thrown into a dark, eerie world filled with challenges and must cooperate (or compete) to survive. The game features a unique art style, intriguing lore, and demanding gameplay mechanics that test creativity and strategy.

[h1] Story and Atmosphere [/h1]
The game’s lore is subtle yet engaging. Players are stranded in the Constant, a mysterious world filled with strange creatures and environmental hazards. The story unfolds through exploration and scattered clues, leaving much to player interpretation. The gothic hand-drawn art style and atmospheric music amplify the eerie, survival-focused tone.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
At its core, the game is about survival—gathering resources, crafting items, and fending off dangers such as hunger, darkness, and hostile creatures. Multiplayer introduces new dynamics, requiring teamwork to split tasks, defend against threats, and manage limited resources. The challenge increases with changing seasons, each bringing unique obstacles like freezing winters or scorching summers.

[h1] Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Unique Art Style: The hand-drawn, Tim Burton-esque visuals stand out.
    [*]Replayability: Randomized worlds and dynamic challenges keep the experience fresh.
    [*]Multiplayer Depth: Cooperative gameplay adds layers of strategy and fun.
    [*]Challenging Yet Rewarding: Success feels earned due to the game’s difficulty.
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1]
[list]
    [*]Steep Learning Curve: The lack of hand-holding can overwhelm newcomers.
    [*]Resource Management Pressure: Balancing food, sanity, and health can feel repetitive.
    [*]Team Dependency: Multiplayer can frustrate if teammates are inexperienced or uncooperative.
[/list]

[h1] Final [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a creative and challenging survival experience that rewards teamwork and strategy. While it may not suit players seeking a casual experience, fans of survival games will appreciate its depth and charm.

[h1] Score: 87/100i [/h1]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1735769946}, {"review_text": "The goal of Don't Starve Together is to find and fight all ~ 26 boss monsters, a lot of which can be more or less hidden.

Two of these bosses are considered "final bosses" in the sense that killing them is the big accomplishment of two separate journeys with many different steps, one taking you deep in horribly dangerous underground dungeons and one taking you all around the sea.
After each of these 2 bosses, new content is added in the form of new "post game" world modifications that each gives new bosses, new mechanics, new weapons, armor and technologies to use.

I wanted to start by describing that because DST looks deceptively more simple than it truly is when you first take a look a it, when in truth it actually is quite complex, rich and intricate!



In this game, surviving is tough and difficult and requires you to understand a lot of different specific steps, and understand how many resources are tied together or meant to be exploited in strange and unexpected ways.
At first it feels like learning to stay alive during each of the 4 seasons is the game, and it won't necessarily make you feel like it's super deep because it is actually only step one. It's supposed to be simple and slow! It's possible to survive a year without too much trouble in a kind of baren base with not so much stuff at your disposal, but that is very far from the goal, which is about learning to thrive and accumulate wealth in order to get out there and fight bosses (that won't come to you unless you come to them.)

There are lots of different resources you can take from the world and bring back home, creatures who'se homes you can move, beneficial structures you can acquire, all kinds of things that are meant to saturate you in food, tools, weapons and armors for your many expeditions.

But the game never holds your hand through any of it at all. Learning can be really unclear and counter-intuitive (who would think that butterflies are the most basic and most essential source of food early game, or that you are supposed to relocate pig houses around a pen in order to have a steady supply of armor every full moon? No one, at first!) and every step of the way can make you think "is that it?" just because you may likely fail to see the link between things for a while, or how you are meant to abuse the heck out of them, or how they are just stepping stones towards something bigger.
It's a game that you just won't be able to enjoy if you struggle with challenging yourself. You need to throw yourself out there, be active, be looking to learn and practice survival techniques and get busy trying to do things on a grander scale, or do research about which bosses should be next and how to reach them.
Knowledge is either difficult to acquire on your own or requires you to practice several times to get it right, and then so much better than right. It can be intimidating, which can make you become a bit too passive and invite boredom because you're nowhere near having completed all there is to complete, but you may not understand how to get there, or how to learn.

Nothing research and interacting with the community can't fix though!
I regularily give many tips and explanations to people from a particular discord community server, it's a great vibe.



All in all, I recommend this game with all of my heart with the knowledge that it really may not be for everybody, especially if you tend to be too passive or can't bother with putting too much effort into trying to overcome challenges. 
It's my own favorite survival game out there specifically because it gives survival so much purpose and so many steps, because of how much effort you can put into learning and how rewarding it can be; but it can put some people off.

There's a lot of ways to achieve the same things. Tons of different knowledge, a bunch of different mechanics that you will likely gloss over for a couple hundred hours until you start using them and start realizing "why have I never bothered doing this awesome thing before" (like taming and riding big cows to become the ultimate war machine) 
There's fun in joining random worlds and seeing how you can contribute, fun in starting over and doing things better and quicker or in different order, fun in practicing the same skills because they're tough and require good habits, fun in seeing how everyone's lack of knowledge can create so many shenanigans due to lack of preparation, lack of resources, lack of having made enough structures in time, and fun in modding the game and tweaking the little things along the way.

There's lots to love!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1744153365}, {"review_text": "[h3] Okay guys, I played a little bit... It's time to finally write a review. I promise to be concise. [/h3]
This game is annoyingly obstinate in theme, design, and user interface. It comes packaged with a flimsy combat system, deliberately useless-sounding/actually-useless tools & structures, and a slightly uncanny and weird art style that's honestly something you just have to see for yourself.

[h3] This game is also kind of... hard. Maybe in a bad way. [/h3]
Seriously? Well, this is a positive review. I'll explain. Nothing gets explained to the player, and players basically just have to point and click on random stuff, make some random tools, and either die of darkness, or die of boredom once they've been sitting at a campfire for 8 minutes straight. If they survive longer, then they die of hounds. Live a little longer? Die to insanity. If somehow they make it to Winter... well, you can guess. I don't have any large praise for this game design, as while I look at this learning process fondly now... it's really frustrating at its core to be entirely honest. I was definitely interested in the game a LOT, don't get me wrong. There's no way I could have possibly played as much as I have now and probably more in the future if I didn't enjoy this, but this game is deliberately difficult: accomplished through ignorance and severely punishing mistakes. Y'know, as a solo-player game, I'd leave it at that, but there's more.

[h3] This game was not meant to be played alone. To that end, it is a lot like another game we all know and love. [/h3]
Minecraft. I think it's a lot like Don't Starve -- maybe not in genre -- but in the sense that the way players learn how to play the game is shockingly a bit similar. In Minecraft, not a whole lot is really explained, and I feel like, to a stranger, you can only really explain it as a game where you play with lego blocks and make crappy log cabins... like, forever (sounds boring?). 

Anyways, No One Learned How To Play Minecraft On Their Own. Seriously, how did anyone learn how to build their first nether portal? How did anyone figure out the ending of the game and all of the steps that led up to defeating the ender dragon? We all learned it through each other. Older siblings, friends, school peers, those crappy Minecraft journals at the book faire, ONLINE guides? That's how we learned, and that's how the public understanding of Minecraft became so advanced, for an otherwise obtuse and poorly explained game. 

[h3] That's Don't Starve. [/h3]
Dropping in on public servers, toiling away like a dolt, barely surviving with a few other, dull campers until some Enlightened Soul steps in to your base to actually organize it and show you the ropes of the game. You'd learn about crockpots, iceboxes, you might really get into base-building. Later, you'd learn about all the biomes, find out how to survive the seasons, start exploring the caves, etc. All at the advice of others in public lobbies or on the internet. All of the pitfalls of Don't Starve's deliberately difficult design and the obscure knowledge that players have to learn are all elements that make mentors and collaboration even more valuable. We all taught each other, and while this game did not truly start out as a multiplayer game... 

[b] I think I can at least say that the experience of sharing knowledge, learning the ropes, and tutoring new, acolyte survivors in this stupid, obtuse little survival game was truly valuable in the end. It's a solid remaster. The visual overhaul breathes new life into these RTS classics while maintaining that distinct Command & Conquer aesthetic. Both Tiberian Dawn and Red Alert plus their expansions are included, giving you plenty of content to work through. There are some rough edges here and there, but nothing that ruins the core experience. The price point feels just right for what you're getting.

The gameplay holds up remarkably well despite its age. You're still building bases, harvesting Tiberium, and commanding armies in that familiar rock-paper-scissors dance of unit counters. The pacing strikes a nice balance between resource management and combat, though you'll spend a good chunk of time waiting for your economy to ramp up. Your units die fast and hit hard, so positioning and timing matter more than raw numbers. It's a satisfying loop of expansion and destruction that keeps you coming back.

The remastered soundtrack by Frank Klepacki is the standout feature. The original compositions were already iconic, and this enhanced version amplifies everything that made them memorable. The music seamlessly shifts between industrial menace and triumphant marches, perfectly matching the on-screen chaos. 

What's genuinely shocking is EA's restraint here. No forced account creation, no always-online DRM, no microtransactions - just a straight remaster that respects the source material. The quality-of-life improvements like unit queuing and improved pathfinding modernize the experience without fundamentally changing it.

Overall, Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection is how remasters should be done - a faithful recreation that enhances rather than replaces.

This review may be long, so I'll try to cover the most important parts here in the beginning:

This 25th anniversary collection contains the very first game from 1995 (also known as Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn or C&C95) and its prequel, the original Red Alert. Both have fundamentally identical gameplay to the originals, but there are many Quality of Life features, bonus content including Behind the Scenes and Missions exclusive to the console ports, visual overhauls, and audio improvements. If you play this, you must keep in mind that the PC RTS genre was merely 3 or 4 years old when these were released. The gameplay tries to be as faithful as possible, so have an open mind about possibly dated level design.
That being said, this collection is an utter triumph as far as quality remasters go. More importantly, it's a glorious bright spot in the past 15 years of (mostly) neglect this franchise has faced from the holder of its Intellectual Property. EA did the fans right this time. They asked for community input and oversight and involved the Former Westwood Creators. If you're on the fence, this game frequently goes on sale for a bargain.
Please also consider the Ultimate Collection, which includes all 17 major PC releases (RIP Sole Survivor) including the ORIGINAL Win95 compatible versions ONLY of C&C95 and RA1. If you buy that one on sale it's technically less than $1 a game because of expansions. Finally, The Modding Community is excellent for many games in this series. Seriously, Mods revolutionized things for me once I discovered them. The dedication of the community is keeping this franchise alive even with a decade and a half of relative silence.


With that out of the way, I'm going to devote most of the rest of this to C&C95, so I want to quickly mention my thoughts on Red Alert 1. RA1 is probably the more approachable of the two. It has a fantastic competitive scene with a high skill ceiling (mostly on CNCnet). It can be fast-paced, and marks the birth of the Tank Rush. There are a multitude of missions. There is more variety of technologies and unit types, and the two factions are quite distinct. From a singleplayer/casual standpoint, feel free to experiment. I think it probably has one of the more impressive soundtracks in the series too, especially tracks from the Aftermath. (I have other personal favorites, but that's trying to look at it objectively). All-in-all, Westwood took a large step towards solidifying the identity of the series when they released it in 1996, and while it may be challenging, the gameplay holds up pretty well and the package here in the Remastered Collection has wonderful presentation.



Now, on to the main event. Command & Conquer 1 holds a special place in my heart. I am the same age, though I didn't realize how close until a few years ago. I didn't actually play the PC version until I got "The First Decade" collection from 2006. I DID however play the Nintendo 64 Port as a child, and I struggled with it. Most of my experience came as I grew up watching my Dad get wrecked by Kirovs in Red Alert 2 until he finally figured out how to prepare anti-air in time and subsequently defeat hard enemies. He showed me how to surround my base with pillboxes, and thus began my long history of turtling. I also yearned for Yuri's Revenge and Generals, which my cousin had. Naturally, I got a lot better with time, and once I got the First Decade, I was able to catch up on all the other games I'd missed. Nowadays I've become our family's resident LAN game and C&C Mod expert, so this series has remained very important to me. TFD is when I started to play C&C1 for real, and it was a journey that helped me improve in other games too.
So, most people would probably find C&C95's level design to be annoying, cryptic, or punishing. Why? In my opinion, it's a Puzzle game as much as it is an RTS. It quickly gained a reputation for me as "the game where you never have money." You will ALWAYS run out of money unless you farm or make bold moves. I am a shameless turtle, and I like the former method, but there are some impressive ways to humiliate the AI. (Please look up guides from Nyerguds, he loves this game even more than me and he's a pro.) In base-building missions, you need to micromanage your harvester so your Tiberium Field is not consumed. only harvest in diagonal "checkerboard patterns" and the resources will slowly grow back. If you don't, then the field will either be permanently gone or take an absolute eternity to grow back with only a Blossom tree.
When there is no base, or if you're strapped for cash, here's the other fun part about this game. YOU MUST MAKE EVERY UNIT COUNT... most of the time. I went back to the N64 version later, and I distinctly remember the GDI mission where you start with a few grenadiers on the beach taking out the three turrets so your MCV can arrive. I moved to the right and started getting some minigunners and a guard tower, but I didn't have enough money for a weapons factory. Then an early flame tank ate my infantry for breakfast and buildings for lunch. That left an impression on me that every choice I made in that game mattered. You will struggle to find the right strategy for every situation, but when resources are tight and you are put in impossible situations, you will come to appreciate the niche of every unit. You are also rewarded for keeping your units alive through micromanagement. Most of the series will let you slide by with tank spam, and if you're good enough you can probably get away with it here too (or maybe bike/buggy for Nod,) but this game will actually test you. It's the little things too, like the garbage HP and absurd cost of the Bazooka men is offset by excellent ability to take out tanks and guard towers if you can place them at the perfect range, or facing away with Mammoth Tank turrets to maximize the rocket attack. This is a game where the design is wholly different from everything that came after, and while that means it shows its age, C&C95 has solidified itself as one of my favorites in the whole series for the unique flavor it brings to the table.
Aside from gameplay, it was a pioneer in both CD Audio Music and Full-Motion Video in PC games, and has a story which fits the period of the mid-90s well. Most of the characters were simply Westwood Employees on green screen. Joe Kucan is timeless as Kane, but he initially planned to simply direct rather than also star as the villain. The plot is not too exciting if you want a modern drama with twists, turns, and inter-character dialogue, but it does a great job of dropping you into the world and letting you see how war is changing with the proliferation of Tiberium. It's a slow drip-feed of information--you learn things as they develop. The finales are also rather brief and open-ended, leaving the consequences of either Kane and Nod's defeat or their discrediting and humiliation of GDI up in the air. (That is, until Tiberian Sun or the Mod Twisted Insurrection.)

In closing, Command & Conquer 1 may not be for everyone, but as the codifier of the RTS genre, it leaves an indelible legacy on everything that came after. It may be tough, but like most things in life it becomes much more enjoyable when you invest the time to get better at it. You can analyze the subtleties of units, learn their strengths and weaknesses, abuse and cheese the AI, micromanage your units, and do the impossible--even the Covert Ops missions which still give me trouble.
I'm enough of a nerd that I have a 486 DOS PC and installed the REAL original from 1995. (By the way, it's a little slow so it's better to at least have a Pentium) I wholeheartedly hope others will come to appreciate this game for what it is. This Remastered Collection is an excellent way to do so.

The story is as simple as an IKEA chair manual: a couple on the verge of divorce is magically turned into dolls. To become human again, Cody and May must learn to work together. Sounds adorable until you find yourselves yelling at each other in perfect harmony.

The gameplay is a constant experiment. One level has you shooting nails and swinging on ropes, another has you steering a tiny minecart, or even fighting a talking vacuum cleaner. Yes, an evil vacuum cleaner. Probably the one I forgot to clean for years.

The visuals are bright and vibrant, as if the artists binge-read children’s books while drawing... and maybe took a bit of, let’s say, inspiration from Madagascar. The levels are so diverse that by the end of the game, you might start to suspect they tried to cram EVERY genre into one box. You’ve got platforming, racing, and even a marriage argument simulator.

But the real star of the game is Dr. Hakim, the talking relationship book. With his charisma and lines like "dance like a butterfly, love like a boss," he’s clearly aiming for the title of the most annoyingly wise NPC of the decade.

It Takes Two is a game that reminds you relationships aren’t just about "press a button and it works." It Takes Two is a co-op adventure where players take on the roles of Cody and May, a married couple on the brink of divorce who are magically transformed into dolls. The game requires both players to collaborate to solve puzzles, defeat enemies, and navigate beautifully crafted environments.

The gameplay is incredibly varied, with new mechanics introduced almost every chapter, ranging from platforming to combat, racing, and more. This ensures that the experience feels fresh and exciting throughout its 12-15 hour runtime. Each character has unique abilities that complement the other, fostering a true sense of partnership.

[h3]🏆 Completion: [/h3]

To fully complete It Takes Two, players will need to explore every nook and cranny for collectibles and achievements, many of which are tied to optional mini-games and secrets. The best part is that each chapter indicates the mini-games if you missed them and guides can offer support in finding the secrets.

review_texts:
[{"review_text": "Witchfire – In-Depth Game Review (9/10)
Developer: The Astronauts
Genre: Dark Fantasy, First-Person Shooter, Roguelite
Platform: PC (Early Access)
Score: ★★★★★★★★★☆ (9/10)

Introduction
Witchfire is a dark fantasy shooter from The Astronauts, a team known for their storytelling brilliance in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter and intense gameplay roots in Painkiller. After years in development, the game finally enters Early Access — and it’s absolutely worth the wait.

Blending gritty action with haunting environments and rogue-lite mechanics, Witchfire manages to carve out its own identity in a genre dominated by titans like Doom and Dark Souls. It’s visceral, it’s beautiful, and most importantly — it’s fun.

Gameplay & Combat – 9.5/10
At its core, Witchfire is a high-octane first-person shooter with tight, snappy gunplay. You play as a Vatican-sanctioned witch hunter dropped into a cursed land teeming with eldritch horrors. What sets the combat apart is the hybrid system of firearms and magic: you’re just as deadly with a flintlock rifle as you are with lightning spells or time-manipulating hexes.

Each encounter feels dangerous and deliberate. Enemies are relentless and intelligently designed, ranging from undead soldiers to grotesque monsters powered by witchcraft. Learning their attack patterns and weaknesses is key to survival — a satisfying challenge that rewards precision and experimentation.

Weapons are customizable and varied, each with its own upgrade tree and personality. Combined with different magical perks and passive bonuses, the combat system offers remarkable depth.

World & Atmosphere – 9/10
One of Witchfire’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The world is meticulously crafted, dripping with gothic horror and medieval dread. Environments shift from fog-drenched graveyards to storm-ravaged villages and warped forests, each filled with secrets and danger.

There is no hand-holding. The world tells its story through environmental storytelling, item descriptions, and subtle clues. This design choice creates a sense of mystery and discovery, encouraging exploration and immersion.

The sound design deserves special mention — thunder cracking in the distance, eerie whispers, and satisfying weapon sounds all enhance the tension and immersion.

Progression & Replayability – 8.5/10
Witchfire employs a rogue-lite progression system: death sends you back to your safe zone, but many of your upgrades and gear persist. This creates a compelling loop of exploration, risk, and reward.

Some players may find the grind a bit repetitive, especially during the mid-game. However, the constantly evolving enemy encounters and new abilities keep things from getting stale for too long.

Frequent updates and a clear roadmap from the developers promise even more content, including new biomes, bosses, and lore expansions.

Narrative & Lore – 7.5/10
While Witchfire isn’t heavily story-driven, the bits of lore you uncover are intriguing. The premise — a holy war against witches in a world where religion and magic collide — is compelling. However, much of the story remains vague or hidden, which can be a double-edged sword.

If you're a fan of FromSoftware-style storytelling (like in Dark Souls or Bloodborne), you’ll likely appreciate the cryptic, environmental approach. But those looking for a cinematic, character-driven narrative might be left wanting more.

Visuals & Performance – 9/10
Graphically, Witchfire is stunning. Built on Unreal Engine 4, the game features photogrammetry-based environments that look almost lifelike. Lighting is used masterfully to build mood — flickering candles, shafts of moonlight, and eerie green glows add to the game’s chilling aesthetic.

Performance is solid, even in Early Access, with well-optimized settings and minimal bugs. The UI is clean and minimalistic, keeping you focused on the action.

Pros & Cons
Pros:

Excellent and satisfying combat system

Beautiful, atmospheric world design

Deep customization and progression

Rewarding challenge and skill-based gameplay

Strong sound design and visuals

Cons:

Story is underdeveloped for lore-focused players

Early-game progression can feel grindy

Some repetitiveness in mid-game loop

Might be too challenging for casual players

Final Verdict – 9/10
Witchfire is a bold, brutal, and beautifully crafted shooter that delivers on its promise of dark fantasy mayhem. With a solid combat foundation, haunting world design, and endless potential for expansion, it’s already one of the best indie FPS games in recent years — and it's only in Early Access.

Whether you’re a fan of DOOM-style combat, Dark Souls-like atmosphere, or rogue-lite progression, Witchfire offers a rich and rewarding experience. It’s not perfect, but it comes damn close.

If that's what you're looking for, Witchfire is the game for you.

The game has a simple gameplay loop. You have a lobby area where you can upgrade your characters levels, research new weapons/spells/equipment, manage your buffs, power ups and test weapons etc. Pretty stock standard basic stuff like you'd see in any other game. Eventually you unlock a shop you can buy supplies from as well.

Then you load into a map. There's initially one map you can load into, unlocking more later through gameplay and upgrades.

The maps are designed with a medieval/fantasy theme in mind. Large towers, islands, old style shipwrecks, rocks, mushrooms and herbs everywhere. The game visually looks very stunning but can become overwhelming when you're getting attacked by a lot of monsters (lots of colours/flashes on your screen).

The gameplay. The gunplay feels absolutely phenomenal and a lot of inspiration was taken from Destiny. Guns feel very unique one to the next, each can be upgraded to have very helpful powerups and there isn't one single gun that makes all other guns obsolete. You'll need to change and adapt depending on the situation.

The gameplay loop works in a couple of ways. You either load into a map and kill enemies/collect resources or else you aim to progress in the story/upgrade arc. You can definitely do both at the same time - you just get dropped in then do what you want.

This game is difficult. It is challenging without it being overbearingly punishing. Health is a resource so you cant just face tank every situation. Bosses are well thought out. As far as I'm aware each map has a sort of "raid" that combines the use of puzzles/thinking as well as at often times genuinely hectic gameplay.

The best thing about this game though - it doesn't feel like a job. You're not competing with anyone. You're not going to get left behind because others progress faster than you. It's the perfect game to kill an hour here or there but also is rewarding for longer gaming sessions in terms of advancement and content.

There are a couple of things that I don't like about it though which are things the community is aware of that hopefully do get fixed in the future.

There are issues where randomly but not often frames seem to crash for about 10-15 seconds. The best solution I've found is to just press escape to pause the game until the frame rate sorts itself out then continue. Happens maybe once every couple of hours for me.

Some general gameplay bugs such as some animations not triggering properly, portals spawning on top of loot making it difficult to pick it up after boss encounters. Minor things that are more of an inconvenience rather than game breaking but in Early Access I'll let it slide.

Pirated this first then decided that I wanted to pay them instead as soon as I got to pilot the game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1753908671}, {"review_text": "I love so much of what we're seeing from this game thus far, but it has some major issues baked pretty deep into its DNA.

The best thing about Witchfire is its premise, it's genuinely a gamechanger. It's a looter-shooter roguelite extraction-shooter amalgamation with free roaming levels, a lot of build customization, and an extremely satisfying core gameplay loop where the hardest challenges that levels have to offer are best done after doing all the easy challenges, but without strictly enforcing that so good players can really show off their skills and builds.

I especially have to give a round of applause to the curse mechanic, where you can effectively bait the witch into launching a curse against you to get a ton of juicy upgrades for a level's raid or boss. It creates unintentional high moments where you get caught off-guard by a curse and need to adapt, it creates intentional high moments where you feel like a mad genius for doing it on purpose and getting richly rewarded for your efforts, it's absolutely brilliant.

Witchfire really is something special, but what I find a bit problematic is that this outstanding high-level gameplay loop is complimented with a much more scrappy low-level gameplay loop, and I mostly don't mean that in a good way.

At the early stages of the game's progression the combat feels like fencing with guns, which is very fun and engaging. The enemies don't overwhelm you with enough projectiles to make sidestepping without dodging unviable, nor are the melee enemies so fast that they have to be dodged away from instead of letting you backpedal and shoot. Your offense is tempered with having highly limited ammo and long spell cooldowns, which plays into the gameplay loop where basic ammo drops become valuable loot.

Then, as the game gets harder, it starts throwing more and more aggressive enemies at you. At first it's knights that lock onto your position and jump at you. Those are actually quite fun since they're the only enemies that do something like this by this point, so they can be fun to dodge then counter.

However, the game ramps this up and up and up to the point where the only enemies that spawn are ones that fire projectiles with aggressive tracking, or launch pillars of silencing lightning that require dodging at the exact correct angle, or fire explosive poison balls that need to be shot out of the air (and by that I mean shot 20 times, not just once), or simply carpet bomb the cramped corridors of the later areas with enough explosives to render positioning almost pointless.

This game is, frankly, not worth it in it's current state. The devs have arguably been proactive in putting out updates to fix the most egregious of problems, but the game is still broken and still unfinished. I have no doubt that it will remain in this state for a very, very long time.

The issue is not that there are a few bugs - entire systems of the game just don't work. 

The old STALKER games were known for having AI that was very intelligent for it's day. They would flank and sneak, use cover appropriately, retreat when necessary and know when to turn up the pressure. Using binoculars, you could watch a team of stalkers fighting a group of mutants and this would be happening all across the in game world, even if you weren't there to see it. Stalkers would have conversations with each other, go on patrols, loot, kill, die and travel - all without the player seeing it. This system, known as the A-Life system, is why the world of the old STALKER games felt so alive. 

This doesn't work in the new game. You will seldom, if ever, find yourself bumping into the same stalkers you met six hours ago at a bar when you go to visit another area. You will almost never see stalkers fighting groups of mutants from far away - you will only ever see this if you are very close to the group. As such, you aren't really a passive observer; you are close enough to the mutants to need to fight them too, you can't just sit back and watch like you could in the old games. 

The AI itself is braindead and glitchy. They will often have pinpoint accuracy behind cover, or in the dark, and therefore be able to instantly kill you without you having any chance to react. Or, they'll be so unaware that you can kill them without any resistance. Be aware that the latter doesn't imply a stealth system - there IS no stealth in STALKER 2. You won't be able to do what you could do in the old games and sneak around with a silenced pistol, sneakily picking off enemies and keeping to the shadows. Stealth is a dice roll, a dice roll that often defies logic or explanation. Do not expect stealth - just expect endless shooting galleries.

Mutants are either so weak that they are trivial, or so overpowered that they are just a chore to deal with. The bloodsucker used to be the most feared enemy in the older games. They had creepy, unnatural, loping strides which made them unsettling to look at. They struck without warning, forcing you to be on your toes once you knew they were around. However, they were quite weak; a shotgun could be used to defend yourself against them. As such, they were a rare enemy that stuck to dark areas and made them more terrifying to explore... but you could kill them. Now, bloodsuckers are so common and telegraph their attacks with the same silly jumpscare that they fail to be scary anymore. They run up to you, make the same irritating (but by no means scary) screech sound, and then appear as if at random. You blast them fifteen times with the magazine fed shotguns like the Saiga, and they die. Or, you jump up on a box and they run around the periphery of the box and never attack you. Fantastic.

The economy of the game is broken beyond measure, and this ties in with the broken quest system. You can go along and do a bounty or fetch quest which can require up to twenty or thirty minutes real world travel time, only to come back and be paid so little that it's not economical to even carry out the task. Stashes contain the same low-level items, most of which are worthless or can be bought cheaply from a trader. Upgrades are arbitrarily limited to certain technicians; this was true of the old STALKER games, but at least you could find the traders easily. 

The world of STALKER 2 is huge, but unlike other huge games like Skyrim or GTA V, you have no easy means of travel. You walk to one side of the map to get the quest from a trader or other named individual, walk thirty minutes to where the quest is, kill whoever or take whatever, then walk back to get the reward. Rinse and repeat. This is further compounded by the stunningly surface level reputation system. There are no side quests for particular factions such as Duty, Freedom, etc. Your reputation with them solely rests on bribing the leader of a faction or doing perhaps one quest for them. You can't slowly build up your reputation with them in exchange for access to new areas or teams of companion fighters. All you do is control whether or not their braindead AI soldiers shoot at you or not. You never learn much about the motivations of certain side characters, their place in the world, or the faction's experiences beyond what a few high ranking members or short voicenotes tell you.

Speaking of voice acting - the English acting is terrible. I kept it on for all of five minutes before switching to the Ukrainian acting. I can't tell you if the Ukrainian acting is any good because I don't speak the language, but I imagine it's much better than the frankly laughable English acting. 

Finally, the performance of the game is absolutely unacceptable. My PC more than exceeds the system requirements, but I am forced into using DLSS setting that turn the game into a fuzzy, fizzing, hissing mess that looks unclear and muddy just to achieve acceptable at best FPS rates. Frame generation is a must for those of us used to 100+ FPS games, and this introduces appalling latency problems. The game's lighting looks poor on reflected water because the forced Lumen raytracing engine has to operate at (in layman's terms) a lower resolution because it's not hardware RT like you mind find in other, better examples of raytracing. It uses software, so to be in any way optimised huge shortcuts have to be made. Baked lighting with an optional hardware RT option for Nvidia users would have been the ideal choice, and still looked good and performed well - instead, we're all forced to use a software RT method that looks poor in many areas and performs even worse. Do not expect much more than 70 FPS without frame generation, even on high end hardware.

As a disclaimer - I am not a new fan of the STALKER series. I played STALKER for the first time shortly after CoP released, and I was so excited for STALKER 2. [hr][/hr]

[h2]Atmosphere: The One Thing It Got Right[/h2]
[b]The environments? Pretty solid.[/b] The Zone is immersive, eerie, and atmospheric, just as much as a post-apocalyptic wasteland can be. [hr][/hr]

[h2]Story and World: Why Should I Care?[/h2]
The story starts off with a bit of intrigue, but it quickly loses steam. I found myself not caring about any of the people I met. There’s no real emotional connection, no reason to invest in their struggles. That would still be fine if the world itself were interesting. But [b]it’s not.[/b] The sense of discovery is completely missing.

Instead of organically exploring, I just followed quest markers, hoping to stumble upon something cool. But every time I arrived at a new point of interest, I found... some ammo. Maybe a bottle of vodka. A few random supplies. No interesting NPCs, no compelling side quests, just a static, lifeless world.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Loot and Rewards: Why Even Bother?[/h2]
I’m fine with the lack of character progression, but at least make exploration rewarding! Instead, 90% of the loot spots contain useless junk. Food, vodka, a handful of bullets. Occasionally, I’d find a gun or armor, but nothing that made me feel like I was uncovering something valuable or meaningful. Even anomaly hunting, which should be one of the coolest aspects of the game, became a chore after getting the anomaly detector. Follow the beeping, grab the anomaly, realize it’s just a minor stat boost, and move on. Thrilling.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Mutants: A Bullet Sponge Nightmare[/h2]
Mutants should be one of the highlights of the game—this is the freakin’ Exclusion Zone! But they’re just a nuisance. [h2]NPCs and AI: Welcome to 2010 (or 2023 Bethesda)[/h2]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts: The Sad Reality[/h2]

[h3]To have accuracy and agility. In a battle. Keep your rifle, soldier. As you keep your life.[/h3]

There is a decent and as you progress, expanding selection of firearms and body armor to give you a lot of variety in how you want to tackle things tactically. And since fighting is the gameplay dujour for most of the game (when you aren't running away in terror), this is super important. But you also have an encumbrance system, so you can't just carry every gun with unlimited ammo. You will need to be selective, and being selective will inform the manner in which you approach this game. I went for a more methodical and stealth focused loadout for the most part. Twenty years of the exact same issues with no apparent ability to learn how to do this stuff properly, only they're even worse with this game due to it being in Unreal 5, which comes with its own issues. 

The compiling shaders thing is just the tip of the iceberg. Yes, other games sometimes do this in a noticeable fashion first time you load a game. With Stalker 2, first time out might take 10 minutes. Might take 30. Might take a couple hours. Who knows? [h1]Introduction[/h1]
Stalker: Shadow of Chernobyl has to be one of my favourite shooters ever made, perfectly combining immersion with exploration and a well-written story that keeps you hooked. So, when the 2nd game, Heart of Chernobyl was announced, you can only imagine the excitement I felt for another jaunt into the Zone. But did the game deliver the same excitement and feel as the first, or was that simply an anomaly?

[table]
[tr]
 [th][b]🟩 Positives[/b][/th]
 [th][b]🟥 Negatives[/b][/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
 [td]🟩A well-written and delivered story that delves heavily into the darker side of humanity and what it truly takes to find freedom in the worst situations.

🟩 Fluid, fast-paced, and fun gunplay that delivers impactful and intense encounters with enemies of all kinds.


🟩One of the most beautiful games I have ever played, to be entirely honest. The open world is enormous and filled to the brim with impeccable detail, and the general graphical prowess of the game is astounding.

🟩 The audio is in the same boat for the most part, delivering truly high-quality audio and immersion to the world with a gritty and realistic atmosphere.[/td]
 [td]🟥 Unfortunately, there are significant bugs within the game. Many of them were apparently game-breaking, but I thankfully never experienced one, and the dev team has been incredibly proactive in updates to improve the experience.
[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[table]
[tr][th]🏆Achievements[/th][/tr]
[td]Stalker 2 is not a super challenging 100% completion by any stretch of the imagination, but it's time-consuming, to say the least. There are a few missable achievements that become unavailable through decisions and some that require new playthroughs or far-back reloads to attain.[/td]
[/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
In Stalker 2, you play as the lone stalker, Skif, who has entered the Zone in search of answers and a new home after an anomaly destroyed his previous one, strangely enough outside of the Zone.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3405713472

Fueled by his thirst for understanding, Skif is thrown into a storyline of enormous proportions and will hold the fate of the Zone in his hands as the warring factions seek control of the anomalous powers for their own. Will you hand over the Zone, or will you fight for its freedom? Either way, a new world has opened and perhaps a place to find a new home along the way.

In my opinion, Stalker 2 is still one of the best-written shooters on the market, delivering a high-octane storyline that grips you from the moment it begins and doesn't let go until the very end, with enormous levels of immersion and atmosphere sewn directly into the fabric of the experience.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Such is life in the Zone.[/h3]
Stalker 2 relies heavily on its realism and immersion, and this is factored into the experience from the first moments to the end. Difficulty plays an enormous role in this, even though even the lowest difficulty, Rookie, can still be a decently challenging experience for those unfamiliar with the Stalker franchise or shooters.

There is an extensive repertoire of guns and tools to utilise on your journey, all of which are useful in their way, and it's up to you to choose the right one for the job. There will be an almost constant stream of upgrades for your character, either from enemies dropping them or buying them in stores with Coupons earned from completing quests and selling resources you find. Enemies of both human and mutant variants can be relentlessly aggressive, forcing you to think on your feet and discover ways to overcome threats as you explore the Zone. It is crucial to remember to repair your armour and weapons frequently. As they wear down, they will begin to jam up more and more often, and that can be the only factor contributing to your death.

On top of the enemies that will constantly harangue you as you explore, you have to also keep your eyes out for anomalies. Anomalies are environmental traps caused by the Zone and affect you in numerous ways. They are mostly easy to avoid, but as you progress through the game and unlock regions closer to Chornobyl, they begin to become more tricky to navigate. Every anomaly has a trick to bypass it, and uncovering these is crucial to your progression and survival. Using a scanner will help you see where anomalies are and also help you uncover artifacts that can be sold for coupons or used to improve your survivability.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3405714199

If you're talking about things to avoid, however, you can't ignore the most consequential and potentially fatal; radiation. Radiation is the most persistent threat in the Zone and will never relent in its attack on you. Keep an ear open for your Geiger counter because it'll save your life more often than anything else, except your guns, of course.

[h3]There and back again.[/h3]
With a map as large as Stalker 2 is, you can only imagine what the exploration is like, and in addition to the map markers, which point out stashes and other points of interest, there are also unmarked locations where encounters, loot and journal entries can be found to uncover more about the world. Exploring the world and locating all of these can be time-consuming, but you never know what you will discover and some of, if not all, the best items in the game come from exploration.

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
Stalker 2 is one of the most visually astounding experiences I've had in gaming. Capturing what are sometimes photorealistic moments and embedding them into this amazing world. Each region of the Zone depicts a different mood with how it looks and feels as you walk through it is truly phenomenal and helps to deliver something truly unique.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3405723522

The audio does an even better job, as I think the experience is more reliant on it than the visuals. Plenty of games capture the graphical aesthetic, but not all of them can capture the immersion that comes from good audio quality and a soundtrack that speaks volumes of emotion.

These factors played a large role in why I enjoyed this experience so much.

[h1]Performance and Specifications[/h1]
Running the game's graphical settings as high as it goes, I was able to hit a fairly stable 90 FPS at 2560 x 1440 and had very little issue with bugs in general. I know a few other gamers who had quite a lot of troubles, and I appreciate that they can occur even after a few major updates.
🟨 Quite a lot of bugs persist according to the general community and should act as a warning for anyone keen to give this one a shot.

CPU: Intel Core i9 14900K 24 Core
GPU: MSI Gaming X GeForce RTX 4090 24GB

[h1]Final Thoughts - Very Good[/h1]
[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2529084785]Review chart here.[/url]
While it wasn't a flawless experience and wasn't perhaps as full as I had hoped to go into it, Stalker 2 was able to deliver another amazing, immersive experience as a whole that genuinely had me captivated from the moment I started it till 170 hours later when I finished it. This isn't a game for everyone and definitely can do with some more time in the oven, but anyone who adored the first game will truly appreciate this experience. DOOM (2016) is a masterclass in how to reboot a beloved franchise. The gunplay is incredibly tight, weighty, and satisfying. The story is simple and wisely kept in the background, which suits DOOM's tone perfectly. That said, Samuel Hayden stood out as a particularly memorable character. [{"review_text": "I saw this game mentioned in the comments of a video of Sseth about Space Station 13 and wanted to play it ever since then. A few months ago, an old friend of mine and I decided to play it together while reconnecting after a long time.

I like this game because it greatly rewards good communication, realistic planning and wise decisions. The way you cooperate with others has many layers and you can learn a lot about yourself this way.

It was kinda hard to get a solid group going after my friend went back to his other games. I started visiting random private servers. But it can be hard to find a public server with a good host. So I started my own public server. I put in the effort to be a good but serious captain, to motivate earnest people and quickly sort out problematic randoms and to plan forward and keep morale high.

With a good amount of patience and diligent, perpetuous attention, I built a solid server out of the random players who came at different times during the weekend. We now have a Steam groupchat and a Discord server. We recently finished the campaign, too, which I didn't get to do with the old friend nor in singleplayer.

We bonded over all kinds of terrible situations and epic clutches. Every single one of us grew in the process. We got to know each other in our highs and lows and learned how to talk about everything with mercy as well as severity. And above all, we learned to function as a team in all kinds of situations. This is exactly the experience I was hoping for and I am very glad that I took the leap of hosting my own server.

Barotrauma is obviously a very niche game and it is a niche I uniquely enjoy. I believe that cooperative multiplayer games with great freedom and complexity like this one bring out the whole spectrum of human behaviour. That is too much for most people, but I enjoy it because it means freedom and opens up the possibility for exchanges and experiences which would otherwise not be possible.

It does take effort to take the brunt of all the strange, dishonest, sadistic or also just kinda daft and unworkable people, to fairly talk it out with all of them, give everyone their just "trial" while keeping up the energy (and managing a submarine of eight other people at the same time), but it rewards you with friends who will stick around for some really crazy unexpected rounds of Europan madness. A Moloch in the deep,
Silent and sleek.
A Basuk it did sink,
In just a blink.

Drugs, guns and hookers but instead of hookers you have aliens trying to kill you. But the drugs are pretty cool.

It’s like Among us meets We Need To Go Deeper.

My wife calls it Space Submarine Sims 4

My wife’s boyfriend says It’s a Death Simulator...

… And maybe a "how to kill your colleague and boss" simulator. 

I'm an experienced domestic terrorist in Barotrauma, so that fits.

Imagine a bunch of idiots that either don't know what they're doing or don't want to do it, in a submarine 4000m deep in the ocean, on a planet where pretty much everything wants to kill you and any mistake can be fatal. Also clowns. 

The best disaster simulation you’ll ever play.

It's an unforgiving 2D Co-op Horror exploration and management game with many ways to die, many ways to survive and many ways to murder anything or anyone you wish… With a submarine editor to make your own ride and mod support to add or remove almost anything you'd want.

But before I go on, let me ask you this…

Have you ever wanted to go on a rampage and slaughter an entire outpost while being so high on several different drugs that you don't feel pain, just to save one guy?
Have you ever ventured too deep into the icy crust of Europa and found something THEY don't want you to know?
Have you ever wanted a pay raise, only for the captain to refuse, so you caused the nuclear reactor to increase the amount of steam produced, causing an explosion?
Have you ever got so high on meth, that you joined a highly controversial and illegal church, that wants to transcend humanity by uniting with a flesh eating parasite?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, then congratulations, Barotrauma IS a game for you!

During the game you walk around this submarine in space and everything and everyone that you aren't directly playing or isn't directly playing you wants to kill you. Disclaimer: Your crew will ABSOLUTELY and WITHOUT HESITATION fire a full on NUCLEAR RAILGUN SHELL at you POINT BLANK, given the opportunity. You need to manage weight, hull strength, cargo space, ammunition, fuel, welding fuel, navigational systems, ship maintenance, and medicine along with having a proper medical practitioner, just to survive transporting f**king 3 clowns to the next station over. You beat the game in campaign mode by killing God with the scraps of bulls**t you've harvested in the course of being a glorified delivery man. You eventually die… In some of the most horrific manners by the hands of ungodly creatures born from the depths of our fears. All the while trying to keep your floating coffin working and armed to hopefully prolongue your nightmare that is life just a little longer. Within an ocean of darkness that hides our fears even inches away from your face.

This is one of the few games where you can do a very simple job (repair everything, keep people healed, etc) and still have a vital role to the mission. It is really satisfying. And then the mudraptors decide they want a hug... 

My wife’s boyfriend has called it a "Drowning simulator" many times. The game is complicated and much of the player skill comes in learning the various systems. Single player it is a submarine and crew management simulator. Multiplayer can be anything from a crew simulator to an RP station or pure clown chaos. There is a tendency for one problem to spiral into many. One example is monster attack and tear holes in your hull, which floods the adjacent rooms, water damages the electrical equipment which cuts power to the pumps.  So you might have to choose between fighting the monsters causing the leaks, fixing the pumps to remove the water, fixing the leaks so more water doesn't come in, or fighting the monsters now boarding your ship! In fact the name "Barotrauma" refers to death by water pressure. This can be very frustrating or exciting as you overcome challenges and survive desperate situations. It is an attitude to gaming made famous by Dark Souls, but with less twitch skill and more cooperation, strategic decisions, and understanding of the game.

The main gameplay loop happens when travelling from one station to another, where you are moving through a passage. You will have to navigate and repair your sub, as well as defend it from aggressive fauna. Each segment is broken into travelling and spending time at a station. At stations you can buy/sell repair and craft items. There are skill trees for each role, and there is an interesting campaign progression based on making sure stations are available late game. 

The average round goes a little something like:

Captain chooses path on map from station. Everyone is ready.

The Captain chose a missions to kill a Hammerhead.

Along the path, you encounter a few smaller monsters that the ships guns handle easily.

You encounter the Hammerhead, it doesn't die immediately and it attacks your vessel.

Here is where it gets fun.

Maybe you quickly repaired your leaking sub and were able to continue.

Maybe someone gets crushed by the water pressure when a room filled too fast and they weren't wearing a suit.

Maybe the navigation console was fried and now you have to drain and repair.

Maybe you weren't able to repair fast enough and you accidentally missed the bottom of the passage and now your sinking towards crush depth in the abyss. Oh and a monster larger than your sub just spawned.

It’s got underwater clown shenanigans, big guns, cool ships, lots of things blowing up and breaking down. Also unspeakable, deep-sea horrors… what the hell are you waiting for?! Have fun.
