There’s something about it that grabs you right from the start, even before you fully understand what that something is. This isn’t the kind of game you dive into for a quick evening of play and forget about. It demands time, attention, and patience, but in return, it offers an experience unlike any other.

Basically, Barotrauma is a survival simulator set on a submarine, stranded deep in the hostile waters of Europa — one of Jupiter’s moons, where death can strike from anywhere: reactor malfunctions, oxygen leaks, grenade-wielding clowns, or an open hatch at the wrong moment. Every mission is a struggle for survival, set against the backdrop of technical failures and internal chaos. It’s less about action and more about managing constant disorder, where teamwork is your only chance to stay afloat. Sometimes it feels less like commanding a submarine and more like desperately trying to keep it from falling apart. And that's where its charm lies. You don’t return to Barotrauma because it’s easy, but because it’s endlessly interesting. Every session is a new story, a new disaster, a new “almost made it, but…”

Visually, the game is more intriguing than frightening. It doesn’t push you away; rather, it charms you with its muted color palette and clean, minimalist art style. The simple yet expressive 2D graphics work perfectly with the sound design. There is music in Barotrauma, with each outpost having its own unique track depending on its specialization. This creates an atmosphere that makes you want to linger there just a little longer before embarking on your next dive. Outside these areas, there’s the game’s tense atmosphere maintained through sounds — muffled thuds, creaking hulls, footsteps — each contributing to a feeling of unease without ever drawing too much attention to itself.

This is one of the few games where, even after hundreds of hours, you can still stumble upon something new — a mechanic, an event, or a bug you didn’t know about before. And that’s a rare and valuable thing. This unpredictability keeps every run feeling fresh and prevents the game from becoming stale.

Each role is an invitation to experience something different. Not only does each new profession provide a reason to learn new mechanics, but I often found myself choosing the more attractive initial branches in the skill tree at the expense of overall efficiency. The game leaves room for improvisation, and no one is afraid of making mistakes — those are just part of the learning process. Sometimes you’ll be patched up by others, sometimes you’ll figure things out on your own, but it always gets more exciting as you progress.

Every parameter can be adjusted individually, allowing you to truly customise the gameplay experience to your style.

The AI won’t fully replace a real player, but it performs admirably in most of its duties — especially considering the developers are continually improving it. Solo campaigns aren’t as vibrant as multiplayer, but they provide a safe space to learn the ropes and experiment. It’s convenient to switch between roles and gradually familiarize yourself with each of them. However, it’s the multiplayer that really makes Barotrauma shine. This is where the game truly comes into its own. Every role — from engineer to medic — is vital, and teamwork isn’t something forced upon you, it’s simply necessary for survival. Each session with a new team feels like a fresh playthrough. The replayability of Barotrauma is exceptional. Even after dozens of runs, you’ll want to come back — try a new role, a different submarine, or a different way of interacting with the world. Peace.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1761091036}, {"review_text": "The planned auction house is a terrible idea.  This game is monetarily predatory enough with battle passes, loot boxes, and the Gaijin Market.  There's already plenty of interesting content that's arbitrarily locked behind these three paywalls.  We do not need a fourth that will end up being even more expensive.  Stop scamming people with this false FOMO nonsense.  There is no scarcity with these items.  They are not limited edition.  They are pixels on a screen and their circulation in the game is based entirely on the developers' whims.  Gaijin, fix some of the fundamental issues your game has before trying to introduce more monetary systems.

Speaking on those issues:

The rate at which you earn silver lions and research points is far too slow.  If you don't buy premium, you might as well not even bother trying this.  God help you if you're trying to get to top tier as a free-to-play player.  You will basically be pulling a second shift every day for months to unlock anything modern.  Even with premium and premium vehicles you're still going to be grinding incessantly.  There's a mechanic in this game called Convertible RP.  You earn it slowly in every battle and are meant to be able to use to unlock anything in a tech tree.  In a sane system, one like their sister game Enlisted, this is something to give back to the players who are willing to waste hours of their life grinding.  It's meant to buffer the tedium that is switching to a new nation.  In Enlisted, this Convertible RP is completely free for the player to use.  At one point they wanted to place a cap on the amount you could store.  The players revolted and the developers, to their credit, actually listened.  In War Thunder, to use Convertible RP you have to spend their premium currency.  The conversion rate?  It's 1 Gold Eagle (the premium currency) per 45 RP.  I have a little over 3.5 million Convertible RP.  It would take me slightly less than 78 thousand GE to use it all.  The largest pack of GE is 25 thousand and it costs $114.  So three of those wouldn't even cover all of my Convertible RP.  The highest rank vehicles (12.0) cost 400 thousand to research.  Ok, you don't want me to complete half a tech tree for free, that's fair.  Then decrease the rate at which Convertible RP is earned if it's free!  Heck, even if you were to make the conversion rate better like 1 GE to 500 RP, I'd be happy.  Give us anything!  Enlisted also has a feature where you can converted their free Convertible RP to silver (the free currency).  The conversion rate is awful but it's at least something!  War Thunder fails to include a similar feature despite being on the market for three times as many years.  

Compression.  Please, for the love of all that is holy, stop compressing based on player stats.  Actually look at how the vehicles perform and balance based off that approach.  If you've added in too many vehicles to do such, stop adding in more vehicles until you balance what you have!  I could list numerous examples of vehicles that are poorly placed in their BR (why is the Pershing and Super Pershing both at 6.7?) but I'm sure their are plenty who'd disagree with me when it comes to specific ones.  The solution to make everyone happy?  Decompress the matchmaking.  Turn our top tier tanks from 12.0 to 15.0.  Do the equivalent for air as well.  I can't speak on naval's balancing, as I don't play it, but it seems to have a host of other issues balance-wise.

Speaking of matchmaking.  Give us more flexibility with Custom Battles.  I'm going to bring up Enlisted again because Gaijin is that game's publisher and it offers an ideal alternative.  In Enlisted, Custom Battles give you experience still.  I believe it's at a lower rate than normal matches but it's something at least.  In War Thunder you don't get anything.  Give us something with the Custom Battles.  I'd love to be able to play games that are set up where it's purely WWII vehicles vs WWII vehicles.  Or Cold War vs Cold War.  The battle ranking system War Thunder has doesn't allow for that and if I were to instead play Custom Battles, I'd be wasting time that could be spent grinding.

The maps suck.  They let you ban one map from your matchmaking when you have premium.  I wish I could ban like ten.  There are so many that are simple Call of Duty three lane maps and it just doesn't fit vehicle combat.  It's even worse when you have modern tanks in these tiny maps that were made for WWII vehicles.  Enjoy being spawn camped repeatedly.  Also, screw Mozdok.  All my homies hate Mozdok.  Worst map in the game.  If you removed it I wouldn't shed a tear.

Keen Vision.  Crew Skills in general are straight up bull with how blatantly pay to win they can be.  Sure you can grind them.  You'll inevitably get to the max rank for each of your crew.  But while you're doing that you're straight up handicapped.  You start new nations with crews that are all at level 1.  For pilots, 75 is the max skill level.  For tanks, it's 150.  When you start that new nation with your level 1 crew members you will be going up against players who have thousands of hours in this game and have max ranked crews.  They will kill you not just because they have more experience/skill, but because you are statistically inferior to them even if you were to use the same vehicle.  They will reload faster.  They will aim faster.  When you hit them, they will repair faster.  It's bad enough you'll be using a stock vehicle against one they already likely have spaded (which adds various upgrades to their vehicle in addition to your crew skills).  This brings us to Keen Vision.  In War Thunder this skill could more accurately be called "Keen Senses".  It doesn't just apply to what you see (which is what it's description would have you believe).  It impacts what you hear too.  As you upgrade this skill you increase the rank at which enemies are rendered in game.  Players who have this maxed out will see AND hear you before you hear them, despite being an equal distance away from them.  If that is not outright considered pay to win I don't know what is.

Oh wait, I do.  

Bushes!

Bushes are a cosmetic item that is far from cosmetic.  Players buy them and then use them to turn their tanks into mobile pieces of shrubbery.  Big deal, you say.  Except imagine how much harder it is to hit the weak spot on a tank that you can't even see.  It'd be one thing if these could be earned normally, but to do so requires you to grind the war bond shop.  This is an in game shop that is tied to the battle pass.  Battle passes cycle out every three months and the war bond shop updates with every new one.  You can earn the separate currency (war bonds) through the battle pass.  Unlock enough and you can buy a whopping ONE bush every six months (because the shop that lets you buy bushes cycles out only bi-annually as far as I'm aware).  Oh and the bush you get is random.  If you don't like that, you can always fork over 500 golden eagles (per bush) to make your tank look like the guy who shot JFK.  

Make the bushes like fictional camouflages Gaijin.  Let me toggle off their visibility.  Tanks should not look like cha cha cha Chia pets.

That's all I have for now.  The game could be so much better than it is.  The foundation is there, it has been for over a decade.  They've done some really good things but the many bad, greedy decisions they've made makes it hard to continue to support them.  This auction house idea is the straw that breaks the camel's back.  It's so utterly ludicrous that this even was considered and, in light of the various other issues I have, I can't help but feel this game won't ever improve. Let's cut the straight bullshit: War Thunder had everything to be the most epic military game ever. Tanks, planes, ships—spanning from fucking WWII to today. It’s literal wet dream material for history and combat fans. But Gaijin Entertainment? Oh, they didn’t want a good game. They wanted a cash-extraction simulator. They turned it into a pay-to-win, broken, soul-draining piece of garbage. If you’re even considering downloading this shit—stop. Just stop.

“Historical Accuracy” My F*cking Ass

Gaijin loves to boast about realism—except when it gets in the way of profit. Those premium vehicles? The ones that cost you half a brand-new game? They’re mostly fantasy bullshit. Armor that never existed, fire rates that break physics, all so some rich kid can dominate without skill. Meanwhile, you grind for weeks to get a tech tree vehicle just to get one-tapped by a paid noob. And when the community riots? Gaijin ignores it. They throw out a corporate “we hear you” and then go right back to counting money. Historical accuracy? More like historical exploitation.

The Grind is Designed to Make You Give Up or Give In

You need 150,000 RP for a top-tier vehicle? Cool. Here’s 600 per match—if you win. That’s 250 matches. For one vehicle. And don’t even fucking start with Silver Lions. Repair costs are so absurd you lose money even on good games. So either you treat War Thunder like a second job, or you suck it up and buy Golden Eagles. This isn’t a progression system—it’s a fucking trap designed to frustrate you into spending.

Balance is a Joke & Balanikov is Clueless

And holy shit, the balance. It’s like nobody at Gaijin even plays their own game. Top tier is a premium-infested wasteland where skill means nothing and wallet means everything. But let’s talk about the man behind the madness: Balanikov. This dude is the fucking poster child of greedy game design. Under his “brilliant” leadership, we’ve seen some of the most tone-deaf, player-hostile decisions ever. Economy nerfs? Broken battle ratings? Event vehicles that cost $200? Thank this guy. He doesn’t see a game—he sees spreadsheets and profit margins. He’s the reason why playing top tier feels like getting punched in the dick repeatedly.

The Game is a Buggy, Unoptimized Mess

The game’s been out since 2012. You’d think it’d be polished by now. Nope. Texture flickering, ghost shells, shells that hit but don’t do damage, tanks phasing through the map, invisible walls—every match is a new episode of “What’s Broken Today?” And Gaijin’s response? “We’re aware.” Then they drop another $70 premium and call it a day. They don’t fix the old shit. They just pile new, expensive shit on top.

They Despise Their Community

They reversed it only because the backlash hurt their image—not because they actually care.

Final Verdict: Don’t Play. Don’t Pay.

Yeah, sometimes—rarely—War Thunder is fun. A good flank, a clean snipe, a dogfight that gets your heart pumping. Balanikov and his team aren’t game developers—they’re monetization specialists. And you’re the product.

This game is fantastic in some points of view. It has lots of military vehicles with relatively correct models thus good for collection purposes. It has unique game mechanics (damage modules, air & land battles, etc.) that attracts lots of players. It lasted more than twelve years till now, for sure has its strengths. 
It is a PvP game so there will be endless fun. But most of the fun is based on other player's pain. Sometimes you can get satisfied from playing this game, while sometimes you can be very frustrated. Of course, you can practice more and try to improve your skills (that goes my 7000+ hours), but it takes lots of time and it does not always depend on your skill level. 
PvP games relay on player bases more than PvE games do. However, in the recent few years, the game managers care less and less about the players. They turned a deaf ear to player's voice (I admit players' voice may not be incorrect all the time) and they changed the game based on their preferences regardless the fact that they do not play the game. The game managers clearly have some bias towards certain countries/fractions in the game and gradually shifted the game mechanics to favor their preference. They made up parameters that are largely off from reality, even though reality is one thing they advocate for this game. I play other games and I am aware that game developers always have bias and hidden buffs for their own nation, but in this game this behavior is not that friendly and hurts lots of players (unless you are enjoying that bias). When you try to report the imbalance or bug, they only take the ones meet their preference, and the others will be labeled “not a bug” and get ignored or banned. Such arrogance is not a polite way to treat your customers. 
This game need lots of grinding, and you can easily meet players that have spent thousands of hours and hundreds of dollars on it. Especially when it comes to modern or nowadays vehicles that still in service (or even have not been in service yet), the grinding is really hard. Each new vehicle requires hundreds of games to research before you obtain the qualification to purchase. For casual players like me this can take up to a year. By the time I reach to that vehicle, it is not as strong as when it first came out. There are newer vehicles that came out later beat it. Then the endless loop cycles. Switching nations in the game also requires lots of resources. You basically have to start from beginning. It is really painful if you find out the game manager does not like the nation you were grinding and continuously nerf the performance thus you have to switch to another nation in the game. 
Because of grinding, it is almost required to purchase premium vehicles/packs to reach to the top tier, where the newest and strongest vehicles lie. The game managers have been focusing on selling premium packs more and more in the recent few years. In the past, when there is a new major update, there are only two or three new premium packs. Nowadays they added twelve new premium packs in one patch. Based on these reasons, there are large amounts of players who bought the premium packs and rushed to the game for their favorite vehicles. Most of them are new to the game, not familiar with the game mechanics thus get bullied by others and quit the game. This is also hurting others because your teammates all vanish in three minutes making the game ends before you achieve something. At its core, Helldivers 2 is a fantastic, infinitely replayable, co-op horde shooter where the higher difficulty creates an unrivaled feeling of badassery. During the first year and 3 months or so, it remained as such: a shining example of live service done right. Recently, however, the development of this game has devolved into a series of missed opportunities and baffling issues in balance and performance. 

With recent changes, new enemies and environments have been added that feel like they have not been playtested whatsoever. Absurd difficulty and mission softlocking from bugs with objective equipment have led to the new Into the Unjust content being pulled entirely for rework. This could be passed off if it was the first time new content fell flat from lack of polish. The Incinerator Corps was too difficult and sparked complaints. The illuminate revamp that added fleshmobs and stingrays was criticized on launch for its difficulty, and fleshmobs still receive criticism for their poor balance. The leviathans post Super Earth invasion are widely hated for their ability to infinitely ragdoll divers from the sky and one-shot players on a direct hit, and they require heavy AP like that of the AT emplacement to kill. Add in some high spawnrate magic, and you get the single most hated enemy in all of Helldivers 2. Now we have the new bug missions that were so unfair and broken that they barely lasted a week before the devs had to pull it. 

New enemies lack exploitable and tangible weaknesses and tend to just be upgraded versions of existing enemies that amplify everything annoying about their predecessors. Automaton war striders are just upgraded hulks that spawn just as often, ragdoll you more, and are only really countered by AP explosives. Terminid dragon roaches are just bile titans that fly, making their weakspots much harder to hit, and set you on fire with their bile, killing you instantly. These also spawn faster than they can be killed. The burrowing enemies in new bug missions would kill you instantly with medium armor in an un-reactable time frame. These enemies cross the line from difficult and intimidating to overly-punishing and unfun to fight. War striders are the least offensive of these new units specifically because I like the grenade barrage for how it shakes up the cover-based gameplay.

Alongside this, the weapon balancing seems to enforce an over reliance on anti tank equipment for most situations with alternative playstyles being punished for no good reason. Gunslinger builds took a recent hit where movement heavily effects the sway on your secondary for a few seconds after you stop. This sounds fine on paper, but it suffocates the run-and-gun punch that draws players to gunslinger loadouts behind gunplay that is unsatisfying to play around and destroys the speedy utility of the gunslinger passive. Melee weapons have had their armor penetration downgraded recently, meaning the days of stunning hulks and chargers have ended. Taking down these heavy enemies with melee weapons wasn't easy in the first place, but apparently, it even being possible was too much for Arrowhead. Melee loadouts were a joke in the first place, but with enough tenacity one could succeed with them. Now, any melee weapon, particularly the flag, have been reduced to an unfunny gag that wastes 40 minutes of your time and all of your team's reinforcements. Can you tell I love both these playstyles?

Lastly and most importantly, the performance is inexcusable for a game of this nature and has been a constant and recurring issue since the introduction of the first urban maps. BeamNG Drive, a high detail soft body driving simulator, runs better in VR on high settings than this game does on NVIDIA's recommended optimized settings. With a 5070, I can get a stable 80 fps, and when things get hectic, I'll get as low as 40. ON RECOMMENDED SETTINGS WITH A 5070. My friends on 3060 laptop GPUs can barely play the game at all. Stability has also been severely effected with the most recent content update with constant stuttering and freezing during gameplay. Many players other than myself seem to have issues with recurring crashes as well. Stability and performance are the biggest issues with this game and need to be top priority.

Arrowhead, Sony, PLEASE put less focus on new content and live service updates. PLEASE stop nerfing loadouts that are already underpowered or underused with the guise of "realism" or "balance." It's a PvE game; no one cares if people are cheesing hulks with a flag. The game needs to be fun and PLAYABLE before you can rake in the cash with a new warbond.

I'm a huge fan of Tomb Raider 2013 so I definitely wanted to check out the games that started it all. Each game offers its own experience, and I would say that while the first two games are worth checking out, I probably wouldn't bother with Tomb Raider 3.

Tomb Raider 1 is a classic, and while it can be frustrating at times (one level, St Francis' Folly, was an absolute nightmare to navigate when I first played it), it's definitely worth playing at least once to understand the hype. 

Tomb Raider 2 is my personal fave and probably one of my fave games of all time now. It's got great action, fantastic set pieces (from the beautiful Italian and Chinese chapters to the hauntingly atmospheric underwater levels), a solid weapon set, and Lara is at her most sassy and badass. Tomb Raider 2 felt like a genuine globetrotting adventure that I would love to go on again.

Tomb Raider 3 is...a downgrade. All three games are difficult (nothing soulslike, but definitely not easy), but TR3 ramps up the difficulty to an absurd, sometimes unfair degree. Which wouldn't be too much of an issue, except there was a definite point for me when the game stopped being fun. [h1]Tomb Raider I : The Essential, Original, Nearly Untouchable.[/h1]

TR1 on the side of playability benefits most from this remaster, as the original TR1 had further delay to running jumps (the foot had to be on the ground IIRC) which were solved with TR2. Now, TR1 is brought to parity with TR2 by cancelling out that delay, and somersaults in mid-air being possible, making combat even easier.

TR1 is obviously the game to start this whole franchise with. Many people may be partial to the sequels, but they are a steep difficulty spike compared to TR1 which starts easy and becomes decently challenging without relying on incredibly hard-to-react traps or do-or-die situations. It was designed with save crystals in mind, after all, with saves possible every 5-10 minutes of progress.

Despite the lower challenge and complexity, TR1 has one thing that its sequels nor many 3D platformers of the era lack, and it's immaculate level design. I would argue that TR1 does not have a single level that dips below a 7/10, when its contemporary Super Mario 64 is riddled with mid to extremely boring zones. TR1 is indeed extremely consistent, with maybe the first part of Natla's Mines sticking out as a sore thumb.

Unfortunately, what definitely does stick out like a sore thumb are some of the texture work of the remaster. It's a toss up between TR1 & TR2 to decide which one has some of the most "AI-looking" textures of the lot, some of them look blatantly not good. To double that unfortunately, in classic graphics, not only are you unable to play at unlocked framerates (without a mod), there's a lack of texture filtering from the old PC version. These two at least came back for the last Remaster of 4-6, but has yet to be introduced here.

[h1]Unfinished Business : You Are (Not) Alone[/h1]

UB released after TR2 at the time. I don't remember whether Core Design or an internal team at Eidos handled this one (Eidos handled TR3's expansion), but in any case, the first part of this expansion is a little reminescent of TR2's design philosophy of "action everywhere", except with Atlanteans.

TR1 is not an especially action heavy game, and UB feels jarring for this reason. Atlanteans are considered the worst enemy type of that game for their fast movement and access to weapons, you either hate or tolerate them. As someone who tolerates them, I welcome the challenge, but be warned there's a whole set of two levels dedicated towards shooting everyone of them dead, and there are dozens upon dozens of them to dispatch.

And contrary to the original UB, this remaster puts the level order back to its intended form, meaning you start the extremely difficult combat heavy stages with a pair of pistols, then lose all your pickups by the end of level 2 to get to Egypt next, the first Egypt level being fairly rehashed in level design on its TR1 counterpart. [h1]Tomb Raider 2 : Tomb Raiders (many times plurals)[/h1]

One thing that happened in the mid 90s with 3D platformers is that control systems seemed to go in two separate directions. In one direction was the Nintendo influenced analogue system, where controls had the character move in the direction you pressed the stick, with large degrees of inertia and looseness. The other direction was the Dpad focused “tank control” system, where the up button made the character move forward, the back button back-peddled, while the left and right buttons steered the character in said direction. While the tank system was the standard for a while (including in the new FPS titles of the time), in the end the analogue stick system won out. This left a lot of the older, typically PC or PlayStation focused titles, feeling rather old. By the mid 2000s, the control system was more or less dead in the mainstream.

Here is the Tomb Raider main conundrum: It was a tank control game. To climb to the top of a cliff you can see, you are likely to not just dart about, hitting the jump button and watch as your character magnetizes to a point. You are going to have to fine tune your positioning for a run up, take the leap, then because you were slightly early in your jump, Lara will hit the wall face first and plunge to her unceremonious death. Tomb Raider is brutally unforgiving with its systems and unless you respect them, it will not respect your time.

In many ways though, this clumsy and picky control system is why Tomb Raider works. It lives in a region where I yells “git gud” and it is then down to the player to see if they can reciprocate. In a lot of ways it has the trappings of an old home micro Euro platformer. The challenge is the platforming in and of itself and it does not really care if you want to be easily entertained: There is a building and you need to climb it to move on. The game will not tell you to do any of this, it just expects you to figure it out. While the later Tomb Raider games would entertain you with quicktime events of Lara parachuting down an exploding mountain while avoiding falling boulders, the bits between the quicktime events would have you do a rather on-rails traversal of a tower. This is the crux of how to advise the Tomb Raider collection. Some say they don’t like hand holding titles, but do you really want that? If so, these old Tomb Raider titles really are just game spaces that exist purely for the sake of letting you get lost and figuring out its firm “my house, my rules” mindset. If you really want to dive back into Tomb Raider’s past, this collection is a great start.

As for each game? My bias is a simple one: Each game was technically better than the last, but felt less interesting to play. name: Mega Man 11
short_description: Mega Man is back! The newest entry in this iconic series blends classic, challenging 2D platforming action with a fresh new visual style. The new Double Gear system boosts Mega Man's speed and power for a new twist to the satisfying gameplay the series is known for.
categories: Single-player,Steam Achievements,Full controller support,Steam Trading Cards,Steam Cloud,Steam Leaderboards,Family Sharing
review_texts:
[{"review_text": "I'm a bit torn on MM11. On the one hand, it's a bold new entry that shakes the formula up for the first time since MM7. On the other hand, it's far from the best game in the series due to important MM staples being underwhelming or missing outright. Regarding positives, the game looks pretty good most of the time. I believe this is the first 2.5D numbered entry. There are some cool visual effects from abilities with more depth to the animated backgrounds in levels. Bosses are much more complex even having multiple attack types and forms they take on as the fight goes on. The charged Mega Buster is back with an additional charge for a larger stronger blast and it's awesome. There are some great very challenging levels here as well with Torch Man's stage being my personal favorite. All the new abilities from bosses are awesome and even add additional movement options like the Pile Driver doubling as an air dash. The Double Gear system is cool and fun to use. This is a welcomed new addition. Being able to not only strengthen the classic Mega Buster even further, but also strengthen all other abilities.

The speed gear is where issues come up. It really REALLY mitigates a lot of the challenge of most bosses and platforming sections since you can upgrade it so you move at a normal speed while everyone and everything around you moves slower. This allows you to bombard enemies and bosses with attacks shredding them in seconds before they even have a chance to respond. That's not to say the game is easy. The challenge is fairly close to what you expect from a Mega Man game. Rumor has it, our Normal is their Hard mode just renamed. Not sure if that's true. My issue with the difficulty is that without using Double Gear, the game can stomp you hard. With Double Gear, the shop, and upgrade system it's one of the easiest games in the series.

Some stages absolutely stink with Bounce Man's being one of the worst in the series. It's incredibly annoying being bounced around constantly, but the general look of the level is just uninspired. What is the theme here? At one point it looked like I was in an indoor bouldering room. What does that have to do with bouncing? The boss was absurdly easy too. The Wily Stages were fairly tough, but the bosses left a lot to be desired. There's just nothing new here. Yellow Devil from MM1 returns. Then there's a boss gauntlet of all of the same bosses you just fought to get here. Then finally you fight the Wily Machine 11 which looks nearly identical to the Wily Capsule from previous games. There's no surprises here. I think they played it a little too safe with the final fortress.

The biggest issue by far is with the soundtrack. It's not that the compositions are bad. They just sound too soft and don't fit Megaman's usual style of rock and metal. It's a problem. It all just blends into the background. The mix sucks too. The music doesn't cut through enough to stand out even with turning down the two other volumes to hear it better. It's just not Rock Man. It reminds me of the awful PS1 version of MMX3's badass soundtrack. The voices and sound effects are too loud by comparison. At least the voice acting is adequate which is an achievement after the infamous "acting" featured in MM8.

It's nice to have new Mega Man and I hope we get more, but I really want to see something different in regards to bosses and levels with the return of the classic characters. Where is Proto Man? Where is Bass? There are no unlockable characters to play as like in MM10. More creative bosses than the typical lineup of fire-type, bomb-type, electricity-type and ice-type. And maybe it's time to move on from Wily. We've been fighting him for 11 games now and that's not including spin-offs. I like the new additions and I would recommend this to fans of the series. (6/10)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752003482}, {"review_text": "It's a decent game, but definitely not worth it at full price.

definitely check it out, especially if you're a fan of the mega man series or action platformers.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761693721}, {"review_text": "9/10 - A worthy sequel and a much needed refresh on the formula.

Mega Man 11 is an incredible game, what a sequel should be. It elevates the series to a whole new level, which got me excited for future installments.

As I got my intro to the whole series with the Mega Man X games, playing the original MM titles can feel like a downgrade. The achievements of this game are also another great part of the experience, they range from pretty regular to very challenging, but it was really fun to hunt for them, and coming back to the difficulty, playing the game on Superhero mode was a really great experience, where I had to use all tools in the arsenal to get through the end of the game.

Mega Man 11 is by far a great sequel, and even though I have yet to finish the game as of this writing, I still recommend it because it really is unique in how it plays.

I like the fact that the gear system enhances the other weapons, and I also like the ability to slow time so I can better time jumps. I wish the gear system was a feature in earlier Mega Man games, or even Mega Man X, Zero, Battle Network, etc., but it isn't.

This is one of a few Mega Man games that doesn't go with the pixelated aesthetic, and AFAIK the only one in the baseline Mega Man series (starting with the NES versions) that is not styled as an 8-bit or 16-bit platformer, going for a 2.5D look instead. The graphics look and feel great, however, and it still manages to pay homage to earlier titles.

The story line is actually kind of nice; it explains some about the history between Dr. Wily and Dr. Light. That said, I do feel that it is loosely tied to past story lines, as it doesn't really cover anything from past Mega Man games. It would have been more consistent if Capcom had decided to integrate stuff from other Mega Man titles into this game, but then again that might not make it stand out very much on its own, which I think is the point of each Mega Man title. From the bottom of my heart, Deepnest, The Hive - eat sh1t.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 25, "timestamp_created": 1759306599}, {"review_text": "From a small indie studio in Australia came a game that would redefine what people expect from the Metroidvania genre. Hollow Knight is more than just a side-scrolling adventure—it's an atmospheric, emotionally resonant experience wrapped in layers of combat, exploration, and mystery. It’s not just one of the best indie games ever made—it’s one of the best games of the last decade, period.

Hollow Knight keeps its combat system deceptively simple: you have a nail (essentially a sword), a jump, and eventually a few magic spells. But don’t be fooled—this minimalism allows for incredible depth. Enemies are fast and unpredictable, and boss fights are challenging tests of reaction time, pattern recognition, and precision.

Each victory feels earned, and even basic enemies can be lethal if you let your guard down. The game balances difficulty beautifully—harsh, but fair. And when you finally overcome a tough encounter, the feeling of accomplishment is unforgettable.

Set in the ruined insect kingdom of Hallownest, the world of Hollow Knight is vast, interconnected, and absolutely bursting with secrets. From the forgotten crossroads to the fungal wastes and the haunting City of Tears, every area is distinct—both visually and mechanically. There's no in-game map until you find the cartographer, reinforcing the sense of being truly lost in a crumbling empire.

Exploration is king here. There are hidden paths, breakable walls, and entire zones that many players will miss on their first run. The interconnected nature of the world design rivals Dark Souls, and the non-linear progression means players are constantly rewarded for curiosity and persistence.

Visually, Hollow Knight is breathtaking in its simplicity. Hand-drawn characters and backdrops exude charm and gloom in equal measure. Despite a palette heavy in blues, greys, and shadow, the environments never feel dull—each region has its own emotional tone.

The music by Christopher Larkin is nothing short of masterful—subtle, sorrowful, and sometimes triumphant. It underlines the loneliness and faded grandeur of Hallownest without ever overwhelming the gameplay.

Sound design also plays a key role. From the tinkling footsteps of the Knight to the skittering of bugs in distant tunnels, every audio detail deepens immersion.

Hollow Knight doesn’t hand you a story—it whispers it from beneath the earth. Lore is hidden in dialogue, item descriptions, and environmental storytelling. Themes of sacrifice, decay, and forgotten glory permeate every corner of Hallownest.

Your silent protagonist, the Knight, might seem blank at first, but over time, a moving and tragic tale unfolds—one of lost kingdoms, ancient pacts, and a desperate attempt to hold back an unstoppable infection.

short_description: Morimens is a roguelite card-building game inspired by the Cthulhu mythos, where you craft a versatile and intricate deck tailored to your playstyle. [{"review_text": "[UPDATE: After almost 2 months playing, I felt the need to adjust a few things.]

tl;dr: It's very good IF you have the heart for gacha. This is a dupe heavy game (details in the comments).

Honestly, I did not expect this game to be any good. The first time I saw it, a couple of months ago on my discovery queue, I remember thinking "ugh, another gacha trash" and moving on instantly because I prefer to avoid the genre.

But I came across it again last week and was drawn in by the art and the atmosphere before remembering I had already seen it. So I ended up deciding to give it a try, to see how egregious it could be and because I'm a sucker for card games.

There are a few caveats but I gotta say I am positively surprised. I expected way less of it than what it offers. Let me start with the caveats because, y'know, bad news first. That's just basic manners. 

First of all, gacha's gonna gacha. Morimens is surprisingly non-agressive about it and offers a good amount of free resources for you to play with IF you have the patience and the heart for it. If you are prone to gambling addiction, have poor impulse control or little patience for the free resource management, just do yourself a favor and stay clear of it. It has all the trappings of the "gacha genre", which is basically a bazillion of different time gated resources for you to juggle and both character and equipment lotteries. This means the main way to acquire and upgrade both characters and their equipments is through gambling with limited, time gated (or real money gated, if we're being honest), resources. So, yeah, this is potentially very dangerous and can be very damaging.

It is possible to stay free to play. And Morimens seems to be more accomodating in regards to that than others in the genre. But if that is your intention, you have to be smart about how you use each of your resources. There are even guides for it in one of its discord channels (Mythag University) and the community in both discord channels that I frequent is, usually, quite helpful and friendly.

That being said, Morimens is pretty good at what it does. So much so that I decided to spend some money in it  the game just to show my appreciation and support (yeah, they got me, dammit). There's real effort here. The art is beautiful. The music is good and fits the setting very well. The voice acting oozes quality and care. The story is well presented in a visual novel style and, as far as I have read it is well written (mind you, I have partially lost my vision a couple of years back, so I've been skipping some of the story. But I do intend to read it later, it's just that it takes extra effort. But I digress). The animations for the characters and their special moves (here called Exalts) are truly remarkable (or just endearingly goofy. Karen, I'm looking at you!). There are various activities to do and, as far as I can tell, there's almost always an event with good rewards going on.

With all of that out of the way, the core mechanics of the game are pretty good. Before each Investigation (which is basically a mini-dungeon with events and a shop that work for that instance, various enemies, maybe an elite enemy and a final boss) you choose a team of up to four characters. Each character has five cards (one strike, one defense and three personalized cards. You can, and should, upgrade these up to 6 times) with various energy costs (the base energy, here called Arithmetica, you get each turn is 5) and an Exalt (which is a special move you can use after you fill a bar with Aliemus by playing some of that character's cards or through special means. The exalt can also be upgraded up to 6 times) and your avatar, the Keeper, has a support ability called Posse (each card played fills its bar with Keyflare. There are also a few other mechanics that can do it). 

The characters can belong to 4 different "Realms" (color coded for your convenience) and each Realm has a special mechanic associated with it (your team can belong to two Realms at once, which usually gives you a slightly downgraded version of both Realm effects. Unless it's Chaos, aka yellow. They mix with any other Realm without downgrading their abilities). Each character can also equip two cards, Wheels of Destiny (as far as I could notice, each character has one golden WoD, rated SSR specific to them. Although not essential, they usually gel really well with their mechanics as envisioned by the developers), and a Covenant (which can be a pain to assemble and upgrade. This is one of the main resource sinks in the game. Late game stuff).This is the very core of it but there are quite a few more details I'm leaving out. The end result is quite good and fun to play. Organizing the teams itself is interesting and the characters are usually good in different ways, with the best characters usually being those that have more options and that can be useful in more situations or resolve specific problems that no one else can. 

The initial group you are given and the characters from the standard pools (the ones that are always available and are easier to get) are all viable to finish the story, especially the first arc (which has nine chapters). They do vary greatly in quality though, as do the Realms themselves, and there are many guides and tier lists about them. I recommend reading through content from different people and making some tests yourself when you become able to afford that becuse although there are a few unshakable consensus, everyone has their biases, both regarding the individual characters and their Realms. And sometimes those biases can blind people and lead them to weird extremes.

There is also a PvP mode, for those so inclined, with completely different rules from the PvE game since it aims to be balanced and fair. The only mechanical advantage one player can truly have over another in it, as far as I could tell, is to have more unlocked characters and that is not a huge issue (it is an issue but it is both solvable with time and, well, most players will be in this same situation, so, it kinda balances out). The rewards for it are also pretty good. I haven't played much of it though because it's hard to play the cards fast in my condition. But I plan to, eventually. Just have to find the patience to figure out a team composition and memorize the cards effects.

One last issue that plagues the game is the translation. It changes from time to time and with it,  so do the terminology in the cards, sometimes for the worse. Nothing too egregious or unreadable but it has become the source of many memes and recurring jokes among the community. The developers say that they will focus on making a quality translation of the storyline in the near future. How that will go, only time will tell.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1747741845}, {"review_text": "Disclaimer: I don't recommend any gacha, but this one deserves a positive review.

Interesting things about Morimens:

- Ever heard of an indie gacha game? Now you have. Apparently they came close to shutting down a while back, which makes me feel sympathetic toward them. Scrappy underdog and all that.

[{"review_text": "Despite i think the flaws that I think most people say (which I think most of them are exaggerated) I think Victoria 3 fills in a niche within the Paradox game set. And I think it's important to set the expectations straight for people who want to buy this game:

Victoria is NOT:
A war game (like Hearts of Iron)
A world conquest game (like Europa Universalis)
A in depth politics about interpersonal relationships (Like Crusader Kings)

Victoria 3 is a simulation of economics and society, set and themed in the Victorian Era.
It's focus on demographic and societal change is something that you wouldn't be able to get form any other game, and honestly really love the game for it.

If you're looking for a straightforward strategy game where you can just paint the map after stacking modifiers, this game probably isn't for you. 

it's potentially a niche game, but if economics and society simulation sounds like something you'd like. Then I'd highly recommend this game!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1749759485}, {"review_text": "This game can be summarized in one word: Unpolished

I really want to love this game however in its current state it really is unloveable. If you plan to buy this just be aware that you'll "only" get a few hundred hours of fun out of this game as opposed to Paradox usual thousand. And this will not change for a long (at the time of writing this, presumably a few years of) time.

Every nation feels and mostly plays the same and its unpolished state applies to both game mechanics AND [nation]flavour.

If you want to know how you'll play 90% of games if you want to do decently well it will look like this: 1. Pick a great power, 2. liberalize, 3. build an economic based on a construction bubble (Iron, steel, tools) and 4. repeat.

Minor nations are even less playable because by the time you fixed your nation the game is already or close to over.

Im gonna list every Problem I have with this game just do demonstrate the unpolished state of the game however be aware this is by far not every problem the game has to offer:

1. The Warfare system is boring, now theres a lot of criticism for the warfare system by the community however this is one of the features that is in my opinion the least in need of fixing. It is oversimplified into a basic frontline attack/defend feature.  Military Research should actually affect your units instead of changing your production method (the Ultra Historical mods fix this).UPDATE: A lot of previous issues I have were fixed or got a bypass now in the latest DLC, good job.

2. The game runs super slow by the time you reach 1890 [depending on your PC, +/- ~10 years]. This is especially annoying because it means you get cut off from a lot of cool action. It essentially means you'll rarely see your fruits of labor pay off. Want to play Germany and establish colonies? By the time you've unified Germany and have done all the important other things the game is already slowing down. Want to play as a socialist country? By the time you're ready to become socialist your game is so slow that waiting for laws to pass is no longer fun but just annoying. Want to be Japan? By the time you implemented the right laws the game is too slow to start Japans historic rapid industrialization. Want to play as an American trade empire? By the time you unified America you'll at best have time to get the South Americas into your sphere of influence.

3. The economy system sucks. Want to build an economy as any Great power? Heres how, 1. build iron/coal mines and logging camps, make tools, repeat. 2. Unlock Steel, steel needs iron and coal, iron needs tools, make more tools using steel. 3. Unlock Dynamite, make sulfur mine, make fertilizer factory. Dynamite needs fertilizers which you make with sulfur, then you use the dynamite production method to get more resources out of mines.... resources like sulfur. UPDATE: As of the latest DLC trading got reworked, giving you incentivizes to diversify into certain products and making it less of an Autarky simulator. 

4. The politics of this game are super boring and lame, if you want to be decently successful you have 2 options: Capitalist Liberalism to focus on a game with a lot of GDP or Communism to see that standard of living go up. There is no incentive to play anything else. Monarchism and other Authoritarian ways to play only compensate you with "Authority" which are points you can use to implement decree's that buff you in a selected state in a bunch of different ways however quite frankly, its useless. And while its obvious that playing as a Theocratic Ethnostate will have little benefits, there is absolutely no reason other then larp to pick them.  Theres no specific unique buff, no odd situational event, nothing. They could have went with something like Monarchies uniting the populace causing less Radicals from political movements or Ethnostates/Theocracies giving less radicals from Standard of Living for the Primary culture but more for oppressed cultures but they chose nothing and hence you are always forced to pick the same old boring policies.

5. The game lacks utter immersion. Despite this game being set in unarguably one of the most important and most rapid changing times of humanity you, the player, feel nothing about it. Are you an industrial great power? Are you a small, non industrial tribe? Are you an oppressed puppet/colony? It "feels" the same. The game lacks utter immersion, while even hoi4 tries to immerse you in its setting with news events like the olympic games, the Hindenburg, etc. no such thing is going on in vicky, add this with the already distant experience from the Global Strategy approach and you're in for a dissapointment. Very very rarely do you feel like you're in these turbulent times. Events that are supposed to immerse you rarely work to do that. The only events that do make me feel immersed are that of nihilism, positivism and communism. However 2 of these rarely fire. And it is just as bad for nation specific immersion. As Prussia/Germany, you'll never feel like you're uniting people that want to be united, you just start 3 wars, get an event and annex lands. Or as Japan, you do not get experiences that make you feel like your world was basically turned upside down when the Europeans [yes Europeans because America will not even reach you] open up your country. There is a massive missed chance of adding visual novel'esque events [or news events like hoi4 does] that immerse you. Imagine how great it would be, you play as Japan and suddenly you're forced to open up. And while you change your laws you keep getting pop ups about people/interest groups describing their perspective of a changing Japan. You could see how displeased the Samurai's are getting with each event, how they feel about losing their privileges while for the Peasantry you feel their sweeping optimism as  they went from the bottom of the hierarchy to a respected group. Ultimately this is a huge missed potential that is also surprisingly not alot talked about in the community. UPDATE: In the newest dev diary they announced they want to change the game content into a more narrative driven game, if they implement this and continue with it, then this might go a long way into fixing this point.

heres a lot more to say and criticize but I've reached my steam word limit... yeah that one sentence sums up the vicky 3 experience.

All in all this game just quite frankly sucks due to a lack of polish. Usually mod's fix this in other games but it is to severe in this game to fix. You need different major mods for every single aspect. I personally run the entire 5 or so Ultra Historical mods to fix research, combat and the lack of a historical ai. The better politics mod to make politics slightly less repetitive (they still are). Various Quality of life UI mods, performance improving mods, Event and Flavour mods. As it is, you get a few hundred hours out of playing different nations and getting familiar with the game mechanics until you realize its all the same.

Before, it was a game that I personally found interesting, but I wouldn't recommend it to other people. I now think that the game is good enough for me to recommend it. 

The best change that came from the update is the treaty system. It allows for so many unique strategies, and being able to negotiate with countries makes diplomacy feel more real than before. What I've been doing as the USA is signing treaties with every small country, guaranteeing their independence in exchange for a power bloc embassy and trade privileges. All three of those articles increase leverage, so my power bloc is growing rapidly; it overtook the British Commonwealth before 1900. That's just one example. You could also use treaties to gain a lot of income, you could use treaties to purchase land, etc. It's very fun.

The changes to trade and companies are also amazing. Building trade centers to trade for you is drastically better than setting up every trade route individually. And prestige goods, company charters, and executives make companies feel important rather than just being a small stat boost like they were before.

My only criticism of the update is the military. I think the new front line system is hit or miss. In most cases, it works fine, although it is weird seeing multiple fronts being grouped together as one front; there could be a better approach to front lines. And there are still some edge cases in which the front lines are horrible. Invading Canada as the USA is a good example. Half way through the invasion, the front line splits into two, and my armies almost always leave one of those two fronts wide open, allowing Canada to take back a ton of land for free; it's like invading Mexico before update 1.9 all over again. I would still say the new system is an improvement from the old one, though. It's only bad when you're dealing with extremely large fronts that are prone to being split. 

I also don't like war in general. Countries should be able to join ongoing wars; if real life followed Victoria 3's war system, World War One wouldn't have included Italy, Bulgaria, or America. And more countries should be allowed to negotiate peace than the two that started the war. A recent example I had that highlights this was when I defended Ethiopia from being annexed by Britain. My recommendation would be to allow every country to have different goals for the war and to turn peace treaties into a negotiating table where every country pushes what they want until a compromise is eventually found. Countries that contribute more to a war would get more say in the final treaty, and countries that capitulate would get no say. 

Overall, Victoria 3 still has a lot of work to do, but it is in its best state yet. disclaimer- this review is primarily addressing underlying concerns with the gameplay of Victoria 3. I am fully aware that the launch and the first few years of this game were abyssal trash, which plenty of reviews already have covered.

Call me (Mc)Stupid, but I feel like this game is greatly over hated. If you are coming to this game expecting a sequel to Victoria 2, or a game that is adjacent to EU4 or HOI4, [b]I cannot inherently recommend this game to you.[/b]

Victoria 1 and 2 both advertised themselves as economically and politically focused strategy games, but ultimately feel like the Europa Universalis Franchise with more focus on economies and politics. Victoria 3, however, focuses entirely on internal politics and economy, often at the expense of both diplomacy and military(although id argue with treaties that Vic3 has some of the most in depth diplo of any paradox game). these features have often been cornerstones of the paradox franchise as a whole, and that coupled with the classic paradox release experience led the autism map game community to assume that the game was a waste of time, and it may be, for them.

Feels like a scam, scummy business practice borderline false advertising.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1736233243}, {"review_text": "After 1000+ hours i REALLY wanted to recommend it. 

And i plan to after these Conditions are met: 

1. The military game must be fixed.

Then they need to do for Victoria what they did for Stellaris.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1735524939}, {"review_text": "The game is one of the best economic simulators out there and deserves a better score and more effort from Paradox.

I am a Paradox veteran with >2000h combined in Imperator Rome, CK, EU, HoI and Stellaris. In my opinion, Victoria 3 is way deeper than all these titles regarding economics and society simulation. Supply/demand curve, market competitiiveness, literacy, discrimination, life standard expectancy - it's just a small portion of factors you have to deal with here.

There is a number of issues with this game:
- The launch in 2022 has been faulty and pushed players away. The game has improved a lot since then.
- War may feel too simple in contrast to other Paradox games. However, it is not a big issue. The primary focus of all Paradox games is to colorize the map. All except Vic3: developing tall and growing soft power is possible and sometimes even more profitable than mindless expansion here, just like in real life.
- Learning curve is a bit sharp. Sometimes strange things will happen that can be thought of as bugs. E. g. a profitable building reduces its workforce. However, most often it is not bugs, but tooltips not being descriptive or accurate enough. A new player has to read a couple of wiki pages to comprehend all mechanics.

By writing this review I hope to improve it's reputation a bit so that Paradox may put more effort into this game, as its economics simulation foundation has huge potential no other modern Paradox game can offer.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1736067330}, {"review_text": "I dedicated a lot of time to Paradox games. Thousands of hours across multiple campaigns in multiple titles. The true near infinite sandbox replay value. Some are better than others, of course. Victoria 3 fells like the worst, least interesting and most half-baked of the bunch.

Average people think that all Paradox games are "boring map games", an opinion I strongly disagree with. Victoria 3, however, is incredibly boring, even for a long time fan of the genre. Then again, Victoria 3 is the disgrace of Paradox games.

The early game consists of waiting for a building queue to finish, meanwhile your economy slowly falls apart due to AI countries sucking up whatever useful ressources your market had in positive supplies, causing your economic buildings to all bleed away money due to the previously correctly priced ressources now being incredibly expensive, due to the ressources magically vanishing into foreign markets, to the point where you have virtually nothing left to supply your own country, within the first few weeks of the game. Time to fix this...

Oh no, you don't have workers available for your buildings, because hundreds of thousands are essentially serfs wasting away their time in unimportant fields for the nobles, creating nothing of value for the economy. Only farmers working in official food producing buildings, count as producing food or grain. The land owners only exist to watch their serfs doing nothing in their empty plots of land. Time to reform the government and start fixing this mess...

Oh no, the law passing system is a frustrating RNG nightmare, devoid of logic. Simple reforms over basic laws require years of in-game time to get passed and are full of RNG events that can either advance the law passing, delay it or give your entire country negative buffs that last for years. These events can happen in a loop, depending on nothing but dumb luck.

Exemple of illogical gameplay nonsense: You want your country to have "interior affairs" and a national guard, granting certain positive buffs in exchange for a cost in admisistrative points (that you pay for with administrative buildings, paper and wood, basically). Normal government procedure, right? Any other game would have this normal state upgrade available by spending ressources, or researching a technology. But not in Victoria 3, because the 8% of "intellectuals" in the country, who strongly oppose any kind of "interior affairs", become radically angry as soon as you try to pass the reform law to unlock it. Does it lead to events involving player choices and negociations? No. Instead, as Prussia, 8% of pencil pushers, being unhappy about the proposed institution of "interior affairs", trigger a massive civil war, where they start with Berlin and most of the country already under their control, including 77 out of Prussia's 128 regiments.
Absolute, immersion breaking, nonsense.

Going into the topic of wars, in this game where world powers can regularly fight each others across continents, with their full armies, either over who gets to control a trade port, or over less than 10% of the population being angry with a mild government reform, there barely is any "gameplay" involved, really. Sure, you can influence warfare with technology and supplies of extra ressources like booze and candies for your armies, but you don't actually get to control what they do. Less experienced players have a lower entry threshold, and veterans can still take on individual challenges. It's time to create the ideal society of the 19th century.

Personally, I like the Crusader Kings series the most, but I couldn't pass by Victoria 3 indifferently. After all, you have to try your hand at everything. And it was worth it, because the game immediately surprised me with its accessibility, which had not been seen in Paradox titles so far. If we add great graphics and music to this, we get an engaging production for thousands of hours, during which we will not fully discover the whole thing anyway.

Victoria 3 is a new beginning for new players.
The main menu of Victoria 3 was my first surprise. This production does not immediately send us to the world map to choose a country, nor does it display any buttons for personal configuration (although this is of course possible). Instead, we have the following options: "Learn the Game", "Economic Domination", "Hegemon", "Egalitarian Society" and "Free Mode". The first four impose goals from the outset, which consist of learning the game, becoming an economic or military power, and creating a modern society in which all citizens are equal. In each case, several countries are proposed that have been deemed the best for the given task.

When we choose one of these modes, the game log will start to show hints directing us to what we should do next. This makes it easier to find our way around it all and learn what to pay attention to if we want to achieve a given goal in our gameplay. People who are not familiar with the genre or those who are dealing with Victoria for the first time will definitely benefit from the precisely defined and described challenges.

In general, Paradox's productions are the hardest to start playing. Even if we go through the tutorial in other titles from this studio, it can still be hard to figure out what to do next. Where to start, what to look at, what to focus on. Without the help of someone who already has experience, you can easily get discouraged. Especially since when playing, we often deal with a waiting simulator and sometimes it's best to do nothing, which is not obvious.

We move to the world map, choose whatever we want, and we can start "painting" the map, deal with society and the political system or do whatever comes to our mind. The full Polish language version helps in all this.

Although you can create an empire by conquering other nations, armed combat is not the main aspect of Victoria 3 and we will not "color" the map like in Europa Universalis. In the latest game by Paradox, internal politics and creating the kind of society we dream of are definitely more important. Of course, it is not that easy.

Victoria 3 is definitely the prettiest game from Paradox
The beautiful visuals of the game are no surprise to anyone, since Victoria 3 is the studio's latest title. Despite everything, the graphics make a very positive impression. Especially since the map is constantly changing with the appearance of new cities, mines and agricultural areas. Even something as simple as running trains and trees moving in the wind adds to the atmosphere. The visuals may not be the most important thing in strategies of this type, but it is still more enjoyable to play when you see the changes introduced related to the development of the country.

The same care was taken with models representing specific social groups. A peasant, a worker, a clergyman, a soldier - they all look different, also in other parts of the world. An official in Great Britain will have a completely different model from his counterpart in China or Egypt.

Pros.
+ Victoria 3 looks really phenomenal.
+ The music is memorable and builds the atmosphere.
+ The Polish language version helps you find your way around the game.
+ There are also additional modes to learn.
+ Building a society is an interesting theme.

Cons.
- Technological development is the same for all nations.
- Laws and politics as well.
- War seems to be an aspect ignored by the creators.
- Higher level of inaccessibility (You really have to understand a lot)

Short summary.
Victoria 3 is a very good game at its core and I admit that the fun of creating a society, changing it as you please, is really addictive. I did not encounter any strange bugs that prevented efficient play. The interface is also clear and it is easy to find your way around the various options. If we have a problem, the game itself tries to help us - and that is why it is worth testing scenarios with clearly defined goals first.

11/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 372, "timestamp_created": 1736279181}, {"review_text": "It started like this: no minimap, no player marker, just a weird map, a compass, and a vague sense of direction. 200 hours later, I still don’t exactly know where I am half the time - but I’ve led squads confidently into ambushes, driven into trees at 100mph and exploded in the most hilarious ways, regularly driven my car around like a lost tourist shouting for the navigator, and somehow had more fun than in any shooter in years. Coming from Squad, HLL, and the BF2:PR days… Reforger feels like chaos, community, and comedy pretending they planned it that way

I don’t usually write reviews as you can see from my profile, but this game deserves one - for the direction it’s heading, the modding scene, and the ridiculous amount of fun it regularly delivers on every play session.

After more than two decades of gaming—from OG Battlefield 2, Project Reality, to newer titles like BF1, BF4, COD: Warzone, Squad, and Hell Let Loose - I can honestly say Arma Reforger has quickly become my favourite strategic-teamwork-big player but small squad FPS. I’ve sunk nearly 200 hours into it in just two months, despite a busy personal and professional life. That should say something.

Early on, I stuck to vanilla for the first couple of weeks, just to get a proper feel for the game. And honestly, it was the right call. No GPS, no map marker, no night vision it all felt a bit punishing at first, but it’s manageable. Eventually, those limitations become part of the immersion. Daytime-only servers help a lot if you’re new. Don't jump into mods before you've spent a good 20-30 hours in vanilla, because you won't go back.

Then I moved over to modded servers - mainly WCS - and that’s when things really clicked. The mods bring variety, polish, and quality-of-life improvements that make the experience smoother and deeper. All the things you expect, map visibility, direction pointers, compass bearings, night vision, the lot. 
The performance has also been solid for me on my mid-ish-spec rig (i7-11700 + 4080 super): crashes are rare, and desync only shows up now and then, usually while in a vehicle or crossing sync zones of some of the larger maps like Everon- but it isn't always there and does not affect the whole server or your gameplay, it's small, brief, and periodic - much less than what I often experiences in Squad with Heli's flying around at times. I'm sure they'll fix it too as it's seemed to improve. Firefights on the ground are smooth and reliable. Solid gun work and feel to everything. 

When things line up, (which is multiple times per 2-3 hour play session and even more if you find a discord group of friends, which you will), people using mics, decent teamwork - the game delivers incredible, unscripted moments. It’s hard to explain, but you know it when it happens: a coordinated push, a perfectly timed flank, or even a chaotic skirmish that somehow works out. It's a great balance between travel time and action on many of the maps - I think that's what really helps keep the magic going constantly.

That said, be prepared to shop around for servers. Some are unmoderated, and I’ve run into the usual nonsense - mic abuse, racism, etc., even on official servers. I nearly walked away from the game at one point because of it. But stick with it. There are excellent servers out there with great communities and regular players. Once you find your spot, it feels like home. For me, that's the official WCS servers.

I’ve essentially retired from Squad and HLL for now. Reforger isn’t a full-on milsim - it’s less rigid, more forgiving - but that’s part of the appeal. Vehicles are a blast to drive. Chaos and comedy happen often. Combat is intense but doesn’t punish you for every mistake. You can usually get back up, heal, and rejoin the fight. It strikes a balance that other tactical shooters haven’t quite managed.

Of course, it’s not perfect. The squad and map systems are confusing and could really use a redesign. The upcoming commander role could be a huge boost for deeper cross team coordination, it's next on the list but it’s not here yet. Comms are limited - more mic channel control would go a long way for those times when you platoon chat is going crazy. You can mute your radio easily, but I haven't found a way to mute just the Platoon chat and not my Squad chat. And the arsenal system is just plain unintuitive until someone explains how to navigate it. (Spoiler: inspecting your weapon is your friend.) 
Thankfully, modded servers remember your loadout, so you only need to suffer through it once per server. Someone dropping you their kit, you picking it up and saving, actually bypasses all of that in seconds anyway. 
Server queue time is the thing, it takes on average 40-60 seconds per player in the queue ahead of you, so you can be queuing to join the most popular servers from anywhere between 10-25minutes - so factor that in, boot the game, join the queue, and deal with a bit of housework or scroll reddit.  The good thing is if you disconnect, you can normally reconnect and skip the queue if done within a few minutes, so crashing isn't as bigger deal as it was a few months back before they fixed this.
Sometimes there is then a queue to join one of the teams if you are picky, normally each server will have a "good team" and a "public team", where it's regular players will gather and join the same team, but I have noticed servers and people starting to rotate teams more between maps, so I think this will balance out.
Finally, there is no way really to track your kills and deaths in game with a score board, you get used to it, even if I do wish they'd add something.

But here’s the thing: none of that stops me from playing. If I were reading this, I’d probably be put off by that list. But in practice, the good far outweighs the bad. And the community - at least in the right places - is full of players who are happy to help you get your bearings, team up, and take on the objective in whatever way you suggest. People are happy to tag along, or for you to tag along with them.

Reforger is already a great game, and it’s clearly on track to become something special. It’s not there yet, but it doesn’t need to be. The foundation is solid, the devs are active, and the modding scene is carrying it in the best possible way.

If you’re after a shooter with strategy, depth, and the kind of moments that can’t be scripted - this is it right now.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1750384469}, {"review_text": "Arma Reforger isn’t just the best shooter I’ve ever played, it’s also the funniest. It's got all the pros and none of the cons of Hell Let Loose, Battlefield, CoD, and Squad. It's Arma 3, but actually playable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1741542350}, {"review_text": "Pros:

Graphics & Performance: The Enfusion engine is a major upgrade. 
Lighting, terrain, and animations are beautiful, and the performance is surprisingly solid for an Arma game (as long as your rig can handle it).

Multiplayer Experience: Playing on Everon with friends is nostalgic and exciting. The dynamic events and role-based teamwork capture the essence of the Arma experience.

Modding Potential: The new Workbench tools open the door for endless modding possibilities. It’s already impressive to see what the community has created, and it feels like we’re just scratching the surface.

Cons:

Content: This is a barebones experience compared to previous Arma games. There are limited weapons, vehicles, and gameplay modes, which might leave casual players wanting more.

Bugs: It wouldn’t be an Arma game without bugs, and Reforger is no exception. Expect some rough edges, especially in larger battles or custom scenarios.

Price vs. Content: At its current price, some players might feel there isn’t enough content to justify the purchase, especially if they’re not interested in modding.

Final Thoughts:
