And even after going through BG3, I still found it really really great.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1739478149}, {"review_text": "It’s rare for a game to reach legendary status while still feeling fresh years later. But Divinity: Original Sin 2 – Definitive Edition is exactly that—a genre-defining CRPG masterpiece that, even in 2025, remains one of the finest examples of what turn-based fantasy storytelling and player freedom can achieve.

Built by Larian Studios (now riding high off the success of Baldur’s Gate 3), Original Sin 2 isn't just an RPG—it's a sandbox of storytelling, strategy, and systemic brilliance, with every action, spell, and dialogue choice carrying real weight.

At its core, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a tactical turn-based RPG with deep character progression, party-based exploration, and a world that bends to your creativity.

Combat is where it shines brightest:
-Elemental interactions: Set oil on fire, freeze a blood pool, electrify water—it's a playground of cause and effect.
-Verticality matters: Height grants advantage, line-of-sight becomes puzzle-like.
-Status effects are everything: You’ll juggle armor types, crowd control, and positioning constantly.

It’s the kind of combat that makes every encounter feel like a battle puzzle, and no two fights ever play the same way.

You can create a custom character or choose from six rich origin characters, each with their own backstory, personal quests, and perspectives. Whether it's:
-Sebille, the ex-slave assassin seeking vengeance
-Fane, the undead scholar from a forgotten world
-Ifan, a former soldier wrestling with guilt

Or your own hand-crafted hero with custom tags and dialogue paths

Your companions aren’t just sidekicks—they’re potential rivals, lovers, or threats, depending on your choices. The writing is sharp, emotional, and often laced with dry humor or existential weight.

Every dialogue option feels meaningful, and choices echo throughout the world.

From the cursed island of Fort Joy to the war-ravaged ruins of Arx, the world of Rivellon is densely packed, beautifully hand-crafted, and reactive. There’s no filler here—every inch hides secrets, lore, and unexpected moments.

The Definitive Edition includes:
-Improved quest flow and pacing
-Polished combat encounters
-Expanded endgame content and rebalanced fights
-Fully voiced dialogue for every line (a massive feat even by 2025 standards)

And despite its linear chapter structure, the game constantly feels open-ended. How you solve a problem is often left entirely up to you—fight, sneak, talk, or blow the room up.

This is a game where:
-Killing a main quest NPC is possible—and accounted for.
-Speaking with animals via a skill might unlock entire subplots.
-Using teleport to bypass a locked door can break the quest in your favor.
-Playing as undead requires wearing a hood in town… or face panic and hostility.

It's the most reactive RPG world since the Ultima days, with a modern layer of cinematic polish and turn-based refinement.

You’re constantly encouraged to experiment, break systems, and try insane ideas—and the game almost always rewards it.

While it’s a 2017 title, the Definitive Edition’s art direction and lighting design hold up impressively. Character models are expressive, spell effects pop, and environments are rich with fantasy flavor.

The voice acting is superb across the board, and the soundtrack by Borislav Slavov (who would later score BG3) is emotional, sweeping, and unforgettable.

You can play Divinity: Original Sin 2 solo or in drop-in/drop-out 2–4 player co-op, both online or local split-screen.

Multiplayer adds unexpected chaos and brilliance:
-Players can split up, tackle different quests, or even work at cross-purposes.
-One player might charm a shopkeeper while the other robs their house.
-PvP choices (even within dialogue) are possible.
-It’s one of the most collaborative and creative RPG co-op experiences ever made.

Any Weaknesses? Just a Few:
-Inventory management can be tedious, especially in co-op.
-The learning curve is real: the game assumes you’ll experiment and fail.
-The final act (Arx) is sometimes criticized for being slightly rushed or cluttered in comparison to earlier chapters.
-If you're not into reading, tactical combat, or slow-burn storytelling—you may bounce off.

But these are minor issues in an otherwise stellar package.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 – Definitive Edition is still, in 2025, a masterclass in RPG design. It’s complex but rewarding, beautifully written yet player-driven, and packed with memorable characters, world-shaping choices, and strategic depth.

Whether you’re a diehard CRPG veteran or new to the genre after Baldur’s Gate 3, Original Sin 2 is an essential playthrough—a shining example of how to build a living, reactive world where every action matters.

Pros:
-Deep, tactical combat with system-based creativity
-Excellent writing and memorable characters
-Massive replay value and roleplay depth
-Incredible co-op experience
-Fully voiced, beautiful world with impactful choices

Cons:
-Steep learning curve for new players
-Inventory/UI bloat, especially in late-game
-Final act less polished than earlier chapters
-Not ideal for players who dislike reading or tactical pacing

Divinity: Original Sin 2 – Definitive Edition isn’t just one of the best CRPGs of all time—it’s one of the best RPGs ever made, period. Rich, reactive, and relentlessly clever, it’s a journey worth taking again and again.

I have no idea what I'm doing, but I 200% am having A LOT of fun doing it! :D", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759620699}, {"review_text": "A word of advice about difficulty level: This game is a lot harder than BG3. Do not do Tactician unless you are the type of person who likes to pick up everything, obsessively upgrade your gear, optimize TF out of your builds, ruthlessly farm XP, and carefully position your units for every fight. And even then, don't do it unless you, like me, enjoy pain and suffering. 

I think where people are most likely to have a bad time with this game is if they are too proud to play on Classic or even Story mode. Classic mode gives you a lot more leeway to not have to think about the most granular optimization aspects while still being PLENTY challenging. I'd say my experience playing this game on Classic is about comparable to what my experience playing BG3 on Tactician was, or maybe *slightly* easier. 

So yeah, the biggest downside of this game in my view is that you really have to hunt down XP, and it's not intuitive about how to do that. Sometimes elaborate quests will only give you a fraction of the XP that other ones will. Other side quests won't give XP at all. Still others will wildly vary in reward based on how you complete them, and there's no consistent set of rules about how that works -- sometimes you must kill everyone, other times it's better to spare, sometimes you must be good or be evil and very often a lot of the XP hides behind extremely optional aspects of the mission. The game RARELY follows the principle that quest completion should be the lion's share of XP, which I think is it's biggest miss. It's hecking difficult to stay leveled in this game unless you look up online how to do it, which is the main reason I recommend Classic for most players. On Classic you can actually pretty easily punch a level above your weight if you're fairly cunning and good about hoarding gear + minmaxing. On Tactician it's WAY harder to do that. 

That gripe aside I now want to ramble that I love this game. Every square inch of scenery is beautiful. I'm not just talking "good graphics" (though yes the graphics are great); this game bothers to add a ton of atmospheric detail that just delights the eye at every turn. Whether you're on a beach stumbling across talking frogs or in some rich lunatic's basement admiring every individual stone and torch between his mountain of excess riches, the whole thing is just packed so tightly that every single location feels unique even to a jaded cynical eye. 

And now a word on NPCs -- DOS2 has a lot of them, and not since Fallout: New Vegas have I felt such a sense that not a single one is wasted space. The majority have unique dialogue; even those that don't contribute to atmosphere, commenting on current events or the smell in the air in a way that really makes every setting feel ALIVE. DOS2 follows a simple principle I've always believed in: the more you engage with every tiny detail, the more immersed it makes you feel. In other games looking around like that might collapse the illusion, but here it always enhances it.

DOS2's combat is a fun DND-like romp that mostly centers on crowd-controlling by using your minmaxxed party cleverly. Another word of advice: you will have one stat that you want to increase way above all your others, and that will be whatever stat you do damage with (STR, INT, or FIN). You will then probably want to dump the other 2, slightly boost Memory, and possibly dump or boost Wits depending on your overall build. Constitution is only worth an investment if you need it for shields. 

That said, I do think my gripe is that the most effective way to do combat in this game is to do it in a predictable and boring way where you use the same tactics repeatedly to maximize damage. In that sense, it feels behind not just BG3 but also DOS1, both of which are a bit more focused on rewarding creativity IMHO. I want to emphasize that I'm nitpicking and still consider it one of the most fun combats in any game I've ever played.

And of course I can't ignore the companions. Full disclosure, I've not played with Beast/Ifan and I've also not finished the story of Red Prince, but I can say that all of what I've seen has been wonderfully engrossing. Sebille in particular is possibly my favorite-written character in an RPG party. If you liked Astarion or really any of the BG3 companions, you'll LOVE Sebille as she is the OG "breaking free of an old abuser" backstory executed to perfection. This helps, this helps alot. But there is a wrong way and a right way to play kovaaks. Playing the wrong way can really fuck up your aim if you don't realize what you're doing for a long time.

This is what happened to me when I initially purchased this game and started getting into aim training. I initially started around 4 years ago, on and off, but i never really started grinding until last year. I now realize that the 4 years on and off blindly aim training set me back really bad. 

I used to uncontrollably flick left in right whenever i'd get into any aim duel. While this is also a symptom of panicking in-game and not keeping calm, there are mouse movements I sometimes could not (and still can't, to a degree) stop myself from making. It had become instinct. This was because for those four years I thought grinding close fast strafes and scenarios much higher than my skillset would help me.

You will hear people saying "Kovaak's doesn't work" or "Kovaak's ruined my aim" - This is true if you don't know what you're doing. 

It's much more obvious, known, and easier to get into these days, but if you're looking to start aimtraining, a nice google search to start with is: "voltaic kovaaks". Voltaic is an aimer community with lots of resources and information revolving aimtraining and kovaaks. 

Remember to disable your high score bar sometimes
Always listen to music*
Prioritize undershooting
Hold your mouse like you would hold an egg
Track your target with your eyes like you would track the blade of a spinning ceiling fan

dont just try to flick to your target because you're losing score. this is a cope tactic, and one that will ruin your aim. do not worry about your score. worry about how you're training yourself. keep in mind the muscle memory you are teaching yourself. read the descriptions of scenarios if there is one. i had to came back to this review to update it because i found myself making the same mistake again, and i wanted to really get this point across.

Unless you want to do even a minimum of crafting. It's kind of insane that such a basic feature is locked behind a subscription - it's not like the game is free-to-play. If you can practice extraordinary meticulousness with your looting and inventory management, and have no desire whatsoever to do any crafting, you can get by without it. But your inventory and bank space can fill up real quick.

Mount speed not being account-wide is awful. No big deal right? Just visit a stable master once a day right? Except each time you visit you can upgrade only one of three stats, and they improve by a meager 1 point each time. Why? I think I know why - because you can buy a pack of 10 "Riding Lessons" on the Crown Store for 1,000 crowns (roughly $10). 18,000 crowns (over $120) to fully max out your riding skills FOR A SINGLE CHARACTER this way.

Oh, and don't you worry. Albeit optional, ESO's got loot crates too! Let's review the financial model:
* Buy the game
* Subscription required to not be hamstringed
* Pay for convenience due to outrageous decisions like locking riding skills to a single character
* Loot crates.

Enough about the unabashed greed on display. The game itself seems to have a healthy population, I never had to wait in a queue for a dungeon or trial terribly long. Quests are unique, the story is... OK. Some dungeons are also pretty unique. Each zone has it's own character but the art design kind of results in them feeling a bit samey, with some exceptions of course. A lot of them have a sense of drabness that I can't quite put my finger on.

Combat is bad. Really bad. Floaty, impactless. Popular meta involves exploiting what I can only imagine was an unintentional flaw in design - animation canceling. Fortunately there are builds (that are also meta but much more niche) that can forgo this exploitation.

When I first started I was really thrown off by my starting stats. Why were they in the thousands already, I'm level 1? Why is my damage in the thousands? It's level-scaling. 	I've spent nearly 10,000 hours in The Elder Scrolls Online (ESO), roughly a year of my life in-game. As a veteran player, I love the game's enormous world and the amount of content it offers new players. However, for veteran players deeply invested in the endgame, ESO feels increasingly neglected. While ZeniMax Online Studios has focused on attracting newcomers, the endgame community has been forgotten, as if they no longer mattered. We face persistent issues such as server lag, an easy-to-abuse ban system, and a lack of meaningful content updates.

The New Player Experience:
	For new players, ESO is a treasure trove. The game's massive world, rich lore, and seemingly endless number of questlines provide hundreds of hours worth of engaging content. I always see new players exploring Tamriel, and it's nice to see the game's newbie community grow.

Endgame Woes, Performance, and Optimization:
	For veteran players, the experience is far less satisfying. ZeniMax's focus on new players has come at the expense of endgame quality-of-life improvements. Things that seem simple in the grand scheme of the game have been persistent problems for years. One of the most glaring issues is unplayable in-game lag, particularly in Cyrodiil during high-pop times. This isn't a standard latency issue, but a slideshow-like drop in framerates similar to dropping thousands of cheese wheels in Skyrim or meshing props in Garry's Mod. Even high-end hardware (like an RTX 5090 or AMD 9950 processor) can't overcome this lag. These issues come from poor server hardware, outdated netcode, and a lack of optimization. These issues have been consistently raised on ZeniMax's forums, but over the past two years, moderators have ignored us. Locking and removing almost everything related to these issues. This suppression of feedback alienates the community and stifles meaningful discussion about the game's shortcomings.

Community and Moderation Issues:
	ESO, being an MMORPG, should encourage player interaction; however, ZeniMax's moderation policies and terms of service have created a toxic environment. The in-game ban strike system is easily abused, with minor trash talk or emotes resulting in permanent bans. Known groups of players exploit this system to target other players they dislike or simply aren't as skilled (you know who you are), baiting them into rule-breaking behavior. This forces players to walk on eggshells, as even friendly veterans like myself and my friends have been targeted by these "ban groups." Imagine... Thousands of hours and dollars invested in the game just vanish, all because you T-bagged someone, or because you told them off after harassing you or a friend. This makes ESO feel less like a game and more like an overly policed social credit society.

PvE Content: Repetitive and Hollow:
	ESO's PvE content feels repetitive and lacks depth. Players will eventually end up chasing achievements/high scores in trials/dungeons. This is their downfall. This repetitiveness leads to rapid burnout, with many PvE players quitting after completing new content and only returning for the subsequent trial or dungeon release. And when new stuff releases, it always follows the same formula, whereas most lack meaningful choices or alternate endings. The lack of engaging, replayable content fails to keep veteran PvE players invested in the long term.

PvP: Neglected and Unbalanced:
	The PvP scene in ESO is in dire straits. Open-world PvP in Cyrodiil is dying due to years of power creep from group-based sets, allowing large, unkillable groups to dominate and create lag-heavy zones that render skilled play impossible. Exploits like keep defense AP manipulation further skew leaderboards, ensuring the same small group of players monopolize Emperor status in the primary campaign. 
	Imperial City, while a lucrative area for PvP players, remains underpopulated due to incentives favoring solo or duo play, causing players to log out when factions grow too large.
	Battlegrounds, the one and only PvP mode receiving any attention, suffers from excessive queue times (20–50 minutes) and consistently one-sided matches. There are several theories behind long queue times, but a high percentage of players believe that the population is just overall discouraged. Some because of simple wait times, and some because of skill balancing between teams.. Battlegrounds entirely relies on a single guild, Deathmatch, without which it would not function.

The Crown Store: A Cash Grab
	The Crown Store, ESO's microtransaction hub, is where ZeniMax focuses most of its efforts. Players spend real money on cosmetics and quality-of-life upgrades, and I've personally invested around $3,000 since launch. Unfortunately, there's little evidence that this revenue is being reinvested to improve the game's servers, netcode, or content. The prioritization of monetization over core gameplay improvements leaves a bitter taste for veteran players.

Advice for Players:
New Players: Dive in and enjoy ESO's vast world! Join a guild, connect with other newcomers, and explore the game's rich content. You're in for a treat.
Veteran Players: If you're feeling frustrated, you're not alone. Many of us feel stuck, torn between quitting or speaking out, only to risk being silenced or banned. The ESO community needs a safe space to voice grievances, and platforms like this review are one of the few places we can do so freely.

Conclusion:
	ESO is a game of extremes: a paradise for new players but a frustrating slog for veterans. Persistent lag, an exploitable ban system, repetitive PvE, neglected PvP, and a cash-focused Crown Store have alienated the endgame community. I hope ZeniMax addresses these issues and reinvests in the game's core systems. Until then, I'll keep playing, hoping for change. And maybe for At'avar to come back with that milk. As someone who has been playing since the launch of this game it really pains me to see the state that the game is currently in and where it is heading. Your time is better off playing a game where the devs actually care about their playerbase.

Itemization: There is over 650 unique item sets in the game and only a handful are being used. While there will always be a meta in video games this is less of an instance where a handful of sets just outperform the rest by a little bit and thus make them the meta; this is a case where the other sets have had the numbers lowered to the point where the sets that are meta are the meta because they are the only usable ones. For instance there was a new mythic item added to the game that interacted with a sorcerer ultimate ability that replaces your light and heavy attacks. This mythic item works by boosting heavy attacks by 50% and thus boosted the power of the ultimate. This was simply a fun setup that was good, but not meta for some of the endgame content, and yet they removed the mythic item working with the ultimate. Meanwhile there is another mythic item that reduces your light and heavy attack damage by 99% and this mythic had and still reduces the ultimate damage by 99%. These are the decisions that the developers choose to make where anything that benefits the player they take away and give us no replacement but anything that is detrimental is kept.

Classes and Skills: There is no longer unique ways of playing the game or distinction between classes and specs as it has all been streamlined and homogenized to the point where everything plays the same. Sub classing has been one of the worst things to ever happen to this game. They already had issues balancing the base classes but letting you choose one line from two other classes meanwhile doing nothing to boost base classes to make up for the opportunity cost forces you to subclass to keep up. Unfortunately there are skills and skill lines that are leagues better than others and picking certain skills and ability lines means that you are actively giving up and opportunity cost that gimps you as a player. We've had this system for a single patch and this upcoming patch should  have been a patch that focuses on tuning things that are blatantly overpowered such as the Arcanist class ability fatecarver (the best AOE and Single target spammable in the entire game for PvE) they instead chose to nerf things that were helping other classes keep up and even nerfed some of the class skill lines with a sub 5% pick rate for endgame PvE content AND PvP content. The week one patch notes were hit with so much backlash by the player base that they decided to walk back some truly awful changes, but then refused to walk back some others. They were then so scared of even more backlash that they gave us NOTHING for the following 3 weeks of the PTS cycle except for a few minor NERFS. The current state of pure classing is in shambles with some classes such as necromancer not being able to use it's own abilities. Necromancer works by having some abilities generate corpses and other use the corpses. They decided that the corpses that are core part of the necromancer rotation should count as pet and capped them at 10, with the oldest corpses you generated not being despawned if you try to summon another when you are at the cap, this means that if you use the more than a single corpse generating ability you rapidly hit the pet limit and are just not allowed to use your abilities due to being at the limit. It has been like this for months and they have done nothing to fix this outside of making it so that you don't use resources if the cast fails due to being at the pet limit. 

Update cycles: Updates in this game happen four times a year, usually with around three months between them. For some reason the developers refuse to hotfix anything, such as the above stated Necromancer issues, UNLESS it positively impacts the players. For instance there have been patches where there is an issues with the code that allows players to get more items than intended or something in the crown store at a lower price than intended. These will rapidly be hotfixed within hours and players that benefited from them will be banned. This means that if something negatively impacts a class or playstyle then you will  have to wait for at least three months or even more before the issue is addressed. For instance the above stated necromancer issues have been ongoing for three months and they have no intention of fixing them for at least another three months at a minimum. There have been so many cases over the years where certain sets and classes have been left in unplayable states for upwards of an entire year. 

Developer team: The developers are plain and simple not a part of the player community. There is little to no communication with the dev team and any player based feed back gets thrown in the trash unless people start mass cancelling the subscription. The dev team is also just generally not knowledgeable about the game. The most blatant instance of this was the lead combat developer not knowing that heavy attacks restored resources, something that is taught to the player withing the first 5 minutes of gameplay. Another instance of the team behind ESO's incompetence was when the Community Manager actively and publicly shamed a large content creator to the point that he quit the game as a whole. 

Monetization: To put it in one word it would be "predatory." The premium currency has such little value that the minimum buying option will buy you a single pack of crown crates "lootboxes" that have basically a 0% chance of giving you anything of value where you need to drop hundreds of dollars to get enough pity currency to buy a single on of the high tier items. There is also a free to play equivalent of the pity currency where you will need to play everyday for nearly a year to buy one of those higher tier items. outside of the crates you have things like in game houses costing hundreds of actual dollars to purchase in the game and to top it of they FOMO so many of the extremely pricy things. Another issue is with their change of content releases. In the past we had two dungeon packs, a main expansion, and a DLC zone. While you always had to pay for that year's expansion, you would get access to the two dungeon packs, the DLC zone, and all past dungeons, DLC zones, and previous years' expansions included with the ESO subscription. This year they upped the price of the expansion and instead of this price hike being due to the zone being bigger etc its because they are forcing you to buy the dungeon packs AND the DLC zone to buy the expansion. You cannot simply just buy the expansion without buying the other things that are already included with a subscription. While this may be nice for people without the subscription, let me start off by saying that a one month subscription is the same amount of money as the cheapest pack of premium currency and not only does it give you access to all of the subscription perks but it also gives you more of the premium currency than the premium currency pack. This means that if you wanted to eventually not have a subscription but still have access to the content it is more cost effective to pay for a subscription and buy the dungeon packs and DLC zones with the premium currency you get from the subscription. Now it might make some people upset that the mechanics of this game aren't the most lore-friendly, being that this game is the only case where we can grow spikes out of our backs, but Nirn [spoiler] canonically isn't real, [/spoiler] I say anything goes.

There are a couple of things that make your character, race, and class, race has some stat effects and its own set of passive skills you can unlock, while classes will give you exclusive skills that are both active and passive. Each class has 3 skill categories, their DPS skills, their Tank skills, and their Support skills. DPS skills do damage, duh, and apply effects onto enemies, Tank skills draw aggro and protect you from damage, and then support skills provide utility to your group, not always just healing, but still mostly healing. Then there are weapon skills which are attacks and passives exclusive to that weapon, and then there are armor skills which are just passive and improve the performance of armor, and then there's a whole load of secondary skills that are unlocked by doing certain activities and are by far the most painful to progress, especially the crafting skills. The combat-related skills can be very fun to progress as you try to figure out your playstyle and optimize your character, but the rest of them are a huge pain, they involve immense repetition and it can get very stale, very quickly, but the payoff is pretty good, having a well-made character is super fun to play with, especially in a group.

Your gear is another very important thing, there are a few ways to obtain weapons and armor: Craft it, find it, receive it as a quest reward or random drop. The gear you're gonna want is gonna belong to sets, which give you stat buffs depending on how many pieces of the set you have equipped, and based on how many stat buffs a set maxes out at, you can get about 2-3 full set bonuses when fully kitted out. You have 2 weapons, 6 armor pieces, and 3 jewelry slots (2 rings and one necklace). Pieces of a set can be obtained two ways, boss drops in dungeons and then crafting, and there is no overlap, specific sets can only be found in dungeons while the others can only be crafted at specific stations in specific parts of Tamriel, some of which require DLCs to access. But it doesn't matter how you end up getting your gear, crafting is very important. Crafting is super simple, you only need two types of items to make it, the item which determines the quality of your gear which just determines the level of your gear and then the style material which is purely cosmetic but you still need one to craft anything, just one style material per item though, so don't worry. In order to craft higher level gear you need the necessary skills unlocked in the crafting category for that specifc type of crafting, there are 7, 4 of them are for gear, the other 3 or for consumables, each takes their own materials (except style materials) and need to be leveled up separately, this can be done by crafting items that belong it that category, disassembling gear, (gear made from other players and gear with bonuses listed for disassembling will give you the most XP for it) and doing writ quests, which require you to craft some specific items for rewards, you get one per crafting category per day. You can also put secondary effects on gear, which require their own items which you find through various means, and the only way to craft gear with these effects is to destroy gear with the effect to research it, which is put on a timer, which is an exponential increase each time you do it, going up to a month, it's really not that fun. The grind for gear is probably one of the most tedious parts about it, it's not hard, just time consuming, use some add-ons if you don't want to be searching forever for crafting materials, Zenimax allows it so it's fine.

The actual gameplay is actually quite fun, you end up getting two weapon slots for double the amount of skills you can use, just push a button to swap weapons and now you have different skills to use, what I often do is have my setup skills on one weapon while all of my attacks are on another. The name of the game is use your skills effectively, most classes have a "spam skill" that you're meant to use repeatedly when you're not using something else, and some classes are built around the spam skill, like the Arcanist, where each time you use the spam skill, you generate something called crux, and some skills consume it, and they get more powerful the more crux it consumes, I really like it and I think it's super fun. The game is most fun when played with a group, dungeons are 4 players, and then Trials are 15, and Trials are my favorite, especially when they're planned well, and it feels super good to win them, its really where the MMORPG magic shines. I also don't recommend playing in first person, it might feel more like Elder Scrolls that way, but you're putting yourself at a disadvantage, you'll be losing a lot of sight that way, and the game seems built around third person despite defaulting to first.

The graphics are much more cartoony than the other Elder Scrolls games, they don't look bad necessarily, Elder Scrolls games never looked that bad when compared to games of the time, but the ESO artstyle is different, and I think it fits well.

The Soundtrack isn't super special, it's mostly just rehashes of old songs from the series, but that doesn't stop it from sounding pretty good, all Orchestral and whatnot.

The writing in this game is pretty balls, it's very clear that story was not a huge concern for Zenimax, at least not in the dialogue, I never bothered listening to it, the stories were never that engaging, some of the story moments can be really cool, be it the bossfights or the end of the main story, but overall it leaves a lot to be desired, I love good stories, games like RDR2 and Cyberpunk 2077 have some of my favorite stories and my ears were wide open and listening to all the dialogue even though the games were dozens of hours long each.

This game is not lacking in content by any means, the base game alone will give you a couple dozen hours, both by doing the main story and going through all of the zone stories, I'd recommend doing a good chunk of the Base Game before deciding on buying any DLCs.

I will share this info in case it is useful for anyone else who want to enjoy the game and to have some more visibility. Thanks to Cryio on Needforspeed subreddit for the fix.

[b] Step 1: [/b] 
Go to Documents > Criterion Games > Need For Speed(TM) Most Wanted > Open config.NFS13Save ini file with notepad

[b] Step 2: [/b]
Disable Vsync by changing VsyncInterval to 0 (VsyncInterval=0)

[b] Step 3: [/b]
Documents > Criterion Games > Need For Speed(TM) Most Wanted > Save > 1004299468619 (could be different for you) and Open controls.NFS13Save ini file with notepad (you might need to open the game first and change some settings for this to show up)

[b] Step 4: [/b]
Lower the right most value of STEERLEFT, STEERRIGHT, ACCELERATE, BRAKE, HANDBRAKE, NITROUS   from 1.00 to 0.10

For eg, in my case it ends up looking like this:
STEERLEFT=0,KEY_A,0.00,0.10
STEERRIGHT=0,KEY_D,0.00,0.10
ACCELERATE=0,KEY_W,0.00,0.10
BRAKE=0,KEY_S,0.00,0.10
HANDBRAKE=0,KEY_SPACE,0.00,0.10

[b] Optional Steps: [/b] 
To disable the horrible screen tearing the game has when disabling vsync, use Borderless gaming app to play in Borderless fullscreen which will eliminate the screen tearing. 

In NVIDIA control panel, set low latency mode for the game as ULTRA

There is a fine line between "ambitious" and "hubristic," and Cities: Skylines II has built a beautiful, eight-lane superhighway directly over that line... which promptly leads to a 15-frame-per-second traffic jam.

As the heir apparent to the undisputed champion of modern city-builders, CS:II had one job: to be CS:I but bigger, deeper, and better. It is, unequivocally, bigger. The "deeper" and "better" parts, however, seem tobe stuck in simulation-limbo, still waiting for a patch to load.

The Performance: A PowerPoint Presentation with Good Intentions
Let's address the elephant in the room—an elephant so large it has tanked the entire city's performance. This game is not "unoptimized" in the way we've come to expect. It is a work of technical audacity. It seems to believe that every player is running a dual-CPU quantum supercomputer cooled by liquid nitrogen.

My rig, which can comfortably render parallel universes in other AAA titles, sputters, chokes, and begs for mercy at the mere sight of a medium-sized suburb. We were promised a deep simulation; what we received is the world's most demanding slideshow. The game is meticulously simulating the dental records of every citizen, the thread count of their bedsheets, and the existential dread of their cat, all while forgetting that the player needs to be able to move the camera smoothly.

The "Deep" Simulation: A Puddle Pretending to be an Ocean
The core promise was a revolutionary economic and citizen AI. We were told every "cim" would live a "full life." This, it turnses out, is technically true. They are born, they get a job (which they may or may not drive to), they mysteriously generate wealth despite the entire city's economy being on fire, and then they require a hearse... which may or may not arrive before the next ice age.

The economy is a baffling magic show. Industries demand workers, but no one wants to work. You import... something... and export... something else... and your bank account either swells to the size of a small nation's GDP or collapses instantly. It's less "complex economic simulation" and more "pulling a lever on a very confusing slot machine." And the new land value mechanic? A fantastic way to ensure your entire population becomes homeless millionaires overnight.

The Foundation Is Here (The Rest Is Sold Separately)
Make no mistake, the bones of a masterpiece are here. The new road tools are (mostly) a dream. The scale is breathtaking. The potential for creation is vast.

But that's the key word: potential.

This feels like a game built for its next five years of DLC. Gameplay and Mechanics
The game's core mechanics revolve around crafting, combat, and strategy. Players gather resources, craft weapons and items, and engage in battles with other players or AI-controlled creatures. One of the game's significant challenges is its player base. Outside of Korea, finding matches can be time-consuming, and the community's activity varies by region. Monetization and Progression
Eternal Return is free-to-play, with monetization primarily through cosmetic items and character unlocks. While the game offers a battle pass and seasonal content, some players have found the progression system to be grindy, requiring significant time investment to unlock all content .

Final Thoughts
Eternal Return is an ambitious title that successfully merges elements of MOBA and battle royale genres. Its unique gameplay mechanics and appealing visuals make it a standout in the free-to-play market. However, issues with matchmaking, character balance, and progression may deter some players. review_texts:
[{"review_text": "Way too many people sleeping on this game just because 66L exist, despite this game is one of the most feature complete fighting game out there.

Rising has:
- Rollback
- Crossplay
- Free Version
- Tons of cosmetics from the progression system
- Single player content
- Minigames", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1747805457}, {"review_text": "I'll be honest, after playing this game for a full year, GBVSR is sick.

I can't tell how many things GBVSR does well compared to other fighting games of this era and yet, it's not as popular despite all the good things we have in this !  
It really feels like a polished game overall.

- Menus are working well and everything is accessible easily without having to search for decades.

- Good online, rollback, matchmaking, lobbies, no issue ! (It's almost fun to just walk around and talk with people in the lobby)

- Ranked is also working well. (although it has a lot of wifi warriors and AFK players in lower ranks.)

- Lots of different modes outside of online battles. (story, arcade, figure, Grandbruise although there is not enough mini games and not many people to play with, robomi and we are getting survival mode in 2.0 ver !)

- Many Characters, all created with lots of love to the source material. (Vikala even has a JustinWong meme reference) 
Each character has a lot of different color and weapon skins.  

- Balancing is overall pretty great ! We had some busted characters and still have 66L spam but the devs are listening and after playing this game for a full year, I think it was great compared to other games. (and also the fact fighting games are HARD to make and balance.)

- Training mode has a lot of options although I would add a frame meter just like SF6 does. (a mod exist for that at least)

- Lots of different input options and macros available to play exactly like you want !

- A generous FREE version of the game is available and simple controls makes the game easy to access, they are well implemented and don't feel clunky or limited like other fighting games.
I introduced so many friends to fighting games thanks to this game. (some of them still play to this day !)

- You may have heard fighting games have DLC and battle pass issues, but GBVSR let's you buy the DLCs with the in game money !
You need to grind a bit but it won't take you months and months to get what you want. (If you want every DLC though... Good luck lol.) 
For Battle Passes, the content is overall great for those who want them, it's completely optional and the free version is also cool.
I'm not really the type of player who will buy the BPs but none of them made me feel like it was a scam and they now sell you the content of older BPs as DLC if you missed one of them.

Overall, I really like this game because it's one of the rare ones where I just like to hang out in it, play a couple of games, have fun with Grandbruise for a little break and tchat with others.
I traveled in tourneys for this game and I lived so many great things because of it.

The devs are communicating well with the players and creates really fun things for us. (See their April Fools Joke as a reference, it was a fun thing !)
It's useless but they did it anyway, It just feels like they also have fun creating the game and it's just so cool.
We will even get Pop Team Epic crossover for lobby avatars ! Why ? Don't know but it's amusing ! 

Thanks for all the hard work you have done GBVSR Team, Arcsys and Cygames.

Thank you so much.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1740402581}, {"review_text": "So, think Street Fighter if it was made for people who like an anime art style. It isn't an anime fighter, there are no airdashes, mix is kind of basic and while combos can get quite long, that's about as close as it gets to your Guilty Gears and Blazblues.
Granblue Fantasy Versus is a fighting game made for a gacha game, and Rising is the upgraded version of the original Versus, with rollback netcode and some updates to the formula.

This game has one button specials, for the people who that matters for, though you can do the regular inputs for pretty much no benefit besides comfort. Character movesets are quite unique and frequently come with significant gimmicks that you need to keep in mind, and damage is for the most part on the low to middling range, though TODs and 70%+ combos can be achieved in rare situations or by certain characters with plenty of meter to spare.

There is a block button, though it's not necessary to use besides for its 'Dodge' function, as there is also a universal unblockable option that costs a secondary resource; the punishment for losing which is taking additional damage, and getting hit by this unblockable option, getting hit by supers, or using the 'get off me' button will use this secondary resource. While it markets itself as an accessible game that's very beginner-friendly, that's not to say that it lacks any depth. This has turned out to be one of my favorite types of fighting games, or really just games in general. Fairly low skill floor, insanely high skill ceiling. It won't take long for you get some exceptionally sweaty people to face off against both in ranked and casual matches, but that's where everything Rising provides comes in handy. Everything from its detailed but easy-to-understand character guides and combo lists in training mode, frame data, tutorials for pretty much every single mechanic in the game, it's all here. Technical inputs exist, and in many ways, mashing your face onto your controller as we all do when we start off will get you killed, just as it was in the OG GBVS, but simple inputs make timings much easier to chain your normals into your specials. The addition of the Bravery Points system for raging strikes, raging chains, and how these points also interact with supers and how much damage you deal the less of it your opponents has is a great addition, and more than makes up for the removal of a universal overhead. And the U-versions of your cooldown skills are also a great addition, giving you much more options with your meter outside of just using supers. It also helps that compared to the OG GBVS, you get a TON of meter now. It used to be that filling your meter took basically the entire round, and it was mostly only ever used for supers despite it having other utilities that have since been removed. There's a lot to consider, but none of it ever felt overwhelming, and that's even considering how much faster the pace of Rising is now compared to the first game. Even if Cygames themselves likes to meme on this game being centered around "one button for easy kills" like that hilarious April Fools trailer, the game's far more than that. The addition of dash attacks is currently one of the more controversial things about the game, and I admit, it does feel like 66L is way too good for literally every character, but for the most part, it hasn't felt like the "I Win Button" that a lotta folks seem to frame it.

But all that minutia's for the sweats. I'm a filthy casul, so let's move onto Rising's story mode and some of its other features. Rising does get rid of the old RPG Mode which makes for a leaner experience for its story, though I do miss being able to select basically the entire roster at the end game when I wanna fight certain bosses, and there's no longer the Tower of Babyl for some extra challenge either. It's definitely leaning heavier now on being a visual novel with some occasional cool animated cutscenes and bosses to fight. The additional chapter they added doesn't even have trash mob quests anymore, but I think for its short run time, those weren't necessary, and they weren't the best part of the original story mode anyway. I like that this new chapter just focuses on the most important characters and events, raises the stakes far more than the original did, and just has the VN-style chapters leading into all the different boss fights.

Without spoiling anything, this game now has quite possibly my two favorite bosses in any fighting game, both in terms of how cool I think they are as characters, how satisfying they are to beat up, and most importantly, how they play. A lotta the times, fighting game bosses break the rules in ways that aren't that fun. They go from just standing or floating there, letting you wail on them for a bit, before they do boring things like raise their arms to conjure up some high damage projectile, or even leave the arena to make you fight someone else in the roster. I'm lookin' at you, Kronika. But that's not the case with Rising. The final bosses have actual movesets. Hell, they're playable in ranked for a reason. It's just that they hurt way more, have way more moves that have armor, and have that good ol' Overdrive mechanic. Without the old RPG Mode's elemental weapons and levels to consider, it is much easier to just straight up fight everything now, but the Hard mode for the story bosses is still a decent challenge.

All of this, and you're rewarded with a strange, Skyrealm-shattering tale that somehow kinda still makes sense, despite involving epic Biblical levels of gods and angels fighting each other, parallel universes colliding, some genuine emotional drama, and the mandatory cutesy anime trash. I love it. All this just so we have a proper lore excuse to have the male and female versions of the Granblue Fantasy MC being able to meet and fight each other online, as well as explaining the mirror matches, because this is still a fighting game.

For the most part, everything in Rising is a vast improvement over the original, and with its addition of crossplay on top of rollback, even though I'm already over a year late to this party, I'm still getting a ton of matches daily, there's still lobbies getting full at peak hours, and even when I'm at a losing streak, they've added a lotta other features that take my mind off it. Modes like Grand Bruise, which is the blatant Fall Guys ripoff that's genuinely pretty fun if you're willing to wait a little while to be matched up with several other people, or just the larger, more expansive, and way prettier lobby to wander around in, or the minigames. And my god, that Figure Studio. That's my end game now. It's basically a photo mode that lets you play around with 3D assets ranging from every character in the roster to side characters, to even just world objects. I'm still gonna play online, get salty, try to escape A rank with Vira and B rank with Beatrix, but the end goal now is to get every possible figure so I can take funny screenshots with my favorite waifus in the roster.

I'm glad Granblue Versus got this second chance. Back then all I and a lot of other people wanted was rollback. I have never been particularly close to the Resident Evil game franchise. I watched all the movies with Milla Jovovich, but I’ve only heard something about the games somewhere, and they never really left a deep impression on me. The hype around the Resident Evil remaster passed me by because it didn’t evoke any nostalgia or positive emotions. As a result, my opinion about the game will be an honest reflection of its core without sugarcoating.
I would like to start with the positive aspects. What really surprised me was the unusual setting of the game. When I first launched RE 2, I thought it would be a game in the style of Dead Space, but how mistaken I was. Naively shooting all my bullets at useless zombies and thinking I no longer needed to conserve ammo because there were no enemies I couldn’t handle, I encountered him… Tyrant. At that moment, my gameplay turned upside down because now I was not the hunter — Mr. X became the hunter. He didn’t react to gunfire in the usual way; instead, he punished even the slightest delay with a brutal death animation. From that moment on, there’s no room for error when he appears — you can’t afford to waste time studying the map, because he’s always nearby. Even if you think you’ve hidden successfully, he mysteriously appears behind your back at the worst moment, scaring you out of your mind. Most likely, my gaming experience was influenced by the fact that I thought I’d be playing a different game — and how awesome that was!
I was definitely pleased with the nice graphics, engine physics, and storyline. But with all due respect, why is the game so short? I understand it’s just a remaster and that we have access to a second storyline, but I still wanted more. Surely those who bought the game at launch were left asking themselves: “Is that it? Even with AAA games we tend to have a big list of games we still need to play. And some great titles such as RE 2 can easily end up on this list. I purchased this one 2 years ago but I have only managed to play it recently. Initially, I wanted to use the word "complete" but I only did one story run with Leon from start to finish which is nowhere near when it comes to the things you can this in this remake.

[b]Biohazard[/b]

The first RE was number 4 for me. But when it was initially released for PC... boy did it look ugly! Then we played number 5 with a friend at least 3 times. 6 was a chore and we hated it. I had enough of the series after that, to be honest, but with 7 I enjoyed it once again. In fact, RE 7 was the one where I have all DLCs. I was reluctant to continue with number 8 for some reason. I didn't like the direction they went with but the remakes were more interesting to me. 

[b]Comparison[/b]

I checked some videos and in addition to the technology (which is obviously an upgrade compared to the 1998 version) I understand they retained the A and B scenarios. Story-wise, you play the same campaign with Leon and Claire but you take different routes. In order to see the true ending you need to complete both. There are character-specific alterations so once you complete the story with Leon (scenario A) you can switch to Claire and pick the "2nd run" option already (scenario B). This is already an interesting concept, something that increases longevity and additional options / modes will be available after you have done the 2 scenarios. But more on them later.

[b]Controls[/b]

Oh yes, no more tank controls and this also means no more fixed camera angles. Are we feeling comfortable with controlling Leon then in his fight against hordes of zombies? Well, yes and no. I mean, close-combat became more and more interesting in later episodes. I think in number 6 you could hit and even kick. There were ways to do melee combat without wasting any bullets.

But remember those games had more sophisticated enemies! We are back to walkers here, most of the time. And you have those clickers and zombie dogs that can quickly jump at you. Headshots with the zombies are a must. You can also destroy their knees and try to get around them. The game is a pure survival horror where every battle can be deadly and conserving ammo is a must!

An interesting concept while holding different firearms is to equip so-called sub-weapons. You need to hold SPACE and after that you can throw a flashbang, a grenade or just melee with your combat knife. In case enemies capture you, you don't necessarily get hurt but you have the option to use the aforementioned tools to push away the enemies. It's fun when you stab a zombie only to remove the knife later on from the corpse. Or you put the grenade in its mouth which can  explode with a well-aimed shot.

[b]Graphical evil[/b]

The game looks fantastic! Zombie come in many forms (as in body shape and clothing). Shots hitting them can chip away pieces of their bodies (heads can be blown off, hats can fly off, limbs can be torn off). The way their body interacts with the environment is just great! That includes us: for instance, imagine that we do a headshot and the zombie in front of us immediately dies but its body falls onto us. Leon feels the weight of the dead body and pushes it away with audible disgust in his voice. 

[b]Scripted evil[/b]

Some of the dialogues are as cheesy as they get. Especially, when we team up with another person later in the story. Other than that the game has a lot of cutscenes with great voice acting and 3 main locations to go through. It's best not to rush the story as backtracking can be very rewarding when you find a special keycard or any other item that allows us to access a new location (e.g. a room, a locker) with a new weapon. Upgrade parts can be found in safes that make our weapons deadlier. Our inventory is limited: be on the lookout for hip pouches to increase its size.

[b]Longevity?[/b]

Yes, multiple playthroughs are needed for all achievements. You can do a fast run to get an S+ rank (my "casual" run granted me a C rank only) and there are achievements for completing the game on hardcore difficulty setting. So if you complete Leon's and Claire's 2nd run, too, and a hardcore walkthrough that is at least 6 playthroughs.

Then we have "The Ghost Survivors". 4 additional but short campaigns with different NPCs we met with Leon and Claire, all of whom died. These stories are a sort of "What if?" scenarios: they are all given a chance to escape and go through locations we got familiar with during the main journey. Only 3 are available at the beginning - the last is a bonus with a guy who needs to eliminate 100 zombies instead of reaching an extraction point. All these focus heavily on the action.

[b]Any annoying bits?[/b]

Of course, it's an RE game! Puzzles can be interesting but the backtracking for a new weapon or weapon upgrade can be tedious sometimes. Going back to locations previously cleared can make some new zombies spawn or those already shot will just wake up. Even with the hip pouch upgrades, inventory limit is often reached so it's best to look for the typewriter (which allows saving) as it is usually in rooms where there is also a big chest allowing us to store what we cannot take with ourselves. Try to store these items instead of discarding them which is always an option.

I found the police station the best and most interesting part of the game and I was annoyed to meet a creature later on in the story that keeps patrolling and chasing us. It is impossible to defeat this monster but we can only immobilize it for a short period of time to escape. After progressing with the story it disappears for good and we can still return to RPD to collect anything we left behind.

[b]Summary[/b]

RE 2 is a fantastic game. Is it better than the original? I don't know, I never played that one. Hardcore fans have probably already shared their view on this. One of the aspects I appreciate most is the amount of content available: there is always something to do, such as races, challenges, seasonal events or even just driving around the map enjoying the scenery, which can often be therapeutic.

Driving feels smooth and responsive, making the game accessible to newcomers and still rewarding for experienced players.

But unfortunately not everything is perfect. If you, like me, use an NVIDIA graphics card, it is worth knowing that the game still suffers from random and unpredictable crashes. This is purely based on the gameplay etc. 

TLDR:
BDO is a great concept and a visually beautiful game, built on an outdated engine. This loot grinder MMO has 30 unique classes to choose from, 26 of which have 2 different specializations.  It's mostly a single player PvE experience with a selection of large/small scale pvp content. Find a class that works for you and get to grinding. Better gear = better grinding = more upgrades. PvP on the other hand is an extremely polarizing experience. While classes are fun to play and extremely satisfying to master, the desync and pvp balancing can really make pvp feel unpolished. To top it all off BDO has a RNG % based upgrade system. Love it or hate it, that's what the game has. One day it's punishing you and the next it's giving you a handy. It's not bad when you start off, but gets worse the closer you are to the gear ceiling.  All in all a pretty solid PvE/PvP experience with one of the best combat systems in any MMO. It has the potential to be the best combat-based MMO available, but suffers from performance issues and bugs. 


Character/Gear Progression:
Probably the hottest topic whenever BDO is being discussed. This is a game all about GEAR, not character level. When it comes to combat performance, the gear will provide a vast majority of your stats. Character levels beyond level 62 are pretty much pointless. As long as you have enough skill points(obtained separately from levels) to get all skills for your specialization, 62 is the last level that provides any combat bonuses. From there going forward, it's all about the gear. This gear can be copied to one additional character via the "Tagging" system for a small amount of in-game silver. Allowing you to experience other classes at the full power of your main. 

Basically enhancing works like this:
Every item has a base enhance chance for it's current enhancement level(pretty low %). You add items called "Failstacks" to increase the chance of success(there's a softcap where failstacks beyond a certain point will net little +%).  So essentially there is a "max" % chance an item can be enhanced.

Then there are items call "Cron Stones" that "protect" the enhancement. Cron Stones are the bread and butter for endgame enhancing and can be acquired in game with silver, from events, or via P2W. So there is a cost to protecting your important items. Whether you are a whale or a F2P player, it's still RNG. Although you only Cron Stone certain items. Most items are not worth cron stoning. 

Lastly, is Pity. This is the maximum enhancement attempts you can make on an item before the game feels bad and gives you the enhancement at 100%. Every item in the game has a pity. You pray you don't hit these...but it will happen. They added these about a year ago and thank effin god. Before you could fail forever and it sucked!

There will be a point in your gear progression where buying the upgrades will no longer be available....then you must gamba enhancement levels whether you like to or not. This will be quite a ways down your adventure path, so don't let that be the "make or break" on you trying the game. Just know that's how current end game progression works. At the peak gearscore, expect most enhancements to be <5% or some as little as .6% with adequate failstack applied.

Enhancing is the biggest make or break for people. It's a lot better than it used to be, but still can be pretty disheartening. Thankfully the Pity system ensures you will get the upgrade after x amount of fails.

PvE:
PvE is a pretty enjoyable experience with a long term gearing curve. You will be spending a lot of time PvE'ing in this game as it is your primary source of obtaining money to upgrade your gear. Even if you play this game to PvP, you will be PvE'ing or Lifeskilling to get them upgrades. The better you can PvE the faster you can obtain upgrades. Thus creates the loop of this game - grind to grind better. Once you have enough upgrades you can go to a new zone. Rinse and repeat. If you only play this game to PvE/Lifeskill(which a lot of people do), you can really do the gear upgrades at any pace you would like. Each step is just a chapter in your own book. No reason to rush. Just take it all in and try out all the zones and lifeskills YOU want to do. There's a lot of different options, choose what's fun for you. Freedom of choice in the mid game is what makes this game great. Enjoy this time before your end game progression becomes more linear(for better or for worse). 

PvE Bosses:
This game offers a lot of solo/4man bossing content....unfortunately it's mostly trash. The rewards are good, but the bosses can be frustrating. Dysnc'd instakill moves, buggy mechanics, and some bosses living in immune frames really make bossing one of the low points in this game.

PvP:
This is where the sweat comes from. My personal favorite piece of the game. PvP. 

Capped :
AOS (3v3 arena)
T1 Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
T2 Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
T2 Siege (attacker/defender battle over castle 100+ players)

Capped content, as the name suggests, puts limits on your total base stats like Attack Power, Defense Power, Evasion. These are made for all players. Reaching these caps varies on the content. The 3v3 arena for example can be done with no gear! While the T1 and T2 caps give two different gear limits. These requirements are very easy to hit for a new player. T1 caps can be hit within a month and T2 will generally take 2-4 months to acquire. If you only want to do capped PvP content, you really don't need to PvE a whole lot once you reach the caps and have your crystals/artifacts/lightstones squared away. You can just log on to PvP and use the PvP currencies to buy consumables for future PvP. Kind of a nice feature if this is your goal.

Uncapped:
All open world pvp(unorganized 1v1 -> 100+)
Uncapped Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
Uncapped Siege (attacker/defender battle over castle 100+ players)

Uncapped content the sky is the limit. You are competing with the whales and no-lifers here. This is in my opinion the pinnacle of BDO PvP, but also is the hardest to reach. If you aspire to do this content you will need to invest a lot of time or a lot of money to get to this point. You will be optimizing your silver per hour and AFK lifeskilling while you are not actively grinding. I would say the entry level for uncapped is ~1 year if you grind a few hours a day. If you're a gamer dad playing a couple hours on the weekend and you are not willing to whale, it would probably take you 2-3 years to get to this gearscore. All that being said, this is a gamba upgrade system. You could get MEGA boosted for very little effort....but the likelihood is low. 

PvP is all around extremely satisfying in this game. PvP has unique CC(crowd-control) mechanics, allowing you to CC unprotected opponents.  Learning your classes protections and CCs makes the skill expression S+ for BDO. Although BDO has great diversity in its 56 specialization, the dev has shown that it's near impossible to balance them all. On top of this, the game engine struggles with desync and frame drops in large scale content(100+ people on screen).  Pretty much all serious PvPers need a graphics preset that reduces the games fidelity by 90% to play at decent FPS. You could have a gaming rig made by jesus himself and still get <30 fps in siege...I'm not kidding. 

7/10 (9/10 with an engine update)
+PvE
+PvP(still fun)
+Long term progression
+Gear does not become obsolete like "raid tier" style MMOs
+Looks Great
+Best darn action combat system in any MMO

~ Enhancement system is RNG but now has max fails via the Pity.

[{"review_text": "Sins 2 is a good game and is heading in the right direction, so my move against recommendation is more to do with release and marketing practices rather than an indictment of the game itself. TL;DR, I would wait about a year (or even two!) before buying just to let the game settle and for some good mods to come out, currently very difficult in this development environment.

In short, I think Sins 2 released "officially" on Steam far too early, and that a lot of the development that's happened between now and then has been largely remedial, but is marketed to us as "new features."

What's good about Sins 2?

The game generally looks gorgeous, especially zoomed out.

It's somewhat controversial, but I think they made the right call to take out some of the 'mandatory' gameplay aspects by now having resource extractors exact a logistics slots cost; diplomacy's pacts are gone, seeing as they were just strictly better to have than not have; stuff like starbase constructors have been removed in favour of instant placement.

The combat model, with simulated ballistics/missiles and real-time turret tracking and lines of fire, is much more interesting than its predecessor. You get to have those Battlestar Galactica moments of watching flak turrets spin to intercept missiles, with some punching through anyways.

And finally, the game is moving in a good direction overall. It was fun to play on 'release,' and has only gotten more fun since then. The devs are responsive and communicative, there are opt-in betas for most patches, adjustments take community feedback into account.

So what's the problem?

Sins 2 had an official 'release' on Steam last year in August, but the way things have gone since then, it's clear that the game was not ready to officially launch, and the magnitude of certain changes clearly demonstrates that. My understanding is that the official launch coincided with the addition of the third race, Advent, to the game.

I'm going to gloss over the AI art, addressed well elsewhere. What I will say is that the new UI is generally soulless and lifeless compared to the first game, the colours of which, while goofy and animated, made the game feel a lot more vibrant than this sober slate blue we have to stare at everywhere we go.

More importantly, the Advent factions almost immediately had to be reworked because they were poorly differentiated between one another, and their major race feature also had to be significantly rebalanced. This rebalance still isn't done, by the way, and they have plans to further differentiate the two. It's admirable that they're committed to fixing these issues, but it doesn't feel good to invest time into a race that you know is going to change significantly in the coming months.

In the same way, gameflow has changed considerably. In the time from Steam launch, we have gone from a slow early game leaning heavily into capital ship spam and the extinction of mixed fleets, to a fast early game into cap spam with high lethality, then to a system that bottlenecks caps with high lethality (meaning large fleet battles were over in the blink of an eye), to the current 1.41 patch, where we have bottlenecked caps and low lethality, meaning more considered and thoughtful battles -- not to mention the addition of the Population mechanic which has drastically affected the impact of culture on the player's economy and is now non-optional if you want to keep up.

People will say that, yes, of course RTSs go through changes and adjustments throughout development. But these are larger than changes and adjustments, these are gameplay changes through which the devs are trying to nail down what they want Sins 2 to feel like at base -- and that would be fine for a game that is still IN DEVELOPMENT. But Sins 2 is supposed to be finished, and finished games don't tend to have these crises of identity.

As it stands, players are not simply learning a new meta from patch to patch, they are almost getting new takes on the design philosophy underpinning the game with each major update.

So the core flow and feel of the game is not yet stable, though it seems like it's getting there. What else?

One of the early official updates headlined the addition of visual destruction debris when your capital ships, starbases, and titans are destroyed. Really? This seems like a basic element of the visual oeuvre you'd expect to find in a large-scale RTS and should not be a headline of a major patch, and probably should have been there before the game's official release.

Patch notes will also have little gems like updated planet visuals, updated ship visuals, certain audio cues being added. To be clear, these are not pitched as bug fixes or retroactive development updates, they're pitched as new additions to the game. But it's clear that what was being updated was not intended for full release, but was simply a first-pass from the game's development phase. 

Finishing passes to visual and audio which are not bug fixes are a part of development, not an "upgrade" that the customer is receiving for free.

Other updates are borderline. We sometimes get new planet types. Great. Others are "new," but they're just restorations of what existed in the first game, and any returning player might have reasonably expected to find them in Sins 2 on release. So for much of 2024 you would not have found uncolonizable gravity wells like space storms, or at least not as many as are currently in the game now, which, again, is somewhat unbelievable to hear as a returning Sins 1 player.

Finally, many road map updates are padded out with these kinds of "features," essentially finishing passes spun as "updates." More egregious is the promise of a whole new Advent minor faction (these are like city-state factions in Civ) -- which should NOT be a road map update feature but an expected part of the base game. Why? Because the game still lacks that Advent minor faction only because the Advent are the newest race to the game at launch -- they clearly didn't have time to design the corresponding minor faction for the race as well.

I don't want to lose sight of my original thesis -- the game is good, but it released too early. Even their new scenarios DLC did not release with multiplayer functionality -- something they're going to add eventually (it's on the road map!), but it probably should have been considered a basic feature of the package to launch with, not spun as a free upgrade coming down the line eventually.

I want to reiterate that all of the above is fine, expected even, for a game early in its life cycle. But Sins 2 is still at the stage where it would be more appropriate to consider it an Early Access title: one that is probably close to completion, but isn't quite there yet.

If I had paid Early Access pricing to play this version of the game, knowing it would still be under heavy development and balancing, all would be forgiven. BAR, another RTS on a grand scale, is probably just as rough as Sins 2 is, maybe even rougher, and I have no complaints about BAR because they didn't charge me money to beta test for them.

I don't expect free Sins 2. I do expect to receive a finished product if I buy the game at full retail price. Give them another year or two at minimum to work out all the kinks, and you will have at last a complete game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1745422187}, {"review_text": "This is my favorite 4X Space Strategy game! If you enjoyed Rebellion this feels like the natural next step keeping the spirit of the original intact while refining the experience in all the right ways.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1737951305}, {"review_text": "Get it on sale, or even better, wait for new content [b]and[/b] a sale.

I do think performance is better in long and large games though so that's one positive.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761060158}, {"review_text": "This is somewhat tough, as on paper in a mechanical sense, Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a GOOD sequel. It follows the design philosophy that a sequel should be more of what you like, but iterated upon. Planet management has a deeper scale to it, fleet compositions are less spammy, and faction differences (Aside from the loyalist/rebel unique techs) are more complex.

Controlling and managing multiple fleets feels more streamlined and less granular without losing complexity, and early game exploration is heavily rewarded. Queuing researches and build orders is easily done and altered. It is a GOOD sequel. If you liked Sins 1, you will like Sins 2. 

However, what is a terrible shame and an absolute travesty is the sheer amount of AI generated images in the game, and something I cannot condone supporting. Especially when the first game had so much charm in it's programmer art and colored concepts.

Once noticed- it's impossible to look past. At first the Balenciaga stare on some of the portraits- then that odd uniform light shading. The constant tilt shift on anything that's supposed to look granular. Odd, in-congruent positioning and posing in images where figures are supposed to be interacting with each other. Figures staring at the camera and screaming. That telltale 'figure standing in front of a bulbous space ship' that doesn't match the design of the rest of the game.

The portraits you select when in the set up lobby have lost all of their unique charm. Sure- there's more of them, but what's the point when they all look vaguely the same? Thirty nearly identical portraits will never be better than 5 filled with personality. Even the in loading screen 'ads' for upcoming DLC's have a clearly AI generated figure within it. (Look at the eyes of the green eyed woman in the paths to power DLC banner.)

The UI is too clean, some of the buttons do not look like buttons. It is serviceable, but lacks the gritty charm the original had. The steam page states that: "This game used AI to help quickly iterate through designs for some UI elements using our own artwork as a baseline. AI is also used to help translate the game."

And this feels like a lie. The UI design does not feel iterative- and the amount of AI images used when you supposedly have an artist on payroll just screams 'We only wanted to pay them for a quarter of the work we wanted done.' 
If you have an artist, you have an artist. And even then, quirky programmer art will always be preferable to soulless AI generations.

One also has to wonder if some of this AI usage affected the visual designs of the ships themselves. Why did the Advent lose nearly all of their nautical theme?
(The hangar defenses- for instance, are now just wedges, rather than evocative of sea shells.)
Why did the Vasari ships lose their insectile appearance?
Why do the turrets on many of the TEC ships look like they were tacked on as an afterthought?

Were these conscious decisions from a person, or- did an AI simply smooth out the edges without understanding why those notions were present?

It's questioning like this that makes it hard to recommend.
