I’ve played my fair share of them, and still do, but usually drop most of them at some point. Right now, there’s only two that have a tight hold on me: Arknights, and Limbus Company.

I started this game because I heard they would collaborate with Arknights, and solely because of that… and oh boy, I wasn’t prepared for what I was getting into.

Let’s set aside the glaring elephant in the room (the gacha) for now, and focus on what really grabbed my attention: the setting.

To begin with, Limbus Company is the third game in a series. To my knowledge, it all started with Lobotomy Corporation (a SCP-esque management game), and continued with Library of Ruina (a deck-building roguelike). All three of them share the same universe, as a continuous timeline.

The stage is set in a dystopian, corporate-driven world… Which just sounds great, doesn’t it? Despite how it actually sounds, it’s what really drew me in as I began learning more about it.

Our playground is ‘The City’: an urban complex comprised of twenty-six districts, each of them ruled by a ‘Wing’ (the most powerful corporations around). The very concept of these corporations is really fun, as each of them have their own ‘Singularity’; a piece of technology unique to each of them, and so important that it’s pretty much the very backbone of their influence over a district.

Add to that Fixer Agencies (mercenary offices, so to speak), with their own rankings and distinct beliefs or creeds, Abnormalities (monstrous entities, manifestations of the human mind), or the mysterious Head (the ones at the top, overseeing The City with apparent omnipresency) and you have a pretty intriguingly built world.

As for the story itself, we play as Dante, the amnesiac, clock-shaped-head manager of the LCB (Limbus Company Bus), and we’re accompanied by a, huh, merry band of twelve misfits labeled as the ‘Sinners’ (each of them based on a literary work, by the way!)

This is one of the key aspects that, for me, separate Limbus Company from other gacha games, and one that keeps me really invested in the plot. 

Contrary to other games, where the new, shiny unit gets to be the focus of the story for a bit and then completely vanishes, in Limbus Company things are a bit different. 

Here, the twelve Sinners are the only playable characters, and the game keeps them both prevalent and relevant. What you pull (gacha) for is Identities: alter ego and ‘possibilities’ from different worlds, and their EGO (basically, ultimate moves). Since the cast is so ‘reduced’ (despite being twelve, bear with me), I could really get attached to them. 

Each Canto (chapter) focuses on one of the Sinners, going through something related to them, such as their past. Seeing their character development, or the interactions between them, is what drives me to keep tagging alongside them. It helps a lot that each of the Sinners has their own personality, background, and goals, as they’re very well developed thanks to their prevalence.

As for the gameplay, it’s… an acquired taste? The story sections are all reading, like a visual novel, but the combat is an interesting mix of turn-based and strategy with a bit of luck, and despite looking very simple, it can get deep real fast. 

It has various mechanics to be mindful of, like the speed of your Sinners and their enemies, their sanity, and other things I would have a lot of trouble explaining. Basically, you deploy your units and select all the skills they’ll use on your turn, using them to ‘clash’ against your enemies’ skills in a round of dice-rolling.

I prefer to not confuse anyone with my poor explanations, so I’ll end it at that. Still, it can get very fun! …And sometimes, hard.

On a more technical aspect, the art direction is also really good at setting the ambience. Bloody corridors, dark backstreets; it all sets the mood so well. Add to that the sound effects… I simply love it. 

The character designs are top-notch, and a high plus for suit lovers (no comment). The music itself is perfect, with tracks from the band MILI for the opening and most of the Canto boss fights. These songs even loop or change depending on the fight’s paces and all, it’s great. There’s also voice acting (though only Korean), and it’s actually really good!

So now then, let’s talk about the dreaded gacha. What I can say is that it’s not THAT bad, but hear me out. 

While other gacha games have a ‘sparking system’ (basically, pulling accumulates a currency you can exchange for the character, or things along those lines), Limbus also has a shard system.

This system allows you to collect shards of each Sinner to exchange for their different Identities or EGO, and it’s a currency you get by acquiring duplicate Identities on the gacha… or by farming the Mirror Dungeon! (a rogue-like-ish mode). 

This means you can pretty much get almost, ALMOST, every Identity or EGO for free just by playing. It does take grinding, and it depends on how much time you’re willing to spend (and buying the $11 battle pass increases the shard acquisition), but not many games give players an option like this to begin with.

All in all, I think it’s a phenomenal story with endearing, cool characters, an intriguing, yet dark world, and tons of rewarding moments. It helps a lot that the game had two other previous entries as a foothold, so the world-building only expands upon that, and does it expand geez.

Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is not your typical FromSoftware game, even though it shares the studio's signature difficulty and atmospheric storytelling. Unlike the Soulsborne titles, Sekiro leans heavily into action and precise combat rather than RPG elements. There are no stats to grind—just your own skill to sharpen.

The swordplay is incredibly tight and satisfying. Every encounter feels like a deadly duel where posture, timing, and reflexes matter more than raw damage. Boss fights are intense and memorable, and the learning curve is steep but fair. Death is part of the process—each failure teaches something new.

The game world is stunningly crafted, with gorgeous, varied environments inspired by late 1500s Japan. The level design encourages exploration, and the verticality introduced by the grappling hook adds a fresh dynamic to movement and combat.

Narratively, Sekiro tells a more direct story than previous FromSoftware games, but still leaves room for interpretation and mystery. The voice acting and music are excellent, further immersing you in its unique world.

However, there are some powerful enemy attacks like thrust, grab, sweep and lightning which cant be guarded and some of them even cant be deflected so you should dodge/jump/mikiri counter for some not all. Thus, the game at first glance feels a bit hard maybe frustrating as well but the main thing is knowing the every enemy’s attack set and imply your strategy according to it. The only variety comes from prosthetic tools and skills you find/learn through the journey.

[b]Prosthetic Tools:[/b] There are 10 prosthetics tools and you can upgrade them to change the usage they have. You can use them for a defensive or offensive purpose according to the boss or enemy you encounter. There is a currency for the prosthetic tools and every prosthetic tools have a cost per usage. This currency is called as “spirit emblem” which can also be required to use advanced combat arts like mortal draw, ninjutsu techniques or spiritfall buffs. You can buy spirit emblems in any sculptor’s idol (bonfire or site of grace) inexchange for sen which is the gold currency of the game, but there is a limit you can carry with you (15 at the beginning, maxed at 20). In addition, you can use ceremonial tanto to refill your spirit emblembs to a max of +5.

[b]Skills:[/b] There are 5 skill trees focusing on stuffs like combat, stealth, prosthetic tools etc., and 3 ninjutsu technique skills which can only be used after a backstab. [b]Vitality/Posture:[/b] It is simple, your vitality and posture increases as you collect prayer beads and using per 4 of them. There are total of 40, so you can increase your vitality and posture 10 times.

Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice suffers from none of these flaws. The player character feels amazing to control, and the combat is so tuned, and so reactive that I suspect it will difficult for me to enjoy another action game for quite a while. 

Something I see frequently in the discussion surrounding this game is that you can't level up, and there isn't any loot that makes you more powerful. This simply is not true, and I'm not sure why it comes up so often. There are multiple skill trees. You can increase your vitality, posture, and attack power. However, the sentiment behind this statement IS correct. The story is substantially less obtuse that the standard FromSoftware lore soup that usually pervades their games. You won't have a to watch a 40 minute YouTube video to understand what happened. I didn't play this game for the story, but I thought it was effective for driving the gameplay.

The Japanese voice acting is great, bordering on exceptional.

I came into the souls-like genre relatively late, starting with Lies of P (9/10) and later The First Berserker: Khazan (9.5/10). Both taught me patience and respect for the genre while proving that even a brutal challenge can be beautiful.
When I began Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, I felt I was stepping into something legendary. It was also my first completed game from the masters at FromSoftware, which made the whole experience feel even more meaningful.

It’s clear that the game comes from the PS4/XONE era, yet its visual direction, lighting and artistic style completely transcend its age.
The cutscenes are captivating, the characters and story pull you in right away, and the atmosphere is soaked in unmistakable Japanese spirit. Among Japanese games from that era, Sekiro’s story stands out as one of the best — powerful, symbolic and full of moments that stay with you long after the credits roll.
I fully understand why Sekiro is considered a “holy grail” among action games.
And yet, I can’t shake the feeling that it’s slightly overrated. Not in terms of quality, but in how uncompromisingly some fans worship it without acknowledging its extremes.

Pros
• Stunning environments and art direction. The fusion of feudal Japan and spiritual mysticism works beautifully, and every location feels like a painting.
• Outstanding cinematic presentation. A film-like rhythm, attention to detail and characters that truly leave a mark.
• Unique combat system. The parry-based rhythm and posture mechanics are demanding but brilliantly designed and deeply satisfying.
• Excellent PC optimization. Smooth performance, fast loading times and virtually no bugs.

• Extreme difficulty and frustration. Not everyone has the patience for repeated boss fights; sometimes it feels more like a test of endurance than fun.

For me personally, it’s a game I admire more than I love — and maybe that’s exactly what makes it special.

Absolutely not, but the people who are truly interested in the lore could potentially recommend this game as a perfect launch point for a larger, more casual audience to be introduced to the world of Warhammer 40K.

This game also lacks in quality-of-life features, but luckily, the ones I list here can be fixed by mods. Going down this list, however, it's baffling that some of these are not in the game by default:
- Playing offline with bots (you can only play this game online, and if you have bots in your games, you can't modify them in any way)
- Loadout names (all you have are icons)
- A database/better descriptions for buffs and debuffs (what is rending? brittleness? strength?)
- Scoreboards/uptime indicators (although this was omitted intentionally to prevent toxicity, it would be beneficial to know your own stats and see where you could improve or what perks have the most impact)

- Ping/latency indicators (some of the combat in this game requires precise reaction time, and if your ping is off, you could die to something you thought you dodged, since this game is online only)
- HUD customization (do you want parts to be bigger or smaller, or more/less information to be displayed? you're out of luck, unfortunately)
- Accessibility features (hope you like clicking left mouse button over and over for semi-automatic weapons or for chaining light attacks)
- Mission briefings/lore excerpts/tips in loading screens (loading screens are everywhere, and there's plenty of information to learn how to play this game correctly, so why not have it as an option other than catechisms like "blessed be the mind too small for doubt")

I do appreciate that all of the cosmetics are lore-accurate and there's no Call Of Duty tone-deafness situation going on with them. Updates and new content are also slow to release, and some systems aren't addressed fully or become outdated, which is counterproductive to the live-service approach this game has. The Arbitrator class, which released in June 2025, has still not received any cosmetics as of the time writing this review (UPDATE: Fatshark has responded to this complaint saying that this is due to Arbitrators' design. review_texts:
[{"review_text": "Just like PoE1, GGG again fails to understand that their top 2% of players aren't the right indicator of game balance.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1749469633}, {"review_text": "This review is for those with experience playing Path of Exile 2; new players are encouraged to play the game to develop their own opinions.

To be clear, Path of Exile 2 has the potential to evolve into something great… the greatest ARPG ever in fact. Even small design shifts like the introduction of a dodge roll have added substantial tactical depth to the gameplay. But despite these improvements, the game’s publicly stated design philosophy is increasingly at odds with the actual gameplay experience. 

GGG has repeatedly insisted that PoE2 is meant to be slower and more deliberate. That’s a fine vision; but in reality, endgame mapping and enemy speed blatantly contradict this claim. The pace remains just as frenetic as it was in PoE1 and there’s just as much onscreen effects which can make it exceedingly challenging at times to even know what’s going on. If the intent was to slow things down, then loot distribution should have been adjusted to match. It hasn't been. On the contrary, this current iteration has made currency even more scarce, doubling down on grind without commensurate reward. The trade system? Still a disaster, faithfully carried over from PoE1 with all its archaic inefficiencies.

GGG seems unwilling to internalize a lesson that should be fundamental by now: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. Many systems are saturated with negative modifiers that drain momentum and morale rather than inspire mastery. Nowhere is this more obvious than in end game mapping, where stacking mods can paradoxically make a map less playable due to sheer mechanical overkill. Several mods outright mean that if you luck into the wrong map suffix you will automatically be throwing that map in the trash (I’m looking at you temporal chains).

Yes, the game is in early access, but GGG seems to have misunderstood what early access is for. It’s supposed to be a testing ground, a sandbox for players to explore systems, theorycraft, and search for broken interactions. In a  game that’s loot dependent, that requires access to resources. Instead, loot is miserly. I constantly run over 100% magic find and still see abysmal returns. Divines are rare. Exalts bizarrely drop more often than Chaos, Regals, or Alchemy orbs. Orbs of Annulment or Chance? Nearly mythical (I say this after playing for over 420+ hours).

Crafting is nonexistent in any meaningful form as the entire system has been reduced to pure gambling. The tools are there and were shown to work in PoE1, but in PoE2 there’s no actual semi-deterministic crafting so experimentation dies on the vine. 

Defense stats in PoE2 remain deeply imbalanced. Armor is still underwhelming, scaling poorly in the face of high incoming damage. Evasion is serviceable. Meanwhile, energy shield continues to dominate across most content. This persistent asymmetry undermines build diversity and reinforces a stagnant meta. This is further exacerbated by the aforementioned lack of currency and crafting, which often leaves players stuck if they’re not wealthy enough to regear their characters in a different manner.

The Trial of the Sekhema is one of the more baffling screwups in the game. The central mechanic, an “honor” meter that diminishes when you’re hit, actively punishes entire archetypes of play. Builds that rely on taking damage as part of their identity such as anything melee related, thorns-based, armor-heavy, or self-damage synergies, are effectively penalized for functioning as intended. The concept of "honor" in combat might make sense thematically, but from a gameplay perspective it's incoherent. “Oh but honor isn’t an issue if you stack honor resist”, ok, stacking “honor resist” is a lazy workaround, not a solution. “Well you can do the Trials of Chaos then”, sure, let’s talk about the ToC.

The Trials of Chaos continue the trend of stacking punishment under the guise of difficulty. Layer upon layer of negative modifiers are applied to both the player and the environment, creating scenarios where success often feels less like a result of skill and more like surviving Jonathan’s spite. Once again, the issue isn’t that the trials are difficult, it’s that GGG confuses misery with difficulty. These trials don't challenge a player's decision-making or adaptability so much as test their tolerance for suffering. Some of the modifiers will 100% of the time be a death sentence, which is ridiculous for a game mode that demands you run a gauntlet.
To reiterate: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. And until GGG takes that distinction seriously, much of the game's potential will remain unrealized beneath the weight of its own contradictions.

And then there’s the death penalty: a flat 10% XP loss. It’s an outdated design relic that punishes players disproportionately, especially in a game this unstable. The optimization is rough; CPU usage spikes inexplicably, screens freeze, and enemies with invisible on-death effects can wipe you before you even register the threat. The game already limits player through currency scarcity and map restrictions, why stack another misery mechanic on top of it all? Literally nearly every one of my high level deaths has been due to the game freaking out and freezing for a split second at the most inopportune times. This is the mechanic that makes me rage quit. This is the mechanic that makes me put the game down and leave it for extended periods of time. This is the mechanic which makes me rethink spending money on stash tabs, cosmetics, mystery boxes, etc.

Let me be absolutely clear here: the XP penalty is not just frustrating, it’s demoralizing. It actively discourages continued play and reveal a fundamental disrespect for player time. Once you hit the late 80s or early 90s in level, even fully juiced maps roll several levels below your character level, making XP grinding a slog. Combine that with PC performance issues and what you’re left with is a bad experience. And yes, I can already hear the diehard fanbase trotting out the same tired defense: “There have to be consequences, otherwise people will just spam content and they won’t learn how to get good.” Sorry, but no. That argument falls apart under the most basic scrutiny. Players can’t spam the same content; maps are gated behind RNG & limited runs. The system itself is already self-limiting. You don’t need an additional punitive XP penalty to “preserve challenge”; you need a well-balanced game that respects player time and rewards effort instead of eroding it in a hot instant.

Things I would like to see:
• Campaign Skip After Completion
Once a player has completed the campaign, they should be allowed to skip it on subsequent characters. 
• Make the Remaining Campaign Choices Reversible
In both Act 3’s, characters are forced to make two decisions regarding stats that are currently permanent. This design is incoherent, especially given that ascendancy choices can now be changed freely. Please allow these decisions to be changed as well (Let Doryani be the interface to make the changes).
• League Character Imports
The requirement to re-run the campaign for each new league or character is, again, tedious. A solution could involve importing characters back into a new league; either starting fresh at level 1 or with a baseline (e.g., level 60 with 500k gold and access to early maps). 
• PoE1 Atlas Skill Tree
The Atlas passive tree in PoE1 was amazing. The current iteration in PoE2 is by comparison a poor imitation. Bring back that depth!
• Boots: movespeed is necessary, so make it an implicit
• An Actual Early Access Philosophy: Treat the current state as a live experiment, not a soft launch. [list]
[*]Clearer & Smoother Progression

 [*]QoL Improvements
        Reconnect feature is a game-changer—no more losing progress due to crashes or disconnects.

 [*]Endgame Potential
        The core gameplay loop (maps, bosses, loot hunting) remains addictive, and new mechanics add fresh challenges.

❌ The Bad: What Needs Fixing
[list]
 [*]Post-Death Effect Overload
        Killing mobs shouldn’t feel like navigating a minefield, yet PoE 2 insists on filling every encounter with delayed explosions, lingering ground effects, and stacking DoTs.         The endgame map variety is shockingly bad. Out of dozens of maps, only four (Savannah, Oasis, Rustbowl, Steppe) feel truly open.   [/list]
[/list]

⭐ Verdict: A Strong Sequel That Needs Polish

Its an absolute adrenaline rush for me,  So many battlefield like moments occur at that level", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1753754233}, {"review_text": "“Good, [strike] bad[/strike] and ugly"

As someone who enjoys playing the Men of War series, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront immediately felt familiar. It’s a real-time tactics game set on the Eastern Front of World War II – gritty, grounded, and utterly relentless. You command squads of infantry, tanks, artillery, and everything in between in brutal and historically grounded battles.

What makes this game shine for me is its authenticity and attention to detail. The visuals, the sound design, the pacing – it all comes together to recreate the look and feel of warfare in a way that’s hard to match. The units behave like real soldiers, the armor feels weighty and vulnerable at the same time, and each engagement feels personal and intense. The penetration and damage model are spot on.

As a self-declared historical nerd, I adore the sheer variety of equipment. Whether I’m fielding early-war Panzer Is or later beasts like the Tiger I and II, the game constantly feeds my need for historically accurate gear. The same goes for the Soviets – T-26s, KV-1s, and the mighty IS-series make appearances in all their brutal, riveted glory.

One of my favorite aspects is the dynamic campaign mode. It's not just battle after battle – there's an economy to manage, a tech tree to develop, and meaningful strategic decisions to make between missions. It adds depth and consequence to every victory (or defeat), and scratches that long-term strategy itch without getting in the way of the core combat.

I still remember one battle where my defenses were holding just fine – until a Soviet KV-1 rumbled onto the field. My 50mm PaK AT gun couldn’t even scratch it. It was like watching history unfold – just like in real life, the KV heavy tank series was a shock for the Germans early in the war, a machine that could shrug off nearly all early AT weapons. I was forced to scramble, reallocate units, call artillery, bait it into a minefield – whatever I could do. It was a desperate, cinematic moment that ended in victory, and I swear I had a wide grin on my face afterwards. Moments like that are why I play these games.

Now… let’s talk about the ugly. Because yes – the UI. It's bad. No – ugly. The interface feels like a relic. It’s like someone dropped a toolbox on the screen and said “good luck.” It takes time to get used to, and even after that, it feels like a major missed opportunity. A cleaner, more streamlined UI would be most welcome.

Still, despite the interface struggles, Gates of Hell – Ostfront delivers one of the most immersive, satisfying, and historically rich RTS experiences I’ve had in years. If you’re into WW2 tactics and love games that reward positioning, timing, and authenticity – this one's for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1754395539}, {"review_text": "this game made me realize how stupid I've been for spending 800 hrs on Company of Heroes 2, desperately trying to "patch" the game with "realism" mod such as Wikinger n Spearhead, when this exist all along.

Huge Upgrades:
+ Particle effects
+ Textures
+ ANIMATIONS (They're so much better omg)

This is probably the best RTS in its genre. The [b]attention to details[/b] is amazing, the [b]atmosphere[/b] and historical accuracy you feel like you're really there. It feels great to play, [i]up until[/i] it doesn't.

[h2]Why I'm so frustrated[/h2]

The game gets ruined by an [b]immense amount of AI spamming[/b] in some missions. It gets to the point where it's literally unplayable. Strategy doesn't matter when the enemy gets infinite units, as the game just turns into a meatgrinder where you focus on endlessly killing AI tanks and hoping yours survive.

To make things even worse, sometimes your own AI just picks a weird path and runs straight into the enemy for no reason. So you're fighting an enemy that's a perfect micromanager, while also trying to stop your own guys from getting themselves killed like idiots. It's frustrating as hell.

A lot of these missions are likely meant for co-op, but [b]you can't host your DLC missions for friends who don't own them[/b]. Since the game's missions are mostly locked behind DLCs, I was forced to play them alone. I can micromanage a few squads, but trying to defend a huge area against an overwhelming amount of AI attacking you (on a mission where you are the one supposed to attack) makes me uninstall this game.

And when the AI starts spamming, the performance starts to show some cracks. It all just becomes a huge, laggy mess.

[h1]Final verdict[/h1]

Basically a hit-and-miss game.

We, the players who actually paid for this game — the ones who put money down on day one because we believed in the damn franchise — got completely shafted.

Back in the day, you bought a Halo game, you got the whole package. Campaign, multiplayer, unlockables, cool armor — it was yours. You earned it. No bullshit. No nickel-and-diming. Just you, your friends, and hours of grinding that felt worth it.

But Infinite? Nah. They cut the game in half, slapped a $60 price tag on the campaign, and then turned multiplayer into some predatory free-to-play battle pass scheme. They shoved armor coatings, color palettes, and even basic-ass helmets behind paywalls. Shit that we used to unlock through playing the damn game is now locked away unless you open your wallet. And if you did pay for the campaign? Congrats, you get absolutely nothing extra in multiplayer — you’re basically on the same footing as some free-to-play tourist.

It’s insulting. We didn’t just buy Halo Infinite, we funded their excuse to gut the series and chase live-service trends. And the cherry on top? They drip-feed content at a snail’s pace, while charging more for cosmetic bundles than old Halo map packs used to cost.

They didn’t just betray the old-school Halo fanbase — they sold us out. Hours played: 2,000+

I’ve been playing Halo since Halo 3 back in 2007, so this series means a lot to me. Even though I enjoyed Halo Infinite early on especially around Season 3 and the Spirit of Fire operation I can’t help but feel disappointed with where this game has gone. The newest operation, “Operation: Infinite,” is finally releasing some coatings that were in the game files since launch but were never available unless you paid absurd prices in the shop or waited for them to show up in an operation pass.

Remember when 343 said they had a 10-year plan for this game? That fell apart almost immediately. At launch, Infinite felt fresh fun gameplay, fluid movement, and a lot of promise. But after 2,000 hours, you start to see all the cracks.

Ever since the so-called “network update” about a year ago, the experience for me as a PC player has been steadily going downhill. Anything above 80 ping and the game becomes borderline unplayable constant blanks, heavy aim, broken hit registration, grenades disappearing midair, and rockets that simply don’t fire or explode. The gun-play feels great mechanically, but the networking and desync completely ruin it.

343 has had control of the Halo franchise for over a decade now, and after three mainline games, it still feels like they’ve learned nothing. “One step forward, three steps back” should honestly be their company slogan at this point. Infinite nails the fundamentals the art direction feels closer to Bungie’s golden era, your Spartan feels agile and grounded, and movement is crisp like Halo 2 and Halo 3 not the hyper-speed, twitchy mess of Halo 4 and 5. The insider flight tests were amazing, the community feedback was overwhelmingly positive, and everyone was saying, “Halo is back.” Then the game actually launched… and it was the exact opposite of what we were promised.
The live service model is a desperate cash grab. Six years of development, over a hundred developers, and half a billion dollars yet Halo Infinite still has less content than most $40 indie shooters. They marketed it as “free to play,” but still charged $60 for the campaign which itself launched incomplete, lacking mission replay, co-op, or proper progression for months.

They promised “Halo Reach-level customization” and delivered a system where 85% of all cosmetics are locked behind paywalls or FOMO-limited event passes. You either grind through uninspired event challenges or pay up. And even then, the shop prices are ridiculous.

There’s just no motivation to play anymore. I only log in when there’s an operation or limited-time event, just to grab cosmetics I’ll probably never use. And even during those, I end up frustrated desync, heavy aim, disappearing grenades, and constant blank shots make matches infuriating. [{"review_text": "⚠️ Background:
This is a review of the 4.0 overhaul. It maybe belongs on the Biogenesis expansion page, but requires spending £20 to put it there. I followed the development of this release very closely. I read all the diaries. Dev forum comments. Watched the streams. Followed discord dev messages.

📜Review:
4.0 ("Phoenix") left the game in a grim place. Biogenesis itself seems excellent and was clearly QA tested - the expansion team did very well! ...But they have been caught in the custodians' crossfire - catching flak for things that aren't the expansions' fault.

[olist]
[*][b]The primary objective[/b] of 4.0 was to resolve Stellaris' performance issues (pops now, and a fleet patch coming later for that half of the problem). Understand that performance is a promise the developers have made before, particularly with 2.0 and 2.2. And after both of those patches Stellaris ended up with worse sim speed and lower frames. Whatever gains the studio made were lost with scope creep and new ideas. Eladrin and his modern team knew this history. So to promise the same thing again in 2025 demonstrated real confidence. The result? Oh dear. 4.0 performance is not better than 3.14. In fact it's not even on par. In fact it's [b]considerably worse[/b]! Unbelievable.

[*]Before Christmas PDX polled the community on a number of exciting reworks and improvements to various game systems. Long awaited features. High potential areas. Internal politics. Espionage improvements. Warfare resolution. Fleets. [b]Immediately after[/b] christmas they announced 4.0: Affecting nothing listed and instead shipping a rework to the planet GUI [i]for a third time[/i] which was already fundamentally sound and had no one asking for changes. Time wasting.

[*]Around New Year PDX reflected on the fact that 2024 had been a messy year with lots of very large DLCs that didn’t have the time for quality they should have. They reassured the community that they would scale back for 2025. Give things more quality control. Breathing room. [b]Immediately after[/b] (a matter of days!) they announced 3 massive DLC's for 2025, non negotiable launch dates, 4.0 squeezed in the middle and the busiest year to date.

[*]The new “District Specialisation” system is convoluted. It doesn't reduce clicking and it doesn't help the AI. Have fun guessing which buildings go where. Have fun with dry and flavour-less "x support" specialisations.  The change nullifies the past half-decade of AI and planetary automation improvements. The rework had nothing to do with the new performance-relating pop changes and [b]was not necessary[/b]. When asked multiple times why it was being enacted PDX were unable to give more than two or three meaningful applications in the entire game.

When asked to add new districts in 4.0 (e.g. research districts), a hotly requested feature that would have been quick to implement and has all the same benefits as their bloated rework, the Phoenix team explained that they too loved the idea! It's what started this whole thing! But what concerned them was GUI space. So instead they enacted this massive time sink of an overhaul, with all the implementation, bug fixing, and balance costs (still ongoing), that allow you to [i]customise[/i] a district. This is staggeringly poor decision making because:

[list]
[*]UI space is not an issue for additional districts! Even with 10-20 district types. The selection area can be made scroll-able, and once the first is built it can be pinned to the top of the list. In 99% of situations the player never has to scroll again. This is perfectly usable. District expansion mods are extremely popular and have been for years. They are “solving” an issue that doesn’t exist.
[*]The only reason the planet GUI is limited is because it must conform to 720p (or 800p) resolutions. When asked to relax the limit here in 2025, by both the community and his own UX designer, Eladrin has said no.
[*]The 4.0 planet rework hasn’t produced a more useable GUI regardless! Just as with performance, 4.0 delivers a worse experience. Myriad stats, buttons and options are now buried in secondary tabs and nested menus when they used to be on the main screen. Yes, you read that correctly. This rework started by quibbling over a little district scrolling and now instead half the planet GUI tools are buried behind multiple clicks. (Update: As of 4.1 some of this has been resolved. Personally I am OK with the interface now.)
[/list]
[/olist]

On three personal notes, there are some more subjective elements I loathe about 4.0:
[olist]
[*]The unnecessarily massive numbers. 1000's of pops and jobs. Stellaris used to be elegant. 1 food for 1 pop. Now it's messy and tedious to parse. These off-putting numbers are so bloated they couldn't fit into the UI when first shown and the tool-tips look [i]ridiculous[/i]. The studio argued this was necessary because they felt fractional pops wouldn’t make sense. When of course they do. They also argued that reading lots of decimal zeroes/integers on pops would read poorly, so we get inflated zeros on [u]every[/u] planetary management mechanic! Baffling.

[*]Trade as a resource is a half baked idea trying to do too many things. It’s logistics, shipping, galactic credit and wealth stockpiling all in one. As with many custodian initiatives (such as paying "unity" for leaders) the story considerations were not made. Then there are energy-credits. For the purposes of all the dialogue, stories and events already in the game that’s still the only currency. It’s an obvious half measure, but the team didn’t want to comb through all the files.

[*]Civilians are poorly implemented. They muddy the waters with unemployment. They spam relentless warning notifications that players are being asked to ignore (resolved in 4.1). They have broken the slavery mechanic. They conflict with empire role-play. They are fuzzy to develop/manage, and so far in practice they're basically just power creep.
[/olist]

These are all examples of sloppy, flat-out badly designed systems. The custodians, whose remit was to [i]support the DLCs[/i] and provide fixes, have ironically driven a bulldozer through Biogenesis with poor quality work. And while certain elements of 4.0 (like the currently broken AI, balance and bugs) may be resolved in upcoming patches, the wonky aspects I've reviewed here are permanent. Stellaris is stuck like this now. Forever.

Not recommended.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1747654359}, {"review_text": "TLDR; Stellaris is incredibly fun and allows for many playstyles and an unrivaled amount of customization, but don't get it if you don't have the patience or if you aren't prepared to shell out quite a bit of money (or wait for sales).


I just reached 1000 hours in this game so I thought I would write a review finally. I will probably have to change it soon though since tomorrow is the release of the 4.0 update.

Stellaris is a very fun game to play on your own or with other people (if you can ever get someone to play with you) and I would absolutely recommend it. That being said there are a few things. Stellaris is not a game for people who like completing a match in half an hour, which makes sense because it's a strategy game. You can play it for like half an hour at a time but a full game of Stellaris can take days to finish if you have it on the default time settings. Also the DLC scheme is a little annoying. The base game is really not worth paying 50$ for if you aren't going to buy at least a few DLC over time. I would recommend waiting for a sale to buy it since you need at least like 3 of the DLC for it to be enjoyable long term.

Now that I've gotten the bad out of the way there are a lot of great things about the game:

1. Replayability: Replayability in a game is really important and Stellaris has a lot of it. Every time you play the galaxy is completely different with different events, systems, planets, and empires. Even if you played the exact same empire every time your experience between two games would be fairly different. 

2. Customization: my favorite part of Stellaris is how customizable it is. I went into the game expecting it to be like a lot of strategy games with a few empires you can play as. The game is way different and allows you to completely create your empire from scratch; including your species, your government type and ideals, your origin which can drastically change your playstyle, and the look of your units and flag and stuff. In one playthrough you can play as a peaceful race of bird-people with psionic powers, and in another you can play as a collective of mass murdering machines who kill everything that breathes. 

3. Appeal to different playstyles: Stellaris is a game that can be fun for very different people with different wants out of a game. If you are interested in being a peaceful nation of diplomats there are very in-depth mechanics that deal with diplomacy. If you like trade and capitalism then there you can do a lot of that. If you like playing strategy games just to murder everyone then you can be a purifier and go total war on everyone with the in-depth war mechanics. 

4. Mechanics: the mechanics of Stellaris are very original in a lot of ways. The tech "tree" is more random and has a lot of mechanics dedicated to getting research of different types and specializing leaders to get the techs you want. The tradition tree mechanic gives you cool ways to customize the ideals of your nation and get different bonuses depending on how you want to play. You also get ascension perks for completing them which give you interesting new mechanics or massive bonuses. The game doesn't do turns or grids but instead uses an interconnected web of systems that ships can move about freely, and has everything happen in real time instead of being turn-based. I could go on and on about all the interesting and original mechanics but basically its very good and fun.

Basically Stellaris is a must have for anyone who likes any kind of strategy or roleplay, but requires a bit of a monetary investment.


If you have decided to get the game then this is the part where I give unsoliscited advice on which DLCs to get (you're gonna need a few). These are my top 10. 

1. Utopia: 
Basically everyone says to get Utopia first. This is for good reason because without it you basically aren't playing stellaris. 

2. Machine age:
Machine age is a massive addition to stellaris. The DLC adds machine empires (as an alternative to synthetic dawn). It adds the cybernetic and synthetic ascensions which are super good. It adds a new megastructure that produces some minerals (arc furnace), 3 new fun origins, and a new Crisis path that allows you to leave the universe for a better one while annihilating the old one and anyone who stands in your path.

3. Federations:
Federations is important not just because of the mechanics, but also because of the origins. Federations adds the most origins of any DLC (8) and almost all of them are fun. It also adds federations (duh) which allows you to become allied with other empires and get useful bonuses. 


4. Megacorp:
some people don't like megacorp (they are wrong) but personally it is my favorite way to play. Megacorp adds a few great things. It adds Ecuminopolis worlds which are worlds that are encased in a massive city, it adds a bunch of megastructures, it adds the caravaneers which are like space vegas, and finally it adds Megacorps. Megacorps are a style of government where you are governed by a massive company.  This is THE DLC for trade empires and is a must have if you like money.

5. Overlord:
Overlord is a great DLC if you like conquering and war because it expands the vassal system. Even if you don't like war this is a good DLC to get because it adds the conclaves. The conclaves are independant groups that help you in different ways. 

6. Paragons:
I didn't get why paragons was so useful until I actually got it. The DLC makes leaders actually good by letting you choose which skills they get as they level up. It also adds some cool leaders who you can hire periodically which can be really great. 

7. Grand Archive:
I would put this one on par with Paragons honestly. Grand Archive adds a few really cool things. First of all the archive itself gives you a fun scavenger hunt to find specimens which give you good bonuses. The DLC also adds two more types of space fauna who are really cool, and even adds space fauna as ships which are a different and really fun way to play (though they may be overshadowed when Biogenesis releases).

8. Ancient Relics, Leviathans, & Distant stars:
These three DLCs are all basically on par. Ancient relics adds a ton of new archeological sites, and relics which make for powerful bonuses. It also improves the precursor system by a ton. Leviathans adds massive space entities that rival planets in size and adds a fun challenge to fight them. Distant stars adds a whole host of new features. It adds the L-Gates which are a really cool mid-game event. It also adds a huge host of new anomalies, special interactions, and interesting scenarios over the galaxy. 

9. Nemesis:
Nemesis is such a cool DLC to play if you want to become the Crisis. It was the first DLC to add a crisis path and it is genuinely a very fun path. The Crisis path allows an empire to make entire star systems go supernova one by one in order to collect enough dark matter to build the aetherophasic engine and rip a whole in the universe. This DLC adds some cool interactions with the galactic community as well. The only snag is that cracking star systems goes from "super cool" to "boring and tedious" quickly once you need to crack like 100 of them.

10. Synthetic Dawn:
Synthetic Dawn is the OG robots DLC. It adds the machine intelligence government and robots, as well as a ton of interesting civics for robots. Obviously now Machine Age adds robots but you should still get this DLC eventually because it adds a bunch more stuff (Driven assimilator, 2 Origins by 4.0, and a genocidal civic for bots).

All the other DLC are kind of whatever or just didn't make top ten. I would especially avoid cosmic storms, some of the species packs (Necroid, Aquatic, and Toxoid are the cool ones imo), and Apocolypse because you never actually use any of the stuff in it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1746417497}, {"review_text": "This is my favorite game, but I can't recommend it due to the way paradox seems to handle major updates recently.

There are 3 major issues I have with 4.0: pops, buildings, and performance.

That system was, in all aspects, an upgrade. It made the game more enjoyable and allowed game-play to be much deeper and expanded in ways that were not possible before. It was simple and easy to understand. The new system is none of those things. The update makes understanding the UI much harder at a glance. Now onto buildings. This system did not need an update. I get what the developers were thinking with the new system, i really do. Having individual districts have their own building slots is a neat and novel idea. It feels raw. Wild. Personal. From the moment you crash-land on that island, the game drops all pretense and just lets you exist in it. You’re not being guided. You’re not being handheld. You’re alone, cold, and immediately in danger. But somehow, that danger feels real in a way few games manage.

The forest is alive in a way that creeps up on you. Trees sway with the wind, shadows stretch across the dirt, animals roam freely, and then there’s silence. Real, heavy silence. Sometimes you’ll hear breathing that isn’t yours. Or see movement in the distance that you hope was just wind. Everything in the world responds to you, but nothing caters to you. There’s something deeply unsettling about that.

Building in this game is incredibly satisfying. It’s not about dropping pre-made blueprints and watching walls appear. You’re cutting down actual trees, splitting logs by hand, laying each piece down yourself. Structures feel earned. Even a simple shelter feels like a project. Over time, you start to take pride in what you’ve made. Not because it’s pretty, but because you bled to protect it.

Combat is tough. Every swing matters. Every shot has weight. Enemies don’t charge blindly. They watch. They test you. Some scream to call others. Some creep behind you without a sound. And some just stand at the edge of the woods and stare until you do something about it. It makes you hesitate. It makes you paranoid. And it works.

You’re not completely alone, though. Kelvin is your companion, injured and silent. He can’t talk but he helps. He gathers materials, follows your commands, and sometimes just sits and rests when he’s overwhelmed. There’s something deeply human about him. Then there’s Virginia. She doesn’t take orders. She observes. Eventually, if she trusts you, she’ll help. She’ll bring you food. She’ll fight alongside you. And when she does, it’s not just useful. It’s emotional.

The island changes constantly. Weather, seasons, even the tone of the game shifts over time. Winter isn’t just a visual effect. It’s survival on hard mode. Food disappears. Animals vanish. Water freezes. Everything becomes still. The sense of isolation hits harder than any enemy ever could.

The story unfolds slowly and without much explanation. You’ll find bodies. Mysterious bunkers. Technology that doesn’t belong in the woods. You’ll piece together what happened, if you care to look. It never interrupts you. It just waits for you to dig deeper. The horror comes not from jump scares, but from slowly realizing the truth behind what you're seeing.

Playing with others turns this all into something completely different. You can build massive compounds together. You can split up and get lost. You can survive as a team or fall apart in the face of chaos. It’s messy. It’s unpredictable. And it’s endlessly engaging.

There are moments of quiet that hit harder than any action scene. Sitting by a fire while rain falls around you. Watching Kelvin rest while your shelter creaks in the wind. Catching a glimpse of Virginia dancing in the distance like she’s forgotten what the world is.

Sons of the Forest is not easy. It’s not polished in the traditional sense. But that’s exactly why it’s so memorable. It’s uncomfortable. It’s rewarding. It’s dangerous in a way that makes you lean in. There’s no flair. No filler. Just survival in its purest form.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1752970101}, {"review_text": "The first Forest game was a one of a kind game that I put quite a bit of hours into exploring the island and building structures and cowering in the corner while cannibals ravaged my base. This one expands upon that experience in every way and does an even better job.

Especially regarding the building mechanic, this game has the most detailed building system I think I've ever seen in a game, which makes it real fun to make whatever structure you want the way you specifically want it. It can be a bit tedious if I'm being honest, but I've never personally had a problem with that since I enjoy the manual work of chopping the trees down and then the individual logs into the size I need. One thing I will say that got kinda annoying with the building, is that a bunch of the blueprints require all different kinds of wood sizes, some of which are only small parts of the log, which means that afterward you're left with a whole ton of leftover cut logs that you can't really use for anything else unless you're building a blueprint that specifically requires whatever it is you have an abundance of, and even then, you're typically still left with some. I had so many different log pieces at once before that I wasn't even able to walk out the door of my house lol. With that said, I for one am really fond of building and decorating within games, and if you truly wanted to, you could play this game purely for that reason and play it as nothing more than a building sim.

Most people likely aren't going to buy this game purely for the building system though, which brings us to the survival and horror aspect of the game. If you're not a builder and don't care about spending 20 hours building a 3 story cabin on a small island in the center of a lake with a fully furnished houseboat that can't even go anywhere due to the fact the lake only leads to a waterfall... then the exploration and surviving side of the game is super fun too. Now I've seen a lot of people complain that the map is actually *too* big (which isn't a complaint you typically hear) and that it isn't filled with enough stuff for it to justify the fact the game area is very big, but honestly, I never once had those same thoughts. In fact, I would get distracted often while exploring just because I'd keep finding stuff, whether that was a cave or a bunker, cannibal camp, some other odd area, or even a pretty area (the environment is gorgeous). There is a lot to find and to do, and I feel that the people who complain about the "empty" map are the same type of people that complain that Elden Ring is "empty" just because it doesn't have something at every step. And it's not like it's difficult to traverse the map either when the game gives you multiple means of transportation such as the golf cart, the knight V, or even the hang glider which can get you across the map in a minute.

Back to the main point though; if you want a solid survival experience, where not only does the cannibals and other unimaginable horrors pose a threat, but also your food, thirst, and sleep bar, then this is the game for you. For the most part, I'm someone who prefers clear goals and story beats to progress towards. I tend to lose interest in large open worlds where you can do the same activities hundreds of times, as it quickly starts feeling pointless. But for some reason, [i]No Man's Sky[/i] and its theme of pitting you against the vast open universe manages to overcome this, even though it really is a quintessential open world game. It has a story (with two different paths, even), but while it's suitable, it's a very sparse affair that mostly serves as a tutorial for game mechanics, and otherwise consists of a lot of "fly here, talk to this person, repeat" sequences. Completing the story is not really what the game is about, it's about making your own fun in an endless sprawling galaxy.

I was never aboard the hype train when this game was announced and I didn't experience the disappointing release myself, but the game's redemption arc is well-known by now, so I don't need to dwell on that. Many, many updates later (with no announcement in sight that they're done expanding, by the way), the game is now teeming with enough activities and events that it should have something for everyone, provided you like open world games. Because make no mistake, this is still a game where you'll be doing the same things over and over again with minor variations. For example, the first time you board a derelict freighter is cool -- the haunting atmosphere, the freezing cold of space, learning of the crew's fate through log messages. But the second time you do it, it's immediately obvious that it's the same event, just with the messages and the room layouts rearranged a bit and a new coat of paint on the enemies, which is not enough to keep things fresh. And, of course, in a galaxy with quintillions of planets, you're not getting any hand-crafted content beyond the basics. Every (regular) space station is the same, every partially buried ancient ruin is buried the same way, every crashed freighter has the same containers behind the same doors and only the loot differs. There is enough variety in flora, fauna and general atmosphere to give planets a bit of identity, but to some extent, if you've seen one deep-frozen iceball you've seen them all (if you can see anything at all through the storms), and if you're expecting a unique adventure every time you land somewhere you'll be disappointed.

The game has been accused of being miles wide and inches deep, and while that's not completely untrue, it's not completely fair either. Every so often you do come across some event, space anomaly or oddity on a planet surface that makes you sit up and take notice, and I think it's this, combined with the promise of exploring the great unknown however you please, that makes me accept the repetition in [i]No Man's Sky[/i] where other games falter. The first time you take off from a planet's surface and launch yourself into space (which the game seamlessly handles, by the way) that realization that the whole universe is at your command and you could encounter anything is something magical. There are plenty of things to strive for if you like setting your own goals: perhaps you want to make the most pimped out base, colonize the most planets, bake the tastiest cake, catch the biggest fish, command the largest fleet of ships from your freighter, become a notorious pirate, build the largest fossil exhibit, or just make it to the center of the galaxy on your own power. The game forces you to do none of these things, but they're all things you can explore, and you can keep yourself plenty busy stacking goals and missions on top of each other. It's one of those games where you can zen out without having to devote your full attention to what's going on on screen (provided you're not in combat, of course), and whether that's a good or bad thing really depends on what you want from a game.

I was lucky enough to experience [i]No Man's Sky[/i] on a free weekend, and I'd recommend "try before you buy" to anyone in this case. If the first few hours of the game can't command your attention long enough to keep playing, it's not likely you're going to find the experience as a whole satisfying. On the other hand, if you find yourself intrinsically motivated to push on and see what's next, the game will probably manage to throw enough variation your way that you're going to be playing a whole lot more. Infinite planets, alien ecologies, interstellar dogfights, deep lore, and multiplayer adventures. What players got, initially, was a lonely, shallow space sim that felt more like a tech demo than a finished game. Fast forward to today, and No Man’s Sky has become one of the most remarkable comeback stories in gaming history.

Hello Games didn’t just patch the holes—they rebuilt the starship mid-flight.

At its core, No Man’s Sky is a procedurally generated space exploration game. You travel between planets, gather resources, upgrade your gear, build bases, fight pirates, discover alien life, and trade across the galaxy. What’s incredible is the scale—there are over 18 quintillion planets, each with its own ecosystem and terrain, generated by complex algorithms.

Initially, this scale felt empty. Now, thanks to years of updates, it feels alive.

The introduction of base-building, freighter fleets, co-op multiplayer, living ships, story-driven missions, and even VR support has turned the game into a sprawling sandbox. Whether you’re role-playing as a space trucker, a biologist cataloging alien creatures, or a pirate lord terrorizing trade routes, the galaxy feels like it’s finally yours to shape.

No Man’s Sky has a unique, vibrant art style that draws heavily from 1970s sci-fi pulp covers. Planets can be serene, horrifying, or outright bizarre—neon fungi forests, frozen deserts, and floating rock islands abound. The game doesn’t chase realism; it aims for wonder.

That said, the visuals can occasionally feel repetitive, especially after dozens of planets. Some textures are still a bit rough, and creature animations can be wonky. But considering the sheer scope and procedural complexity, it’s often jaw-dropping.

What makes No Man’s Sky special is its sense of solitude. Unlike most games, it’s not afraid to let you be alone with your thoughts. You’ll spend hours mining minerals, jetpacking across alien landscapes, or simply flying through space while synth-heavy music pulses softly in the background.

It can feel like a space-age nature walk—until you stumble upon a derelict freighter haunted by corrupted AI or get ambushed by Sentinel drones.

The game’s loop—gather, upgrade, explore, repeat—takes time to click. But once you’ve built your first planetary base or discovered an uncharted paradise planet, the hook sinks in deep. The grind is real, but rarely feels punishing. The latest updates have also added better tutorials and quality-of-life features that ease new players into the galaxy’s rhythm.

Despite its transformation, No Man’s Sky still suffers from some long-standing quirks. Inventory management can be a pain, menus aren’t always intuitive, and the sheer amount of content can be overwhelming. Performance hiccups can pop up, especially on older hardware or during multiplayer.

Also, while the narrative has grown deeper with the Atlas Rises and Echoes updates, it still can’t compete with more tightly scripted RPGs in terms of emotional storytelling.

No Man’s Sky today is not the game it once was—it’s better, bigger, and infinitely more interesting. It’s a testament to what a small, passionate team can do when they commit to their vision and their community. What was once a cautionary tale of overhype has become a shining beacon of perseverance and transformation.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? Yes, I would. This game has come a long way since its disastrous release, and I can happily say that the current iteration of [i]No Man’s Sky[/i] is well worth both your time and money.

I actually waited over a year before picking it up back when it first launched, just to give them time to fix the broken state it was in. Since then, it’s only grown bigger and better with every update. The team lost the goodwill of gamers at the start, but instead of giving up they put their heads down, fixed the issues, and steadily rebuilt that trust. They’ve gone above and beyond, delivering a genuinely great game and focusing on giving us something worthwhile, rather than chasing dollar signs like so many AAA studios do these days.

As for the current state of the game, I don’t really have any complaints. Playing solo, the game runs really well. I haven’t had any major crashes or bugs to speak of, except for a single crash when going through the galactic centre on my permadeath run. But given the sheer size and scope of the game, the overall performance is fantastic.

When it comes to the narrative, it can feel a bit confusing unless you go out of your way to check out extra content [i](like on YouTube)[/i] or really dig deep to piece everything together. That’s probably the only downside for me. But once you start putting the pieces together, the lore and story are actually really interesting and quite melancholy.

Graphically, the game is excellent. The colours are vibrant and the visuals are consistently strong. The only small gripe I have is the reduced vision during storms. I know there’s a setting to turn it down to 35%, but I wish there was a way to remove it completely, maybe through a late-game mod or upgrade. It’s not a huge issue, but it can be a bit irritating. On the flip side, the sound design is great and I have zero complaints there.

Gameplay-wise, the amount of content in the current version is huge. You can explore, build bases, fight, fish, and even build your own ships now. While exploration is still the main focus, all the other mechanics slot together really well, and the team keeps improving on them with each update. This game has grown into a content powerhouse, and I love to see it.

It’s worth saying again: this current version is the result of years of consistent, free updates from [i]Hello Games[/i]. That effort has taken [i]No Man’s Sky[/i] well beyond where it should have been at launch. That doesn’t excuse the bad release, but it does show just how far they’ve taken things. Because of this, it’s always my first choice when asked about [i]“Labour of Love”[/i] games. The way they’ve handled this project also gives me a lot of confidence for whatever future games they decide to make.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
The achievements can look a bit daunting at first, mainly because of the permadeath run and the grind tied to the extreme survival milestones. Outside of those, most achievements will come naturally as you play.

For permadeath, the hardest part is just surviving the starting planet. Once you get off it, the run becomes much easier. There are plenty of guides to help you through, but my best advice is to take your time and make use of caves for cover. If you’re still struggling, you can always use the duplication method to stock up on resources and items, which makes things even simpler. Personally, this run took me about 10 hours because I spent time building bases and picking up S-class gear and ships. But you could speedrun it in around an hour and a half to two, if you wanted.

The extreme survival milestones are the other real grind. You’ll need to stay on an extreme-weather planet for 43,200 seconds [i](12 hours)[/i] exposed to the elements. [{"review_text": "A classic in the Resident Evil line with a fun story and good characters and if your a fan of extra unlockable content, then this game has it! 

Something to bare in mind for newcomers to the franchise or people who have only played the later games/remakes, this is when the games where extremely trial and error and you had to be very resource mindful. You are not (nor do you need to) supposed to kill every enemy you see or rush through the game. There are some fundamental things you must understand about the legacy games before you play them as I have listed below:

These games are not meant to be beaten in 1 sitting as fast as you can. Take your time, make notes of things and take breaks.

Adding onto what I said above, keep a notepad be it virtual or an actual notepad with you. Maybe even have a print out or digital version of the in game map. Write down what enemies are weak to when you discover it, write down where you found things, the answers to puzzles and where tricky enemies are. Pay attention to what enemies you NEED to kill and which ones you can simply avoid. Information is key to beating resident evil. 

Don't be afraid to load up a save or die. Make multiple saves (you have 10 slots so use them) but don't over save since you have limited ink ribbons to do so. Take a risk like I mentioned above, the game is very trial and error so you are bound to make mistakes or even soft lock yourself on the first playthrough. So BE SURE to use all your slots up instead of saving over 1 slot. Don't take death as another set back but instead treat it like a lesson. What did you learn from your death? did you discover where some useful items where? did you find out the location of enemies that are important? did you solve a tricky puzzle? Death is common in this game, if you view it as just a set back then your going to keep failing. Use and write down all the info you learned and try again using your new knowledge.

NEVER JUST DROP SOMETHING! Seriously there is an unwritten rule with these games I see almost nobody mention. The game has an interesting mechanic few people seem to either pick up on or mention to newcomers. Whenever you pick up and use a key item be it an actual key or some piece of equipment, you will be asked "this item is useless now, would you like to discard it?" this means you no longer need it and so you are safe to throw it away. The other instance of this is automatic discarding meaning you use an item and the game disposes of it without your permission. [{"review_text": "Enshrouded, as an Early Access title, does some things well and some not so well, but it is all subject to change. We'll see how things go over the next few years. Overall, it's fun enough, and the developers have been very forthcoming with game additions and are also very open and responsive to player feedback. This game does Early Access right.

Pros:
-Gorgeous visuals
-Gorgeous world, procedurally-generated and then lovingly populated with hand-crafted locations
-Incredible, detailed and interesting dungeons to delve through, filled with puzzles and environment hazards
-Beautiful, if inconsistent, armor and weapon designs, which are fun to collect.
-A fairly robust building system, with benefits to decorating and constructing a base that you then populate with craftspeople and villagers
-Simple, but satisfying combat
-A leveling system that revolves around perks instead of stat increases (though you can still boost your stats from the perk tree)
-Dedicated cosmetic slots for your armor, with options to hide both your headgear and your gloves
-Fully cosmetic clothing sets to find behind exploration and bosses
-A food-based buff system, wherein the food you eat increases your stats and stat regeneration
-Lots of lore to discover through characters, locales, obelisks and books throughout the world
-Highly customizable game settings, including the ability to turn off weapon and tool durability or turn on starvation mechanics

Cons:
-The bonuses from armor and weapons are largely pointless, or too small to make much of a difference. Some are even entirely pointless, such as one set that offers a small 10-20% bonus to unarmed damage, with unarmed attacks dealing only 8 damage to enemies (when your mace is doing over 400 per swing, and swings faster than your fists)
-There are tons of weapons, but there are very little differences between weapons of the same class: All one-handed weapons use the same three-swing combo, regardless of what the weapon actually is, and even legendary items don't have anything to differentiate them outside of their raw damage and visuals
-The few weapons with "unique" effects are things like 5% lifesteal, 1 point of health regen, or some bonus critical chance and damage. None of the weapons are build-defining or unique in any meaningful way. For example, the "Dragon Sword", found only one hidden place and tied to a piece of esoteric lore found in your travels, just adds a flat +7 fire damage... Five times in a row. The Dragon Sword is a weapon with nothing going for it except minuscule damage bonuses that don't even interact with your perks.
-Extremely linear item and location progression: New areas are blocked off by "Deadly Shroud," a gas that simply kills you if you haven't leveled up your base enough yet (using the heads of bosses and regional materials). Essentially, your ability to explore the "open world" aspect of the game is heavily restricted by boss progression.
-Heavily reused enemies with very limited attack variety
-The magic system is bland, being exclusively ranged elemental attacks and two healing spells. There is no utility magic to speak of, outside of a single knockback spell
-The perks you gain from leveling are very restrictive in what they affect, very strictly confining their offerings to their respective stat tree (Strength, Intelligence, Dexterity) with very little overlap
-Every quest is a fetch or kill quest with some lore sprinkled around it. "Skyrim quest" is how I would describe them: Talk to a person, go to a place, get a thing, repeat until you run out of quests", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1737240401}, {"review_text": "I love this game, I just wish the 6 friends who forced me to buy it for $30 didn't stop playing it after 2 hours.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 112, "timestamp_created": 1752445584}, {"review_text": "🛡️ Enshrouded – 100+ Hours Later, Here’s Where It Stands (June 23, 2025)
I've been playing Enshrouded with friends for over 70 hours now, and while it’s still in development, I think I've seen enough to share some impressions. Consider this a snapshot in time, not a final verdict.

✅ The Good
🎨 Graphics & World Design
Of all the base-building/adventure games I've played recently, Enshrouded feels the most polished visually. Lighting, textures, biomes, and building decor all come together beautifully. Compared to Valheim or V Rising, where things eventually start to feel repetitive, Enshrouded keeps things visually fresh and interesting longer.

🧠 Optimization (esp. on AMD)
I first tried the demo when AMD users were getting warning messages. That’s changed. Now the game runs remarkably well, and honestly feels smoother than many full releases.

🏠 Base Building
This is one of the game’s strongest features. Even though we’re not exactly mansion-building architects, the system was intuitive and fun enough to inspire creativity. I’d love to see Valheim-style physics introduced eventually — where structural integrity matters — but even without that, base-building is satisfying.

🪂 Traversal
The glider system is brilliant. Way better than Valheim’s slow boating and swim-heavy travel. It cuts down tedium and encourages exploration without frustration.

🤔 The Mixed Bag
⚔️ Character Building
I was excited to see proper skill trees, unlike the minimalist approach in Valheim. But they don’t quite synergize as they should. It feels like a half-finished system — pick some random perks and you're more or less fine.

🌍 The World Feels Empty
Not the Shroud — the actual world. Outside of rescued NPCs, there’s little to discover in terms of life, story, or dynamic events. No traveling traders, no ambient world events, no quest-givers. It’s beautiful but feels underpopulated.

🥊 Combat
Not bad, just barebones. Needs deeper class synergy, spell combos, buffs, and combat depth overall. Right now it’s functional, not exciting.

📚 Storytelling
There is a story, but it’s mostly told through journals and logs. After a while, I just stopped caring. A more engaging delivery method would go a long way.

🎮 Controller Mapping (Especially for Building)
Default controls are awkward. I had to remap everything manually for it to feel right, especially during building. Thankfully, that fixed it.

🌐 Server Performance
Works fine with 3-4 players, but becomes spotty beyond that. Needs optimization.

❌ The Frustrating Stuff
📦 Chest Grinding & Loot Progression
This broke the game for us. The best gear can be looted from static chests that you can reach early on. We got OP too fast, which made the rest of the content trivial. Yes, you can choose not to loot them — but in a group, if even one person does, you’re out of balance.

Top-tier gear should be earned, not found lying around. Tie it to hard quests, crafting blueprints, or endgame dungeons.

Also — why does 95% of loot from chests feel like junk?

🧾 Quests
They’re all fetch quests. It’s 2024 — surely we can do better than "bring me 5 mushrooms."

🧠 Suggestions for the Future
⚔️ Harder group dungeons with puzzles and unique rewards — mini-raids, basically

🐾 Pets or companions

🐧 Native Linux support for dedicated servers

🌈 HDR support — the game is gorgeous and HDR would make it pop even more

🎯 Final Thoughts
Despite its flaws, we thoroughly enjoyed our time in Enshrouded. In the open-world action builder genre, it’s one of the best out there right now. It builds on its predecessors’ strengths (Valheim, V Rising) and meaningfully improves in areas like traversal, building, and polish.

There’s a lot of potential here. If the devs keep improving on the weaker systems (combat, world depth, loot balance), Enshrouded could become a genre classic.

Thanks for reading — hope this helps someone decide whether to jump in!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1750638015}, {"review_text": "I'll start by saying this is a beautiful with devs that work really hard and care alot about their project.

The first steps:
If you are totally new to survival crafting games, you will be utterly lost in this game. When you start out, you don’t have any tutorial to walk you through the game, and it most certainly doesn’t hold your hand in any way. You have to figure out stuff by picking, chopping, looting, killing and crafting stuff along the way. 

User interface:
The UI is very easy to use. Not much to say here, even a total noob can figure this out.

Moving about:
This game gives you wings! You can travel over land very fast in this game if you make use of your glider and strategic spires and hills. Otherwise you will have quite the adventure tracking over lands and channelling your inner mountain goat.

Combat:
The combat is in it’s way very simplistic and there are no combo’s or funny buttons and special skills. It’s just straight forward stabbing, slicing and shooting. That said, it is very enjoyable to just go into a stabbing frenzy when you duel wield (like I do, hehehe).

Skills:
It does have a skill tree where you do branch of into your three major groups: tanky, healy and damagy. And it also offers stamina and magic skills alike. It’s a fairy small-med sized skill tree, and doesn’t need any special builds or manuals to be optimum in any way. Players are free to build as they want.

Survival:
Food is a bonus to have, but not as a means to keep you from starving. There is no dying in here when you don’t find food, or having a grumpy character when you’re not eating a balanced diet. The foods boost your character stats and are helpful in surviving the great outdoors.

Farming:
Yes, there is absolutely farming in this game. If you’d like to grow your own ingredients you can easily do so, with hardly any limits, except time. Patience with farming is extremely rewarding. Where some things will be ready for harvesting in a day or so, it is best to leave others to grow for a while to better reap the benefits.

Building:
I’ll say this. If you love building in games where you have no limits, you’ll have a blast in here. It does offer a wide selection of building materials and furnishings with no caps and restrictions, so long as you build within your flame radius. It could however use a bit of a fine tweaking tool and more rotation options for blocks, but other than that, it is thoroughly enjoyable to build masterpieces in this game.

Scenery:
There are some very, very beautiful and well thought out places in this game. Even though it does have some re-use over some building exteriors, like the spires, there are equally places that are very unique and you can immediately feel the love and effort that was put in to create some of these spaces (e.g. a beautiful woodland cave when you’re heading to the tar swamp)

Gameplay:
After playing this game for some time, I found it to be very enjoyable (especially if you play with someone else who also enjoys it).
