Baldur's Gate 3 isn't merely a great role-playing game; it is a structural anomaly. It is, in effect, a proof-of-concept that demonstrates what happens when a major budget is deployed not in pursuit of the live-service treadmill, but in absolute service to player agency. 

Larian Studios took the chaotic, magnificent spirit of Dungeons & Dragons and rendered it with systemic integrity, solving the decades-old issue of the illusion of choice that plagues the modern RPG genre. The triumph here is not its narrative, though it’s often compelling, but its terrifying mechanical consistency.

[h2] The Freedom of Choice[/h2]
One of the reasons why Baldur's Gate 3 is successful is its refusal to treat player choice as a mere series of dialogue prompts. Where other titles offer a tightly curated set of branching paths, Larian delivered a simulated reality governed by D&D 5E's core rules. If a character is meant to be unreachable, they are not protected by an invisible wall; they are simply separated by geometry and elevation, obstacles that can be overcome with a simple Misty Step, an improvised jump, or a strategically placed oil barrel.

This systemic fidelity grants players the genuine, unsettling freedom to break the game's intended path, and the underlying code is trusted to calculate the consequence. This is the difference between performative agency (AKA when dialogue leads to the same outcome) and true consequence. This approach generates those singular, emergent moments (like the infamous scene involving Halsin, or the bizarre solutions to dungeon puzzles) that are unique to the player’s session, proving that the digital medium can finally emulate the chaotic collaboration of a tabletop campaign. It sets the standard for interactive design by demonstrating that the designer's job is not to dictate the story, but merely to construct the responsive simulation.

[h2] Atmoshpere[/h2]
The art direction shifts between the grimy, oppressive environments of the Goblin Camp and the breathtaking, bioluminescent splendor of the Underdark, establishing a clear mood for every narrative beat. Crucially, the camera's shift from the isometric viewpoint to the tight, cinematic focus during dialogue acts as a crucial validation mechanism. It signals to the player that their decisions are being treated with the same industrial-scale seriousness as a major pre-scripted cutscene.

With two million words of recorded dialogue, the quality is often exceptional—particularly the companion performances, which carry the majority of the game’s emotional load. In a game designed to let you talk, sneak, or murder your way out of every encounter, the quality of the dialogue delivery must be consistent to maintain the player’s immersion in the responsive simulation. The orchestral score, while expertly crafted, serves primarily as an effective, atmospheric support layer, underscoring the player’s action without dominating the soundscape.

[h2]The Pacing Paradox and the Narrative Debt[/h2]
However, such radical ambition inevitably encounters the untenable volume required to sustain it. While Act I and Act II thrive on a tight, interconnected geography, Act III marks where the simulation’s sheer weight begins to crush the narrative's structure.

The urgency of the main plot [spoiler](the ticking mind flayer parasite clock)[/spoiler] is utterly contradicted by the administrative load of the finale. The game implicitly requires players to wade through thirty or more hours of companion resolutions, murder mysteries, and urban political intrigue to cash in the emotional and narrative debt accumulated over the previous two acts. 

Crucially, many vital character moments are tied to the Long Rest mechanic, forcing the player, in a moment of narrative crisis, to repeatedly retreat to camp just to ensure companions receive their overdue emotional cutscenes. In my playthough, this resulted in making the plot's climax feel less like a roaring crescendo and more like an abrupt conclusion following an exhaustive slog through content administration. But, everyone's playthrough is different.

[h2]Why We Won't See This Again[/h2]
This brings us to the uncomfortable truth and that is Baldur's Gate 3 is a profound exception. [b]We will not see another game of this specific caliber for at least the next decade.[/b]

Larian Studios is privately owned meaning they are allowed the luxury "freedom". A six-year development cycle, an eventual team size of 450, and the ability to fund the game through the success of their previous independent IPs and a long, stable Early Access period is what made Baldur's Gate 3 the game it is today. A game which sold a complete, single-player experience with zero monetisation hooks, simply does not fit the modern spreadsheet.

The game’s creation required producing over two million words of voice-acted dialogue and animating hundreds of unique cinematic scenes designed for outcomes only a fraction of players will ever see. For your typical AAA studio, this is not something they would do - they operate on the principle of the Minimum Viable Product, maximising monetisation on predictable, repeatable structural foundations. 

[h2] Conclusion[/h2]
In the end, Baldur's Gate 3 is an astonishing work of art—a towering monument to the possibilities of player agency. Its flaws are the scars of its own radical ambition, the inevitable trade-off when simulation dares to surpass scripted narrative. It is a masterpiece, not because it is perfect, but because it exposed how far the industry had drifted from simply making great games for the sake of making great games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1759721606}, {"review_text": "One of the most detailed and freedom-giving RPGs I’ve ever played. [b]This game is amazing[/b]. The story is (for the most part) true to the lore and well-written. Sure it's not perfectly faithful to 100% of the lore - there are some clear exceptions if players are seasoned DnD fans - but these differences are mostly made in favour of playability. [h3]The customization:[/h3]
The game offers a wide selection for customization, allowing you to choose your race, background, and class, with the option to multiclass. You can even customize your voice, body type and your wiener. Dialogues are influenced by your origin, race, and class. Wizards and sorcerers can make fun of each other, drows can intimidate others, and companions might banter with you about whose god is the better one.

If you don’t want to create your own character, you can play as one of the 7 Origin characters. I recommend creating your own character or trying "The Dark Urge". He is unique as he is the only Origin character who doesn’t appear in the story, offering a unique playthrough you won’t experience on a normal playthrough.

The animations and facial expressions are impressive as well, they bring life to both human and non-human races. Even characters like dragonborns have expressive facial expressions.

[h3]Companions:[/h3]
The game features a huge cast of companions (10), each with their own distinct personalities and backstories. Over time, these companions evolve from strangers in your party to allies, friends, or romantic interests. Companions dynamically react to your choices and to each other, leading to surprising dialogues and conflicts. Bringing specific companions to encounters can change how they unfold, and you can influence their fate—helping them stay on their path or stray away from it. The voice acting is also phenomenal. Romances also features options for polymorphic or same-sex relationships, (so no one missies out on Shadowheart or Halsin).

Spoiler Alert: If you don’t want to miss an easily missable companion:[spoiler]When you meet a drow named Minthara, and if you get into a fight, switch to non-lethal combat and knock her out instead of killing her.[/spoiler]

[h3]Open World and Exploration:[/h3]
The game does an amazing job with its story, covering a wide range of topics, with its central themes being trauma, trust, and personal growth. There are three acts, each offering many beautiful and memorable locations to explore. Its open-world design lets you roam freely, and NPCs dynamically react to your actions. 

The world feels alive, with consequences for your actions. After 200+ hours, I’m still finding hidden dialogues and secret details that surprise me, making me appreciate the developers’ attention to detail.

[h3]Gameplay and Mechanics:[/h3]
The game offers many difficulty options, from "Explorer" for those who just want to enjoy the story to "Tactician" for the min-maxers. You can also play the game solo or in co-op, giving you the opportunity to experience the story with your friends.

Combat is highly creative, with spells and abilities that interact with the environment. For example, you can set up explosive barrels before an ambush or use water to create electrified surfaces. Players can tackle obstacles in numerous ways—combat, stealth, magic, or conversation. This variety ensures you can tailor the story to your own playstyle.

[h3]Flaws:[/h3] 
[list]
[*]As with many open-world games, bugs can arise due to its complex and detailed structure. For example, after killing a character, NPCs might still refer to them as alive. In one instance, I exposed a thief disguised as a guard, only to have him arrest me for stealing.

For quite some time, I have been avoiding BG3 completely. Of course, the huge popularity and high appraisal of this game didn't pass me, yet I didn't have much interest in it. I can't explain why exactly. Maybe I wasn't in the mood for turn-based combat. Maybe I was "afraid" of the sheer size of this game and didn't want to commit too much time to it. Maybe I was a dumbass trying to be "not like everyone" and not play what was popular.

Time passed, one of my friends got a gaming PC, and we started to think about what games we could play together. We were looking through what Steam could offer us, and nothing interesting popped out, except for BG3. Suddenly, I thought, "Well, if I didn't play this game myself, we could try coop, I guess". And after that short thought, the month of non-stop BG3 gameplay started for us both. I just lived in the mode of "I hope the end of my work day comes faster, so I can play BG3 with my friend". 

Despite not having the best-in-class graphics, the game still looks very good. As always, creativity and designers/artists can bring a lot to the table without taxing players with immense hardware requirements. I liked how characters look, how armor and weapons look, spell effects etc. The locations and landscapes were stunning.

The sound design was good for my limited knowledge and taste. The musical score is amazing, magical even. As always, after beating a game with good OST, I went straight to a streaming service just to listen to said OST on repeat. I only wish the music was more "present" during the gameplay and more frequently "took the stage".

Overall, I liked the gameplay, even though I can't really critique it, because I didn't play many of the similar games; Only Divinity Original Sin comes to mind. My friend and I played on Tactician difficulty, and even with our subpar, non-optimized builds, we managed to beat the game (I know, I don't have the achievement, yes, we briefly dropped difficulty for the fight with Apostle of Myrkul, but then switched back to Tactician and stayed on it to the end). The combat is interesting and engaging, with a lot of combos and possibilities. There are only so many classes and mechanics we experienced and explored in our 100+ hour playthrough. If you get stuck and think that the fight you faced is impossible to win, it's most probably not. Don't be afraid to experiment, study your enemies, and don't hesitate to use potions, scrolls, environment etc. The game provides all these things to make your life easier (except for explosive kegs abuse, that one doesn't count as fair play). Of course, there were a couple of annoying things, like characters missing their shots/hits in the most comical manner ever, characters not having enough mobility etc., but all of these come from the fact that our builds weren't the best, us not using all the mechanics and items, plus it's just the nature of the games with the dice. Even with a 99% probability of hitting the enemy, you can still miss (and it's right, because that is how probability works). You just need to get used to it.

Exploring the maps was interesting. As I mentioned, the locations were really well done, in my opinion. The only gripes I got with exploration were episodes of camera freaking out in buildings with several floors, and those ladders, which can be used only by one character at a given time.

Also, as in every other self-respecting RPG, you can fight with your words in this game. I will remember for a long time how my friend who had high charisma just verbally un-alived that sick doctor in Act 2 in the hospital.

And now for the most interesting part - the story and characters. I will never get tired of realizing how important good and interesting characters are. At first, I was kinda afraid that the writing part of this game would not be that good, because in my mind it was like that - "it's built upon D&D, in D&D people create new stories/characters every time, i.e. characters may not be as defined, the game may be 'faceless' etc.". I can't explain why I had something like that in mind, and thank God I was wrong. I absolutely love the characters in this game. Yes, maybe they are stereotypical here and there, but I don't really care. They were interesting to me, I wanted to listen to their dialogue, do their quests, I worried about them, so on and so forth. For me personally, it's one of the most interesting parts of such games - to see the stories of your companions unfold, taking part in it, helping them, building relationships with them, having their unique input about different situations and such. It's amazing. I liked how the majority of your companions' stories unfold throughout the course of the entire game, gradually giving you new story bits. The voice actors did an outstanding job in bringing said characters to life. Worth saying that not only companions are done well, but the majority of the NPCs. And of course, I enjoyed my romance with Shadowheart. It was really nice, how it slowly progresses together with her story and such. Also, that celebration at the very end of the game, when Withers gathers all of your companions - you can clearly see that the developers knew what they were doing, and they too understand the importance of our companions and how players can get attached to them.

I think the story was good. We played the "good" route, and maybe it wasn't as deep and fresh, but it felt fulfilling. I enjoyed my journey, truly. Sidequests were very interesting to do.

In my profile you can see how much I was glazing The Witcher 3 in my latest Steam review, and now I think I shouldn't have done it. Don't get me wrong, I like CDPR work a lot, but that review was written under strong emotions. I think that BG3 offers much more, and other game developers should take notes. Baldur's Gate 3 is packed with content, has amazing art design and music, good stories and lovely characters, a lot of interactivity in its world, variety in both gameplay and narrative. Add to all of this the countless number of mods and good replay value, and you get a game that can be played for hundreds and thousands of hours. I am already planning a new playthrough with mods, where I will recruit every companion (we didn't get Wyll and Minthara), try different classes etc. From a story perspective, I will probably make the same choices and romance Shadowheart again and again, but you can do things differently. And this is the beauty of this game - the player's freedom to shape their story in whatever way they want.

This game doesn't really need any recommendations, everyone has heard about it and knows that it's worth playing. Playing this game with a good friend of mine was a truly special experience, living through all these adventures together - it was amazing. BG3 easily became one of my favorite games ever.

Also, I should just point out one bit. In my country, the game costs like 20–30 dollars, which is basically a steal. I don't know how Ukrainian gamers earned such generosity, but thank you devs. Add to this the fact that the game has full Ukrainian text localization, which is rare on its own, and even more rare for a game of such a scale with so many text lines - I can't be grateful enough. Definitely recommended.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1748539881}, {"review_text": "⭐ 10,000+ hours later... my crops are still thriving and so is my soul ⭐

There’s something magical about Stardew Valley.

I bought it thinking, “Eh, I’ll play for a weekend and move on.”
That was 7 years ago. I now have a farm more organized than my real life, a digital wife who loves me unconditionally, and a shed filled with 300 jars of ancient fruit wine. I don't know what day of the week it is in real life, but I can tell you exactly when the traveling cart shows up in the Valley.

This game isn’t just about farming. It’s about healing.

You start in the chaos of modern life, burned out and tired. Then you inherit your grandfather’s farm and escape to the gentle rhythms of nature. The music calms you. The villagers surprise you. The world breathes with life. And before you know it, you're fishing at 2AM, debating whether to plant cauliflower or parsnips next season, and attending the Flower Dance hoping someone—anyone—will finally accept your invitation.

🌾 The pixel art is charming.
🎵 The soundtrack is soothing.
💌 The stories are deeper than you expect.
🎣 The content updates? FREE. And HUGE.
🛠️ The modding community? God-tier.
💖 ConcernedApe? A one-man miracle.

This isn’t just a game. It’s therapy. It’s a warm blanket. It’s home.

If you’re sad, anxious, tired, or just need a place to breathe—Stardew Valley will be here for you.
Rain or shine. Winter or Spring.

That's definitely how I felt when I first decided to give this game a shot when Space Age dropped near the end of 2024. However, I quickly realized how wrong that initial assumption was from my end.

The most daunting thing about booting up Factorio for the first time turns out to be its hotkeys and its sprawling tech tree. In terms of its hotkeys, it's much like any graphic design software where initially some hotkeys seem so unbelievably specific its almost absurd. After some time with the game (in my case, 400 hours in and I'm still picking up new hotkey tricks) you'll probably end up surprised with how naturally you've adapted to their use. So, no rush there.

The tech tree, if you stare at it long enough when you start your first world, might seem a little nauseating. Your mind may spiral a bit trying to understand how you'll prepare to make components, or plan to use structures, that are hours of gameplay down the line from the start. It may help to look at the tech tree as a series of courses that the game will serve you during your playtime instead. The game is gating you, presenting you with a challenge at each step. "How do I stop needing to manually feed all my furnaces and get more smelted products?", "How do I keep up with my demand for gears and circuits?", "How can I improve my power supply and access to distant resources?".

This series of compartmentalized challenges is how this game ropes you in. All of those videos and images you've seen of crazy mega-bases and efficient train networks aren't gated behind some genetic predisposition to being talented at Factorio. Rather, they are the result of approaching each of these small, bite sized challenges the game presents you with as you progress through its tech tree. Before you know it, you'll be producing answers to questions this game asks you that you weren't even aware were a possibility 20 hours prior. The pieces will keep falling into place for you over and over and over again, and after 400 hours playing this game, they haven't stopped for me.

If you let it, Factorio will take you on a journey of endless problem solving, where the problems you solve only grow more complex and where your answers only become more elegant and clever. It comes highly recommended from me, it is one of the most rewarding and fascinating games I have played in my life.

The biggest negative I could assign Factorio is how its post-endgame content functions. With space age especially, what drove me in this game was rounding out and perfecting my main base, along with discovering and conquering new planets and optimizing them as I went along. However, at a certain point, as the tech tree begins to fizzle out into repeatable researches, the end game content simply becomes a game of pushing your production values higher.

This works for some people, but doesn't work for me (at least, not yet). And from what I've seen of the modding community, there are countless ways to customize the game's content to mitigate this issue. I don't think its necessarily a bad thing, how vanilla Factorio concludes, it's just not for me.

A tower defense game utilizing anthropomorphic plants to defend your home from zombies.

A simplistic tower defense (with small mini games and puzzles as extra content) using 6 rows across your yard, backyard, and roof that lead to your house. If the zombies get in, game over.

This game is a classic.

A zombie invasion is happening, chaos is everywhere and how do you defend against it? With Plants, of course!

This is a Tower Defence game that is exactly what the name implies, you help your definitely sane friend Crazy Dave, by collecting sun and using multiple Plants to defeat a variety of Zombies. 

It doesn't matter if it's on the lawn, backyard or even the roof, or if it's day, night or with fog, or even if they're inside vases. The Zombies are coming, and you better be ready to get set and plant your Peashooters and Sunflowers to victory!

Anyways, let's get to the pros and cons.

Pros:

- Almost every level gives you something new to play with, maybe it's a Plant, a new Minigame, or the ability to access Dave's shop. Thanks to that, it keeps you engaged throughout the whole experience.

- Several minigames that changes how you would normally play, there's even one that allows you to play as the Zombies instead.

- The Soundtrack is fantastic, every music fits the area and more instruments are added if there's a lot of Zombies on the screen. My personal favorites are Crazy Dave (the main theme), Ultimate Battle, Grace the Roof, Zen Garden, Brainiac Maniac, and Zombies on your Lawn.

- The Artstyle is gorgeous, all the Plants look cute and charming, even a flower pot has eyes and a face. As for the Zombies, despite them usually being depicted as scary in games, they look goofy and simple in this one.

Cons:

- The game is way too easy, most Zombies are barely a threat, the lawnmowers can also defeat any Zombies on an entire lane. Even something like a Balloon Zombie, which can fly, gets affected by it. The game is so easy in fact, that it can be completed without ever using Sunflowers and Sun-Shrooms. Some of the plants are also way too powerful, speaking of which...

- Overpowered Plants.

> Puff-Shroom is a 0 cost Plant, yes, a free Plant, that attacks similarly to a Peashooter, with the only downsides being that it doesn't have a lot of range and it doesn't work on daytime. This Plant single handedly turn night levels into a joke since you can just spam it.

> Ice-Shroom freezes most Zombie types on screen for several seconds. After the freeze is gone, the zombies are still chilled.

> Doom-Shroom is just a better Cherry Bomb, having more range than it, with the only downside being that of preventing you from planting in that tile for several seconds.

> Cattail, a slightly more expensive Repeater that can hit zombies on any lane, and also counters Balloon Zombies.

> Starfruit is a slightly more expensive Peashooter that shoots in five directions at once, spam it and you win.

> Winter-Melon does high damage, has splash damage and slows Zombies down, insane.

> Gloom-Shroom is a close ranged Plant that attacks in all directions and demolishes anything that gets close to it.

And on the opposite end of the spectrum we have...

- Super niche or very weak Plants. 

> Chomper takes forever to finish eating a Zombie, understandable if it's on a tanky one, but it takes the same amount of time regardless if it was a Browncoat or Zomboni.

> Plantern is designed to counter fog and nothing else, this plant feels like a Quality of Life feature more than anything else.

> Cactus is made to counter Balloon Zombies and that's it. If that zombie isn't in the level, then Cactus is just a more expensive Peashooter with the same stats.

> Blover defeats Balloon Zombies and temporarily gets rid of fog, does nothing else. Same problem that Cactus has.

> Hypno-Shroom hypnotizes a zombie to fight for you, cool effect but the only Zombie worth doing that is Football Zombies, more problematic ones are immune to this plant. Better off just using Jalapeno.

> Split Pea is supposed to counter Digger Zombies but it lacks the firepower to do so, outside of that it's just a more expensive Peashooter.

> Umbrella-Leaf counters Catapult and Bungee Zombies and does nothing else.

> Gold Magnet just collects coins for you, pretty much just a Quality of Life.

> Marigold produces coins, that's it. Should have just been exclusive to Zen Garden.

> Sea-Shroom is a slower recharging Puff-Shroom that can only be used on water and during night time. 

> And other plants that only do one thing, such as Grave Buster, Coffee Bean, Flower Pot and Lily Pad.

Combining both the really strong and weak plants leads into..

- Bad replayability. The game is fun to play through the Adventure mode, but after that there's not much reason to do it again. Crazy Dave does force you to use some random Plants in the loadout if you go into Adventure again, and levels are longer than normal with problematic zombies showing up more often, but that's about it. Game also suffers from being really slow to play, a button to increase the game speed would have been appreciated.

In Conclusion:

Despite all that, my final score is a 8/10, pretty solid game with only a few issues here and there.

This is a classic that stood the test of time. Sad to see how this franchise is in such a sad and deplorable shape nowadays, at least this game still works like a time capsule of the good times we had back then.

🌱Happy birthday of 16 years.🌱

[{"review_text": "This game is how every triple A game should be. However, Ghost of Tsushima is more than a masterpiece. It’s is ART.

The combat system in Ghost of Tsushima has got to be the smoothest of any game I have ever played. No hiccups, no jittery movements. Every button and action used smoothly transitions from one to the next and honestly it’s just amazing. 

The game direction is the best I have ever seen. No stupid marker on the screen in your face. No UI for the most part of travelling. The game uses the wind to guide you through Tsushima and Iki Island. It adds a level of immersion I hadn’t ever thought possible in a game.

The game itself is beautiful. Everywhere you go in this game and in any weather looks fantastic that a screenshot from anywhere anytime can look like PURE CINEMA. The trees, the grass, the sun as it sheds its light on everything just looks… wow!

Throughout my gameplay of this game I have encountered only two bugs. On Iki island there was a rock and you could see a few pixel gap where you could see through the world. But honestly it is super easy to miss. The other was a fault of my personal settings so I won’t include it.

The story is one that hits home for me. Balancing what is right and what is not and of one’s own honour. It is amazing. Literally goosebumps whenever I play or watch the game. I bought Ghost of Tsushima in a real tough time in my life and had no spoilers and thus NO REGRETS.

The music is on another level. I’ve never really stepped into the Japanese genre of music before and this game has it dialled up to 100x. The music gives goosebumps every time, it matches the feel and the action the game is going for at every turn. It is hard to put into words how good it is. How AMAZING it is!

Japanese culture is somewhat inaccurate as the whole Honour theme wasn’t prevalent until 200 years after the Mongolians attempted to invade the mainland after conquering Tsushima and Iki. But their faith, their traditions, the way the armour looks and how many times you hit an enemy with your katana to kill them is really realistic. As blades back then were too thin to cause real damage.

This has changed my opinion on games and is officially my favourite game of All Time!

Just a moment ago you might have been fumbling and tripping in real life, but now you are Jin Sakai, cutting down Mongols like it’s nothing, as if you've been training with a bamboo sword under a waterfall your whole life. The game is stunning, cinematic, and almost a spiritual experience... unless you take into consideration the fact that you stop during a fight to pet a fox. 

The Director’s Cut is essentially the same game, but with an amplified effect of everything, more island, more narrative, more wind dramatically blowing through your cape as you contemplate honor and trauma. The Iki Island expansion is Jin’s journey in therapy, which is cleverly disguised as a side quest. It is aesthetically pleasing and tragic at the same time, and sometimes it can be the “my dad didn’t hug me enough” energy. 

The visuals are worth discussing. This game doesn’t have graphics, it has art. Every single frame could be a piece of art that people museum it and they silently say “wow, the composition.” You might find yourself in the middle of a fight and suddenly stopping to take pictures because the sunset is just too beautiful. While you’re technically supposed to be saving Japan, you are here instead, like a feudal times influencer, adjusting filters and focal depth. 

The fight? Exquisitely sharp. It’s a combination of ballet and murder. Each stunt and every sword strike is real and believable. You’ll transition from button, mashing panic to perfect timely parry that will make you say “yes” quietly to yourself at 2 a.m. They even have a standoff mode where you can basically act as the main character of every cool samurai movie you’ve ever seen, with the difference that you are the one who doesn’t fail and misses. 

Also, the dual, audio Japanese voice acting? The best. If you opt to play in English, that’s ok but playing in Japanese and with Kurosawa mode on is an absolute vibe. Black and white, film grain, wind that is blowing dramaticaly, it really gives you the feeling that you are watching a masterpiece from the 1950s, except without the smell of the film burning. 

The Director’s Cut is not a major overhaul of the game, but a kind of a mirror polish. Emotionally, the weight comes from Iki Island and a handful of new gadgets, and on PS5, ‘blink and it’s done’ would be a pretty accurate description of the load times. It’s essentially the same game, only smoother, prettier, and slightly sadder in a good way. 

Essentially, Ghost of Tsushima: Director’s Cut is the result of art, combat and open, world design teaming up to form a boy band. It’s gorgeous, emotional, and at times, silly, in the way that only a game that lets you write haikus about death next to a waterfall can be. 

Play it. Then play it again. And don’t forget to pet every single fox, they really deserve it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1760839628}, {"review_text": "I didn't really have expectations going into GoT, and for the first few hours it didn't blow me away. It does suffer from the common problem in action games where the combat can feel shallow in the beginning, but as you get a grip of the mechanics and unlock more "abilities" you can mix up each fight massively. You switch between stances in a way that's not clunky, you have batman-like gadgets as well as your sword and bow, everything feels so fluid and smooth to use. When you get the ability that lets you use slow-mo when aiming your bow it becomes even more fluid where you can headshot multiple people from a few feet away in under a second the instantly throw down a smoke bomb and assassinate another two - it's more thrilling than I'm giving it credit for and that's just one of many "techniques" you can use. Hard to believe Ghost of Tsushima lost Game of the Year to The Last of Us Part II with all its controversie, but I guess that’s subjective.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761494914}, {"review_text": "Ah yes, the Japanese Assassin's Creed Ubisoft wishes it had made.

Just how the Spider-man games make you FEEL like Spiderman this game really makes you FEEL like a Samurai.

However, I realise that this is something I should have started doing a while ago. I really enjoy it and it has helped me a lot in defending myself from my wife’s boyfriend!

I first played the game during the pandemic and it was the perfect game for me during lockdown. I would just wander the countryside and take in the scenery. I would chase foxes to their shrine, and wear different outfits depending on my mood. I would zone out to the ambient shakuhachi flutes, and bang my head to the taiko drums. I would compose haiku under the stars, and perfect my showdown stances. The whole game felt organic and natural. When I finished the game, living there in that little hut, with all the trophies, I indulged in the memories of each one, like having a glass of wine with an old friend. When I originally played it in 2020, I felt it was my favorite game of that decade. Have yet to play a game in the last 2 years I love more. Those touches were MAGICAL for the first hours. The first time I wrote a haiku was an experience that made me reevaluate how I view video games. The whole thing was like I was playing one of my beloved Samurai movies. I would get excited when I saw the Fox dens, since it meant there was a chance I could pet one.(love giving animals scratches in games) The stoic characters felt authentic to the the type of old school Samurai movies they were seemingly inspired from. And having the guiding wind to help you to your objectives was a very nice touch and really innovative way to get rid of quest markers. The mythical tales are excellent, and so are the duels that come with the quests. This is where the game really shines, as it is able to combine the best of the great visuals and good combat into memorable segments.

The game sure has several of the open world tropes that studios are apparently tied to these days, But it’s a lot less bloated than the recent AC games. In AC I would always be rushing from A to B trying to get the traveling over with. In this you get full trilogy, all DLCs included with enhanced graphics. And there is no series like this one, from the very beginning it really feels like it was meant to be a three part story.
For the whole series I must say it looks good, soundtrack fits what is going on the screen, story is amazing, the characters are very well written, sidequests are interesting and I enjoyed gameplay. And what is most important: YOUR CHOICES MATTERS! Feels good beeing able to shape your character your way.
As for the cons, I encountered few minor bugs and I don't like some changes they made across the titles.
It's kinda hard to talk about whole trilogy so I'd like to say few words about each part.

[h1] Mass Effect 1 [/h1]

As befits the first part, we are introduced to the main character and the world in which the action takes place. We get to know some of the lore and we meet our most important companions. This game is a great beginning to something really big that comes later. That's how series start should look like.
This game has the best RPG elements in whole series imo. There are plenty of abilities for each class and companions and there is a lot of equipement you can find. There are different type of armors, good amount of weapons and addons to them, you can also find different types of ammunition. Not only that, there are different levels of each item so you can find upgraded one with your character levels up. So it's important to look for a loot and bring on a mission someone who can hack/bypass locked containers or terminals.
As for combat it's good, you can always take different approuch to enemies but it's not very challenging even on the hardest difficulty. I'd say that enemy SI is not so good and that's why.
My only complain is about planet exploration, it's really basic and gets boring pretty fast. It could get some more love.

[h1] Mass Effect 2 [/h1]

This one has the best part of the story (for me). From the start of the game you know what you have to do and what your final destination will be. You just need to recruit necessary companions and go on a suicide mission with your crew, sounds fun. AND IT IS! Great recruiting missions, even better companions missions and amazing final mission. I absolutely love quests you get here.
As 1st game felt too easy this is the hardest game in trillogy. In a wrong way, it's basically taking cover simulator. You really can't do anything else, just take cover, shoot some, hide. I'm not a fan of that. I also don't like the change they did to omni gel. In 1st you could use it to heal yourself or to revive knocked down squadmates, in this it can only be used to revive squadmates unless your omni gel is fully upgraded and here comes the other complains about the changes...
There are no different armors, only couple of weapons with no addons, type of ammunition became an ability. Only loot you can find are resources or technology. With it you can buy upgrades to weapon, armor, body or said omni gel. It's mostly +some% of dmg/health etc.
They also removed planet exploring (not counting few side missions) and replaced it with scanning system. You fly to a planet, scan it and send a probe to collect resources.
They also changed abilities system, now you only have couple of powers you can upgrade and there is almost no build variety per class.

[h1] Mass Effect 3 [/h1]

The Grand Finale. For me all the missions were really good until the very end, but the ending was kinda disappointing. What I mean is only one choice make sense and the others are... let's say weird. Nonetheless it's very good closing to the story.
In this part they upgraded abilities system so now you can actually make different builds, they also improved scanning system but didn't bring back planet exploration sadly.
Combat seems much better but there is one thing I don't like. It's spacebar button, one key that does too much. You use it to interact, to sprint, to take cover and to go over the cover. That's wild and I'm not able to count how many times I died just because i pressed it twice unintentionally so Shepard jumped over the cover to meet his end.
Other things are same or very similar to previous games but one - character interactions. There is much more of that than it was. It's mostly because of the Citadel DLC in which story is less serious and It's one big thanks and goodbye to all our friends and companions. The romances are much more complex as well. i didn't talk about them because in ME1 and 2 it was just couple of dialogues and a short scene just before the final mission and here in ME3 it is much more than that. What I love the most in this part are: the party during Citadel DLC and dialogues during our last mission.

[h3] Final words [/h3]

Getting 3 games in a price of 1 is a great deal and this game is very often on sale for like 5 bucks, that's a steal. And for a games like that absolutely worth it. When i was near the end I felt somewhat sad because i knew it will be over soon and there will be a little emptiness. It's always like that with games like these. But I'm glad i finished it, it's absolutely amazing and i don't regret a second.

Risk of Rain 2's primary verbs are the same as its predecessor: search and fight. You search for items that make you better at searching and fighting, search for the teleporter to proceed, and fight enemies to remove threats and make money. What spices this up is how enemies power scale over time, so you're incentivized to search and fight quickly as to not let the enemies outscale you in offense and defense. With this basic setup there's an elegant interplay between the systems: movement items make you better at searching and evading damage; damage items make you kill faster; defense items mean you have less downtime in combat. There's also utility items that help you search or make money. You have to find a balance between these priorities. Gaining this understanding of how the game works, and then finding your ideal balance, is part of the game's fun.

On every level there are three phases of gameplay: 1. Fight and search for items and the teleporter, 2. Fight the boss and charge the teleporter, and 3. Search for more items and try to spend all your money. The first phase challenges you to fight and search simultaneously, and make a call on when to start the teleporter based on your incomplete information about what items you might buy and your confidence in the boss fight. If you activate early, you risk being underpowered for the boss; if you do it late, you might gain more money than you can spend on the map, meaning the excess money (i.e. time spent) was wasted. The second phase is a pure combat test, and the third is mostly a test of your searching ability. These phases generally provide moderate, high, and low levels of tension respectively, giving the game a good flow.

This game also takes full advantage of the third dimension, with aerial enemies, dramatic elevation differences and variance in character movement that lets you navigate the environment differently with each one. A lot of 3D games keep the play space relatively flat, so it's refreshing to have a game that makes you fight and navigate in every direction. Heck, I'm not a fan of RoR 1 because searching in 2D isn't that interesting (combined with the very limited movement), and the combat is practically one dimensional (not figuratively).

Items change your run in a Roguelike. In Ror2, you stack them, bringing a whole new layer to the system. The game dares you to break it in the most fun way possible. Wins are possible with every character on every run, but it's still challenging and well balanced. You can have runs that go forever if want. You stop when you choose to, with several different ways to do so (given you don't die). The achievements teach you how to play the game. The artifacts combined with the multiple difficulties, and character variety make each game session spicy. This game is truly great! It has tangible progression despite being a roguelike and (generally) every run starting you from zero like normal. The loot drops also almost always feel fair, even when it's left completely to RNG. Additionally, random placement of stations that are able to fabricate a specific item at the cost of an item or item scrap of the same tier allow you to somewhat tailor your build to your tastes, without ever being fully in control. It is to be commended how varied the ten base survivors are. None of them move or fight in the same way. The freedom to explore open and big maps while maintaining the progression loop of the original creates a one-of-a-kind experience that stands out in the whole rougelite genre. The transition to 3D elevates the gameplay, making every run feel dynamic and immersive.

What makes Risk of Rain 2 truly special is its hidden storytelling. Instead of relying on direct dialogue, the game weaves its narrative through environmental details, lore logs, and the natural progression of events. Each character’s experience feels unique, with endings that reflect their perspective, adding a personal touch to every run.

The soundtrack is another standout feature. some may say it's trash but in my opinion, the mix of atmospheric and intense tracks perfectly complements the gameplay, elevating both the quiet exploration moments and the chaotic, large-scale battles. It’s not just background music—it’s an essential part of what makes Risk of Rain 2 so engaging and immersive. you can never forget stage 5 music, especially considering the fact that this track alone is used by many video essayists even if the video doesn't have anything to do with Risk of Rain 2.

Replayability is where the game truly shines. The endless variety of builds, characters, and artifacts ensures that no two runs are the same. Artifacts in particular are a game-changer, allowing you to tweak core mechanics and create wildly different experiences. It’s a testament to how Risk of Rain 2 keeps things fresh even after countless hours.

However, the multiplayer experience has its flaws. When a player dies mid-run, they’re forced to spectate while enemies grow stronger, leaving them at a severe disadvantage in the next stage. This can make co-op runs frustrating, especially since it punishes the entire team’s balance. Mods like those that allow reviving teammates can greatly improve the experience, and I highly recommend them. While the DLC introduces a character and item that address this issue, tying these fixes to paid content limits accessibility. It’s a step in the right direction, but an inclusive solution would have been better.

Even with these drawbacks, Risk of Rain 2 is a masterpiece. It’s endlessly replayable, innovative, and remains one of the best roguelites in it's genre. It is, in many ways, a love letter to long-time fans, tying together lore threads that have dangled since the original Dark Souls. However, while the narrative and atmosphere reach impressive heights, the game’s approach to build variety feels like a step back, especially when compared to the sprawling arsenal of Dark Souls 2.
On a technical and artistic level, Dark Souls 3 is a masterclass in world design. Lothric’s interconnected, ruined beauty is a haunting sight, echoing the best of the first game’s level design philosophy while improving upon it with smoother traversal and verticality. The lore is rich, weaving in references to past games in a way that feels reverent rather than redundant. Gwyn’s legacy, the Undead Curse, and the ever-repeating cycle of fire and dark all find resolution here, bringing a sense of finality that Dark Souls 2 never fully embraced.
However, where Dark Souls 3 falters is in its gameplay variety. Compared to the sheer level of options in Dark Souls 2, which boasted an almost overwhelming number of weapons and builds, Dark Souls 3 feels streamlined to the point of limitation. The removal of power stance mechanics, the reduced dual-wielding options, and the emphasis on a faster-paced, aggressive combat style cater more to a specific meta rather than the ‘choose your own playstyle’ philosophy that defined the series. While the introduction of Weapon Arts offers some variety, they often feel underwhelming compared to the adaptability and unique movesets from previous entries.
Magic builds also suffer from this streamlining. The separation of FP from individual spell casts allows for more sustained magic use, but the nerfs to spell damage and the overall slower casting times make them feel underpowered, especially in PvP. Meanwhile, faith builds—once a cornerstone of versatility—are left with little to stand on outside of buffs and healing.
Despite these limitations, Dark Souls 3 still provides an immensely satisfying challenge. The boss fights, from the relentless Nameless King to the poetic tragedy of the Soul of Cinder, rank among the best in the series. The combat is more fluid than ever, encouraging a mix of aggression and careful stamina management. While the game may not offer the sheer experimental sandbox that Dark Souls 2 did, it refines what it does have to near perfection.
Ultimately, Dark Souls 3 is a worthy send-off for the series, closing the loop in a way that respects its past while pushing forward into a bleak yet beautiful unknown. It may not offer the same level of build variety as its predecessor, but as a final journey through the dying embers of this world, it remains unforgettable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1743734921}, {"review_text": "What a game! One of the huge flaws in this game which confused me was how the player approaches enemies in a more lethal sniper format. Another large downgrade is the approach to vehicle combat, in this game weapon customization is a very strong boon the player has and the ability to make a suppressed anti-armor rifle is pretty neat, but the interaction between vehicles and the player is extremely limited. The very first level, Atlantikwall introduces you to vehicle patrols right after you complete the tutorial piece of the game and again, at first its pretty neat seeing a traveling patrol of trucks, wagens and bikes roaming around the maps (until it breaks, I'll get that towards the end of the review), but targeting of vehicle weakpoints is extremely hit or miss in SE5, even with Anti-Armor ammo, sometimes it takes up to two, four shots before you blow up a troop truck, even a wagen. Later in the same level, you encounter the first major flaw of this issue, the patrol boat. On the water in front of the beach bunkers is a boat with spotlight and turret.

In previous games, you could target the driver AND gunner of the boat, but in SE5 only the spotlight can be broken and the driver can be killed. The base campaign maps (without DLC) look great – big, detailed, and atmospheric. Some areas are perfect for stealth, but I often wish there were more opportunities for true long-range sniping. The level design is impressive, but replaying missions quickly becomes repetitive.  

For achievement hunters, it can be exhausting. A good example is the “Wolf Mountain” mission with Hitler – killing him in a dozen different ways just to unlock achievements feels like filler content. It adds hours of repetition without much creativity from the developers.  

I’ve logged around 350 hours in the game, and while the campaign is enjoyable, replay fatigue is definitely real.  

---

## ⚔️ Axis Invasion  
Axis Invasion is probably the most exciting addition to Sniper Elite 5. Dropping in as a Jäger sniper to hunt down another player completely changes the atmosphere of the campaign. It’s tense, unpredictable, and often thrilling.  

Unfortunately, this mode suffers from serious balance issues – usually against the invader:  
- You can’t loot fallen soldiers for extra weapons, traps, or grenades. You’re stuck with two grenades, a mine, and a medkit.  
- The invaded player has big advantages: looting gear, using phones to track you, and even seeing hints of where you’re approaching from.  
- Worst of all, “Sniper Focus” feels like an unfair advantage – allowing the invaded player to see your location through walls and prepare an ambush.  

Camping makes it worse. Many players clear the entire map of AI, plant mines everywhere, and then sit in a high spot (like a church tower) with perfect vision. Most of my deaths as an invader were simply from running into yet another mine.  

AI isn’t helpful either. If enemies are shooting at the campaign player, I should get an exact location update. Footstep sounds are also too quiet, making sound-based tracking unreliable.  

---

## 🛡️ Survival  
Survival mode is fun, but it highlights a big flaw across the game: there’s no proper tutorial explaining mechanics, scoring, or what actions give the most points. You have to figure it all out yourself.  

Difficulty scaling is also frustrating. Getting a gold medal feels almost impossible on lower difficulties like *Civilian* or *Very Easy*. Maps are sometimes designed to overwhelm you with enemies from all sides, leaving no chance to respond. The mode is intense, but it lacks balance.  

---

## 🔫 Multiplayer  
I’ve only played a few dozen matches, but the main issue is clear: **everything requires grinding**.  
- You unlock weapon attachments in the campaign, but then you must unlock them again in Axis Invasion.  
- In Survival, you also need unlocks, or you’re stuck with bare-bones gear.  
- In Multiplayer, you have to grind all the way to level 50 to access the full arsenal.  

This system feels unfair – new players are stuck with basic weapons, long aim times, and no attachments, while higher-level players dominate. On top of that, there’s a “Prestige” system where you re-grind levels from scratch for small perks. Honestly, it feels lazy.  

Other issues:  
- **Easy Anti-Cheat** doesn’t seem to stop cheaters, but it does eat resources, cause micro-stutters, and add lag.  
- The **wheel menu** is clunky. In combat, it blocks the screen and wastes time. Hotkeys for ammo and explosives would’ve been better.  
- **Weapon customization** is excellent, but loadouts reset across game modes. And you can’t name custom loadouts, which makes things confusing.  

---

## ✅ Pros  
- Beautiful maps and textures  
- Axis Invasion is exciting and unique  
- Wide choice of sniper rifles and secondary weapons  
- Deep and satisfying weapon customization  

## ❌ Cons  
- Repetitiveness kills replay value  
- Poor balance in Axis Invasion  
- Too much grinding across every mode  
- Easy Anti-Cheat hurts performance  
- Wheel menu slows gameplay  
- Lack of realism in animations, physics, and AI  

---

## 📝 Final Thoughts  
Sniper Elite 5 is a good game – even a very good one in some areas – with beautiful visuals, strong sniping mechanics, and a brilliant idea in Axis Invasion. But it also feels unfinished, with too much grinding, weak AI, and mechanics that often frustrate more than they entertain.  

For me, Sniper Elite 2 / Sniper Elite V2 Remastered still holds the crown for the most satisfying overall experience. Sniper Elite 5 is revolutionary in parts, but disappointing in others.  

My advice? Wait for a good sale, grab the Season Pass bundles, and give it a try. To call Dark Souls merely a game is a disservice. It is an experience, an ordeal, and for many, an awakening. Playing Dark Souls Remastered is not just about rekindling a classic—it is about revisiting the foundation of a trilogy that fundamentally changed how I interpret storytelling in video games. It is a reminder that not all tales need to be told in upfront exposition, nor should every journey be neatly plotted by quest markers. In an era where games like Skyrim sought to guide the player's hand, Dark Souls did the opposite: it let us stumble, fall, and carve our own meaning from the abyss.

 [h2]A World Told in Whispers, Not Shouts [/h2]
What makes Dark Souls so profound is its refusal to speak too loudly. Lordran is a land of hushed myths, decaying grandeur, and cryptic figures who offer guidance just as often as they deceive. Its story is not delivered through cutscenes or a journal of dictated objectives but through ruins, item descriptions, and the silent suffering of those who still cling to existence. There is no exposition-laden Jarl to welcome you, no noble guild waiting to anoint you as a chosen hero. Instead, Dark Souls looks at you with hollowed eyes and asks, Why are you here? What are you willing to endure?
This storytelling philosophy—where meaning is not handed to the player but uncovered—resonates deeply with Nietzschean existentialism. Dark Souls forces players to find their own purpose amidst the decay. There is no singular right way to interpret the game’s narrative, just as there is no absolute meaning in an uncaring universe. The First Flame will always fade, and the gods are not eternal. To persist is to impose meaning onto a world that has none.
 [h2]The Strength of a Community-Built Mythos [/h2]
Unlike Skyrim, where every story is spelled out for you, Dark Souls thrives on ambiguity, and in doing so, it fosters something far greater: a living, breathing myth shaped by its community. It is in the shared experience of piecing together fragmented lore that the game’s narrative finds its fullest form. Players dissect every item description, theorize on the nature of Manus and the Abyss, debate whether Gwyn was a hero or a coward. It is a game where knowledge is just as much a reward as victory over a boss, where every new theory reshapes our understanding of the world.
This communal storytelling turns Dark Souls into something transcendent. It is no longer just a personal journey but a collective endeavor, an eternal cycle of discovery and reinterpretation. In this way, it mirrors how real myths survive—through countless voices passing them down, each altering the tale with new meaning.
 [h2]A Lesson in Perseverance and Interpretation [/h2]
Returning to Dark Souls Remastered in the wake of the series’ legacy only reinforces what was already apparent in 2011: this game is a monument to the power of interactive storytelling. The feeling of finally besting Ornstein and Smough, the dread of descending into the Tomb of the Giants, the quiet, sorrowful notes of Gwyn, Lord of Cinder’s theme—these are not just moments of gameplay, but moments of personal revelation. They are tests of will, framed within a narrative that allows players to define their own understanding of struggle and triumph.
To play Dark Souls is to wrestle with the abyss and emerge changed. It is a game that does not tell you what to feel but allows you to discover meaning in your own perseverance. Dark Souls isn’t just a game — it’s an experience. Specifically, the experience of being repeatedly and unapologetically bullied by medieval architecture, undead warriors, and the very concept of hope.

So let me break it down, both from the perspective of someone coming in new to the franchise, and a vet Diablo player. 

Story - (4/5 for newcomers, 1.5/5 for vets) - Blizzard probably assumes no one currently gaming played Diablo 1 and 2. Otherwise, they wouldn't have copied the plot ending of D1 and part of D2 into D4. As it is, the game has a limited and recurring cast of baddies, and a plot that repeats the Hero/Mysterious Wanderer's endgame (albeit with a different outcome) is bound to feel jaded. 

For newcomers, though, the biggest question is why this game is called Diablo. There is no Diablo in the picture (so far) and instead we get Lilith and Mephisto. Otherwise, the story is decent. Lilith comes across as perhaps the most morally ambiguous antagonist, which makes lack of any meaningful decisions in the game makes the game feel like something out of Sunday School. You can probably predict the ending of the story halfway through the game, with only minor variations dragged in. That said, if you don't use your brain too much, the game has a fairly engaging storyline IF you joined the bandwagon with D3 or this is your first Diablo game. 

Graphics (4/5 for all) - It's a point and click game so breathtaking details are probably not what anyone expects. They're a climb up from D3, and that is probably all that matters. Max settings at 4K don't really demand a beast of a GPU, though you'll need a fairly beefy CPU for those Infernal Hordes waves when there are dozens of enemies on screen. Effects have been improved, and the transitions are also better. Together with some excellent background scores, they provide excellent atmosphere. 

Gameplay (2.5/5 for newcomers, NA for vets) - Those unfamiliar with point and click games would probably have some difficulty persuading their wrists to click hundreds of times per gaming session. Beyond that though, the gameplay is, well, classic Diablo. Nothing much has been changed since D3, or even D2 for that matter, in terms of core gameplay mechanics. You choose a class, and depending on it, you have some core mechanics that you have to repeat time and again with better and better gear to take down more and more powerful enemies. The skill trees are simpler than POE/2, but they can be daunting at first. My advice would be to use your common sense to build your first seasonal toon, and then go for build guides in the endgame. 

The endgame used to be a long slog to Level 100 after Level 50. That has been replaced by the more familiar (and comfortable) Level 60 + 300 Paragon levels. Most players don't manage to go beyond Paragon 250 in any season, as it takes an insane amount of xp. But by that time, you should have filled up everything on your skill tree and paragon board (a kinda extended skill tree) to make you truly badass.

Finally, the difficulty system has been made even more convoluted, and not necessarily for the better. Normal is very easy, Hard is easy, expert is hard, penitent is very hard, and then you have the torment difficulties where difficulty rises exponentially. The goal is to get better gear, hone your stats and push the pit till you unlock the next difficulty. Reach the highest one, and you're facing tormented bosses that can drop mythic items. Collect mythic items to complete your gear journey and then melt everything on the map that has a red health bar over it. 

Next season, rinse and repeat. 

Conclusion - Diablo continues to do what it has done for the past decade - churn out what was a decent story once, and keep making variations of it as if the scriptwriters were asked to work on half pay. [{"review_text": "I'm not generally a person who plays games for the difficulty. I like a challenge, but for me, the main draw to any single-player game is the story. If the difficulty prevents me from experiencing the narrative, I'm not going to enjoy it.

I have played through Lies of P probably three or four times now.

There's something about this world the developers created, something that keeps making me want to come back, even though I've experienced nearly everything there is to see in this game.

The gameplay is incredibly fun, the characters are engaging, the music is phenomenal, and the twist on the Pinocchio story is beyond interesting. It's gripping.

I cannot wait for the DLC to release just so I have a chance to experience something new in this world.

This is the first review I've ever written for a game. And there are games out there that I love, games that have literally shaped who I am as a person.

But for some reason, I was compelled to write something about this one.

More lore can be discovered if you're willing to venture a little off path to explore.. It created an emotional journey that actually made me a little teary eyed and had some pretty memorable characters on top.

The environment is a stunning, gothic fantasy landscape that had me constantly stopping to take screenshots (and getting smacked in the back by a lurking puppet way too many times) There is just so much life to the different areas that it feels like it was a once very lived in city. I knew going in that it was a great game —the reviews, the visuals, the hype —but actually playing it? It was even better. I loved every single second of it.

The story was surprisingly well done...simple enough to follow but still packed with some emotional moments that actually hit. Normally in Souls games, I just go around slashing anything that moves and barely know why I’m doing it. But Lies of P? I actually understood what was going on ...kind of like Sekiro in that way. It had me hooked from start to finish.

Enemy design is another strong point ...there's a great variety and they’re both creepy and creatively designed. Most of the boss fights were intense, memorable and incredibly well done (except the swamp monster... that thing can go sink back into whatever cursed bog it came from. Still salty )

The music and sound design also deserve a shoutout. Some of those boss themes go hard and the general soundscape ...from the clashing metal to the unsettling puppet noises, added so much to the atmosphere. And man, that sharp, clean clang when you perfect deflect an attack is so damn satisfying, it makes every successful parry feel 10x cooler.

Exploration was decent ...not the game’s strongest suit but still enjoyable. That said, Krat is a hauntingly beautiful city to explore, full of atmosphere and little details that reward those who pay attention. 

Like any good Souls game, the game is tough but never unfair. It challenges you constantly but every victory feels earned. And when you die, you usually know exactly what you did wrong. The combat system in this game is more guard and parry heavy than dodge heavy.  That means in combat you won't be dodge rolling around as much in this game as you would in a lot of other soulslikes. I also didn't find it intoxicating to find an unnecessary amount of consumables and the gear isn't that varied, given how armours are almost out of the equation. Do I gag alone when I see an oversized club attached to a sabre handle? The toned-down scope delivers an intimate experience, emphasising characters instead of the surroundings. Yes, I said I didn't like the story, but I'm cool with its inhabitants. And you'll love it, for the combat system is what truly shines.

[h3]Lies of Penitence[/h3]
At the base, it's the same Souls game of predictions and commitments, light and heavy attacks. Except P relies on guard counters, i.e. deflections. Landing those perfectly takes a sharp reaction time. On the upside, you heal by hitting your enemy after guarding, which is called guard regain. I recognise my skill issues and admit that I lack both speed and rhythm, being 40 and brain-damaged. After coming to terms with my ineptitude, I minmaxed, lowering the amount of precise inputs I'd have to ace each fight. O, Dex. Become my blade, once more.

Then I smashed the remaining bosses with my ugly stick, learning nothing from it. I'm just glad they disallowed summons on the final boss. My victory didn't ring so hollow. Ultimately, I'm jealous of people who feel at home here. I admire them as I admire Lies of P. But it's not mine to love. Different strokes.

DRG, at its core, is a class-based co-op shooter set in procedurally generated caves. Your goal in every mission is to collect resources by mining ores and shooting a lot, and I mean A LOT of bugs. There are four classes to choose from, each having their own weapons, movement abilities, and most importantly, role and "job" in the team. You can level up your class by collecting upgrade materials in missions, used to add buffs to weapons and movement tools. 

Now on the whole, that is about as brief of a summary I can give without going into the minutiae of Deep Rock Galactic. There are a LOT of other details about the gameplay loop, class perks, Overclocks, and the roles and quirks of the classes themselves. For those still interested in reading, strap in.

To give some context on how and why I'm writing the rest of this review, I'll start with how I began playing DRG and why I continue to play it. I would give this game not really a thumbs up but not really a thumbs down and there's several reasons that go into this. I've played both ARK Survival Evolved and ARK: Survival Ascended enough time that I feel able to give this sort of review at this point. 

[b] Let's start with the Good: [/b]
[list]
[*] Unreal Engine 5.5 is the current engine of the game as of this review. (I may update this in the future but unlikely.) It has resulted in a gorgeous game visually. 
[*] The developers are releasing all of the maps and content that were originally DLC (paid and free) for ARK SE as free updates to ARK SA, meaning for the box price you are getting everything that came with ARK Survival Evolved (eventually, they have just dropped Ragnarok as of this review, with Gen 1/2, Fjordur, Crystal Isles, and Valguero still to come among a few others.
[*] There is new content being added to ASA that is not going to be added to ASE, including new gameplay benefits, creatures, and cross-platform mod support. 
[*] Development is active, with a pretty active community and a healthy unofficial community as well. 
[*] Crossplatform mods also give rise to Premium mods, are very easy to install from within the game and tend to work... most of the time, with some whitelisted to work on Official Servers!
[*] The developers do maintain an active official network where those who can't afford to rent their own servers or prefer to play with others outside of SP can do so. 
[/list]

[b] Now to the Bad: [/b]
[list]
[*] There are still bugs present in the base game that have existed since ASE, the reasons for these vary, but while some has been fixed not all of it has. If you were hoping for a less buggy game I'm afraid that classic ARK jank is still present. 
[*] The game has been optimized repeatedly since it's initial early access release, but it is still pretty hard on older rigs. I would recommend making sure you have updated hardware. 
[*] No Steam Deck support due to the aforementioned hardware requirements. You can get it to run, it just won't run well. 
[*] MTX. You can call it DLC and it functionally is, but $5 here, $5 there, that's a microtransaction and there's a significant number of them.  
[*] The arrival of crossplatform mods has also meant the arrival of premium mods that you also pay for. This isn't really a sticking point for me, as I love supporting passionate individuals but it is a turnoff to some, especially with many premium mods starting at $5 USD for varying quality.
[*] Though the Official Network is fairly healthy, the developers have begun a pattern of sunsetting inactive official servers, potentially leading to progress loss for those who don't manage to get their characters off onto a different official server. They do kindly offer the saves themselves so you can play with them on SP or load them onto a personal server cluster, but this has been a point of contention for the community. 
[*] The additional DLC that provides gameplay changes as well as unique creatures to tame can be pretty expensive.

Overall I have been a longtime ark fan even if I wasn't around for the 'beta' days. I enjoy the game but I fully admit that it's not a game for everyone. It can be buggy, and if you play on officials (and even then) it can be extremely unforgiving when something bugs out, or you lose progress etc due to server troubles. 

The game has gotten better from its initial release, but that doesn't mean its perfect and as of writing this review it is still in early access and adding yet more content at a pretty blistering pace while translating over older content from ARK SE. As far as the promised content goes, I do believe that promise is being kept pretty admirably but for a lot of other people I fully understand the anger regarding the costs.

It is worth emphasizing that the exorbitant cost of this game is all in optional content that has come across as Pay-to-Win because the creatures involved are very powerful, but locked behind these DLC Passes. If you are someone who thrives in PvP and were hoping for fair fighting grounds, I'd argue this game is not for you unless you have $$$. 

Even among PvErs though, the game is costly if you want some of the really cool critters. This is why I recommend purchasing on a sale if you really want to get into it with all the bells and whistles. to me it's not worth the value that I myself have paid out over time so far. 

As of this writing, total cost to enjoy this game at full price with all new things: (rounded to nearest whole dollar)
Base Cost: $45
Bob's Tall Tales: $30
Fantastic Tames Pyromane: $5
Fantastic Tames Dreadmare: $5
Fantastic Tames Drakeling: $5 (after LC release)
Partner Map Astraeos: $15 (The only map where Maeguanas, a reptilian version of the Maewing that was released as an early access baby trough spawn naturally. Otherwise an optional community map developed by a modder working along with WC as a partner.) 
Lost Colony Expansion Pass (currently w/Veilwyn and Drakeling): $30 USD (Drakeling will be sold separately after LC releases and Veilwyn is only temporarily available until the LC map releases which is its otherwise exclusive spawn.)

There is additional optional content released by WC in regards to cosmetics, one which is available on Steam STore, the other which I've seen on their internal Overwolf Premium Mod offering: 
- Power Rangers Official Cosmetics: $10-20 USD total (not super positive on this one, I feel like the price changed for it.) 
- Official ARK Show Cosmetics: $15 USD

Without these cosmetics and just the main creature DLC though you are still looking at $135 USD just to keep up with their pace of releases and have access to genuinely GAMECHANGING mechanics and devices. Things like a gestation incubator, the ability to tame Pyromanes or Dreadmares or Armadoggos etc, all of which naturally spawn on the otherwise free base maps, the ability to use special mechanics like the shovel from bob's tall tales to hunt for treasure and dig it up. Or even the ability to access new lore notes related to the expansions. 

To be perfectly clear there is plenty of reason to be upset at this level of gameplay being locked behind additional paywalls, but this content also goes several steps BEYOND what was initially promised with ASA, which was simply bringing ARK SE forward in terms of technology and engine. They have accomplished that portion, and as a company need to continue funding development so to an extent I understand it. However it leaves a bad taste in the mouth of many players, myself included when we go beyond the occasional $5  release and announce more 20+ USD expansions. I love the game and I'll still support it at the end of the day, but I won't say the anger is unjustified to an extent.

The worst thing about BTD6 is that you have no idea what the actual stats of towers are. Pierce, damage, bonus damage vs. certain bloons — none of that is shown. Upgrades often just say “increases attack speed” without telling you if it’s 10%, 50%, or 2%. You’re left guessing from the animation. You could argue they want the game to feel less technical, but an option for advanced stats would fix this easily. Some upgrades are even worse, saying things like “bloons will fear you” with no explanation of what that actually means.

You also don’t know which bloons spawn on which rounds unless you memorize them. If you want real info, you basically have to open the wiki.

Each map has way too many “easy” challenges, forcing you to replay them several times if you want a black border (all challenges + CHIMPS without retrying). It’d be nice if we could do multiple challenges at once, especially the easier ones, to speed things up. Personally, I would have preferred if CHIMPS was balanced with Monkey Knowledge for more progression, but it’s fine as is.

The game can flood you with abilities, many of which aren’t explained well, leading to a messy UI with 20+ buttons. The Tech Bot helps automate abilities but costs monkey money and space; there really should be a built-in auto-cast option, similar to what the DLC game mode does.

As a live service, BTD6 has added tons of content — but much of it feels unnecessary. Bosses and Paragons are cool, but they don’t add much outside their specific modes. Paragons are trial-and-error, since you don’t know the degree before buying them, and thresholds are extremely important. Because of their cost, you mostly end up using the same few Paragons while ignoring the rest. Some are only used when the “good” ones are disabled, which feels artificial. Honestly, Paragons and bosses could have been the foundation of a future BTD7, instead of being bolted onto 6.

The in-game purchases also leave a bad taste. They’re not really worth it (which is good and bad), but just having a store in what is mostly a single-player game feels off.
