For one thing, there's a bit more of a focus on platforming in this game compared to other Souls games. You can swim in mid-air for a short time kind of like Yoshi's flutter jump, and thanks to the drop shadows that always appear right below you, I rarely had issues lining up my jumps properly. The grappling hook you get very early on also unlocks more platforming opportunities and is used very effectively with the level design. It all works well and is very enjoyable, with some surprisingly tough platforming challenges towards the end.

This is also one of the very few 3D platformers to actually have good combat. Unlike many other games in the genre where you can just spam the attack button over and over making it feel mindless, you won't get very far if you try to do so in this game. Similar to Souls games, knowing the best timing to dodge, block or strike requires paying attention to the enemy attack patterns then reacting accordingly. Each enemy type has different attacks that keep you on your toes, constantly evolving as the game progresses and remains interesting from beginning to end.

The combat isn't without its issues, however. The camera can be rather problematic sometimes, occasionally obscuring the view of the enemy you're targeting, leading to me getting hit when I can't even see them. I've also had times where enemy AI gets confused and doesn't really try to attack as they should, leading to me getting some very easy hits on them when I shouldn't. Fortunately, these issues don't happen too often and aren't bad enough to ruin the experience.

Scattered throughout the ocean are various shells you can wear. Simply equipping one will drastically reduce damage taken, but each one also comes with their own skills you can activate with an Umami charge. You can hide in a shell to protect yourself from damage, which goes to the shell instead, but will break after taking too much damage so you may be better off dodging if you can. Parrying is possible by leaving your shell just as the enemy hits, but can be very tough to time so I usually don't bother unless I do so by accident.

The game looks very nice. I loved the ocean setting this game uses and is full of its own personality. Characters are expressive and well animated, each environment feels unique, and the real time cutscenes, when they do show up, are entertaining to watch while also having voice acting that usually gets the job done. What I certainly wasn't expecting, however, was a short mini-documentary of sorts about aquatic ocean life when I booted this game for the first time, yet it still somehow fits into this game's narrative perfectly.

True to the Dark Souls series, this game is tough. Enemies hit hard and you'll die very quickly if you don't "get good" at combat. Microplastics, which are this game's Souls or Runes, can be used to level up at Moon Snail Shells, which are this game's Bonfires or Sites of Grace, but you'll drop every single one on death. You can go back to collect them at the spot you died at, but you'll lose them for good if you die again before doing so. Although punishing, it's never unforgiving, and it helps that dying at a boss will respawn you right before the boss, allowing you to try again quickly without having to go all the way back.

If you do find this game too difficult at any point, however, there are assist options that allow you to reduce damage taken and/or increase damage dealt. There are settings to disable losing Microplastics, as well as giving you a gun to shoot enemies with if you find melee combat too frustrating. However, I "got good" and was able to beat the entire game without them, and I'm glad I did as it made conquering every single challenge feel like a satisfying accomplishment, which I would've felt deprived of had I resorted to changing these settings to make it easier on myself.

New Game Plus becomes available after finishing the game which increases enemy damage drastically and changes enemy layouts, with much stronger foes appearing early on where they did not on your first run, but to make up for this, your shells, levels and most items will carry over. An overall nice way to provide replay value for the more experienced players looking to get even more out of it.

At the time of writing this review, my experience with the genre is very limited. The only other Souls game I have played is Elden Ring, and only for a few hours before getting absolutely destroyed by it. I don't know how this game's difficulty compares to that or other Souls games, but if you want a gateway game to get into the genre, this is a good place to start with. Mechanics are much more simple and not so overwhelming, there's a good amount of platforming and exploration to break up the combat, while also maintaining the difficulty the genre is well known for.

Other than the occasional camera hiccups I mentioned earlier, this game runs really well on my computer with very few glitches, short load times and at 60FPS with very few performance issues even when running on the highest graphics settings. I haven't tried running this game on Steam Deck yet, but for those who have one and want to play this on the go, I have heard it runs fine on that as well.

Not only is this overall an easy game for me to recommend to anyone that's never played a Souls game before and want to get into the genre for the first time, but the unique game mechanics, art style and setting also makes this worth playing even for Souls veterans. It regularly goes on sale, but has enough content to make it worth buying at full price unlike many AAA releases nowadays. It's also gotten me interested in checking out the Dark Souls series of games that inspired this someday in the future, and perhaps giving Elden Ring another chance.

Rating: 9/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752403548}, {"review_text": "[h1]The Reluctant Forksman[/h1]
TL;DR: A surprisingly well-crafted game that is everything you could want in an indie soulslike. A little easy for the genre, but features creative combat and platforming systems, great comedy writing, and a story that is more touching than a goofy game about crabs has any right to be.[hr][/hr]
I’m wary of trying out new soulslike franchises, especially when they aren’t from a tested studio like From Software. There’s a fine line between challenging and frustrating, and the slightest bit of jank can be a real turnoff in a genre that demands precision. Despite that, [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] got enough affection from people whose opinions I respect that I opted to wade in. What I found was a genuinely funny and enjoyable game that has a few fresh ideas and punches well above its weight.

In [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] you step into the role of Kril, a true hermit of a hermit crab; he lives in a tidepool on the beach, does largely nothing, has no friends, and is perfectly content. He is ushered into utter turmoil after his shell is repossessed to cover back taxes, and he must brave the sea bed in his quest to recover his home. It’s a goofy setup for a story that is unexpectedly grounded, seeing our hero leave his comfort zone to broaden his horizons and find value in things he had previously scarcely considered. Not only relatable, the tale is woven throughout with humor that lands fairly consistently, as well a fair number of groan-worthy marine life puns.

On his odyssey to reclaim his shell, Kril will be forced to take up the fork in self-defense. The melee combat is pretty standard for the genre, but well enough crafted not to feel frustrating except in a few rare situations where footing can be an issue. There are a few variations, like releasing block at the moment of impact to parry, but the real USP comes in the form of shells. Kril can protect himself with a wide variety of found objects, from soda cans to skulls. These have different stats and weights, but the stroke of genius is that different shells enable different spells, and they have their own durability. It’s not uncommon to find yourself scrambling to jump into a new shell in the middle of a boss fight after yours has soaked a few hits. It’s a fun way to tie systems together, and encourages you to try moves you might not otherwise engage with. By the end of the game you’ll probably have a favorite shell, and you can insure it so you always respawn with it, but collecting the different options and trying out the various moves was a lot of fun.

Exploration is a little more lively than most soulslikes, with 3D-platforming eventually bolstered by swimming, climbing, and a grappling hook. Areas start fairly basic and ramp up to some truly impressive levels, ranging from electrified mining rigs to pitch-black abyssal plains. The environs shape the combat, and as mentioned above, this can lead to some slightly wonky encounters, but that is very rare and seemed to happen most in the first handful of levels. The art direction is cartoonish, and fits the tone and humor of the game beautifully. When the surroundings turn inevitably bleak (this [b]is[/b] a soulslike, after all), the loss of light and saturated colors serve to reinforce the severity of the crisis and the depths of Kril’s alienation. This degree of attention to detail is not something I’d expect from a first-time developer, and it’s both impressive and refreshing.

It’s an overused phrase, but this game is a true indie gem, and well worth your time and money if you enjoy the genre. Even if you haven’t in the past, there’s a decent chance you’ll have fun here, and if you get too frustrated, Kril can always bring a gun to any fight and win in one shot. Introduction
Knights of the Old Republic (KOTOR 1), developed by BioWare, is a game that revolutionized the RPG genre and made a permanent mark in video game history. Set in the Star Wars universe, it offers a simple but incredibly engaging storyline, phenomenal characters and a world that continues to delight despite the passage of years. The game is not without flaws, but it still remains one of the best RPGs of all time.

Plot and narrative
The game's plot revolves around the classic theme of good versus evil in a galactic conflict. While the story's outline may seem simple, its strength lies in great pacing, rich world creation and a variety of quests - both main and side quests. From the beginning, the game sets clear objectives that evolve smoothly, and the narrative draws you in thanks to a well-balanced presentation of events and a natural introduction to the reality of the world. There is no shortage of moments of surprise that enhance the quality of the story, and information is provided in a way that does not overload the player.

Characters
The characters are a real gem - each of them is well written and memorable. From the sarcastic Carth Onasi, to the charming droid T3-M4, to the charismatic Canderous Ordo, they all have stories that we discover as we play. Some, like Mission Vao or Bastila Shan, even get their own quests, which deepens their characters. However, they are not as elaborate as in the sequel, and our influence on their fates is limited. Nevertheless, the companions are distinguished by their personalities and bring a lot to the gameplay.

Gameplay mechanics
The mechanics of KOTOR 1 are based on a simple character development system, which, compared to the more complex Neverwinter Nights, may seem poor. Character level has a real meaning, and skill and Power points need to be spent with your head, as it's impossible to have everything. Combat isn't particularly difficult, but I happened to die or fight on the edge of endurance, which makes it remain satisfying. Also noteworthy is the economy - one of the best I've seen in an RPG. Collecting credits from enemies and chests, or even extorting them from NPCs as an evil character, doesn't immediately make us rich. For a long time I couldn't afford the best items, and by the end of the game, although I had enough money for the top gear, I had to choose what to buy, which added authenticity and motivation to being “evil.”

Game world
The locations are phenomenally designed - from crowded Taris, to desert Tatooine, to the jungles of Kashyyyk. Each planet contrasts with the others, offering variety without overwhelming in size. The game world achieves the perfect balance between exploration, combat and dialogues - there are no hordes of enemies like in Neverwinter Nights or protracted conversations like in KOTOR 2. Side quests are interesting, though not very elaborate - the game relies on the main storyline, and quests are often done “along the way.” The possibility to solve them in different ways, according to the light or dark side of the Force (or something in between), builds a sense of freedom and authenticity of the world. The locations typically focused on combat and exploration are sensitively designed - they don't drag on endlessly or overwhelm in complexity, which keeps the gameplay in a smooth and pleasant rhythm.

Audiovisual setting 
The graphics are slightly inferior to those in KOTOR 2, but they have still aged well. Character models and locations still look decent, although without modifications the game does not support 1920x1080 resolution.  The soundtrack is a Star Wars classic - epic, matching the narrative, and the ambient sounds, such as the din of the cantina on Taris, do a great job of building atmosphere.

Replayability
Replayability is huge. The ability to create your own path - from the noble Jedi to the ruthless Sith - combined with moral choices and an immersive world makes you want to return to the game. The game doesn't moralize - it allows you to take on the role of a real villain, which adds to the fun.

Technical aspects
Technically, KOTOR 1 has problems. The game repeatedly crashed for me, dialogues sometimes skipped on their own, and companions had trouble following me. Fortunately, I didn't encounter bugs that prevented me from completing the game or quests, but the technical condition leaves much to be desired.

Subjective evaluation
KOTOR 1 is, for me, one of the best RPGs ever made. It offers tremendous freedom in character creation, great locations, interesting characters and an engaging storyline with a brilliant twist. Despite its simplicity and technical shortcomings, the magic of this game is unmistakable. Other than Baldur's Gate 3, I don't know of a modern RPG that could top it. I definitely recommend it - it's a classic that every fan of the genre should know.

Summary
Knights of the Old Republic is a game that, despite its flaws, impresses with its consistency, atmosphere and possibilities. It doesn't try to be more than it is, and still delivers an unforgettable experience. The game looks gorgeous, I kinda enjoyed the story mode (not the DLC part though, it's horrible beyond any words), I like the roster, I don't mind the grind and the customization system is fine by me. But no matter what I do I just can't have fun with this game at all, which is pretty sad and frustrating. And the issues this time are not so much on the surface, so it took me a while to figure it out why it feels so bad to play MK1 for me.

[b]I came to a conclusion that the game is just... too hardcore for me, and not in a fun way[/b]. With thousands of online matches in MKX and MK11, I just can't get a grasp on this one, and most importantly I don't want to cause it doesn't feel rewarding.

All the mechanics that currently piled up in the game, and the way they're implemented, and all the long-standing issues, they all together smothering me as a player from all sides. It's like I'm mostly fighting against the game rather than my opponents. I mean, how in such a dynamic game am I supposed keep in mind:
[list]
[*][b]Cameo moves and their shitty delayed inputs
[*][b]Move enhancements
[*][b]Fatal blows
[*][b]Cameo fatal blows
[*][b]Desperate moves
[*][b]Perfect blocks and upward blocks
[*][b]Extra-mechanics of every character on the roster [/b](stances, cancels, trap-setups, portals, you name it)
[/list]

All of this + remembering your regular combo strings and specials.
All of this + your attack won't hit cause the game has no actual hit/hurt boxes and uses cheap solution in form of polygon mesh collision instead.
All of this + sloppy online connection.
All of this + some stings in combos don't schedule for no clear reason and require absurdly precise input timings after the character recovery.
All of this + bdf/bfd/dbf... specials that are difficult to pull off consistently. 


[b]NOW AT WHAT POINT CAN I ACTUALLY FOCUS ON JUST PLAYING AND ENJOYING THE GAME?[/b]


When between all that cognitive load do I have a window to actually think about my opponent's actions, about my or their mix-ups, about zoning, and everything else that fighting games are about? How many hundreds of hours do I need to learn all of the above on the muscle memory level and switch my mind to something that is actually fun in the game?

And then I'm comparing this to previous games, MKX and MK11, where it took just a fragment of these efforts to consistently pull off beautiful satisfying combos that involve several different specials and basic attacks.

I remember how I used to main Erran Black and there was a not so hard string that includes almost all the character gimmicks - shooting, acid, rifle butt strikes, slides. Or MK11 Geras string that I used to spam online that had bed of spikes, time freeze and sand portal in it - all you wanna see from your boi.

Now in MK1 it feels like you have to do twice the effort, and the string you get would be something like "punches combo, legs combo, one special that basically looks and feels like a normal attack, more punches, same special". Make it twice as long by slapping a cameo extender after learning its unintuitive timing by heart.

[h2] What's ASIO? [/h2]
[list]
[*] ASIO stands for Audio Stream Input Output. 
[*] ASIO is a "Software protocol that enables applications to communicate with hardware device directly". It basically bypasses the software mixer of Windows noises, which is known to modify sounds to increase performance over quality.

[*] Want to record / stream yourself playing DJ MAX? ==> OBS will not pick up any audio source from DJ MAX as it tries to capture sound from the windows sound mixer itself which ASIO is not. 
[*] Want to watch a video real quick? (or sent by a friend) ==> You have to exit out of DJMAX entirely to hear anything from your desktop, which is extremely frustrating given the slow loading times of opening up the game.

Story: 5/10

Not much to tell—the game has minimal dialogue since it primarily focuses on crafting, mining, fishing, and grinding for materials. The Core at the center is the only source of guidance, providing objectives and occasionally offering some background story and clues about past events.

Gameplay: 9/10

The gameplay feels like a mix of Stardew Valley and Terraria. The game features Health, Mana, and Hunger mechanics.

Hunger affects max HP, but it's not too punishing when it reaches 0%, unlike other survival games.

Health can be upgraded in various ways, such as wearing armor or consuming rare items that permanently increase max HP.

Mana can be frustrating early on as it depletes quickly. However, its regeneration is fair even without a mage-focused build, and it becomes more manageable with dedicated armor or a build centered around magic and mana regeneration.

Combat feels smooth and accessible, offering a variety of builds and playstyles, whether you prefer ranged attacks, melee, magic, summons, explosives, or a combination. In my opinion, melee and ranged weapons feel overpowered from early to end-game due to their high damage and consistency.

The skill tree takes considerable time to fully max out. It levels up similarly to Skyrim—the more you perform an action, the more proficient you become in that skill. Reaching certain skill levels unlocks passive abilities that contribute to character builds. However, you can't acquire every perk even at max level, as you have a limited number of points to allocate, likely for balancing reasons.

Crafting is straightforward and enjoyable, with a vast array of items to create, including base structures, weapons, tools, and other necessities.

Item drops are well-balanced, with specific drop rates for each item. Some rare items may require respawning bosses multiple times to obtain.

Cooking is one of the game’s best features. There are no restrictions on combinations, and with over 100 ingredients, you can create unique food buffs that enhance combat and activities like mining or exploration.

Farming is decent but could be improved. While there are plenty of seeds available, the yield per harvest is quite low—typically just two seeds per crop. Even after maxing out the Gardening skill, seed drops still feel RNG-dependent.

Fishing is straightforward and serves as the primary method for acquiring fish-based ingredients. Many of the best food buffs in the game come from fish-based meals.

Animal Husbandry is poorly implemented and could use improvements. Some cattle species do not respawn in their designated biomes, while others are overpopulated and scattered across different regions. Breeding is also slow, making it difficult to farm meat efficiently. Additionally, animal drops feel underwhelming—milk cannot be used in cooking, wool can be found in chests, and overall, it's not worth the effort.

The map design is great and simple. The overworld is circular, with the player spawning at the center. There are seven main biomes and six sub-biomes, providing plenty to explore. Fast travel options become available from early to mid-game, making navigation more convenient.

Difficulty: 6/10

The game isn't too difficult as long as you prepare properly before fighting bosses. Food buffs and potions provide significant advantages. Every weapon type can be viable against bosses with the right build and buffs. Boss patterns are predictable if you pay attention, making the fights enjoyable rather than frustrating.

My Verdict: 8/10

This is a fantastic RPG sandbox adventure game! If you enjoy Stardew Valley, Minecraft, or Terraria, it's well worth the price and provides a complete satisfying experience without DLCs. review_texts:
[{"review_text": "This game has a ton of potential. MADFINGER, if you're reading this, please look further below for some more direct feedback.

For experienced players of games like Escape From Tarkov, Arena Breakout Infinite, etc, many aspects of the game will be intuitive. Inventory management, weapon customization, equipment slots (with some additions/changes, like being able to wear a tactical belt) will be quite familiar.

The real draw for this game, in my opinion, is the more free-form style of gameplay in place of "raids". You don't have any raid timer, ever. You aren't restricted by timers or boundaries pretty much at all. You can go where you want, when you want. That is extremely cool to have in a game like this.
I think people underestimate the importance of immersion in the extraction shooter genre (which this game effectively falls within, just in a pretty unique kind of way). Games like Tarkov are successful in part because they build such a convincing world. This game does much the same, just with a very different tone. The fact that you can just "live" in this world without restrictions really creates a special feeling that's hard to describe.

Somewhat on the topic of making comparisons with Tarkov, something I really enjoyed about this game (mostly) is the amount of direction they give you with the tasks. I have completed all but 1 or 2 tasks so far (up to the introduction of Ban Pa, in other words: leaving the starter town) without needing any wikis or anything of the sort. I just read what they told me to do and figured it out on my own. WAY easier to follow directions (for most of the tasks) than Tarkov. I'm unsure if this is due to a language barrier issue or just a different approach in design, but either way it was a refreshing boost in immersion to not have to constantly rely on wikis for basic info.


Criticisms/feedback for MADFINGER:

1. -- The game is extremely unclear with VERY important rules involving death and item retrieval. There are very important specific rules in place that the player must know in order to competently approach retrieving their items after death (because yes, after you die, you're still in the same server and you can go back to attempt retrieving your items). i.e. you have 1 hour before your body despawns, and you can ONLY retrieve your MOST RECENT body's items. If you die 2+ times then you can only loot your most recent body. All others will be marked as "old loot", for some reason. This limitation can be completely circumvented by simply being in a squad with other players and having them take the items off your body and throw them on the ground, making the whole feature kinda pointless except for the fact that it puts solo players at a further disadvantage in a pretty arbitrary and immersion-breaking way. The wording is confusing as well. Since it says "old" I thought that it was based on a timer. I needed another player to explain it to me before I realized that dying a second time caused it.

My personal take here? Just remove the "old loot" thing that gets applied after multiple deaths entirely. This only serves to make the experience more frustrating for solos, especially new ones getting bullied by more experienced players/squads.

2. -- The ammunition and armor systems are very confusing. I get almost zero sense of progression when I find anything new, because there's no clear system for what's better/worse. Even a simple instructional chart or something to decipher what I'm looking at would be nice. A huge part of the progression and motivation for players in a looting-based game is to give a clear "Ah HA!" moment when the player finds something good or unlocks the ability to purchase good gear/ammo of their own. Currently, I only get this feeling with guns, and absolutely nothing else. So far, I have almost zero understanding of how any of the armor or ammunition types work. The most clear thing I've seen so far was a description for ammo describing it as sub-sonic, but with the greatly reduced muzzle velocity, I can only assume that it's less effective in SOME other way, I just don't know what's affected. Penetration? Damage? Bullet drop when shooting at a distance? Absolutely no idea what's affected or how it relates with anyone's armor, and more importantly, I don't have any idea HOW MUCH any of those things might be affected. Someone gave me a plate carrier and told me "that's the best one in the game" and the only difference I could find that particularly stood out was the addition of a little "+" next to the armor class, and I have no idea what that means.

3. -- I really like the design choice of having the "marked as aggressor" status placed on players with varying duration depending on the severity of their friendly fire. However, I think that the game is currently overly harsh in cases of immediate defense.
Example: I was walking into hostile territory with 1 teammate by my side. From behind, someone opened fire at us at about 30 meters out, hitting and wounding my teammate and continuing to open fire into his body, and within ~2 seconds, I swiveled around and gunned down the aggressor, who turned out to be a confused ally who mistook us for the enemies that were a little further ahead. When I shot him, I quickly landed a fatal blow, killing him in defense of my teammate with absolutely zero chance to react. I was given 57 minutes of aggressor status for that, even though I literally saved someone's life while the dude was mid-fire, full auto. While I understand that it is not good to encourage "revenge friendly fire", I think there's a line that needs to be drawn when you're quite literally saving the life of an innocent teammate in defense of a rogue ally, regardless if that ally is intentionally acting out or not. Everyone involved was cool with each other there, no heated emotions or anything, and everyone involved agreed that it was unfair for me to get ~1hr with the aggressor status.


Anyway, thanks for reading. There's way more good and bad I could say about the game, but overall I've found it to be a unique and enjoyable experience, so I recommend the game. I just hope that concerns like these are taken seriously and addressed. [olist]
    [*]I can't count the number of times I've died and amount of gear I've lost to AI pulling off 200 yard, hip-firing 1 taps. It's just ridiculous and it needs to be addressed ASAP.

    [*]Goes with the previous point, but the AI's ability to see through foliage is insane. If I can't see them, they shouldn't be able to see me.

As far as optimization, the main issue I've encountered as well as others are spiking CPU temps. [olist]
    [*]Why am I being tasked to go to locations where the AI is wearing III+ Armor and firing M855, when I only have reliable access to FMJ and at best IIIA armor? [h2]The Good: Why Arena Beats Paper 95% of the Time[/h2]

[olist]
    [*][b]Rules Engine is a Godsend[/b]
    [list]
        [*]No more "Did you tap that?" or "Did you pay for Negate?" debates. The stack resolves [i]exactly[/i] like paper, but the client enforces priority, shows triggers, and auto-taps. Teaching new players the stack in paper? Painful. Here? The client [i]shows[/i] it.

    [list]

    [*][b]Queue Times are Insane[/b]
    [list]
        [*]I'm in Europe, and queues for Standard/Explorer/Historic are 2–5 seconds most of the time. Paper nights? They're a whole evening. Here, I can jam 2 Bo1 games while pasta boils.

    [*][b]Limited is Perfect for Learning[/b]
    [list]
        [*]Quick Draft vs. bots lets you practice archetypes without committing. Premier Draft with humans feels competitive. Sealed queues pop fast. As a paper drafter, this is HUGE. Practicing here made me better in-store.
    [/list]
    [*][b]New Player Experience is Actually Good[/b]
    [list]
        [*]Tutorial + colour challenges do a shockingly good job. You get starter decks, and promo codes/free events (like the recent Dominaria United event) help jumpstart your collection. If you stick to a plan, you can build decent decks without spending.
    [/list]
    [*][b]Variety of Formats[/b]
    [list]
        [*]Standard, Historic, Explorer (Pioneer proxy), Singleton events, Brawl. It scratches most itches.
    [/list]
[/olist]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Bad: Where Arena Falls Short[/h2]

[olist]
    [*][b]The Shuffler is [i]Slightly[/i] Suspicious[/b]
    [list]
        [*]I've tracked 10,000+ games. I'll go 12 games drawing 0 lands in a row, then 8 games with 12 lands. In paper, variance exists, but it feels [i]fair[/i]. Here, Bo1 sessions amplify streaks. If it tilts you, play Bo3.
        [*][i]Not[/i] as bad as people claim, but it's there.

    [list]

        [list]

            [*]Rotate between aggro (fast laddering) and control (Bo3).
            [*]Wildcards are gold, but lands hurt. Craft them [i]first[/i].
        [/list]
        [*][b]Alt Account (Spent $£€200ish):[/b]
        [list]
            [*]Mastery Pass + bundles = 3x faster progress. More cosmetics, packs, wildcards. But it's definitely not [i]needed[/i] to win.
        [/list]
        [*][b]Cons:[/b]
        [list]
            [*]No trading. No dusting cards into wildcards. The Vault is slow. If you want 5 decks, F2P feels tight.
            [*]Crafting 8–12 rare lands for a manabase? Brutal.
        [/list]
    [/list]
    [*][b]Meta is Too Compressed[/b]
    [list]

[h2]Paper vs. Digital: The Real Differences[/h2]

[table]
    [tr]
        [th]Aspect[/th]
        [th]Paper[/th]
        [th]Arena[/th]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Cost/Collection[/td]
        [td]Trade, borrow, proxy. Flexible.[/td]
        [td]Closed economy. Wildcards only.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Speed[/td]
        [td]Shuffling, rule debates, slow play[/td]
        [td]Fast, precise, no take-backs.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Social[/td]
        [td]Table banter, Commander pods.[/td]
        [td]Rope system keeps people honest.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Meta Variety[/td]
        [td]Pet decks, homebrew.[/td]
        [td]Ladder = netdecks only.[/td]
    [/tr]
[/table]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cons That Actually Bug Me[/h2]

[list]
    [*]No 4-player Commander. Brawl is fine but not the same.
    [*]Wildcards are inflexible. No dusting, no trading. Plan your crafts.
    [*]Alchemy cards in Historic. If you want "paper parity," stick to Standard/Explorer.
    [*]Auto-tapper grief. It'll sometimes tap the [i]only[/i] dual you need. Learn to pre-tap.

    [*]Use Bo3 for learning: Teaches sideboarding, closer to paper.

review_texts:
[{"review_text": "I finally played Fable for the very first time and my journey through Fable Anniversary was instantly memorable, showing me how special this franchise is.

I sat down to play Fable Anniversary on my Steam Deck, confident that I was playing the very best version of this classic RPG. After overcoming the initial pains of playing an older, inaccessible title, I quickly found myself falling in love with the world of Fable and its charming, unique blend of serious plotlines and humorous writing. In some ways, Fable feels more like an RPG than many modern RPGs in that I always felt like I was in control of the Hero's destiny.

Fable Anniversary is an expanded and remastered version of the 2005's Xbox 360 Fable: The Lost Chapters, which in turn is an expanded re-release of the first Fable from 2004 on the original Xbox. Released in 2014, Fable Anniversary brought vastly improved visual fidelity, superior performance and load speeds, overhauled controls and UI, and plenty of Achievements to entice new and returning players. It's a great remaster of a game that was 10 years old at the time, but even Fable Anniversary is now over nine years old.

As I said, I played the game on my Steam Deck, which means my experience was even better than those who may have played Fable Anniversary around its initial release. Upscaled to 4K HDR, with FPS Boost bringing me 60 smooth frames per second, the first Fable has never looked or played better than it does on the latest current-gen Xbox consoles or handheld device. Still, no number of facelifts short of a complete remake can fix fundamental game design, meaning it took me a few hours of easing into Fable Anniversary before it really clicked.

Fable is still a product of its time, and that means everything from exploring its world to battling its enemy lacks the fluidity and seamlessness of more modern games. Everything feels just a little clunky and awkward, and it's clear that the scope of the first Fable game was inherently limited by the capabilities of the hardware on which it launched. Fable Anniversary also lacks in-depth accessibility options, with even subtitles being compromised.

As I'm hard of hearing and have auditory processing issues, subtitles are necessary whenever I play any game or watch any media. Fable's subtitles, however, lack customization and strangely only apply to in-game cinematics, meaning I frankly lost a lot of casual NPC conversations and non-cinematic story moments. Beyond these issues, though, I found a game that I wholeheartedly loved, to the point where I genuinely could scarcely stop playing until I finished the entire game over the course of two-three days.

The story of Fable is a simple one: you're the Hero, orphaned at a young age by a brutal bandit raid and raised to be a powerful, productive member of the Guild. As a part of the Guild, you explore the world, taking on quests for various people, establishing a name for yourself as either an evil plight on the land or a pure-hearted savior. To this end, every major decision in Fable is very black and white — you either choose the good path or the bad path, and the consequences of each choice are fairly obvious.

In this way, Fable may confuse players used to more recent RPGs. There's no character creator here, not even as much as a gender slider or a way to choose your name; the Hero is who he is, and that's all there is to it. Yes, you can alter his hair, get tattoos, and change his body build through rigorous exercise or excessive eating, but you're never expected to put yourself into the world of Fable. You're also never confronted with an endless array of vague, questionably meaningful decisions. Instead, Fable asks not that you role-play as a character of your creation but instead control the destiny of a nameless Hero inexplicably involved in the fate of the entire world.

It's the ways in which you can control that destiny where Fable's magic lies. For one, you can romance almost anyone in Fable's world; you can flirt with all the men, women, and people of Fable wherever you go, have people fall in love with you, and marry them. Fable has plenty of stats to inform how many spouses you have, what your sexuality is, how many times you've been divorced, and even how many times you've, ah, gone to bed with other people. If you want to be truly evil, you can attempt to romance everyone in a town and ruin all their collective lives.

You can invest in real estate, including buying and furnishing homes for yourself or renting out to tenants for some passive income. If homeowners or shopkeepers "mysteriously" pass away or disappear, their properties go on the market and can also be purchased. Yes, you can own pretty much everything in Fable, as long as you're willing to reduce the population a tad. It's ridiculous.

Fable also features a healthy number of Expressions that can be used to interact with the people of Albion. From positive affirmations and pleasant manners to spiteful insults and silly dances, there are plenty of ways to elicit reactions out of NPCs. Your Expressions are influenced by your Hero's alignment (how good and evil they are) and how well-known they are. They can be necessary for finding secrets, completing quests, and generally being a part of Fable's world.

There are so many small ways you can influence Fable, despite its modest scale, that makes you feel like you have control. Many of these ways actually make little to no difference to the game's story and are simply ways to have fun amidst all the chaos and seriousness. Fable isn't afraid to be delightfully silly, and it gives the game a wonderful charm that's just absent in many "AAA" modern RPGs — which often insist on being serious and dramatic to the point of exhaustion.

Modern games look and play better than any previous generation of gaming, and developers are becoming more creative and ambitious than ever before. Why is it, then, that Fable Anniversary is lingering in my thoughts so much longer than other modern RPGs? What is it about this 20-year-old classic that remains so fun after all this time?

Many modern RPGs are filled with vast open-worlds and countless quests, discoveries, choices, and ways to personalize your experience, but they also focus unerringly on the completion. It's all about getting things done, all the time. Complete the next quest, unlock the next level, beat the next boss — RPGs are always giving you another thing to keep you occupied, and it's always so aggressively serious. Fable has plenty of serious moments, but it's also filled with minute details that don't matter at all. They're just there because someone, somewhere, will love them.

Video games are constantly striving to become bigger and bolder than what came before, but this incessant push for more often results in games forgetting that there's value in a simple moment of humanity, or in the option to be ridiculous. Making vulgar gestures at a door that won't open, farting to ward off a common bully, posing heroically in front of a gaggle of love-addled fans, and combating the forces of darkness with a frying pan and a chicken hat are all things you can do in Fable Anniversary.

This charm is absent in so many games nowadays despite the mind-boggling technological advancements, and it's likely a large part of why Hi-Fi RUSH is such an incredible journey from beginning to end. Elden Ring is also a great example of this, with its community messages offering a potent, often hilarious contrast to the dark and morbid atmosphere of its world.

Fable Anniversary Edition is an amazing work of fantasy, with a unique atmosphere, a great sense of humor and fun, and an unforgettable world. There are some elements that really show the game is twenty years old now, but on the whole it holds up as well today as it did in 2004. This is a game to fall in love with, and if you haven’t played it yet, I hope you’ll give it a try.

Fable is, and always will be, one of those timeless gems in gaming. There's something about its approach to RPG mechanics and the way it looks. There's no denying it has a charm that hasn’t faded over the years. For anyone wondering, Fable Anniversary is essentially a remastered version of the 2004 classic, bundled with its DLC, The Lost Chapters.

I missed out on playing Fable as a kid, but even now, so many years later, it blew me away. It surprised me in ways I wasn’t expecting, and I’d recommend it to any RPG fan out there, young or old.

This game has a unique feel that’s hard to put into words. The world it creates, the way it lets you interact with everything...it’s like nothing else. Even games like Skyrim haven't managed to match this level of detail. 

Let me explain...
In Skyrim, you can go from being a nobody to basically a God, but the world barely reacts to that. Sure, you might get a few comments from guards, but it’s pretty basic, simple and overall doesn't even add to your immersion. You could walk into a village wearing Daedric armor, and no one would care.
Fable is the complete opposite. Every choice you make. right down to the armor you wear, changes how people see you. Some villagers cheer for you while others run away in terror. And while Fable doesn’t take itself too seriously, it doesn’t lean too hard into comedy either. It hits a balance that feels just right.

+ You start off as a kid, and everything you do leaves a mark. Eat too much, and your character gains weight. Take too much damage, and you get scars. Master magic, and glowing runes appear on your body. Your character changes as you progress, and it makes the whole experience feel alive.

Not the kind that warms — the kind that devours.

It’s the rhythm.
The sound that doesn’t stop.
The footsteps.

Measured. Heavy. Inevitable.

You run until your lungs burn, and still — it’s behind you. Not hunting for food. Not for revenge. Just… to end you.

Walls collapse. Creatures claw through the dark. Streets become labyrinths of debris and blood. You keep moving, not because you’re brave, but because stopping means becoming part of the rubble.

Weapons buy you seconds, not safety. Choices feel like coin flips made in fire. And through it all, that sound returns: those steps, like a countdown you can’t reset.

With that being said, this is still a very good game. A very good game that is tragically bogged down by its short length, it’s re-used assets and locations from the previous game, and by a failure to innovate or bring anything new to the franchise. It’s because of this, compounded by it’s hefty price tag, that despite how good it is in its short run time, it still manages to dissapoint.

Starting with the good, this game has incredibly gorgeous visuals and the detail in the environments and characters are truly jaw-dropping. The facial features of the characters were especially impressive as every gesture, emotion and muscle is captured so well and it really elevates the characters and the story. The combat is very snappy and the feedback you feel when you shoot or dodge is very satisfying. There’s a healthy variety of enemies that keep you on your toes from fear, and the combat sequences are impressive.
 
More importantly than anything though, RE3 has that classic resident evil horror atmosphere that we all know and have come to love. Eerie, somber and gory level design that are still filled with so much detail and color. Environments filled with small claustrophobic dark hallways and corridors that make you feel trapped in closed spaces with horrific undead. Skin crawling horror music that plays as you push forward knowing you will have to earn every room you enter. It is incredible horror and it’s what made Resident Evil a one of a kind franchise. This is all present in RE3 and it is an incredible thing to experience as always.

All of this, ofcourse, is overshadowed by its very short run time of 5 hours. it’s re-used locations from the previous game that wear out their novelty very quickly. its disappointing rework of the nemesis villain that feels forgettable and fails to leave an impression on you like the original. This failure to innovate, when mixed with a hefty price tag, results in a game that feels lazy and incomplete for a full standalone title. For this level of scale and content, this game should’ve been a DLC/expansion to RE2, not a fully priced title.

At full price, I just cannot recommend this game. It just does not offer anything new or fresh enough to justify its price tag, especially compared to it’s predecessor RE2. 

But it’s still Resident evil man, and holy hell do I love Resident evil. Like yes it's got all these flaws but it's still Resident evil. It's still got all the hallmarks that makes this franchise so beloved and so good. 

And that’s why, even though it was disappointing compared to the other games, I still recommend Resident Evil 3.

On deep sale that is.

Overall its good if you played the second one.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762650071}, {"review_text": "Resident Evil 3 takes a more action oriented approach compared to its predecessor, much like the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis did within the classic trilogy. However, even among those older titles, Nemesis was arguably the weakest entry, and unfortunately, this modern remake doesn't manage to elevate its source material in a meaningful way. In fact, it not only falls short as a remake but also struggles to uphold the identity of a Resident Evil game.

Like the Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's not a one to one recreation. It is more like a reimagining with considerable creative liberties, not all of which work in its favor. While some of the original's core ideas are still present, they have been altered in ways that make the game feel more like a cinematic action thriller than a survival horror game. There's a clear emphasis on cutscenes, dialogue, and scripted moments, which gives the game a more "movie like" quality but at the expense of player agency and atmospheric tension.

Visually, there's little to complain about. The RE Engine continues to impress, with highly detailed environments, excellent character models, and realistic facial animations. Zombies, although largely recycled from Resident Evil 2, still look convincing. From a technical standpoint, the game is well produced. But gameplaywise it moves the game further away from its survival horror roots.

Nemesis, the big bad thing you already see on the covers, should have been a standout feature. In the original, his encounters were tense, unpredictable, and often dynamic. Here, he is reduced to a mostly scripted presence. His initial appearance in the city streets is arguably the highlight of the game one of the few moments that captures the chaotic energy of the original. But subsequent encounters are heavily controlled and lack tension. His mutations are less grotesque and feel disconnected from the biological horror that once made him terrifying. Instead of evolving in response to the player's actions, his transformations now follow a fixed, cinematic path, turning him into a quadruped like creature that's visually odd rather than intimidating. It's strange, with the Tyrant from Resident Evil 2, they've already introduced an enemy into the series who has somehow evolved from the original. But here, it really seems to be the case that Nemesis is even better in the original than he is in the remake.

Also Carlos, a side character from the original, plays a much larger role in the remake. His expanded sections include new locations and extended gameplay time sometimes even replacing segments originally played with Jill. While his improved presence could have added depth, these sections often feel more like a generic third person shooter. Armed with an assault rifle and abundant ammunition, Carlos storms through waves of zombies, holding out against dozens of them in a sequence that feels more like a scripted shooter scenario than a survival horror game. It was similar in the original, but here they could go on a different road, instead of making everything more over the top.

Equally disappointing is the removal or truncation of key areas from the original. The clock tower and parts of the factory are missing entirely, and some of the game's characters are introduced so briefly that they leave no lasting impression. The Mercenaries mode has also been cut, and puzzles once a staple of the series have been either removed or simplified to such a degree that they no longer offer any meaningful challenge. You get Resident Evil Resistence instead, a stand alone multiplayer game nobody asked for.

Unfortunately, combat often feels unsatisfying. Zombies are unusually durable, absorbing bullets unpredictably. The game doesn't encourage careful aiming or offer consistent feedback for well placed shots. Critical hits seem to occur at random rather than as a reward for skill. Boss fights are similarly unengaging, typically resolved by unloading the most powerful weapons until the enemy collapses. There's little strategy involved, and these encounters rarely evolve beyond their visual spectacle. The new dodge roll require also less precise timing and makes them far more forgiving and with full control over aiming and movement, there's little reason to flee one of the core survival instincts that the older games used to evoke. While this makes the game more accessible, it also reduces the sense of vulnerability that once defined the series

[h2]GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW:[/h2] 3R picks up the story of Jill Valentine after the events of the first game. Jill is now trying to escape from a virus-infested Raccoon City. Along the way, she meets Carlos Oliveira, a security operative of the Umbrella Corporation. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3535467740
Nemesis arriving early in the game.

This remake retains the shift from the fixed-camera perspective of the original RE2/3 to the over-the-shoulder perspective of 2R, making it easy to navigate the streets and buildings of the infected city. The player starts as Jill, transitions to Carlos for several segments mid-game, then back to Jill. The two characters have slightly different move sets and available weapons.

For each character, zombies and other foes litter the way forward. Just as in the remake of the second game, these walking corpses are quite durable, soaking up multiple headshots from starter weapons. They are also surprisingly fast, shambling toward the player with deceptive leisure, only to lunge and cover the final stretch between themselves and the player in the blink of an eye, so stay alert. Old enemies from previous games make appearances, along with some new ones. The action is gloriously gruesome, with exploding heads and sprays of blood. Player deaths are equally horrific. 3R definitely earns its "Mature" rating, so keep the young ones away.

Puzzles were a hallmark of the early RE games and while there are a handful in 3R, I found this game's riddles laughably easy. This game definitely shifts away from that aspect to a more action-oriented experience. There are some new environmental wrinkles added, such as mobile power carts, which spray an arc of electricity when shot, stunning all enemies in range for a few seconds. The player can use these to slip past large groups without using ammo, though save for the end of several prolonged bouts of combat, I never felt a lack of bullets or healing items while playing on Standard. Resource management is usually an staple in survival horror but I never felt the pinch in 3R. Supply status wasn't much of an issue as long as I picked my fights and ran when I could.

One new feature in 3R is the dodge mechanic. It's a little tricky to get the timing down but once you've done so, it's a very effective method of avoiding damage—and honestly, it's essential for the boss fights, so I recommend a player practice early until they are comfortable with it.

With the exception of one fight against waves of zombies, the boss fights in 3R are against Nemesis in some form or the other. Unlike the original RE3, where Nemesis could appear and attack the player at random, in this version, encounters with Nemesis are fixed occurrences at specific points of the journey. Players can opt to fight him but since Nemesis is a bullet sponge who can't be permanently disabled before the game's end, running is usually the better option. There are several mandatory fights against the hulking menace but those encounters are marked by hallmarks of the genre—wide-open arena-like spaces littered with ammo and healing items—so the player should see these encounters coming. After mastering the dodge timing, I found these fights more tedious than anything.

My real issue with 3R is its incredibly short length. I died a lot, explored every nook and cranny I could find, repeated several segments to get the exact outcome I wanted, and still finished in under eight hours. Replay value is minimal; unlike 2R, there is only one real route here and any subsequent playthroughs will proceed along the exact same path. 

The story and gameplay are adequate but there just isn't enough of either on offer. 3R's controls and interface are much like 2R and (aside from the dodge) doesn't innovate much new ... which would be fine, if 3R had retained the bulk of the story and events from its original version, and clocked in at a 25-hour-plus playthrough. But since it doesn't, it's hard for me to do more than give it a slim thumbs up. RE fans will likely enjoy 3R for what it is—and just as likely be left dissatisfied and hungry for more. I did, and was.

[h2]STORY / WORLDBUILDING:[/h2] This story takes place around the same time as the events of 2R, though the two tales don't intersect. More of Umbrella's experiments and dastardly deeds are uncovered as the player progresses, and the narrative is consistent with the lore of previous games. On the other hand, the 3R setting is a bit light. This remake uses multiple locations and tile sets from 2R. At the risk of repeating myself, this probably wouldn't matter if 3R was a longer game but as it stands, such reuse feels like a lazy corner-cutting shortcut. The fact that 3R slashed so much interesting story and so many locations from the original RE3, like the Clock Tower, Raccoon City Park, and Factory, and the boss fight with the Gravedigger, for example. This reduction in length and content only exacerbates the impression that this game could have easily been a DLC to 2R.

[h2]TECHNICAL ASPECTS:[/h2] Like 2R, 3R is a visual and aural feast. Environments are rendered in fine detail and character animations were fluid on my ten-year old rig. The sound design is excellent. In the early areas, ambient noise alerts the player to nearby threats, by both volume and direction, and fills the background with the sounds of a city falling apart. This is in marked contrast to later scenes, where the silence itself becomes almost oppressive and adds to the tension. Voice acting and dialogue for the main characters is generally pretty good, and far better than the original. In terms of presentation, the game excels.

I didn't have any errors or glitches and the game felt perfectly stable. Steam achievements are generally accessible, though maxing out requires finding all collectibles and speed running the hardest difficulty.

[h2]FINAL SCORE: 6.5/10[/h2]

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare set a new benchmark for first-person shooters when it launched, redefining the genre with its modern military setting and intense pacing. The game departed from its World War II roots to present a fast-paced, high-stakes narrative grounded in contemporary conflict. With its expertly designed missions and cinematic presentation, it quickly established itself as a standout title in the series. The sense of urgency and realism it offers remains impactful even years after its release.
The story follows a gripping narrative centered around global terrorism and military intervention, featuring perspectives from multiple characters across various factions. This approach offers a layered and immersive storytelling experience, moving players through war-torn environments and covert operations. Memorable missions such as “All Ghillied Up” showcase not only technical ingenuity but also emotional depth. The narrative structure successfully keeps players engaged through its tense pacing and dramatic twists.
Gameplay in Modern Warfare is tight, responsive, and highly refined, delivering a balance between cinematic spectacle and strategic combat. The combination of on-rails sequences, tactical objectives, and large-scale battles ensures a dynamic experience. Multiplayer mode became a defining element, introducing the now-iconic progression system with perks, killstreaks, and customizable loadouts. Its addictiveness and replayability set a new standard for competitive online shooters.
Visually, the game was a technical marvel for its time, utilizing realistic lighting, detailed character models, and immersive environments. The attention to visual fidelity helped ground the experience in a believable modern warfare setting. Effects such as smoke, fire, and debris added intensity to every combat encounter. The art direction and animations contributed to a polished and authentic look that supported the game’s tone.
Overall, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare delivers an exceptional blend of storytelling, gameplay, and visual execution. Its influence on the FPS genre is undeniable, thanks to its innovative design choices and gripping presentation. From its emotionally charged narrative to its groundbreaking multiplayer mechanics, it stands as a milestone in gaming history. This title remains a prime example of how to elevate a franchise while pushing industry standards.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare gets an 8/10.

Movement is stiff, sprinting is limited, weapon handling lacks nuance, and shooting does not have the realistic recoil, weight, or sound depth that define the reboot. Compared to the reboot’s fluid animations, tactical sprint, weapon mounting, and highly detailed gun models, COD4 feels basic and almost arcade-like. The reboot provides a level of immersion and responsiveness that the 2007 game simply cannot match.

Multiplayer, once praised as groundbreaking, now feels barebones and unbalanced compared to the reboot. The original’s perk system is limited and easily exploited, killstreaks are basic and repetitive, map design heavily favors certain playstyles, and customization is extremely minimal. Meanwhile, the 2019 reboot features a deeper weapon progression system, extensive Gunsmith customization, richer sound cues, and far more refined balancing. Returning to COD4’s small selection of weapons and predictable class setups makes the experience feel shallow rather than nostalgic.

Visually, the difference is even more dramatic. COD4’s graphics once impressive now look flat, washed out, and lacking detail. Character animations are stiff, environments feel static, and lighting is basic. The reboot’s advanced engine brings cinematic realism, dynamic shadows, modern textures, volumetric smoke, and stunning environmental detail. The contrast makes COD4 look not just dated, but almost unrecognizable compared to today's standards.

The campaign, while iconic, also suffers when judged against the reboot’s storytelling and presentation. COD4 relies on fast pacing and memorable set pieces, but the character development is thin and the narrative lacks emotional depth. The reboot offers richer writing, grounded performances, morally complex scenarios, and a more mature tone. Missions feel more immersive and have greater narrative weight, making COD4’s story seem straightforward and less impactful in comparison.

Overall, while Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare (2007) deserves respect as a classic, it struggles to compete with the Modern Warfare (2019) reboot in gameplay, graphics, storytelling, and technical polish. Except Prestige, since that wasn't in this PC port for some absurd reason. Yay, even less of a reason to keep up with a multiplayer experience from 2007.

Do I hate this game? Absolutely not. CoD4 was a very important game to me, as it came out during a very bad time in my life. My very late adolescence was terrible--worse than most people's, but this hunk of golden age multiplayer from the aughts, was there for me alongside several other decent releases from that year. But I'm not gonna go off about that, you're here for a review about CoD4.

The campaign is your usual Call of Duty stuff: Overly linear missions with frustratingly boring combat encounters, and those juicy bits of story that keep you going. Cool set-pieces, cool weapons, and some real cool characters. We love you forever, Captain John Price.

There's not a day that goes by without yours truly remembering some absurd, insipid moment from playing this game. Getting a taste of Martyrdom, Juggernaut, Last Stand, and the most infamous weapons, and of course, the Godforsaken sniper culture that was born here. Those crazy killstreaks with a bizarre class setup you experimented with for laughs one day, or just having a really hot match that made you look real good in front of a bunch strangers over the internet. Do I recommend Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2025? No.

EN: This game has a dark secret that not many know, which can hinder an optimized and dedicated low-spender, where even a free to play player can be better. 
In this game there is the arena, where you can battle players to "get pictures" of their equipment to fill a scrapbook, the higher the % complition of the scrapbook, the more % EXP you get for your quests and thus the faster you progress. After each arena battle, you must wait 10 minutes or spend 1 cash currency to skip the wait. It turns out, people playing the game on a phone can watch an ad to skip the wait time and they can do this around 50 times a day (this is separate from the 10 minutes cooldown and it ticks down independantly). 
So far so "good", since all f2p games do this. However, a smartphone is not equal a smartphone, since the more valuable your data is (the more you use your phone for different non S&F activities) the more ads you get. So if you have a work phone that only has an authentificator and you use it for nothing else, you'll get around 3 ads/skips a day, if you have a phone that you basically spend your whole life on, you can get 250+ ads a day. Yes, you can only do 50 arena skips a day, but the other ads will give you 3 lucky coins per ad which you can the use to spin a wheel that gives very good additional rewards. So, as a player who spends let's say 15 EUR (more if you pay on Steam) for the 2 starter packs, you'll be significantly weaker than someone f2p who has a valuable phone and gets 250+ ads a day. 
As a test, I was doing arena every 10 minutes for the last 3 days while awake from the new server start, and barely reached lvl 36, someone who had 250+ ads daily got to lvl 51 and got way better stats and items from the additional goodies from the lucky coins.
You'll of course ask now, do I have proof, and yes I do, I had 3 smartphones in front of me today, one S&F account, one phone provider, one internet provider (using the wi-fi). My work phone that I only use for 2-factor and has nothing on it gets exactly 3 ads, another phone from a family member, that is a side-phone and used occasionally, had +/- 30 ads, a phone that is being used the whole time with a lot of apps, network activity and so on, had 250+ ads and I stopped the experiment since they seemed to never run out. And I can confirm, all the ads on all 3 smartphones were the same.
TL:DR If you like wasting your whole day to do an arena fight every 10 minutes and thus optimize your game, and in the end see, you are at the bottom of a f2p guild since everyone else watched ads like crazy and made you realize you wasted 3 days optimizing, go ahead and play. 
If you hate being discriminated for havign a "not-so-valuable-data on your phone" and everyone else will be better than you, even free-to-play, then this is definitely not the game for you. Keep away.
If you want to play F2P or low pay to play or even go full pay to play, make sure you have a phone with a lot of valuable data on it or else you will be at a big disadvantage..
I don't know what total playtime Steam is showing, but I have probably over 10k hours, playing since when there were only 4 classes (currently there are 11)

My personal gripes. Some are just my opinion but others seriously need to be changed for the sake of the games benefit.

- KB&M controls does not have an option to direct attacks to mouse cursor. Targeting in multi mob fights is frustrating more then difficult
- Fast travel points not connected to each other but only to the last one you touch negates the point of it entirely. It causes more backtracking then needed. I want to go through the zones because I want to not because I'm forced to
- Not respawning at your nearest whisper (fast travel point) on death but on the last one you touched is criminal
- Parrying is the coolest thing you can do but this game hates you for trying it. You're not aptly rewarded for parrying enough to justify it leading to path of least resistance
- Giving every other enemy at the start firebombs that have INSANE tracking is a hell of an onboarding choice but there's only one other mob later on that uses an aoe projectile and it's a slow moving fireball. 
- Food being tied to healing is a choice. While I can understand the rpg element to it the friction in other parts of the game can't be denied. This needs another look into because the idea is sound but the reality is not fluid
- Repair cost, in the same vain as food, causes friction. The idea is sound but when learning/fighting a boss having to go back and repair your gear takes you out of the combat. But what really sets it apart?
Performance.

I’m running this on a RTX 5070 Ti + i9-12900K + 32GB DDR5. At 4K Ultra with DLSS on Quality, I’m getting a stable 120fps in dense areas without frame generation. From the moment you land in the blood-soaked jungles of the Pacific or crawl through the ruins of Stalingrad, you know this isn’t your typical hero’s journey - it’s war at its ugliest.

¶ The visual tone of the game is a stroke of genius. The gray filter over everything creates a sense of bleakness, making the vibrant splashes of red blood all the more jarring. It’s not just a visual choice - it’s a statement. Here, war isn't glamorous or thrilling; rather, it's a nightmare, and every gunshot, scream, and eerie moment makes you realize that.

¶ The two campaigns - American and Soviet - are both unforgettable, each offering a unique perspective on WWII. The American campaign drops you into the hellish jungles of the Pacific Theater, where every shadow might hide a Japanese banzai charge. Crawling through the underbrush with flamethrowers roaring and enemies charging at you is equal parts exhilarating and horrifying. Then there’s the Soviet campaign, where you march from the smoldering rubble of Stalingrad to the heart of Berlin. It’s a grim revenge tour, and Reznov’s speeches are pure fire - they make you feel the fury and desperation of a soldier who’s seen too much.

¶ This title really separates men from boys on a veteran difficulty, especially with those grenades constantly being thrown at you.
And then there’s the Zombies mode. Man, I’ve spent hours in Zombies. It’s the perfect blend of tension and chaos, with each round becoming more frantic as you scramble for ammo, repair barricades, and try not to get overwhelmed. It still gives me the creeps just like in 2008 after the main campaign, especially on Verrückt.

¶ Multiplayer is solid, it sticks closely to the formula laid out by Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. The working formula. The progression system, perks, and killstreaks are all here, and while it doesn’t reinvent the wheel, it doesn’t need to. The maps are well-designed, and the gritty WWII setting adds a fresh flavor to the familiar mechanics. My favorite mode? War. There’s something so satisfying about the push-and-pull dynamic, fighting tooth and nail to capture objectives while chaos erupts all around you.

¶ The soundtrack is my personally best in the whole series. Composed by the talented Sean Murray, the music is a blend of chilling orchestral pieces and aggressive, metal segments that crank up the tension in every moment. Those metallic riffs hit like a sledgehammer during intense combat sequences, making the firefights feel even more chaotic and visceral. The game's overall atmosphere of dread and sorrow is further enhanced by the spooky, atmospheric music played during quieter scenes.

[{"review_text": "I Have played this game since day 1 and i can honestly say that right now is the darkest time the game has ever been in. The game currently has a few key problems that are actively killing the game, and I will do my best to summarise them here: 

1. Maxx C, The mere existence of this card completely destroys your gameplay experience. This card warps the format so utterly that it creates an entire mini game within the game itself resting on whether one of you have Maxx C and if the other can negate it. If they negate it you have now lost a card for no reason, and if the do not they instantly lose the game. How this can be considered even remotely fun is beyond me and it has only got worse now that there is effectively 8 copies of this card in an opponents deck at any given time. This has created an absurd meta in which upwards of 17-18 cards of a 40 card deck can be dedicated to this mini game, any QA dev would be crying right about now. 

2. The Meta, Yugioh has had over 26 years of life, over the course of this the game has undergone multiple transformations and has gone from a more controlled, slow paced strategy game to something akin to a match of call of duty black ops 6 at max rank. For many people this can be pretty fun, myself included, but even by most standards this game has gone way too far. The game has a lax approach to the banning and limiting of cards and as a result it has cultivated a format where you must go first or you have a likely chance of losing instantly. The reason for this, besides unbridled power creep, is that the top decks of the game put up an unreasonable amount of disruption that no deck could play through, they then have insane resilience to boardbreakers which should be able to counter combo decks of this manner almost entirely on their own, or at least force out some meaningful interaction. They also have layered boards which essentially means that even if you break one part of their established board they can rebuild it in the middle of YOUR TURN. Couple this all with generic boss monsters capable of winning the game by themselves being entirely unrestricted such as apollousa, and it means the going second experience amounts to drawing the perfect hand or surrendering instantly. 

3. The Format, now everything I just said would not be a problem if there were multiple formats available, but there isn't. You can play ranked, then casual, which is fundamentally the same experience as ranked, you can play duel room, which often amounts to ranked but with friends, then team battle, which is ranked but in a group of 3. A toxic meta is a problem on it's own, but when that is the only format you can play then you can see why the game is haemorrhaging players. Yugioh has many fan-made formats that have been supported by Konami in the past, eddison, reaper, goat, draft, duellist alliance, deck master, time wizard (RIP), tag duels, and most recently genesys format which represents a new hope for the game, and yet they have not, and most likely never will try to implement any of these into the game. Why? Frankly I do not know as it seems like such an easy way to make more money. Events are held every month or so but this does little to break the monotony, mainly because it amounts to 'ranked but only synchro' or 'ranked but only xyz', all the while one of the best events they ever did was the N/R format, something which they refuse to revisit or add into the game permanently even though it would take no effort to do. 

4. The Game itself, When this game was first released it felt very much like a minimum viable product with many elements contributing to the feeling that this game was essentially still in beta. 4 years later and very little has been changed to fix this issue besides them adding more ranks and solo mode gates which in of themselves are utterly terrible. 4 years and nothing to show for it in a live service game, just new things to buy, miserable. 

5. Solo Mode, I could go on forever about this but the truth is that it is a half-baked concept that was never truly realised. Solo mode is the closest thing this game has to a campaign and it boils down to practising a deck before playing against the AI in a duel or multiple duels while watching slideshow cutscenes that have been translated through chatgpt. The bots play incompetently to say the least as the moment you can disrupt them they refuse to play at all. The decks you are given range from competently constructed to utter garbage, often the latter, with some decks going as far as to be anti-synergistic, something that could have been found with any level of QA or just READING THE CARDS. But I digress, this could have been a really fun way to showcase the rich lore in the card game and prep casual players for the firestorm they will experience in ranked, but nah, just make another slideshow and call it a day. Such wasted potential. 

6. Monetisation, compared to other gatcha games this isn't actually that bad, I construct the vast majority of my decks for free and the F2P experience can be enjoyable if a little grindy. Recently though the game has started to demand more. At the game's inception most decks only had 1-2 UR slots max meaning it wasn't too hard to make multiple meta decks. Now every new release has anything from 4-5 to as high as 7 UR slots meaning that the amount of grinding/money you have to put into the game has significantly increased. They also charge for ridiculous things such as bookmark slots or deck slots. All of this is emblematic of a game that is fast becoming a game for whales who will shell out hundreds on the latest decks while the rest of us are left in the dirt, it also explains the lax banlist situation. Limiting Doormouse and Underground does not stop maliss from obliterating you, it simply means they have to play more UR cards to get there. 

7. The community, Master Duel has done it's absolute best to remove player communication in any respect, meaning most players have to co-ordinate on 3rd party apps, for a live service multiplayer game this is unacceptable, especially considering the community of yugioh is the only reason this game has been alive this long. If it were not for the efforts of creators and players combined this game would have no community aspect at all and would be nowhere near as popular. I understand wanting to prevent toxicity but if that is the case then set up robust moderation, do not make it impossible to communicate with one another (insert campaign code here). 

8. PR, Live service games often live or die based on community relations, and in the case of this game, there simply isn't one. Devs do not explain anything, they do not interact with players, decisions are handed down from an ivory tower and you are expected to deal with it. It's childish and shows a lack of interest in interacting with the community that have had such a massive effect on making their game successful in the first place. 

Overall this game had so much potential at launch and it still could if Konami decided to harness it, many of the solutions to this require minimal work. But they won't, because it's not about creating an enjoyable experience, it's about making the most money with the least effort, the implementation of AI commentary into the world championship was proof of that mindset. Based on their current pattern of behaviour, I don't see them changing course and admitting their mistakes. But I for one refuse to continue this abusive relationship with the game any further. I hope something can be salvaged of this game, but for now, it seems that Konami are more interested in a managed decline than taking any real action to fix things, and I refuse to sit on a rotting ship, I'll take my chances overboard thank you.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1759424122}, {"review_text": "It is a well made implementation of the card game, but it would benefit greatly by having permanent playlists for older formats like goat or hat since the modern meta playstyle isn't very fun.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1737733379}, {"review_text": "I summon 1 monster

short_description: Rule a fantasy realm of your own design! Explore new magical realms in Age of Wonders’ signature blend of 4X strategy and turn-based tactical combat. Control a faction that grows and changes as you expand your empire with each turn!

review_texts:
[{"review_text": "Well, here we are. I have played over 1000 hours of age of Wonders 4. I still fell like a beginner and I still enjoy every minute of it. 
I would like to share my experience with other potential players.

This game is unique and simply amazing. The graphics, map, music, gameplay are probably the best in the gaming industry of our time.

You start out with 5 introductory story missions that immerse you in the lore of the Age of Wonders series. (The game lets you play regular maps and factions if you choose not to start the story missions). After that, you move on to your own adventures with pre-made characters and maps or create your own factions and map parameters. I haven't yet purchased a single one of the many DLC and I am still learning new things from each game played. 



When you start a new realm, ( RANDOMIZED MAPS ! ) you are the ruler of a single small town in a beautiful but very hostile world. You must research, develop your cities, explore, expand, exploit and exterminate. (4X) The game is a wargame at its core.
